title: [Perf][Hybrid] 3D-grid tiling of the state-copy Triton kernels
author: fuscof-ibm
body:
## Purpose

Follow-up to https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48110.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48110 optimized the copy of the states for hybrid models using 64bit load/stores. However the state copy is still underutilizing the HBM memory at small batch and the kernel requires 8B-aligned state tensors.

This PR further improves the performance by adding a 3D grid and lift the hard 8B alignment precondition by using a head/body/tail pattern. Those are the main changes:

1. **Tiles the temporal copy across CTAs.** The `uint64` body range of each temporal state is partitioned across `TEMPORAL_TILES` CTAs along a new `program_id(2)` axis. Grid goes from `(num_reqs, total_states)` to `(num_reqs, total_states, TEMPORAL_TILES)`. Small-batch runs (reqs=1..16) now fill the SMs instead of leaving them idle.
2. **Extends the 64bit load/store path to the SD conv state.** SD Conv copies previously went through a separate byte-wise route; they now share `_copy_mamba_state_block` and the same fused launch, with `tile_idx > 0` early-returning so conv still runs single-CTA (it's ~60–80 KiB per block, compared to 1-4MB of the temporal part).
3. **Drops the hard 8B alignment precondition.** `_memcpy_u64_tiled` now splits the copy into head (≤7 B to align dst to 8 B) / body (u64-vectorized) / tail (≤7 B). The setup-time asserts become one-time `warning_once` calls — misalignment is a throughput hint, not a correctness failure.
4. **Refactors the shared body into `_memcpy_u64_tiled`** so `postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel` and `precopy_mamba_align_fused_kernel` so both kernel can use it and the 64 aligned copies can be tested in isolation.
5. **Tunes `TEMPORAL_TILES = 16`** based on a sweep over {8, 16, 32} on GB200 with Qwen3.5-9B and Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B.

Files touched: `vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py`, plus two test files.

**Net Effect:** 3D-grid tiling lifts small-batch kernel bandwidth by 6–7.7× at reqs=1 and pins post-copy throughput at **~72–84%** of GB200 HBM3e  peak bandwidth across reqs ∈ {1..128} (vs. main's **11–79%** swing). End-to-end on Qwen3.5-9B + MTP + prefix caching: **+1.1–1.8% output tok/s** and −0.7 to −1.6% median TPOT / ITL / E2EL across conc ∈ {16, 32, 64}, with MTP acceptance unchanged and no regressions.

## Test Plan

### Unit tests (new):

```bash
python -m pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_memcpy_u64_tiled.py -v
python -m pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_precopy_mamba_align.py -v
```

- `test_memcpy_u64_tiled.py`: byte-identity check of `_memcpy_u64_tiled` vs. a torch slice copy across `copy_size` ∈ [0, 4 KiB], all sub-8B src/dst alignment offsets, and `NUM_TILES` ∈ {1, 16}. Guards head/body/tail correctness and the tile partitioning at the boundaries.
- `test_precopy_mamba_align.py`: existing V1-vs-V2 copy-spec equivalence test, now parametrized over `TEMPORAL_TILES ∈ {1, 16}`. 

### Integration tests (existing hybrid coverage):

```bash
python -m pytest tests/models/language/generation/test_hybrid.py -v
```

### Microbenchmark

Reused the [benchmarks/bench_copy_mamba_state_block.py](https://github.com/fuscof-ibm/vllm/blob/postprocess_benchmark/bench_copy_mamba_state_block.py) developed for https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48110 and extended to support a) multiple models and b) the 3D grid launch. In particular we use https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/36a924e8d190ffd668645c4b44807c0ac5407a84 for 3D grids (as in *this PR*) and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/5cce1bce45c926317da3727932684f81782cfed6 for 2D grid (as in `main`).

Sweep `num_reqs ∈ {1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}` on GB200 to confirm tiling improves small-batch throughput without regressing at large batch. 


### End-to-end

Exact same benchmark as in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48110, but using MRv2.

For the `main` we use 

`vllm bench serve` against `vllm serve` with MTP and prefix caching enabled (which exercises the state copies):

```bash
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 \
vllm serve \
    --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
    -tp 1 -pp 1 -dp 1 \
    --language-model-only \
    --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_next_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2}' \
    --enable-prefix-caching
```

Benchmark workload:

```
    vllm bench serve \
        --dataset-name random \
        --seed 42 \
        --temperature 0 \
        --random-input-len "$INPUT_LEN" \
        --random-output-len "$OUTPUT_LEN" \
        --num-prompts "$NUM_PROMPTS" \
        --request-rate inf \
        --max-concurrency "$conc" \
        --ignore-eos \
        --percentile-metrics "ttft,tpot,itl,e2el" \
        --metric-percentiles "50,90,99"
```

Workload: `--dataset-name random`, `INPUT_LEN=500`, `OUTPUT_LEN=5330`, `NUM_PROMPTS=500`.

The workload is chosen to exercise the `_copy_mamba_state_block` which happens when a block is crossed.
For Qwen3.5-9B the block size is 533. The output length is chosen to be 10x the block size.

Hardware: NVIDIA GB200. Concurrency sweep `{16,32,64}`. At each concurrency we ran the benchmark **4 times per branch and discarded the 1st run** to strip warmup/JIT effects; reported numbers aggregate the remaining 3 runs

## Test Result

### Unit Tests

Unit and integration tests: all passing

### Microbenchmark

Raw results: 

[microbenchmarks_results.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276029/microbenchmarks_results.txt)


## Throughput

Peak = ~8 TB/s for GB200 HBM3e

### Qwen3.5-9B

| reqs | MAIN (GB/s) | PR (GB/s) | Gain | MAIN % peak | PR % peak |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|   1 |  585.7 | 4519.1 | 7.72× |  7.3% | **56.5%** |

| 128 | 6216.5 | 6748.3 | 1.09× | 77.7% | **84.4%** |

On Qwen3.5-9B the PR delivers **> 70%** of the peak starting from `reqs=4` while  `main` requires `reqs=23` to achieve that value.

### Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4

| reqs | MAIN (GB/s) | PR (GB/s) | Gain | MAIN % peak | PR % peak |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

Unlike `main`, on Nemotron-3-Super this PR achieves an almost flat curve starting from `reqs=1`.


---

## Kernel Latency

### Qwen3.5-9B  — Kernel Latency (μs)

| reqs | MAIN | PR | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|   1 |  178.58 |   23.15 | 7.71× |
|   4 |  201.78 |   73.61 | 2.74× |
|   8 |  231.78 |  133.55 | 1.74× |

| 128 | 2153.65 | 1983.94 | 1.09× |

This PR is provides lower latencies at all regimes, with larger gains below `reqs=`16`.

### Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4 — Kernel Latency (μs)

| reqs | MAIN | PR | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|

### End-to-end

Raw results:

[tiled_16.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276073/tiled_16.txt)
[tiled_32.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276068/tiled_32.txt)

Values below are `mean ± stddev` across 3 runs (sample stddev, n=3).
Δ rows compare PR to main; for latency metrics negative is better, for throughput positive is better.

| Metric | Branch | conc=16 | conc=32 | conc=64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Output tok/s | main | 6219.19 ± 10.28 | 9744.67 ± 5.37 | 13848.81 ± 37.01 |
| Output tok/s | PR   | 6331.49 ± 9.81  | 9864.17 ± 10.30 | 14004.27 ± 20.58 |
| Δ throughput |      | **+1.81 %** | **+1.23 %** | **+1.12 %** |
| Median TPOT (ms) | main | 2.407 ± 0.006 | 3.027 ± 0.006 | 4.113 ± 0.025 |
| Median TPOT (ms) | PR   | 2.373 ± 0.006 | 2.987 ± 0.006 | 4.063 ± 0.032 |
| Δ median TPOT    |      | **−1.39 %** | **−1.32 %** | **−1.22 %** |
| Median ITL (ms)  | main | 7.003 ± 0.006 | 8.623 ± 0.012 | 11.773 ± 0.032 |
| Median ITL (ms)  | PR   | 6.890 ± 0.010 | 8.517 ± 0.015 | 11.693 ± 0.021 |

| Mean E2EL (ms)   | main | 13224.01 ± 15.90 | 16889.25 ± 7.79 | 23644.57 ± 32.34 |
| Mean E2EL (ms)   | PR   | 13010.79 ± 8.04  | 16680.60 ± 25.10 | 23416.33 ± 40.85 |
| Δ mean E2EL      |      | **−1.61 %** | **−1.24 %** | **−0.97 %** |
| Acceptance rate (%) | main | 98.68 ± 0.05 | 98.61 ± 0.03 | 98.60 ± 0.09 |
| Acceptance rate (%) | PR   | 98.67 ± 0.03 | 98.51 ± 0.08 | 98.62 ± 0.05 |

## Summary

- **Consistent ~1.1–1.8% throughput improvement** across all concurrency levels, well above the ~0.1–0.3% run-to-run noise (visible from the stddevs).
- **Latency reductions track throughput gains**: TPOT, ITL, and E2EL all improve by ~0.7–1.6%, monotonically decreasing as concurrency rises.
- **Gain shrinks as concurrency grows**: at conc=16  tiling helps more when the 2D grid is smaller
- **Speculative decoding is unaffected**: acceptance rate stays ~98.5–98.7% and acceptance length stays 2.97 on both branches — this is purely a postprocess optimization with no semantic effect on drafts.
- **No regressions** on any metric at any concurrency level.

## Duplicate-work check

Per `AGENTS.md`:

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "postprocess_mamba"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "mamba tiled"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "_copy_mamba_state_block"
```

This PR is a strict follow-on to the earlier `postprocess_mamba` uint64 vectorization PR — same file, same kernel, but pushes past the single-CTA-per-copy ceiling and drops the alignment precondition. Not duplicating any open work.
Tested on MRv2.

title: [Model][MoE] DeepSeek-V4: add opt-in FlashInfer moe_ep expert backend
author: mhoqueanik
body:
Add a FlashInfer `moe_ep` compute path for the DeepSeek-V4 mega-MoE experts, selectable at runtime alongside the existing native `deep_gemm_mega_moe` backend.

- New module `vllm/utils/flashinfer_moe_ep.py`: model-agnostic plumbing only — backend registry and predicates, flashinfer `moe_ep` runtime bootstrap/finalize (bootstrap passes `device=torch.cuda.current_device()`, see review item on the LOCAL_RANK pin), NVFP4 prequant weight packing + epilogue alphas, config validation, and mega-layer construction.
- New module `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/fi_moe.py`: `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExpertsFI`, a subclass of the native `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExperts` (same weight layout + loader; overrides weight finalize and forward with the flashinfer compute path), plus the DSV4-specific helpers (NVFP4 checkpoint detection, prequant pack, routing preprocess).
- `model.py`: pick `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExpertsFI` when an fi backend is active and thread the swiglu activation clamp through; the `use_mega_moe` checks (including sequence-parallel eligibility) test membership in `MEGA_MOE_BACKENDS`.
- `config/kernel.py`: register the two new names in the `MoEBackend` literal and host the `MEGA_MOE_BACKENDS` set next to it. Required, not cosmetic — `KernelConfig` validates `moe_backend` against that literal and rejects unknown values before the model is ever constructed.
- New tests `tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_fi_moe_ep.py`: 11 unit tests (no GPU; flashinfer faked) covering backend registration, the device-pinned bootstrap, SP eligibility for every mega backend, config building, and the fp4 dequant helper.

Two backends are added, selected by `moe_backend` string:

| `moe_backend` | megakernel | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `flashinfer_moe_ep_mega_deep_gemm` | `deep_gemm_mega` | consumes an MXFP4 checkpoint verbatim (e2m1 + E8M0 per-32 scales) — the same recipe the native path uses, so this isolates the integration layer from kernel work |
| `flashinfer_moe_ep_mega_cutedsl` | `nvfp4_cutedsl` | needs NVSHMEM. The checkpoint picks the weight path, not the kernel: an NVFP4 checkpoint is consumed prequantized, MXFP4 weights are dequantized to bf16 and requantized |

Opt-in and off by default: the fi path is taken only when `moe_backend` is one of the two names above, so the native path keeps its own compute. Selection is by backend string alone.

**Sequence-parallel ready; benchmark numbers below predate SP.** Since the numbers below were taken (v0.25.1), main integrated sequence-parallel MoE, which shards the MoE batch across TP ranks — 8x fewer tokens/rank at TP8 — and moves the e2e operating point down the tokens/rank curves in the microbenchmark tables. This PR runs SP exactly like native: mega-MoE eligibility, SP included, is keyed on the shared `MEGA_MOE_BACKENDS` set, with a regression test (without this the fi backends silently ran the MoE full-batch on every rank). On the current stack `fi_dg` holds 0.997–1.008x parity with native across prefill/decode cells on 8xB200. CuTeDSL perf tuning at the sharded operating points (knob autotune at sharded token counts, quantized combine wire) is ongoing and will come as follow-ups — this PR is the correct, SP-ready plumbing.

The native `DeepseekV4MegaMoEExperts` class body is unchanged. Everything in the diff either widens the `use_mega_moe` checks from an equality test to `MEGA_MOE_BACKENDS` membership — which still matches `deep_gemm_mega_moe` — or adds the fi experts class and its config validation alongside the native one.

`flashinfer.moe_ep` is a soft dependency — imported lazily inside the fi code paths, never at module import. The backends need flashinfer >= 0.6.17 (`BootstrapConfig.device`, flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4348), which the vLLM FlashInfer requirements pin will carry; selecting a fi backend against a build without the moe_ep runtime raises a clear ImportError at config time. The fi backends also validate an SM100 device capability up front, and reject `--enable-eplb`, since the FlashInfer experts neither apply the logical-to-physical expert map nor report per-expert load.

**Tests**

```
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_fi_moe_ep.py -v   # 10 passed
pre-commit run --all-files                                                  # clean
```

GPU validation on 8xB200: smoke across MXFP4/NVFP4 checkpoints on both fi backends including remapped `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (the regression case for the bootstrap device pin), the GSM8K gate below, and the e2e cells below, native vs fi.

**Duplication check:** no open PR adds a FlashInfer moe_ep / mega-MoE backend (searched `moe_ep`, `mega moe`, `flashinfer moe`).

**AI assistance was used** in developing this PR; every changed line was reviewed, tested, and is defended by the submitter.

## Reproducing the MoE-EP benchmarks

> The section below reproduces the numbers as measured on **vLLM 0.25.1** (pre-SP stack) with that stack's matched FlashInfer/DSL pins; it is the environment the tables were recorded in, not the requirement for this PR (flashinfer >= 0.6.17 via the requirements pin, see above).

Both harnesses, the patch, and the numbers live in a companion repo on a branch carrying only what a reproduction needs: **[mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark @ `vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2`](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2)**. [RUNBOOK_REPRO.md](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md) is the whole procedure — [§1 prep](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md#1-prep) (clone, image, checkpoints, venv), [§2 microbenchmark](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md#2-kernel-microbenchmark-25-min-per-shape), [§3 e2e throughput](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md#3-vllm-e2e--throughput) (offline in-process, plus the serving-mode server+client sweep in §3g), [§4 accuracy](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md#4-accuracy) — and every number below appears in [expected_results.md](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/expected_results.md) with its tolerance and the SLURM job it came from.

All numbers: **one 8-GPU B200 node (SM100)**, flashinfer `4_5_2-perf-fix` @ `1ee41bcd` (https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4101), **nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.2** — vLLM 0.25.1's own pin. Do not unpin it: the DSL version and the flashinfer branch are a matched pair, and both harnesses assert 4.5.2 at run time. CUDA 12 and 13 both work.

Backend is selected by the `moe_backend` string — one per run, no env gating:

| config | `moe_backend` | checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| native | `deep_gemm_mega_moe` | mx original |
| fi_dg | `flashinfer_moe_ep_mega_deep_gemm` | mx original |
| fi_cutedsl | `flashinfer_moe_ep_mega_cutedsl` | NVFP4 cast |

In serving mode that string is an ordinary server CLI flag. One process serves an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (the decode-1k cell shown; the per-cell engine flags are the table in RUNBOOK §3g):

```bash
hf download deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
    --revision 6e763230a9d263eca2023f1d4a5ce1bfe126cf48 \
    --local-dir $CKPT/deepseek-v4-flash
    
export MODEL_MX_FLASH=$CKPT/deepseek-v4-flash
    
vllm serve $MODEL_MX_FLASH\
    --trust-remote-code \
    --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \
    --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
    --enable-expert-parallel \
    --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe \          # or either fi backend above
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --block-size 256 \
    --no-enable-prefix-caching \
    --max-model-len 4096 \
    --max-num-seqs 1024 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
    --compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 4096, "cudagraph_capture_sizes": [256, 1024, 2048, 4096]}' \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

(fi_cutedsl additionally takes `FLASHINFER_MOE_EP_KNOB_CACHE=<repo>/vllm_e2e/results/knob_cache_ep8.json` and the NVFP4 checkpoint.) A second process benchmarks it over HTTP:

```bash
vllm bench serve \
    --backend vllm --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
    --model $MODEL --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \
    --dataset-name random \
    --random-input-len 128 --random-output-len 256 --random-range-ratio 0 \
    --num-prompts 1024 --max-concurrency 1024 \
    --ignore-eos --seed 0 --save-result
```

The first client pass after boot is discarded as warmup and the timed passes are repeated with the median reported — the native decode baseline drifts run-over-run by more than the fi-vs-native delta, so single-pass serving numbers are quoted nowhere below.

**EP8 throughout, but the two levels reach it differently.** The microbenchmark builds the MoE layer alone with synthetic weights, so there is nothing for tensor parallelism to shard: one process per GPU, `DP8 / EP8 / TP1`, no vLLM and no checkpoint. The e2e sweeps have a whole model to place, so they run `TP8 / EP8 / DP1`. Expert parallelism is 8 in both, which is the axis under test.

One vLLM-side hazard is worth surfacing here rather than leaving in the runbook: **a cell that sets `MAX_CAPTURE` must also pin `CAPTURE_SIZES`.** With the dense default ladder, the cudagraph memory profiler reserves ~48 GiB/GPU for the flashinfer backends against a real ~6 GiB cost — the same ~6 GiB it estimates correctly for native — and the difference comes out of the KV cache. The tell is a backend that is *fast per step and slow overall*: better ITL than native, far worse throughput, because the engine is holding a fraction of the sequences requested. The other two ways to get plausible-but-wrong numbers are [§5](https://github.com/mhoqueanik/moe_ep_benchmark/tree/vllm_repro_8_gpu_v2/RUNBOOK_REPRO.md#5-things-that-will-bite-you).

**`gpt_oss_120b`** — hidden 2880, inter 2880, 128 experts, top-4 — `dg` is `—` throughout: `deep_gemm_mega` requires hidden and intermediate both divisible by 128, and 2880 is not, so there is no baseline to divide by.

| tok/rank | dg | nvfp4 bf16 | +ikr | +combine_nvfp4 | +combine_mxfp8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | — | 93.2 | 95.4 | 97.2 | 97.4 |

| 4096 | — | 379.9 | 383.8 | 329.6 | 339.1 |
| 8192 | — | 697.4 | 697.2 | 541.7 | 607.3 |

**The crossover sits between 512 and 1024 tok/rank on every geometry.** Below it `deep_gemm_mega` wins; above it the CuteDSL variants pull away, and the quantized-combine wires extend the lead further at large batches — `+combine_nvfp4` is the strongest variant above the crossover on every shape, worth roughly a further 0.4x over plain `nvfp4 bf16` at 8192.

**V4-Flash is the least favourable of the five shapes that have a baseline.** The geometry the e2e sweep uses tops out at 1.20x on plain `nvfp4 bf16`, where V4-Pro reaches 1.64x and `deepseek_v3` 1.59x. The e2e numbers below are therefore a conservative reading of the kernel, and V4-Pro's larger end-to-end gains follow the kernel rather than any integration difference.

`gpt_oss_120b` has an empty `dg` column by construction: `deep_gemm_mega` requires hidden and intermediate both divisible by 128, and 2880 is not, so the harness logs the assertion once per token count and carries on with the CuteDSL variants, which are tail-safe down to %64.

## End-to-end results (vLLM 0.25.1, TP8 + EP8, 1x8 B200)

native and fi_dg run the mx checkpoint; fi_cutedsl runs the NVFP4 cast of the same base weights, which is the format its kernel consumes. That makes every ratio cross-checkpoint, which is what the GSM8K gate below is for.

### Offline (in-process `llm.generate()`, median of repeated rounds)

**DeepSeek-V4-Flash** (4096 hidden / 2048 inter / 256 experts / top-6):

| cell | native tok/s | fi_dg | fi_cutedsl |
|---|---|---|---|
| prefill-8k | 38986 | 40225 (1.032x) | 46584 (**1.195x**) |
| decode-1k | 30845 | 31494 (1.021x) | 32741 (**1.061x**) |
| 100K ISL / 1K | 29632 | 30230 (1.020x) | 32913 (**1.111x**) |
| 32K ISL / 32 | 35700 | 36597 (1.025x) | 42028 (**1.177x**) |

**DeepSeek-V4-Pro** (7168 hidden / 3072 inter / 384 experts / top-6):

| cell | native tok/s | fi_dg | fi_cutedsl |
|---|---|---|---|
| prefill-8k | 15240 | 15630 (1.026x) | 20074 (**1.317x**) |
| decode-1k | 12897 | 13157 (1.020x) | 15368 (**1.192x**) |
| 100K ISL / 1K | 12223 | 12453 (1.019x) | 15053 (**1.231x**) |
| 32K ISL / 32 | 14117 | 14435 (1.023x) | 18250 (**1.293x**) |

Latency on the interactivity cells, fi_cutedsl vs native — Flash: TTFT 42.2s vs 49.3s at 100K and 12.8s vs 15.1s at 32K, ITL p50 51.9ms vs 56.1ms and 191.2ms vs 226.5ms. Pro: TTFT 95.0s vs 122.3s and 29.5s vs 38.4s, ITL p50 111.8ms vs 134.3ms and 441.3ms vs 573.9ms.

### Serving mode (`vllm serve` + `vllm bench serve` over HTTP, same four cells)

Same workloads and per-cell engine settings, but the backend is the `--moe-backend` server flag and the measurement is entirely client-side over streaming HTTP — so tokenize/detokenize, HTTP and scheduling gaps are included. Total tok/s, median of the timed client rounds:

**DeepSeek-V4-Flash:**

| cell | native tok/s | fi_dg | fi_cutedsl |
|---|---|---|---|
| prefill-8k | 38074 | 39280 (1.032x) | 45643 (**1.199x**) |
| decode-1k | 29419 | 29958 (1.018x) | 30861 (**1.049x**) |
| 100K ISL / 1K | 29457 | 30059 (1.020x) | 32765 (**1.112x**) |
| 32K ISL / 32 | 35661 | 36518 (1.024x) | 41932 (**1.176x**) |

**DeepSeek-V4-Pro:**

| cell | native tok/s | fi_dg | fi_cutedsl |
|---|---|---|---|
| prefill-8k | 15216 | 15609 (1.026x) | 19860 (**1.305x**) |
| decode-1k | 12408 | 12619 (1.017x) | 14518 (**1.170x**) |
| 100K ISL / 1K | 12190 | 12417 (1.019x) | 14909 (**1.223x**) |
| 32K ISL / 32 | 13976 | 14290 (1.022x) | 18052 (**1.292x**) |

**The two harnesses agree.** Serving lands within 1–3% of the offline absolutes and the fi_cutedsl ratio matches the offline column to ±0.022x on all eight cells (e.g. Flash prefill-8k 1.199x serving vs 1.195x offline; Pro 32K 1.292x vs 1.293x) — the kernel win survives the full serving stack, HTTP included. Interactivity latency over HTTP, fi_cutedsl vs native — Flash: TTFT p50 42.5s vs 49.7s at 100K and 12.9s vs 15.2s at 32K. Pro: 95.5s vs 122.4s and 29.9s vs 38.9s.

**`fi_dg` is the control, and it reads 1.02x — in both harnesses.** It is the same deep_gemm kernel reached through this integration layer rather than a torch op, so its ratio measures the layer and nothing else — parity is the expected answer, and the fi_cutedsl deltas above it are kernel-side. A `fi_dg` far from 1.02x means the run is misconfigured, not that the layer is expensive.

**The fi_cutedsl win grows with model size** — 1.19–1.32x on V4-Pro against 1.05–1.20x on V4-Flash, on identical cells, offline and serving alike.

### Accuracy gate — GSM8K, 200 questions, greedy, both checkpoints

| model | native | fi_dg | fi_cutedsl (NVFP4 cast) | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flash | 0.965 | 0.965 | **0.965** | +0.000 |
| Pro | 0.880 | 0.880 | **0.890** | +0.010 |

**The delta is what gates the throughput claim.** Because fi_cutedsl runs a different checkpoint, its numbers are only comparable if its accuracy is; ±0.010 on 200 questions is two questions. Both models pass.

V4-Pro scoring 0.88 is a property of the model and this eval, not of `moe_ep` — all three backends agree exactly (176/176/178 correct), and it is not a truncation artifact: raising `--max-tokens` 512 → 1024 → 2048 moves accuracy 0.8800 → 0.8750 → 0.8750 while truncated completions only fall 15 → 14 → 13.

### Reproducibility of the numbers themselves

Ratios are stable to about ±0.02x between sessions; absolute throughput moves more with node and thermal state. That tolerance is measured rather than assumed, three ways: repeating the entire offline set on a second pass, from the branch's own scripts against a freshly built venv, reproduced it to within **0.5% on absolute throughput and 0.008x on every ratio**; the serving 32K cell was measured in two independent sessions on different nodes and its ratios reproduced to **0.001x**; and the serving decode-1k cell re-run by hand from the runbook's pasted server/client commands landed within **1% absolute and 0.008x on the ratio** of the recorded sweep. One measured caveat drives the methodology: the *native* serving baseline drifts run-over-run by up to 8% under an identical warm protocol — more than the fi-vs-native delta on that cell — which is why every serving number above is a median of repeated client rounds with a discarded warmup pass, never a single run.

title: [Kernel][SM100] Add a CuTeDSL fused query kernel
author: zhou9402
body:
## What this does

Add an SM100 CuTeDSL implementation of the fused query preprocessing used by DSA
sparse attention (`fused_q`): the packed fp8 MQA query, the indexer query
RoPE + UE8M0 fp8 quant, and the folded index weights — registered as a torch
custom op.

Selected only for the supported dtype/shape combination
(`is_fused_q_cutedsl_supported`); the existing Triton implementation stays the
fallback everywhere else. `vllm/cute_utils` gains one dtype-map entry and two
conversion helpers used by the kernel.

Part of the #48597 re-split — see that PR for the tracker and merge order.

title: [Spec Decode][Perf] Fuse the MTP trailing all-reduce; local-argmax draft tokens
author: zhou9402
body:
Two optimizations on the DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5.2 MTP draft path.

- **Fuse the trailing all-reduce into the final RMSNorm** on the
  non-sequence-parallel path, as the main model already does at layer
  boundaries. The sequence-parallel path is unchanged.
- **Greedy draft tokens via vocab-parallel local argmax** (`get_top_tokens`),
  skipping the full-vocab all-gather in `compute_logits`. The proposer already
  probes for this via `use_local_argmax_reduction`; this adds the model side.

Not a duplicate: an earlier revision also carried the
`index_share_for_mtp_iteration` gates and the V2 speculator lifecycle hooks,
both of which have since landed on main; that part is dropped. Nothing open
overlaps with what remains.

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "MTP all-reduce RMSNorm fuse"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "local argmax draft tokens"
```

## Benchmarks

2×GB300, TP8 across 2 nodes, `nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4`, MTP=5,
`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`, fp8 KV cache, no prefix caching. The baseline arm
is the same tree with the fusion reverted to an explicit
`tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce` + `RMSNorm`; local argmax is toggled with
`--speculative-config.use_local_argmax_reduction`.

**Batch 1 (8192 in / 1024 out, c=1) — no measurable change.** Three runs per
arm, output tok/s and MTP acceptance length:

| arm | fusion | local argmax | output tok/s | acceptance length |
| --- | :-: | :-: | --- | --- |
| baseline | ✗ | ✗ | 456.7 / 451.6 / 463.3 | 4.78 / 4.70 / 4.86 |
| +fusion | ✓ | ✗ | 487.0 / 459.0 / 461.3 | 5.05 / 4.76 / 4.79 |
| +both | ✓ | ✓ | 460.1 / 472.8 / 470.2 | 4.80 / 4.95 / 4.90 |

The arms overlap completely. At c=1 the saved all-gather is one vocab row and
the fused all-reduce is one small tensor, so this is the expected result;
median ITL sat at 9.08–9.12 ms across all nine runs.

**Concurrency 64 (1024 in / 1024 out, 256 prompts) — this is where it pays.**
One A/B pair on the same node pair:

| arm | output tok/s | acceptance length | median ITL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| baseline | 2923.2 | 4.86 | 31.83 ms |
| +both | 3321.1 (**+13.6%**) | 4.69 | 31.32 ms |

The gain cannot be attributed to speculation luck: acceptance length is 3.5%
*lower* in the faster arm. Normalizing throughput by acceptance length
(steps/s) gives +17.8%. At c=64 the draft's per-step full-vocab all-gather is
64 × 151k × 2 B ≈ 19 MB, five times per accepted token — that is what
`get_top_tokens` removes.

Caveats, stated plainly: the c=64 result is a single A/B pair, and a repeat was
lost to cluster contention. Cross-node variability on this cluster is large
(the +fusion arm measured 4226 tok/s on a different node pair with the same
acceptance length as the baseline), so only within-pair comparisons above are
meaningful — do not compare numbers across the two tables.

## Accuracy

gsm8k, 5-shot, full 1319 questions, via `lm_eval --model local-completions`:

| arm | flexible-extract | strict-match |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baseline | 0.9439 ± 0.0063 | 0.9424 ± 0.0064 |
| +both | 0.9431 ± 0.0064 | 0.9409 ± 0.0065 |

Unchanged within stderr, which is the point: the fused kernel accumulates in
fp32 and local argmax breaks vocab-boundary ties differently, so both are
output-affecting in principle.

AI assistance (Claude) was used; every changed line has been reviewed.

title: [Linear] [Kernel] add block-wise scaled_mm
author: zufangzhu
body:
## Purpose

This adds a native, dependency-free torch._scaled_mm block-wise FP8 backend. It needs no extra libraries or per-shape tuning (unlike CUTLASS/DeepGEMM/Triton), and stays competitive-to-best in the compute-bound regime (M≥1024, up to 1.09x faster than the next-best backend on H20).

Add a block-wise FP8 `_scaled_mm` linear kernel
(`BlockWiseTorchFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel`) that routes DeepSeek-style block
scaling (1x128 activation + 128x128 weight) through `torch._scaled_mm`.

This gives a native PyTorch path for FP8 block-scaled GEMM in addition to the
existing Triton / CUTLASS / DeepGEMM backends, and works on CUDA (Hopper).


## Changes

- New `BlockWiseTorchFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel` and registration in the FP8 block
  kernel map.
- On CUDA, restrict support to SM90 (Hopper), matching PyTorch's
  `_check_deepseek_support()` which only implements the (1x128, 128x128) recipe
  for SM90.
- Pad the M dimension up to a multiple of 4 on CUDA (cuBLASLt requirement) and
  slice the result back.

## Test

Added `test_w8a8_block_fp8_torch_scaled_mm_matmul` (SM90-gated) that exercises
the kernel end-to-end, including the M-padding path, and checks numerics
against `native_w8a8_block_matmul` (`rel_diff < 0.001`).

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_block_fp8.py -k torch_scaled_mm

title: [Spec Decode] Add top-k DSpark Markov projection
author: askliar
body:
## Purpose

DSpark computes the base logits for all draft positions in parallel, then applies the Markov bias sequentially over the full draft vocabulary. The repeated full-vocabulary Markov projection is on the serial drafting path.

This PR adds `dspark_draft_topk` for Qwen3 DSpark. It selects the top-k candidates from the base logits once, gathers the corresponding `markov_w2` rows, and evaluates the sequential Markov bias only for those candidates.

The current implementation deliberately reuses the existing dense sampling path:

- Compute dense base logits and select the top-k candidates once for all draft positions.
- Initialize the reusable dense logits buffer to `-inf`.
- At each sequential step, apply the Markov bias only to the selected candidates and scatter the corrected values into that dense row.
- Use the existing greedy or probabilistic Gumbel/rejection sampling path unchanged.

The base LM-head output and probabilistic draft-logits storage remain dense. This optimization specifically reduces the repeated sequential Markov projection while avoiding custom proposal and rejection-sampling plumbing.

Current scope:

- Qwen3 DSpark

## Test Plan

- Compare dense DSpark against `dspark_draft_topk` across lower- and higher-concurrency workloads.
- Check GSM8K accuracy and acceptance length for greedy and probabilistic drafting.
- Profile the decode window to confirm that savings occur in the drafter projection.
- Run focused configuration/top-k tests and repository pre-commit hooks.

## Results

### End-to-end comparison

Tested with `draft_sample_method: probabilistic`, temperature 1, and 7 speculative tokens on GB10.

| Implementation | Top-k | GSM8K strict / flex | AIPerf tok/s/user¹ | AIPerf total tok/s¹ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Initial PR implementation | 512 | 0.82 / 0.83 | 65.3 | 44.6 |
| Initial PR implementation | Off | 0.80 / 0.83 | 53.0 | 40.6 |
| Current simplified implementation | 512 | 0.84 / 0.84 | 78.1 | 52.1 |
| Current simplified implementation | Off | 0.84 / 0.85 | 54.0 | 41.3 |

¹ Concurrency 64, ISL 32768 / OSL 1024.

- At concurrency 64, top-k 512 improves per-user throughput by 23% for the initial implementation (53.0 → 65.3) and 45% for the current simplified implementation (54.0 → 78.1).
- With top-k 512, the current implementation is 20% faster per user than the initial implementation (78.1 versus 65.3). Their no-top-k baselines are equivalent.
- These results confirm that top-k benefits higher-concurrency, GPU-bound decode.
- GSM8K scores remain within the observed run-to-run range; there is no measured accuracy regression.

### Decode GPU profile

GPU time by selected kernel category, in milliseconds, over a concurrency-1 / approximately 8K-context decode window:

| Kernel category | Initial / Off | Initial / 512 | Current / Off | Current / 512 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Drafter projection (`cutlass` / GEMV) | 155 | 105 | 154 | 107 |
| Elementwise / norm | 28.7 | 34.4 | 28.3 | 28.9 |
| Sort / top-k / select | 5.5 | 6.2 | 5.5 | 6.7 |
| Total GPU time | 878.5 | 822.9 | 870.8 | 831.4 |

The profiles confirm that the saving occurs where expected:

- Top-k 512 reduces the drafter projection by approximately 47–50 ms. The top-k selection itself adds only approximately 1 ms.
- Total decode GPU time falls by 6.3% for the initial implementation and 4.5% for the current implementation.
- The initial path adds 5.7 ms of elementwise/index work, while the current implementation adds only 0.6 ms. The profiler reports 35 additional distinct kernels for the initial path versus 14 for the current path.
- Major target-model categories such as MoE routing/GEMMs, dense matmuls, and attention are unchanged within run-to-run variation.

The concurrency-1 profile establishes the per-step compute saving. At concurrency 64 with a 32K-token input, decode becomes GPU-bound and that saving converts into substantial throughput. The current path's advantage over the initial path at high concurrency is consistent with its lower auxiliary kernel/index overhead, although that contribution was not isolated independently.

### Acceptance-length sweep

| Top-k | t=0 (greedy) | t=1 (probabilistic) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | 3.9509 | 3.6582 |
| 1024 | 3.9448 | 3.6573 |
| 2048 | 3.9445 | 3.6472 |
| 4096 | 3.9403 | 3.6455 |
| 8192 | 3.9403 | 3.6556 |
| 16384 | 3.9648 | 3.6473 |
| 32768 | 3.9253 | 3.6568 |
| 65536 | 3.9403 | 3.6429 |
| Off | 3.9253 | 3.6413 |

### Focused checks

- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>`: passed, including Ruff and mypy.
- `pytest -q tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_topk.py`: 2 passed.
- `pytest -q tests/test_config.py -k 'draft_sample_method'`: 2 passed.
- `pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_rejection_sampler_chunking.py -k 'preserves_request_boundaries'`: 1 passed.

### Benchmark caveats

- AIPerf used 5 measured requests plus 2 warmup requests, so exact throughput values have some run-to-run variance. The top-k 512 differences are substantially larger than the observed noise.
- AIPerf and GSM8K runs used `gpu-memory-utilization=0.8`.
- Nsight Systems runs used `gpu-memory-utilization=0.7` because CUPTI trace buffers caused model-load OOM at 0.8 on this node. The decode kernels were unchanged, so the profiles remain representative of the code paths.

---

- [x] Test results are included.

title: Enable ModelOpt FP8 emulation on SM80
author: mikekg
body:
## Purpose

ModelOpt FP8 checkpoints are currently rejected on NVIDIA A100 GPUs before vLLM can select its existing weight-only FP8 execution path:

```text
ValueError: The quantization method modelopt is not supported for the current GPU. Minimum capability: 89. Current capability: 80.
```

This PR lowers `ModelOptFp8Config`'s minimum CUDA capability from SM89 to SM80. On GPUs with capability SM80 through SM88, it also emits one model-level warning explaining that FP8 is not executed natively, that vLLM will use emulation for the model, and that some models may run more slowly. SM89 and newer GPUs retain their existing behavior and do not receive the warning.

This enables a serialized ModelOpt `quant_algo=FP8` checkpoint to load on A100 without a backend override. The exercised model was `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8`. While it may appear counter-intuitive, the emulated FP8 actually shows better performance than the unquantized BF16 model due to the bandwidth reduction achieved for bandwidth-limited GEMMs. (Added a warning because for dense/compute-limited GEMM models, FP8 emulation may lag native bf16 execution due to the dequantization overhead.)

## Test Plan

The before/after reproduction uses one NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, tensor parallelism 1, vLLM 0.26.0, BF16 activations, and an FP8 KV cache. The tested FP8 checkpoint revision was `f8dc1c0afee92f44417695b4f5ddca9afc95ea58`.

Run this command with stock vLLM 0.26.0, then run the same command after applying this PR:

```bash
vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8 \
  --revision f8dc1c0afee92f44417695b4f5ddca9afc95ea58 \
  --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-num-seqs 512 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 25088 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 128 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000
```

Stock vLLM 0.26.0 exits at the capability check shown above. With this PR applied to the same vLLM version, the checkpoint loads, the server becomes ready, and the existing automatic FP8 fallback is selected for both dense and MoE layers. No backend-selection environment variable or command-line override is used.

For the matched BF16 control, start a second run on the same A100 with:

```bash
vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 \
  --revision 2d59de1cbd51c0adf384eb906b766d1aee0e0517 \
  --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-num-seqs 512 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 27136 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 128 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000
```

The two servers use the same GPU, vLLM version, TP size, KV-cache dtype, maximum sequence count, memory utilization, block size, and prefix-cache setting. Their `max-model-len` values differ because each was set to the exercised capacity for that weight format; the GSM8K prompts and generation settings are identical.

The GSM8K evaluator used for the reported results is public at `NVIDIA/srt-slurm`, commit `cb651682117df129162cd276cf567ec70dc57b36`. Clone that revision:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/srt-slurm.git
cd srt-slurm
git checkout cb651682117df129162cd276cf567ec70dc57b36
```

With the FP8 server running, execute:

```bash
python3 src/srtctl/benchmarks/scripts/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py \
  --host http://localhost \
  --port 8000 \
  --model nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8 \
  --num-questions 1319 \
  --max-tokens 16000 \
  --num-shots 8 \
  --temperature 0.6 \
  --seed 42 \
  --save-results ./gsm8k-fp8.json
```

With the BF16 control server running, execute:

```bash
python3 src/srtctl/benchmarks/scripts/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py \
  --host http://localhost \
  --port 8000 \
  --model nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 \
  --num-questions 1319 \
  --max-tokens 16000 \
  --num-shots 8 \
  --temperature 0.6 \
  --seed 42 \
  --save-results ./gsm8k-bf16.json
```

## Test Result

The stock FP8 run failed before model loading with the SM89 minimum-capability error. Applying this PR changed the same command to a successful load and healthy server. The full FP8 GSM8K run and the BF16 control both completed all 1,319 questions with no request failures.

| Metric | BF16 weights | ModelOpt FP8 weights | FP8 delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Completed questions | 1,319 / 1,319 | 1,319 / 1,319 | — |
| Accuracy | 61.1069% | 58.3776% | -2.7293 pp |
| Invalid responses | 0% | 0% | — |
| Evaluation wall time | 539.667 s | 435.493 s | -19.30% |
| Questions/s | 2.4441 | 3.0288 | +23.92% |
| Total output tokens | 588,906 | 611,214 | +22,308 |
| Output tokens/s | 1,091.24 | 1,403.50 | +28.62% |
| Full job wall time | 13:31 | 11:56 | -11.71% |
| Process exit status | 0 | 0 | — |

The FP8 run was approximately 1.24x faster by evaluation time and 1.29x faster by output-token throughput, with a 2.73 percentage-point accuracy reduction in this single full-dataset run. Because the FP8 run generated more output tokens than the BF16 control, output tokens per second is the more useful normalized throughput comparison than total job wall time. These results establish the measured performance/accuracy tradeoff rather than claiming that every model or workload will speed up.

title: [KV Offloading] Back-pressure detection and remediation
author: bnellnm
body:
## Purpose

Add back-pressure detection to the KV cache tiering offloading manager. When a secondary tier (disk, shared storage, P2P) becomes slow, the manager detects saturation via store completion latency and stops cascading new stores to that tier until it recovers. This prevents unbounded job pileup from degrading serving latency.

See associated RFC; https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50031

### Design

- **Detection**: An exponential moving average (EMA) of store completion latency is tracked per secondary tier. When the EMA exceeds a high-water mark (1.0s), the tier is marked as under pressure. Pressure clears when the EMA drops below a low-water mark (0.5s). The hysteresis band prevents oscillation.

- **Response**: Stores to pressured tiers are silently dropped — blocks remain in the CPU primary tier subject to normal LRU eviction. Loads from pressured tiers continue normally.

- **Observability**: Two new Prometheus metrics per tier:
  - `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_backpressure_active` (gauge) — 1 when pressure is active
  - `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_backpressure_stores_dropped` (counter) — number of dropped stores

### Changes

- `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/backpressure.py`: Add abstract `BackpressureDetector` and `BackpressurePolicy` APIs. Implement subclasses for EMA and store skipping.
- `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py`: Add `BackpressureState` dataclass and per-tier tracking. Update `_process_finished_jobs()` to feed the EMA on store completions. Gate store cascades in both `complete_store()` (global tiers) and `_cascade_to_request_level_tiers()` behind pressure checks. Report metrics in `get_stats()`. Reset state in `reset_cache()`.
- `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`: Add `submit_time` field to `JobMetadata` for latency measurement. Add `BACKPRESSURE_ACTIVE` and `BACKPRESSURE_STORES_DROPPED` metric keys.
- `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py`: New test suite (12 tests).

### Test plan

The test suite uses a `DelayedSecondaryTierManager` that holds completed jobs until explicitly released, allowing precise control over apparent store latency. It exercises:

1. **EMA updates on store completion** — EMA starts at 0 while jobs are in-flight, updates to `alpha * latency` after a fast completion.
2. **Pressure activates above high water** — Slow store (5x threshold) flips `is_under_pressure` to True.
3. **Pressure clears below low water** — Repeated fast completions decay EMA below low-water mark, deactivating pressure.
4. **Hysteresis prevents oscillation** — Mid-range EMA (between low/high water) does not toggle pressure in either direction.
5. **Stores skipped under pressure** — Blocks land in primary but are not cascaded to the secondary tier.
6. **Stores resume after pressure clears** — After clearing pressure, the next store cascades normally.
7. **Dropped store count tracked** — `stores_dropped` increments correctly per skipped cascade.
8. **Metrics reported via get_stats** — Prometheus gauge and counter appear in reduced stats with correct values; dropped count resets after collection.
9. **Metrics gauge zero when no pressure** — Backpressure gauge reports 0 when inactive.
10. **Reset cache clears backpressure** — `reset_cache()` zeros EMA and clears pressure state.
11. **Request-level tier respects backpressure** — Request-level cascades (via `prepare_store`) also skip pressured tiers.
12. **Loads continue under pressure** — Lookups still return RETRY and initiate promotion; only stores are suppressed.

```bash
pytest -sv tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py
```

Benchmark for Qwen with various tiering configs:
[backpressure-report.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31228948/backpressure-report.html)

Note: portions of this PR are generated with claude.

cc @varun-sundar-rabindranath

title: [Hardware][AMD] Enable fused bf16→fp32 router GEMM on ROCm
author: mpashkovskii
body:
## Purpose

This pull request addresses issue #50267 by enabling fused bf16→fp32 GEMM operations on AMD ROCm hardware for MoE router gates.

## Problem Statement

The MoE router gate requires `out_dtype=torch.float32` for the `grouped_topk` operation. However, on ROCm, the fused fp32-output GEMM implementation was gated exclusively to CUDA platforms. This caused a fallback to bf16 GEMM followed by a separate cast operation, creating a standalone "bf16→fp32 copy kernel" visible in performance traces between the router GEMM and `grouped_topk` for every MoE layer on each decode step.

## Solution

The changes enable hipBLASLt's `out_dtype` epilogue support (analogous to CUDA's cuBLAS capability) by modifying `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py`:

- Adds ROCm as an alternative condition for `allow_cublas_router_gemm` when: no bias exists, weights are bf16, and output is fp32
- Updates both `__init__` and `set_out_dtype` methods to ensure consistency
- The fused tier now executes on ROCm, folding the fp32 cast into the GEMM epilogue

## Impact Assessment

**CUDA:** No changes; the condition uses `current_platform.is_rocm()`, which evaluates false on CUDA.

**Correctness:** Verified on gfx942 hardware; results match fp32 reference within ~6e-5 tolerance.

**Scope:** Router gate only; expert GEMMs and other fp32 operations remain unaffected.

## Performance Results

Benchmarked on ROCm (gfx942) using the online serving benchmark: baseline vs. fused, 3 seeds each (123 / 456 / 789), max concurrency 4, 40 requests per run (40960 input + 40960 generated tokens). All runs completed 40/40 successful with 0 failures.

Averaged across the 3 seeds:

| Metric                    | Baseline | Fused (this PR) | Δ              |
|---------------------------|----------|-----------------|----------------|
| Benchmark duration (s)    | 343.18   | 337.69          | −5.5 s (−1.6%) |
| Output throughput (tok/s) | 119.35   | 121.29          | +1.9 (+1.6%)   |
| Total throughput (tok/s)  | 238.71   | 242.59          | +3.9 (+1.6%)   |
| Mean TPOT (ms)            | 32.87    | 32.34           | −0.53 (−1.6%)  |
| Mean ITL (ms)             | 32.87    | 32.34           | −0.53 (−1.6%)  |
| Mean TTFT (ms)            | 689.65   | 688.97          | ≈flat (−0.1%)  |

**Interpretation:** Folding the fp32 cast into the router GEMM epilogue removes a per-MoE-layer, per-decode-step conversion kernel from the critical path. The decode-path metrics (TPOT, ITL, output throughput) all improve by a consistent ~1.6%, while TTFT is unchanged as expected since prefill is not dominated by that per-step kernel. Variance across seeds is small (throughput within ±0.2 tok/s, TPOT within ±0.07 ms), so the improvement is stable and above noise, if modest.

## Testing Plan

- Confirm the standalone `bfloat16tofloat32_copy_kernel` is absent from ROCm traces
- Validate router logits match previous behavior within tolerance
- Unit tests added for the modification
speedup_claims: TPOT, ITL, output throughput) all improve by a consistent ~1.6%

speedup_evidence.claim: TPOT, ITL, output throughput) all improve by a consistent ~1.6%

title: [Bugfix] Fix speculative decoding for short_conv (LFM2) models
author: zwischenraum
body:
## Purpose

Supersedes #44296 (rebased onto main with the original commit and authorship preserved — thanks @Tonoken3); that PR has had failing pre-commit since opening and merge conflicts since July 6 with no author activity, so this revives it to make the merge cheap.

Speculative decoding (ngram, EAGLE-3, any method) on `short_conv` (LFM2 / LFM2.5) targets silently corrupts output at the first rejected token: attention KV rolls back, but the conv sliding window retains rejected-token activations. `mamba2` / GDN already handle this via the spec-aware `causal_conv1d_update` path; `short_conv` was never wired in:

1. `MambaStateShapeCalculator.short_conv_state_shape` sizes the conv state `conv_kernel - 1` (no `num_spec`), so there is no room to roll the window back (mirror: `mamba2_state_shape` adds `num_spec`).
2. `GPUModelRunner._build_attn_group_metadata` never injects `num_accepted_tokens` for `ShortConvAttentionMetadataBuilder`, so the layer never sees the accepted-token counts.

Changes vs #44296: rebased onto current main, fixed the mypy failure that blocked its pre-commit (`assert state_indices_tensor_d is not None`), added a regression test for the spec-widened conv state shape.

## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR

#44296 is this fix (red CI + conflicts + stale for 8 weeks; original commit and authorship preserved here). #50146 bundles a rebase of the same target-side fix with 6 further drafter-side changes across 9 files and depends on other open PRs; this PR is the minimal, independently mergeable target-side correctness fix for released models.

## Test plan

- `pre-commit run` (incl. mypy-3.10): pass.
- New `tests/kernels/mamba/test_short_conv_state_shape.py`: pass.
- E2E (we are the model vendor — Liquid AI serving team; LFM2.5-230M fine-tune + trained EAGLE-3 drafter with ~0.9/step acceptance, ROCm MI325X, v0.26.0 + this patch): without the fix, low-concurrency spec decode diverges after the first rejection (doubled/fused tokens, occasionally flipped outputs; under default cudagraphs it degrades to garbage from ~token 2). With it, `--enforce-eager`, `PIECEWISE`, and default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` all produce identical, correct output on fixed-seed content probes.

AI assistance was used to rebase, fix, and validate this change; I reviewed every changed line and am accountable for it.

title: [Kernel][Model] Optimize FA4 mm_prefix range lookup
author: vhagor
body:
# [Kernel][Model] Gemma4: optimize FA4 mm_prefix range lookup and CuTe JIT stability

## Motivation

Gemma4 multimodal models can use FA4 as the backend for all layers, so that both
sliding-attention layers (`head_dim=256`) and global/full layers
(`global_head_dim=512`) use one attention backend. This is required for the
vision `mm_prefix` / PrefixLM bidirectional mask path, and avoids mixing
FlashAttention and Triton attention implementations within the same model.

For video prompts, however, the current FA4 `mm_prefix` implementation scales
poorly when the number of multimodal ranges varies across requests and batches.
In Gemma4 video workloads each frame commonly contributes one range, so batches
may see `max_ranges` values such as 1, 8, 16, 32, 46, or 64 over time.

This is not limited to applications that pre-extract frames outside vLLM. The
native vLLM video ingestion path can also produce variable frame counts. Raw
video inputs are decoded by `VideoMediaIO` / `VideoBackend`, which uniformly
samples up to `num_frames` frames (`32` by default). Long videos usually become
32 sampled frames, but shorter clips, failed frame recovery, JPEG-frame
sequences, multiple videos in one prompt, mixed image+video prompts, or
request-level `media_io_kwargs` such as `fps`, `num_frames=-1`, or a larger
`num_frames` can all change the final number of frames in a batch.

Gemma4 does not have a native video tower in vLLM. After video loading, each
sampled frame is processed as an image and the video placeholder is expanded as:

```text
mm:ss <boi> <|video|>*N <eoi> mm:ss <boi> <|video|>*N <eoi> ...
```

Only the `<|video|>` soft-token positions are marked as multimodal embeddings;
the timestamp, `<boi>`, and `<eoi>` tokens are not. Therefore
`PlaceholderRange.extract_embeds_range()` splits one video into one
bidirectional `mm_prefix` range per frame rather than one range for the whole
video. With default raw video loading, one video typically contributes between
1 and 32 ranges. With multiple videos, mixed images, or caller-provided frame
sequences, the range count can be higher and more variable.

## Problem

The current FA4 `mm_prefix` mask_mod receives a padded tensor of shape
`(batch, max_ranges, 2)` and scans every range for every Q x K score:

```python
for i in cutlass.range_constexpr(max_ranges):
    r_start, r_end = ranges[b, i]
    keep = keep | (q_in_range & k_in_range)
```

This creates two performance problems:

1. `max_ranges` is baked into the CuTe JIT specialization via
   `cutlass.range_constexpr(max_ranges)`. Different video frame counts can
   produce different FA4 compile keys and trigger repeated cold JIT compiles.
2. Even when the kernel is already compiled, the mask work is
   `O(max_ranges)` per score. A request with many frames increases the work for
   every request in the same batch because the tensor is padded to the batch
   maximum.

For Gemma4 video prefill with FA4 and vision `mm_prefix`, this hurts both cold
start and steady state. The GPU can sit idle while CuTe compiles a new
specialization, and the compiled kernel still pays for the range scan on every
masked score.

The old mask work scales roughly as:

```text
sliding_layers * num_heads * L^2 * batch_max_ranges
```

The `batch_max_ranges` term comes from scanning all padded ranges in the
mask_mod. The proposed range-id path keeps the same dense Q x K mask surface,
but each lookup is constant time:

```text
sliding_layers * num_heads * L^2
```

There is a metadata precompute step to allocate and fill the
`(batch, max_seq_len)` range-id tensor:

```text
batch_size * max_seq_len + total_mm_tokens
```

That work happens outside the FA4 score loop. The hot FA4 mask path no longer
scales with the largest frame count in the batch.

## Proposed change

Move range membership lookup from the FA4 mask inner loop into metadata
precomputation:

- Build a per-token range-id tensor with shape `(batch, max_seq_len)`.
- Fill non-mm tokens with `-1`.
- Assign each multimodal range a request-local integer id.
- In the FA4 mask_mod, replace the loop over `max_ranges` with:

```python
q_id = range_ids[b, q_abs]
k_id = range_ids[b, kv_idx]
mm = (q_id >= 0) & (q_id == k_id)
keep = causal_window_keep | mm
```

For Gemma4 sliding layers that clamp the bidirectional block to the sliding
window, keep the existing `(query_abs - kv_idx) < sliding_window` condition on
the `mm` branch.

This preserves the non-overlapping range semantics of the existing
start/end-list implementation while making lookup `O(1)` and removing
`max_ranges` from the FA4 mask_mod compile key.

The complexity reduction is part of the fix, not just a cache workaround. It
removes the range loop from the innermost Q x K masking path, so the FA4 mask
cost no longer scales with the batch's largest video frame count.

## Measured results

The numbers below were measured with the latest vLLM version on one H100 GPU,
using Gemma 4 31B in BF16. The benchmark used FA4 with vision
`mm_prefix`.

This was a pooling embedding workload, not a generation benchmark. That matches
the production use case for this branch, where serving returns pooled scores
rather than generated text. QPS means completed pooling embedding requests per
second.

Workload shape:

- 1000 real requests stress test at concurrency 32.
- Each request has one video and text, in `text + video` order.
- Video frame count varies between 8 and 64 frames, with an average of 48.
- Each frame is 360 x 640.
- The text part averages 885 tokens.

| Path | QPS |
| --- | ---: |
| Existing FA4 `mm_prefix` range scan with CuTe JIT | 0.103 |
| Existing FA4 `mm_prefix` range scan without CuTe JIT | 0.678 |
| FA4 with per-token range ids | 1.307 |
| Triton reference path | 0.743 |

This is a +92.8% QPS improvement over the existing FA4 path and makes FA4 faster
than the Triton comparison path under the same workload.

The gain comes from both parts of the change:

- avoiding repeated FA4 CuTe recompilation when `max_ranges` changes;
- replacing the per-score scan over all padded ranges with an `O(1)` range-id
  equality check.

Correctness checks from the same setup:

- outputs matched bit-exact between old FA4 and range-id FA4.
- Mean absolute difference versus the reference path was about 0.00646, in the
  same range as the historical FA4/Triton difference.

## Implementation sketch

Files touched:

- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py`
  - Add `compute_mm_prefix_range_id_tensor(...)`.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py`
  - Store `mm_prefix_range_id_tensor` in `FlashAttentionMetadata`.
  - Build the range-id tensor from `CommonAttentionMetadata.mm_req_doc_ranges`.
  - Pass the range-id tensor to FA4 as `aux_tensors`.
  - Remove `max_ranges` from `_make_mm_prefix_mask_mod(...)`.
  - Use `q_id == k_id` instead of scanning range start/end pairs.
- `vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4_mm.py`
  - Clear the new FA metadata field on full-attention layers, matching the
    existing Gemma4 `mm_prefix` cleanup.

The Triton attention path can continue using the existing
`(batch, max_ranges, 2)` tensor. This change only optimizes the FA4 path.

## Test result

Unit / local:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_mm_prefix_range_id.py -v
# 4 passed, 14 warnings in 0.85s

git diff --check -- \
  vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py \
  vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py \
  vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4_mm.py \
  tests/v1/attention/test_mm_prefix_range_id.py
# passed
```

## Duplicate-work check

Searched for existing and open work around:

- Gemma4 FA4 `mm_prefix`
- `mm_prefix` range lookup
- `range_constexpr(max_ranges)`
- `compute_mm_prefix_range_id_tensor`
- FA4 Gemma4 video performance

Related existing work covers FA4 enablement, Gemma4 bidirectional vision
attention, correctness fixes for FA4 `mm_prefix`, FA4 FP8 KV cache work, and
text-only backend selection. The duplicate-work check did not find an existing
PR or issue that removes the FA4 `max_ranges` specialization or replaces the
in-kernel range scan with a per-token range-id lookup.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used to analyze the current implementation and prepare this
issue draft.

title: [DSv4 Perf] Remove redundant full kernel for dsv4, 1.88x kernel performance improvement
author: yewentao256
body:
## Purpose

Part of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45861

Passing an out tensor to avoid additional `torch.full` kernel call

## Test

Covered in unit tests

Perf can be seen in this AI generated script

```py
import gc
import statistics
import time
from collections.abc import Callable

import torch

from vllm.models.deepseek_v4.common.ops.cache_utils import (
    combine_topk_swa_indices,
)

# Fixed production-like C128A prefill configuration.
NUM_TOKENS = 8192
MAX_MODEL_LEN = 1_048_576
COMPRESS_RATIO = 128
WINDOW_SIZE = 128
TOPK_WIDTH = MAX_MODEL_LEN // COMPRESS_RATIO
COMBINED_TOPK = (
    (TOPK_WIDTH + WINDOW_SIZE + 127) // 128 * 128
)

# Timing configuration.  The first calls compile/warm the Triton kernel and are
# deliberately excluded.  Rounds alternate provider order to reduce bias.
WARMUP_ITERS = 5
ITERS_PER_ROUND = 20
NUM_ROUNDS = 5

Provider = Callable[[], tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]]


def make_inputs() -> tuple[
    torch.Tensor,
    torch.Tensor,
    torch.Tensor,
    torch.Tensor,
]:
    """Create the metadata seen by one fresh 8192-token C128A prefill."""
    device = torch.device("cuda")

    # C128A reserves MAX_MODEL_LEN / COMPRESS_RATIO columns.  For an 8192-token
    # prompt only the first 64 can be valid, so leave the unused tail untouched.
    topk_indices = torch.empty(
        (NUM_TOKENS, TOPK_WIDTH), dtype=torch.int32, device=device
    )
    valid_topk = NUM_TOKENS // COMPRESS_RATIO
    topk_indices[:, :valid_topk] = torch.arange(
        valid_topk, dtype=torch.int32, device=device
    )

    query_start_loc = torch.tensor(
        [0, NUM_TOKENS], dtype=torch.int32, device=device
    )
    seq_lens = torch.tensor([NUM_TOKENS], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    gather_lens = torch.tensor(
        [min(NUM_TOKENS, WINDOW_SIZE)], dtype=torch.int32, device=device
    )
    return topk_indices, query_start_loc, seq_lens, gather_lens


def measure_batch(provider: Provider) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Return average (GPU event ms, synchronized wall-clock ms) per call."""
    start_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    end_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)

    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    wall_start = time.perf_counter()
    start_event.record()
    for _ in range(ITERS_PER_ROUND):
        result = provider()
        # Drop the old-path output immediately, matching its temporary lifetime
        # in _forward_prefill and allowing normal CUDA allocator reuse.
        del result
    end_event.record()
    end_event.synchronize()
    wall_end = time.perf_counter()

    return (
        start_event.elapsed_time(end_event) / ITERS_PER_ROUND,
        (wall_end - wall_start) * 1000 / ITERS_PER_ROUND,
    )


def report(
    before_gpu: list[float],
    after_gpu: list[float],
    before_wall: list[float],
    after_wall: list[float],
) -> None:
    before_gpu_ms = statistics.median(before_gpu)
    after_gpu_ms = statistics.median(after_gpu)
    before_wall_ms = statistics.median(before_wall)
    after_wall_ms = statistics.median(after_wall)

    gpu_speedup = before_gpu_ms / after_gpu_ms
    wall_speedup = before_wall_ms / after_wall_ms
    gpu_reduction = (1.0 - after_gpu_ms / before_gpu_ms) * 100
    wall_reduction = (1.0 - after_wall_ms / before_wall_ms) * 100

    print("\nResults (median of per-round averages)")
    print("-" * 72)
    print(f"{'Provider':<12} {'GPU latency':>16} {'Wall latency':>16}")
    print(f"{'before':<12} {before_gpu_ms:>13.3f} ms {before_wall_ms:>13.3f} ms")
    print(f"{'after':<12} {after_gpu_ms:>13.3f} ms {after_wall_ms:>13.3f} ms")
    print("-" * 72)
    print(f"GPU:  {gpu_speedup:.2f}x speedup, {gpu_reduction:.1f}% lower latency")
    print(f"Wall: {wall_speedup:.2f}x speedup, {wall_reduction:.1f}% lower latency")
    print(
        "\nThis is the combine-index micro-operation speedup, not full-model "
        "prefill speedup."
    )


@torch.inference_mode()
def main() -> None:
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        raise RuntimeError("This benchmark requires a CUDA GPU")

    torch.cuda.set_device(0)
    topk_indices, query_start_loc, seq_lens, gather_lens = make_inputs()

    compressed_len = NUM_TOKENS // COMPRESS_RATIO
    n = compressed_len
    m = n + WINDOW_SIZE

    workspace_indices = torch.empty(
        (NUM_TOKENS, COMBINED_TOPK), dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda"
    )
    workspace_lens = torch.empty(NUM_TOKENS, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")

    def before() -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        return combine_topk_swa_indices(
            topk_indices,
            query_start_loc,
            seq_lens,
            gather_lens,
            WINDOW_SIZE,
            COMPRESS_RATIO,
            TOPK_WIDTH,
            m,
            n,
        )

    def after() -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        return combine_topk_swa_indices(
            topk_indices,
            query_start_loc,
            seq_lens,
            gather_lens,
            WINDOW_SIZE,
            COMPRESS_RATIO,
            TOPK_WIDTH,
            m,
            n,
            out=(workspace_indices, workspace_lens),
        )

    print("DSv4 C128A prefill combine-index microbenchmark")
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"GPU:                 {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
    print(f"Prompt tokens:       {NUM_TOKENS}")
    print(f"Maximum model len:   {MAX_MODEL_LEN}")
    print(f"C128A index width:   {TOPK_WIDTH}")
    print(f"Combined width:      {COMBINED_TOPK}")
    print(
        "Output buffer:       "
        f"{NUM_TOKENS * COMBINED_TOPK * torch.int32.itemsize / 2**20:.1f} MiB"
    )
    print(
        f"Timing:              {NUM_ROUNDS} rounds x {ITERS_PER_ROUND} calls"
    )

    # Compile both paths and stabilize allocator/workspace state.
    for provider in (before, after):
        for _ in range(WARMUP_ITERS):
            result = provider()
            del result
        torch.cuda.synchronize()

    # The new path intentionally leaves padding uninitialized.  Compare only
    # lengths and valid entries, which are the values consumed by FlashMLA.
    reference_indices, reference_lens = before()
    actual_indices, actual_lens = after()
    torch.testing.assert_close(reference_lens, actual_lens, rtol=0, atol=0)
    sample_rows = (127, NUM_TOKENS // 2, NUM_TOKENS - 1)
    sample_lens = actual_lens[list(sample_rows)].cpu().tolist()
    for row, length in zip(sample_rows, sample_lens):
        torch.testing.assert_close(
            reference_indices[row, :length],
            actual_indices[row, :length],
            rtol=0,
            atol=0,
        )
    del reference_indices, reference_lens, actual_indices, actual_lens
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("Correctness check:   passed (lengths and sampled valid entries)")

    samples: dict[str, list[tuple[float, float]]] = {
        "before": [],
        "after": [],
    }
    for round_idx in range(NUM_ROUNDS):
        order = (("before", before), ("after", after))
        if round_idx % 2:
            order = tuple(reversed(order))
        for name, provider in order:
            samples[name].append(measure_batch(provider))

    report(
        [sample[0] for sample in samples["before"]],
        [sample[0] for sample in samples["after"]],
        [sample[1] for sample in samples["before"]],
        [sample[1] for sample in samples["after"]],
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

And we get

```bash
DSv4 C128A prefill combine-index microbenchmark
========================================================================
GPU:                 NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC
Prompt tokens:       8192
Maximum model len:   1048576
C128A index width:   8192
Combined width:      8320
Output buffer:       260.0 MiB
Timing:              5 rounds x 20 calls
Correctness check:   passed (lengths and sampled valid entries)

Results (median of per-round averages)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Provider          GPU latency     Wall latency
before               0.093 ms         0.094 ms
after                0.049 ms         0.050 ms
------------------------------------------------------------------------
GPU:  1.88x speedup, 46.8% lower latency
Wall: 1.86x speedup, 46.3% lower latency
```

title: [CPU] Bump up CPU kernels to latest version
author: bigPYJ1151
body:
## Purpose

Sync `csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels/` from sglang (`sgl-kernel/csrc/cpu`) to latest upstream `main`, reconciling vLLM-specific patches layered on since the last bump (#41924): MXFP4 W4A16 MoE, AMX GDN dispatch, ISA-portability BLAS fallback, RISC-V scalar/RVV support, chunked-prefill `has_initial_state` fix, DFlash speculative decoding, and batched spec-decode conv-state updates. Also rejects one upstream regression found during merge (a broken `TORCH_CHECK` for MXFP4 scale validation that would have silently weakened a size check).

Adopts SGLang's new pooled-state-indexing `chunk_gated_delta_rule_cpu` signature for GDN prefill: the CPU GDN path now reads/writes the pooled `ssm_state` buffer directly via `initial_state_indices` instead of gathering a local copy first, avoiding an extra copy per prefill call. Made the kernel read `initial_state`'s actual `stride(0)` at runtime (mirroring `conv.cpp`'s `conv_state_slot_stride`) instead of assuming a fully packed layout, since pool buffers can be padded per slot (e.g. Qwen3.5's Mamba cache-align mode).

Not a duplicate of any open PR — searched `gh pr list` for sgl-kernel/CPU-kernel-bump related terms, no matches.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to fetch/diff upstream sglang, reconcile merge conflicts against vLLM-specific patches, and run the validation below. All changes were reviewed and tested by the submitting human.

## Test Plan

- Build: `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu python3 setup.py develop` (`_C`, `_C_AVX512`, `_C_AVX2` targets)
- Correctness: `tests/quantization/test_cpu_wna16.py` / `test_cpu_w8a8.py` model list (12 models covering AWQ/GPTQ/compressed-tensors W4A16, FP8 W8A16 dense/MoE, MXFP4, INT8 W8A8 MoE) via offline inference, before vs. after this change
- `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`: multi-sequence prefill, prefix-cache reuse (`has_initial_state=True` path)
- `vllm serve` + `vllm bench serve` before/after on 4 models (w8a8, w4a16, FP8 MoE, Qwen3.5)
- `lm_eval` GSM8K (200 questions, 5-shot, chat template, `max_model_len=16384`, `max_gen_toks=8192`) on `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`, before vs. after

## Test Result

- Build succeeds cleanly on all three CPU ISA targets.
- All 12 quantization models produce coherent output; 10/12 byte-identical to the pre-bump baseline under greedy decoding, 2 diverge after the first token (`gpt-oss-20b` MXFP4, `Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4`) consistent with quantized-kernel numerics shifting a near-tied argmax, not a functional break.
- Qwen3.5 GDN: coherent generation across fresh-state and prefix-cache-reuse prefill paths.
- Serving benchmarks: throughput/latency within noise (±3%) for the three MoE GEMM paths (w8a8, w4a16, FP8); Qwen3.5 GDN path improved 3-8% across throughput/TTFT/TPOT from the pooled-gather optimization.
- GSM8K: before `0.795/0.785` (flexible/strict exact_match), after `0.835/0.795` — within one standard error, no regression.

title: [Model] Fused mm preprocess normalisation on the Device

## Purpose

This is one of my favorite CV tricks.

1. When normalize is computed on the GPU, it can be fused into subsequent operators, or even if left unfused, it takes almost no time.
2. Currently, image data transmission from the entrypoint to the engine core and then to the GPU uses uint8, rather than the model dtype bf16, and is only converted to bf16 on the GPU before entering input normal.
