title: [Quantization] Layer re-quantization for linear layers through online quantization API (MXFP8 -> FP8 PTPC showcase)
author: fxmarty-amd
body:
Detailed RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59062

## Disclosure

AI assistance was used. The changes were reviewed and tested manually.

## Purpose

This PR allows re-quantizing linear layers to a different precision using online quantization API, as long as the `dequantize_weight` method for relevant `LinearMethodBase` subclass is implemented.

Similar features have been requested previously in specialized cases:
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48427
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51274

and this feature exists on sglang side https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28291 / https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29328.

Addresses the third item of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52167. This PR is adapted from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48427, co-authored by @tanpinsiang.

This change lets `--quantization-config.linear fp8_per_channel` convert selected serialized ModelOpt MXFP8 linears to FP8 PTPC at load time.

The original checkpoint quantization config remains responsible for unselected linears and MoE.

The composition is handled by the existing `resolve_quant_method`, so model implementations continue to receive their original checkpoint quantization config type.

Quantization methods expose an optional `dequantize_weight` method, that:

- raises `NotImplementedError` by default, or
- dequantizes the quant method weights if implemented.

This draft implements it only for `ModelOptMxFp8LinearMethod`.

Such `dequantize_weight` methods implementation can be shared across model producers (quark, modelopt, compressed-tensors, etc.) based on weight quant key, no model producer-specific code should be required.

## Test Plan

```bash
vllm serve mmangkad/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-MXFP8 --quantization-config.linear "fp8_per_channel"
```

or

```bash
vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --moe-backend aiter \
  --linear-backend auto \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --language-model-only \
  --quantization-config.linear fp8_per_channel
```

`pytest tests/quantization/test_online.py-s -vvvvv`

## Test Result

Unit test passing, end-to-end eval to be added.

title: [Quantization] Enable shared expert fusion compatibility with online `shared_expert` quantization (showcase: along Quark MXFP4 routed experts)
author: fxmarty-amd
body:
## Disclosure

AI assistance was used. The changes were reviewed and tested manually.

## Purpose

This PR enables compatibility of online `shared_expert` quantization with fused shared expert optimization. As an example, it implements it for for `QuarkOCP_MX_MoEMethod` (and `INCMxfp4MoEMethod` to showcase extensibility, possibly to be removed).

The main idea is that given https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f27ae25473af7520dde3f8b9e0705041940be0c9/vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_next.py#L168-L180 `self.shared_expert = Qwen3NextMLP` is not defined when using `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1`, we use weight loading in the `RoutedExperts` to capture the shared expert weight loading, quantize it there, and copy the quantized shared expert into the correct quantized fused expert slot.

The original `quant_method` is preserved (e.g. `QuarkOCP_MX_MoEMethod`).

This PR does NOT implement `experts` + `shared_expert` joint online quantization + fusion. `experts` is expected to be already quantized in this PR (loaded through `QuarkOCP_MX_MoEMethod`/`INCMxfp4MoEMethod`)

Main design goal is to be as much as possible quant method agnostic.

We also preserve quant config compatibility checks for fused shared expert, that could be extended to accommodate new precisions e.g. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53161

## Test Plan

Testing:

```bash
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1 \
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES="6,7" \
vllm serve \
    amd/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-MXFP4 \
    --quantization-config.targets '{"*shared_expert*": "mxfp4"}' \
    --tensor-parallel-size 2
```

`pytest tests/quantization/test_online_shared_expert_fusion.py -s -vvvvv`

## Test Result

`test_online_shared_expert_fusion.py` passing `7 passed, 14 warnings in 10.31s`

Displayed to user: `(EngineCore pid=27900) INFO 08-17 10:29:41 [base_loader.py:109] Quantized 80 layers of types: mlp.shared_expert.down_proj: 40 (from linear: QuantSpec(weight=QuantKey(dtype=torch.uint8, scale=ScaleDesc(dtype=torch.uint8, static=True, group_shape=GroupShape(row=1, col=32)), scale2=None, symmetric=True), activation=None)); mlp.shared_expert.gate_up_proj: 40 (from linear: QuantSpec(weight=QuantKey(dtype=torch.uint8, scale=ScaleDesc(dtype=torch.uint8, static=True, group_shape=GroupShape(row=1, col=32)), scale2=None, symmetric=True), activation=None))`

title: [Mamba] Unify FI ReplaySSM STP/MTP/Prefix Caching Lifecycle
author: askliar
body:
## Summary

Adds FlashInfer ReplaySSM prefix caching in `align` mode, including MTP, for Model Runners V1 and V2.
Replay rings remain inside Mamba pages.

- Preserves live state and cached prefixes across partial acceptance, preemption, and request reordering.
- Batches lifecycle work across cache groups and keeps V1 accepted-token counts on the GPU.
- Fixes Mamba page alignment and checkpoint publication before block release.

[Usage, MTP example, and supported configurations](https://github.com/askliar/vllm/blob/d9cd1fd1fcfc5a08d14ff29ba7439f76ad42d628/docs/features/automatic_prefix_caching.md#flashinfer-replayssm).

## Performance

### ReplaySSM OFF → ON

**Super 3, one GB300, TP1, V2, FP32 SSM state, CUDA graphs, no prefix caching.**
Uses the [paper workloads](https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM/tree/73a9592e9d8a2268620e8883a82f5cec7442ed36/benchmarks/replayssm) with current FlashInfer.
Standard decoding generates 1,000 tokens from a short prompt. Natural MTP3 generates 256 tokens per GSM8K question.
Results average two repetitions per mode in OFF/ON/ON/OFF order.

| Workload | Batch | OFF output TPS | ON output TPS | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Natural MTP3 | 512 | 10,950 | 24,037 | **2.20×** |
| Natural MTP3 | 256 | 9,516 | 19,217 | **2.02×** |
| Standard decoding | 256 | 11,412 | 14,631 | **1.28×** |

Output TPS includes prefill and complete generation. MTP gains include higher admission:

| Workload | Peak concurrent decoding, OFF → ON | Per-request decode TPS, OFF → ON |
|---|---:|---:|
| MTP3, batch 512 | **219 → 512** | 61.99 → 59.93 |
| MTP3, batch 256 | **221 → 256** | 60.81 → 97.98 |
| Standard, batch 256 | 256 → 256 | 45.01 → 57.89 |

Concurrent decoding is measured from overlapping request timestamps. Per-request decode TPS is the reciprocal mean time per output token.
All 16 Super runs completed with zero preemptions.

### ReplaySSM OFF → ON with prefix caching

**Same TP1 paper workloads, with prefix caching enabled in both modes.**
Uses Super 3 on one GB300, V2, FP32 SSM state, stock FlashInfer, and normal CUDA graphs.
Each run seeds the exact prompt batch before timing. Results average two runs per mode in OFF/ON/ON/OFF order.

| Workload | Per-request decode TPS, OFF → ON | Decode change | Total output TPS, OFF → ON | Requests with prefix hits, OFF → ON |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MTP3, batch 256 | 60.21 → **91.12** | **+51.3%** | 8,747 → **18,043** | 0 → **256** |
| Standard, batch 256 | 43.88 → **54.56** | **+24.3%** | 11,047 → **13,670** | 256 → 256 |
| MTP3, batch 512 | 60.83 → 57.15 | −6.1% | 10,266 → **20,384** | 0 → 0 |

- **Standard, batch 256:** both modes reuse 13 prompt tokens per request, with zero preemptions.
- **MTP3, batch 256:** ON reuses 19,683 prompt tokens per run with zero preemptions. OFF has no hits and 2–4 preemptions.
- **MTP3, batch 512:** neither mode records prefix hits. ON improves total throughput while decoding more requests together, but per-request decode slows.

Per-request decode TPS is the reciprocal mean time per output token. Total output TPS includes prefill and complete generation.
All 16 prefix-enabled runs completed. These results demonstrate prefix reuse at batch 256.
Gains include differences in cache retention and preemption.

### Prefix caching OFF → ON

**Super 3, four GB300 GPUs, TP4, V2, FP16 SSM state, concurrency one, CUDA graphs.**
ReplaySSM is enabled in both modes.
Workload: 51,200 shared tokens, then 20 turns with 2,048 new input tokens and 1,024 output tokens.
MTP uses three drafts and synthetic acceptance length 3.1151. Values average two repetitions per mode.

| Metric | Prefix OFF | Prefix ON | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| E2E output TPS | 304.76 | 518.88 | **+70.26%** |
| Decode TPS | 589.38 | 611.60 | **+3.77%** |
| Time to first token, mean repeat median | 1,658.9 ms | 249.8 ms | **−84.94%** |

Each ON run records **1,513,680 prefix-hit tokens**. Measurements include first-use checkpoint-store compilation.

### Comparison with main

Same TP4 workload, ReplaySSM enabled, prefix caching disabled.

| Comparison | Main | PR | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| STP decode TPS, identical saved tuning | 239.77 | 239.65 | −0.05% |
| MTP decode TPS | 577.02 | 587.76 | +1.86% |
| MTP E2E output TPS | 303.20 | 301.58 | −0.54% |

## Validation

Manual GB300 validation:

- **71 component tests passed**, with one expected missing-provider skip.
- **17 E2E test identities passed** across tested revisions, covering FP16 TP2 MTP, prefix reuse, preemption, and partial acceptance.
- **Hooks and DCO passed** on `d9cd1fd1fc`; [hosted pre-commit](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/actions/runs/40393393118).
- GPU tests are selected in dedicated CI jobs. Hosted GPU execution remains deferred.

**GSM8K:** Super 3, 1,319 questions, five shots, V2, TP2, FP16 SSM state, stochastic rounding, natural MTP5, and eager execution.
Both modes enable ReplaySSM. Each has zero invalid answers.

| Cache mode | Accuracy | Mean acceptance length | Prefix-hit tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `none` | 93.33% | 4.254 | 0 |
| `align` | 92.80% | 4.266 | 861,972 |

<details>
<summary>Benchmark setup</summary>

Runtime source: `00cf5cb2ab`, based on main `74340c7300`. Head `d9cd1fd1fc` adds documentation only.
Stock FlashInfer: Python `0.7.2.post1`, cubin/JIT cache `0.7.2`, with version checking disabled and no provider patches.
The TP1 runs use BF16 inputs, FP8 E4M3 KV cache, replay window 16, and FlashInfer autotuning.
The TP1 cache modes are `none` without prefix caching and `align` with prefix caching.
The prefix-enabled runs use `prefix_match_unit=1` and chunked prefill to reuse the original short prompts.
GB300 power limit is 1400 W. The paper uses Triton on B300 at 1100 W.

</details>

title: [Feat][Frontend] Add Watchdog for Engine and Worker Monitoring
author: wenjinhust
body:
## Purpose

 Fixes RFC [#56816 ](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56816)

  Add a watchdog mechanism to vLLM V1 to automatically capture all-thread stack
  traces when the engine or worker process stops making progress, making it easier
  to diagnose hangs and deadlocks.

  - **New `vllm/utils/watch_dog.py`**: introduces the `WatchDog` class. A background
    daemon thread monitors a heartbeat (`feed()`); if the heartbeat is not refreshed
    within a timeout (default 300s, checked every 10s), it dumps the stack traces of
    all threads via `faulthandler` into a per-process log file
    (`VLLM_STACK_DUMP_for_<name>_<pid>.log`). Repeated timeouts without an intervening
    feed are logged only once. Provides `feed()` / `dump_stack()` / `start()` /
    `stop()` and a process-wide singleton `get_watch_dog()`.
  - **EngineCoreProc**: creates and starts a watchdog named `engine` after startup and
    feeds it while processing the input queue and before each engine step. The input
    queue `get()` now uses `timeout=5` so the loop stays responsive while preserving
    the original blocking semantics. The shutdown signal handler dumps all thread
    stacks for diagnosis.
  - **WorkerProc** (multiproc executor): likewise creates and starts a watchdog named
    `worker` and feeds it before executing every worker method; its signal handler
    dumps all thread stacks.


  ## Test Plan & Result

### Test Qwen3-8B by TP 1:

- Launch vllm:

```
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
```

title: [Frontend][RL] Track HTTP weight operation outcomes and concurrency
author: Ronald1995
body:
## Purpose

Weight sync is on the critical path of every RL step, but the frontend exposes no signal for how long each weight-transfer operation takes or whether one is stuck. The generic HTTP metrics already count every weight route by status (`http_requests_total{handler,status}`), but their per-handler histogram tops out at 1 s, and nothing is recorded until a request completes, so a hung NCCL transfer is invisible.

This PR adds two metrics, with the same names, labels and buckets in the Python and Rust frontends:

| Metric | Type | Labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vllm:rl_weight_update_operation_duration_seconds` | Histogram, buckets 0.01–600 s | `operation` |
| `vllm:rl_weight_update_operations_in_flight` | Gauge (`livesum` in multiprocess mode) | `operation` |

| Endpoint | `operation` |
| --- | --- |
| `/init_weight_transfer_engine` | `init` |
| `/start_weight_update` | `start` |
| `/start_draft_weight_update` | `start_draft` |
| `/update_weights` | `update` (one per chunk when packed) |
| `/finish_weight_update` | `finish` (includes the optional version update) |

- Each route wraps only its engine call, so requests rejected by validation are not recorded.
- The in-flight gauge is released and the duration observed on success, error and cancellation. Python uses a context manager; Rust uses a guard dropped at the end of the handler.
- Python collectors are created lazily on the default registry, after multiprocess Prometheus setup.
- No request counter is added: `http_requests_total` already covers counts and status. This matches the sleep-mode metrics in #52864.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/entrypoints/unit_tests/test_rl_weight_operation_metrics.py
pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/test_weight_operation_metrics.py  # 1 GPU
cd rust && cargo test -p vllm-metrics weight_operation
cd rust && cargo test -p vllm-server --lib weight_transfer
```

- E2E (1 GPU): a real `vllm serve --api-server-count 2` with the IPC weight-transfer backend. An HF trainer runs eight full syncs over HTTP. `/metrics` must report the exact summed duration counts per operation and zero in-flight, and the multiprocess files must show both API servers recorded, so the counts are cross-process sums.
- Multiprocess (CPU): two real processes each hold an operation open; the registry that `/metrics` serves (`get_prometheus_registry()`) reports in-flight 2, then 0 and two duration samples after both finish. Fails if `livesum` is dropped.
- Cancellation (CPU): cancelling a route task while the engine call is pending releases in-flight and still observes the duration. Fails if the recorder only handles `Exception`.
- Also (CPU): recorder success/exception paths, each of the five routes, rejected input records nothing, lazy registration on the default registry.
- Rust: the recorder guard tracks in-flight and duration; the HTTP lifecycle test checks `update`/`finish` duration counts and in-flight; invalid payloads record no duration.

## Test Result

- Python unit: 11 passed. E2E: 1 passed on GB200.
- Rust: `vllm-metrics` 1 passed, `vllm-server` weight_transfer routes 3 passed.
- pre-commit (ruff, mypy, rustfmt, typos, test tethering) clean.
- No model output path changes, so no accuracy eval.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for this change; the submitter reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

title: [Perf][Attention][MiniMax-M3] Select CUTLASS MSA by EAGLE3 decode shape
author: anish-shanbhag
body:
## Overview

Select the MiniMax-M3 CUTLASS MSA decode path using measured SM103 EAGLE3
crossover points instead of a fixed batch-16 gate. The current patch is
model-local and keeps the original floor for unmeasured shapes and
architectures.

No other open PR changes this decode dispatch gate; #60684 changes prefill
query quantization and does not overlap this work.

## Claims in the current patch

- On SM103 with decode query lengths 1–8 and measured rank-local 64/4, 32/2,
  or 16/1 query/KV heads, use CUTLASS once
  `batch_size * decode_query_len * num_q_heads >= 1024`.
- Keep the existing batch-16 floor for query lengths 9–32, SM100, and unknown
  head geometries.
- Preserve all existing kernel constraints: explicit CUTLASS selection, FP8
  E4M3 KV cache, supported head geometry, page size 128, top-k 16, supported
  query length, and the planner row bound.
- Allow deployments to override the automatic crossover with the model-local
  `VLLM_MINIMAX_M3_MSA_CUTLASS_MIN_BATCH`; unset uses the automatic policy,
  and setting the integer to 16 restores the original floor.

## Validation

Full `pr-checklist` audit: [read the condensed report](https://gist.github.com/anish-shanbhag/e87258c8b3d501ac34195d91335ff1cb).

### Current PR refresh (2026-10-08)

- Added the review update as a fast-forward commit; no existing commits were
  rewritten.
- Removed the global `envs.py` registration and `tests/test_envs.py` changes.
  The final PR changes only the MiniMax MSA implementation and its existing
  kernel test.
- `pre-commit run --files tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3_msa_cutlass_sparse_decode.py vllm/models/minimax_m3/nvidia/msa_cutlass_sparse_decode.py vllm/models/minimax_m3/nvidia/sparse_attention_msa.py`:
  passed, including Ruff, formatting, mypy, test tethering, SPDX, and
  forbidden-import checks.
- CPU-safe direct checks: seven dispatch cases and two model-local override
  cases passed. `git diff --check` also passed.
- The local host does not have the PyTorch/CUDA test runtime, so the existing
  GB300 correctness and benchmark results below remain the GPU validation.

### Original query-length-4 GB300 evidence

The isolated benchmark used one NVIDIA GB300, EAGLE3 query length 4, FP8 E4M3
KV cache, 16 selected pages per token/KV head, CUDA graph replay, 30 warmups,
300 iterations, and five trials. It covered request batches 1/2/4/8/16, 8K
and 200K cached contexts, TP1/TP2/TP4, and concurrent DEP2/DEP4 ranks.

| Local heads | Batch 4 | Batch 8 | Batch 16 | First measured win | Query-head rows at win |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64/4 | 1.069x | 1.545x | 1.875x | 4 | 1,024 |
| 32/2 | 0.800x | 1.100x | 1.642x | 8 | 1,024 |
| 16/1 | 0.600x | 0.800x | 1.099x | 16 | 1,024 |

These conservative ratios charge CUTLASS for standalone BF16-to-FP8 query
quantization. All 130 rank-level CUTLASS-versus-Triton comparisons passed at
`atol=0.02`, `rtol=0.02`; maximum absolute error was `0.00006104`. The
focused GB300 kernel suite reported `41 passed` in 237.40 seconds, and the
focused environment suite reported `9 passed`.

### Query-length 1–8 follow-up (2026-10-08)

A second GB300 microbenchmark swept decode query lengths 1–8, TP1/TP2/TP4,
request batches 1/2/3/4/6/8/12/16/24/32/48/64, and cached contexts 8,192 and
200,064. It used interleaved CUDA-graph replay with the same 30 warmups, 300
iterations, and five trials. Query lengths 1/2/4/8 fit the rule; 3/5/6/7 were
held out. All 1,344 rank-level comparisons passed correctness at
`atol=rtol=0.02`; maximum absolute error was `0.00430298`.

The safe direct-kernel crossover is the first measured batch for which every
larger measured batch wins at both context lengths:

| Decode query length | TP1 / 64 Q heads | TP2 / 32 Q heads | TP4 / 16 Q heads |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 12 | 24 | 48 |
| 2 | 6 | 12 | 24 |
| 3 | 4 | 8 | 16 |
| 4 | 3 | 6 | 12 |
| 5 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
| 6 | 2 | 4 | 6 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| 8 | 2 | 3 | 6 |

The follow-up image (vLLM 0.25.0) first won at 768 query-head rows for query
length 4. The newer vLLM 0.28.1rc1 benchmark used only power-of-two batches,
so its first measured win at 1,024 rows did not test 768. At the shared 512-
and 1,024-row points, the two datasets agree to rounding (approximately
0.889x/0.800x and 1.222x/1.099x for direct/conservative speedup). This is not
evidence of a version shift, but the matching-version evidence does not resolve
the intermediate boundary. The merge-safe rule is therefore the conservative,
directly measured newer-image boundary:

```python
query_head_rows = batch_size * decode_query_len * num_q_heads
if 1 <= decode_query_len <= 8 and measured_head_geometry:
    automatic_min_batch = ceil_div(1024, decode_query_len * num_q_heads)
else:
    automatic_min_batch = 16
use_cutlass = batch_size >= automatic_min_batch
```

The 1,024-row rule produced zero false-positive CUTLASS regressions across all
576 new aggregated cases. It left 61 direct-kernel wins unselected on the
older image, an intentional conservative trade-off. This supports replacing
the `decode_query_len == 4` special case and three head-geometry entries with a
single query-head-row threshold, while retaining every existing capability,
dtype, head, page-size, top-k, maximum-query-length, and maximum-row guard.
Query lengths 9–32 retain the existing batch-16 floor rather than extrapolating
beyond the measured sweep. Unknown head geometries also retain 16.

The selected region has clear margin: among all 318 selected cases, the minimum
direct-kernel speedup was 1.221x and the minimum quantization-inclusive speedup
was 1.098x. The 24 cases at exactly 1,024 rows measured 1.221–1.223x direct and
1.098–1.101x with standalone quantization. Median per-case trial CV at the
boundary was 0.020% for Triton and 0.019% for the conservative CUTLASS path;
the maximum CVs were 0.199% and 0.063%, respectively.

The current commit implements the conservative 1,024 query-head-row rule for
query lengths 1–8. The 768-row rule remains a later candidate, but it should be
adopted only after measuring that intermediate point on the same vLLM build
used by the PR.

Complete tables, all trial JSON/CSV artifacts, methodology, and runnable
benchmark/analysis scripts are in the [benchmark Gist](https://gist.github.com/anish-shanbhag/3ce54e7314995b38b22612ab0100b260).

Matched MiniMax-M3-NVFP4 disaggregated EAGLE3 runs of the original fixed-16
policy versus an earlier blanket batch-4 experiment showed approximately
+3–5% p90 per-user output-token rate and +1–2.5% total TPS/GPU. That experiment
supports the opportunity but does not isolate the final dispatch policy; the
microbenchmarks above provide the shape-specific evidence.

## Details

### Root cause and implementation

The existing metadata builder used a fixed `batch_size >= 16` dispatch gate,
so common EAGLE3 verification steps fell back to Triton even when CUTLASS was
faster. A blanket lower floor is unsafe because tensor parallelism changes
rank-local query/KV head geometry and therefore the crossover. The current
model-local helper selects a conservative floor from query length, device
capability, and head geometry. The metadata builder resolves the optional
environment override once at initialization and passes it to the existing
dispatch predicate.

### Design fit and trade-offs

The implementation stays within MiniMax-M3's NVIDIA sparse-attention path and
does not change shared scheduler, model-runner, or KV-cache interfaces. The
automatic speedup is deliberately limited to the measured SM103 EAGLE3
query-length and head-geometry region; all other shapes keep the prior
batch-16 behavior.

## Checklist

- [x] Change is model-local and does not add complexity to shared core components.
- [x] Dispatch boundaries have targeted regression coverage; the integer
  override remains a model-local rollback.
- [x] Existing CUDA correctness and benchmark evidence exercises the changed path.
- [x] Query lengths 1–8 now have a genuine CUTLASS-versus-Triton microbenchmark.
- [x] Current lint, typing, test-tethering, and CPU-safe checks pass after rebasing.
- [x] Performance scope, fallback behavior, version calibration, and end-to-end limitations are explicit.
- [x] Commits are signed off and include AI-assistance attribution.

## AI assistance disclosure

This change, benchmark support, rebase, and PR refresh used OpenAI Codex. The
human submitter remains responsible for reviewing every changed line,
reproducing GPU validation as needed, and defending the implementation and
evidence end to end.

title: [Perf] Add fused DFlash2 grouped convolution
author: mgoin
body:
## Summary

- Fuse DFlash2's grouped dynamic convolution in one Triton custom op, keeping the existing Torch CPU fallback. The kernel stays in `qwen3_dflash2.py`.
- Use row-aligned tiles: 1024 elements for at least 128 rows with hidden width divisible by 1024, otherwise 512. Four warps; no autotuner.
- Cover non-power-of-two dimensions, strided coefficient views, multiple tap counts, and both tile paths in FP32/BF16.
- Add real-checkpoint GSM8K accuracy and acceptance-length coverage to the existing H200 35 GB DFlash nightly job. Keep this case excluded from its AMD mirror; the Speculators/MTP job is unchanged.

The implementation docstring credits LightSeek TokenSpeed PR https://github.com/lightseekorg/tokenspeed/pull/1399.

## End-to-end validation

One NVIDIA B300, TP=1, V2 model runner, compilation and CUDA graphs enabled. Target: `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`; unchanged BF16 draft: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`. Full GSM8K: 1,319 questions, 5-shot chat, thinking disabled, temperature 0, max output 256 tokens, max model length 4,096, max batch 32, seven speculative tokens.

| Implementation | GSM8K accuracy | Mean acceptance length |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original Torch convolution, NVFP4 target, run 1 | 92.0% | 6.14 |
| Original Torch convolution, NVFP4 target, repeat | 91.2% | 6.13 |
| Fused kernel before final tuning, NVFP4 target, run 1 | 91.1% | 6.13 |
| Fused kernel before final tuning, NVFP4 target, repeat | 92.2% | 6.14 |
| Final row-aligned kernel, NVFP4 target | **92.2%** | **6.14** |

All passed. Acceptance length is `1 + accepted_tokens / draft_steps`. Accuracy varies across runs; this is not an exact-output-equivalence claim. The compiled draft graph was inspected to confirm it invokes the convolution custom op. CI checks accuracy >= 90% and AL >= `6.14 * 0.95` (5.833).

The NVFP4 target reduces reported target-plus-draft model-load memory from 54.0 GiB to 22.85 GiB; this is not total serving/KV-cache memory. The case runs in the existing H200 35 GB DFlash nightly job, with its 90-minute timeout unchanged, and remains excluded from the AMD mirror. H200 has a Marlin weight-only fallback for the NVFP4 target. Local validation was on B300; H200 execution and memory fit remain unverified.

Earlier BF16-target validation also passed: original Torch convolution 92.2% / AL 6.19; initial fused kernel 92.0% / AL 6.19 in two runs. CI now uses the smaller NVFP4 checkpoint instead.

## Kernel performance

### Initial fusion versus Torch (before the final row-aligned tuning)

Actual checkpoint shape: hidden size 5,120, BF16, block size 8, group size 16, two taps, strided coefficients. B300, FlashInfer CUPTI timing, CUDA graphs, cold L2, four alternating-order trials; median latency. Baseline is the existing expression under `torch.compile`. Correctness checked before timing.

| Batch | Torch / Triton latency (us) | Torch / Triton effective GB/s | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.889 / 1.920 | 103 / 101 | 0.98x |
| 2 | 2.064 / 2.016 | 179 / 183 | 1.02x |
| 4 | 2.176 / 2.112 | 329 / 339 | 1.03x |
| 8 | 2.496 / 2.320 | 566 / 609 | 1.08x |
| 16 | 3.296 / 2.720 | 851 / 1,032 | 1.21x |
| 32 | 4.576 / 3.599 | 1,222 / 1,554 | 1.27x |

Effective bandwidth counts each input once and the output once: `2 * (2*rows*5120 + rows*2*320 + 2*5120)` bytes, `rows = batch*8`. These are kernel-only gains, not end-to-end speedups; batch 1 is approximately neutral.

### Final row-aligned tuning versus the posted fused kernel

Integrated confirmation on all 11 surveyed hidden-width/block-size pairs, at batches 1/32/256, BF16, group 16, two taps, strided coefficients. B300, CUPTI, CUDA graphs, cold L2, four alternating-order trials of 100 ms. Compared with posted commit `fd19503785`: batch 1 is effectively unchanged; batch 32 is 1.006–1.172x faster; batch 256 is 1.078–1.328x faster.

Representative batch-256 results (posted fused kernel → final tuned kernel):

| Hidden / block | Tile | Useful GB/s | Latency (us) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2560 / 8 | 512 | 2649 → 2856 | 8.384 → 7.776 | 1.078x |
| 5120 / 8 | 1024 | 3038 → 3921 | 14.624 → 11.328 | 1.291x |
| 6656 / 16 | 512 | 3300 → 3610 | 35.057 → 32.049 | 1.094x |

Useful bytes = `2 * (2*rows*hidden + (2*rows-batch)*(hidden/16) + 2*hidden)`, excluding unused second-tap coefficients at block starts. This is an ideal useful-bandwidth estimate, not measured HBM traffic. These remain kernel-only speedups. Block-7/anchor/MoE entries in the shape sweep are kernel coverage, not full-model compatibility claims.

## Tests

All GPU workloads used `chg run -g=1 --`; no `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` overrides. Commands below assume the checkout's Python environment is activated (including its `bin` directory on PATH):

```bash
chg run -g=1 -- .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash2.py -q
chg run -g=1 -- env VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn .venv/bin/python -m pytest -v -s tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dflash/test_dflash.py -k dflash2
pre-commit run --files .buildkite/test_areas/spec_decode.yaml tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dflash/test_dflash.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash2.py vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py
```

- Focused suite: **16 passed**, including the aligned 1024-tile path and non-aligned 512-tile fallback.
- Integrated scratch boundary sweep: **570/570 bitwise comparisons passed** against the posted kernel. Covers all 11 model shape pairs, FP32/FP16/BF16, empty/one-row inputs, strided inputs/coefficients, ragged rows/widths, 1/2/3 taps, log-scaled values, and 127/128/129-row boundaries.
- Full NVFP4 model test: **1 passed** for each of the five runs above, including the final tuned implementation (**226.52 s**, including startup). First NVFP4 runs took about 5.5 minutes due to compilation/autotuning; warm-cache runs took 3.5–3.7 minutes. The smaller checkpoint is not a claim of faster CI.
- Changed-file pre-commit: **passed**, including mypy, SPDX, forbidden-import and CUDA API checks. CI YAML parsing/selection checks passed.
- Local environment: PyTorch 2.13.0, Triton 3.7.1, Transformers 5.15.0, FlashInfer 0.6.17. Initial startup failed on both branches due to a missing generated FlashMLA Python module in the worktrees; linking the existing installed artifact fixed the environment without code changes. The first NVFP4 attempt on both branches also stopped before evaluation because `ninja` was missing from PATH; using the already-installed venv `bin` directory resolved it without dependency/code changes.

## Duplicate work

Rechecked open vLLM PRs for `dflash2 conv`, `fused grouped conv`, and DFlash2 GSM8K/acceptance coverage. No other open PR implements this kernel/dispatch or this CI case. The companion TP-reduction and packed-top-k PRs remain separate.

AI assistance was used to analyze the upstream implementation, implement the change, and write/run the tests and benchmarks. Human submitter review is required before merge.

title: [XPU][Kernel] Tune Triton W8A8 block-FP8 GEMM for Intel B70
author: pmanczak
body:
## Purpose

Follows the pattern established in #53065 (XPU Triton fused MoE tuning): port
`benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_w8a8_block_fp8.py` to Intel XPU and ship tuned
Triton kernel configs for the W8A8 blockwise FP8 GEMM (`block_shape=[128,128]`)
on **Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B70 Graphics**.


## Changes

- `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_w8a8_block_fp8.py`: XPU support (platform
  assert, `device_type`, guard `torch.cuda.init()`, and a curated
  `get_xpu_tuning_space()` — 96 configs vs. 1280, since per-config Triton
  JIT compile time on B70 is ~1-8s vs. sub-100ms on CUDA; only used when
  `current_platform.is_xpu()`)
- 26 new tuned config JSONs under
  `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/configs/` for
  `device_name=Intel(R)_Arc(TM)_Pro_B70_Graphics,dtype=fp8_w8a8,block_shape=[128,128]`
  (comparable to MI300X's 28 and H20/H100/H200's 23-26 for this kernel),
  covering dense-linear shapes from DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V2-Lite
  (TP=1), Llama-3.1-8B (TP=1, packed QKV/gate-up), and Qwen3-8B's two
  shapes not already covered by Llama's

## Results

Intel Arc Pro B70, fp8. Baseline is the kernel's built-in default config
(`BLOCK_SIZE_M=64, GROUP_SIZE_M=32, num_warps=4, num_stages=2`, used when no
tuned JSON is found); tuned uses the generated JSON. Per-batch sweeps (10
sizes, matching the tuned grid) for two DeepSeek-V2-Lite (tp=1) shapes;
geometric-mean speedups are **2.73x** (`N=576,K=2048`, kv_a_proj_with_mqa /
kv_b_proj) and **2.00x** (`N=22016,K=2048`, gate_up_proj):

| batch | N=576,K=2048 | N=22016,K=2048 |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 5.08x | 2.67x |
| 4 | 2.62x | 1.93x |
| 16 | 5.17x | 3.28x |
| 32 | 3.21x | 2.99x |
| 64 | 3.21x | 2.22x |
| 128 | 4.18x | 1.50x |
| 512 | 2.89x | 1.69x |
| 1024 | 1.31x | 1.25x |
| 2048 | 1.02x | 1.69x |
| 4096 | 2.02x | 1.69x |

Numerical validation: every tuned config was checked against an FP32
reference GEMM using deterministic FP8 block-quantized inputs (relative L2
error < 2e-2). DeepSeek-V2-Lite passed 60/60 batch-size x shape
combinations; Llama-3.1-8B passed 60/60; Qwen3-8B's 2 newly-tuned shapes
passed 40/40 (its other 2 shapes reuse Llama-3.1-8B's already-validated
configs, see below).

### End-to-end

Served `yiliu4/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat-Block-wise-FP8-Test-Only` (block-FP8
checkpoint) on a single B70 card. Both rows use explicit
`--linear-backend triton`, comparing Triton's built-in per-shape heuristic
(baseline) with the tuned shape-specific JSONs. Workload: 512 input tokens,
128 output tokens, 32 prompts, inf request rate; 1 warm-up run discarded, 3
measured runs per arm (seeds 2-4):

| model | shape | TP | baseline | tuned | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat` (block-FP8) | all dense linears (7 shapes) | 1 | 109.63 tok/s | 140.88 tok/s | 1.285x |
| `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` (block-FP8) | all runtime linears (4 shapes) | 1 | 36.99 tok/s | 84.20 tok/s | 2.276x |
| `Hunyuan-MT-7B` (block-FP8) | all runtime linears (4 shapes) | 1 | 37.04 tok/s | 84.55 tok/s | 2.282x |
| `Qwen3-8B` (block-FP8) | all runtime linears (4 shapes, 2 newly tuned) | 1 | 36.29 tok/s | 82.89 tok/s | 2.284x |

For reference, the default (oneDNN, `auto`) path is substantially faster
than tuned Triton on all four models (roughly 2-5.7x), confirming the
"Note on scope" above: this PR's value is the tuning pipeline plus configs
for whenever Triton is the selected/needed path, not a claim that Triton
should replace oneDNN on B70.

## Test plan

- Tune on XPU with
  `benchmark_w8a8_block_fp8.py tune --tp-size <tp> --batch-size <bs>`.
- Verify every generated winner against an fp32 reference
  (relative L2 error < 2e-2).
- Confirm serving with `--linear-backend triton` loads the exact JSON
  (`fp8_utils.py` logs `Using configuration from ... for W8A8 Block FP8
  kernel.`).
- Compare the kernel's default config and tuned config with identical
  inputs at the tuned batch-size grid.
- Compare heuristic and tuned Triton E2E with identical workloads and fresh
  engines.
- Keep CUDA/ROCm behavior unchanged; XPU pruning is guarded by
  `current_platform.is_xpu()`.

title: [Frontend][EPD] Use JSON arrays for multimodal metadata
author: gty111
body:
## Summary

Send EPD placeholder metadata as numeric JSON arrays instead of torch/base64 tensors. Accept arrays only for model-declared metadata fields, preserving legacy base64 embedding inputs and the proxy's raw-media path.

Python-only prerequisite extracted from #55842, which now contains only Rust frontend changes. No scheduler, model runner, or EC transport changes. Duplicate checks found no other PR implementing this Python contract. Related to #52409.

## Motivation

- **Performance:** Avoid `torch.save` / `torch.load` and base64 encoding/decoding for small metadata arrays. The MUIRBench comparison below observed **2.59% higher throughput** with JSON, with no aggregate accuracy regression; different node pairs prevent attributing the entire gain to this change.
- **Router and Rust frontend integration:** Provide a language-neutral metadata format for future EPD support in [vllm-project/router](https://github.com/vllm-project/router) and the Rust frontend (#55842). Both can handle metadata as JSON arrays without depending on PyTorch or implementing its tensor serialization format.

## Validation

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/unit_tests/test_chat_utils.py -k 'image_embeds or json_metadata or json_arrays' -q
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/ec_connector/unit/test_epd_proxy_round_robin.py -q
```

17 + 11 tests passed; applicable pre-commit hooks passed.

MUIRBench, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B + Mooncake RDMA, 4E+4PD, V2, concurrency 96, CUDA graphs through 16384 tokens (no eager): 200 warmup questions, then five repetitions of the first 1200/2600 questions.

Base64 → JSON: accuracy **59.02% → 59.10%**, mean throughput **60.48 → 62.05 req/s**; both **0/6000 failures**. Sequential runs on different node pairs, so the throughput difference is not an isolated causal estimate.

Prepared with AI assistance (OpenAI Codex).

title: [Perf][MiniMax-M3] Triton indexer: decode grid retune + SM12.0 split-K
author: venkywonka
body:
## Overview

Two changes to the Triton MiniMax-M3 indexer (`vllm/models/minimax_m3/common/ops/index_topk.py`):

1. **Decode launch-grid retune.** `TARGET_GRID` goes from 512 to 4096 (decode index score) and `TOPK_TARGET_GRID` from 64 to 512 (decode top-k). This applies to every CUDA GPU on the Triton MiniMax-M3 indexer, not only SM120. ROCm uses its own `amd/ops/index_topk.py` and is not touched. Folded in from #49229 with its author's agreement; original commit by Zijing Liu, co-authored by Kyle Liang.
2. **SM12.0 prefill split-K.** On SM12.0 only, the prefill index score (`_index_block_score_kernel`) splits its K loop across CTAs when the launch grid is small, as it is for short chunked-prefill extends. Other GPUs keep the unsplit launch.

This PR was closed after the concurrency-12 point showed no gain, then reopened and narrowed:
- FP8 index-cache support and the operand casts are in #59081 (supersedes #47665).
- The fused decode top-k and the router change are dropped.

## Claims

Faster decode at higher batch sizes on the Triton indexer (grid retune), and faster short-extend prefill on RTX PRO 6000 (SM120, split-K).

## Validation

- **E2E:** MiniMax-M3-NVFP4 + EAGLE3 on 8x RTX PRO 6000, InferenceMAX recipe at c10 TP8.
  - Grid retune: removing it costs 4.6% throughput (tput 0.954x). Decode step p50 at 10 requests is 49.2 ms without it and 39.6 ms with it, matching the reference stack's 39.6 ms. #49229 separately reported +44% at B300 TP4 c24.
  - Split-K: short cached extends take 263 ms per iteration without it and 200 ms with it (reference stack 192 ms). This comes from a leave-one-out of the earlier fused-top-k + split-K version; split-K is the only part of that version on this path.
  - This PR as a whole: the split-K-only confirmation run already included the grid retune, so it measures exactly these contents. It reaches 0.985 tput / 1.004 interactivity vs the InferenceMAX reference stack, and per-request TPOT 0.997 [0.975, 1.008] vs the earlier fused+split-K version (n=1).
- **SM120 tests:** `pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py` gives 95 passed, 0 failed, 58 skipped. Main gives 92 / 0 / 58; the only difference is the 3 new prefill cases, and outcomes on the shared IDs are identical. `test_decode_index_topk_correctness` passes all 6 cases with the new decode grids (256 score chunks; up to 16 top-k chunks). All 4 prefill cases take `USE_SPLIT_K=True`.
- **CI:** `test_prefill_index_topk_correctness` forces the split path on any CUDA GPU (incl. an uneven split), so L4 runs it.
- **Lint:** `pre-commit`, including mypy-3.12, passed.

## Details

- Decode chunk counts stay shape-constant, so the launch is still CUDA-graph safe. At 2 or fewer decode requests the score grid is unchanged, because both values hit the 256-chunk cap.
- The split count is `split_k = min(max_block, 48 // (n_q_tiles * batch * heads))`, on SM12.0 only.
- Each CTA writes a disjoint range of per-block maxima, so no reduction is needed.
- Splits past a query tile's causal window exit early.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Route softmax MoE top-k, including fused shared-expert sigmoid, through AITER topk_gating
author: mjkvaak-amd
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

On ROCm, softmax MoE routing uses AITER's legacy `topkGatingSoftmax` launcher. This routes `FusedTopKRouter` and the fused-shared-expert router (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1`) through `aiter.ops.topk.topk_gating` instead, which keeps selected-mass renormalization in-kernel (ROCm/aiter#4460), has the E=512 `prefill_n` dispatch (ROCm/aiter#5334), and with ROCm/aiter#6306 scores the shared-expert columns with sigmoid in the same launch. `dispatch_topk_softmax_func` decides per launch between `topk_gating` and the legacy `topk_softmax`. This PR makes the selection the default on CDNA3 and CDNA4 (gfx942, gfx950); every other architecture keeps the legacy launcher. gfx950 is the main sweep; gfx942 (MI300-class) was verified more lightly (see the gfx942 section). The blast radius is implicitly limited to Qwens, because based on my search other models won't use the `topk_gating`.

Not a duplicate: searched open PRs for `topk_gating` and `aiter topk softmax`; no other PR routes softmax top-k through `topk_gating`. #57246 fixes the eager `torch.topk` fallback in `fused_topk_bias`, and #55147 fixes the width of the `topk_ids` buffer AITER's kernels write; neither changes which AITER launcher is used.

## Claims

- On the same nightly, with only this PR and ROCm/aiter#6306 added, `topk_gating` is **+0.7% to +1.5% output-throughput geomean per cell** for Flash-Next (E=512, top-10, one shared expert) at TP2 with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS` 1 and 0, at three `max-num-batched-tokens` (2048, 4096, 8192), and **+1.3% to +1.9%** for Qwen3-30B-A3B (E=128, top-8) at TP1 in two passes per cell, over the four rows that repeat. Single-stream decode (1k/1k, concurrency 1) is the largest effect: +2.0% to +4.4% in every cell.
- Kernel: for E=512 / top-10 with one shared expert, `topk_gating` is 37–47% faster than `topk_softmax(..., "sigmoid")` at T ≤ 1024 and level at T = 2048–4096 (AITER op test, table below).
- No directional accuracy change: GSM8K on all 9 cells, paired, 134 problems fixed and 126 broken in total (net +8 of 11,871), no cell below p = 0.12. The six cells of the Qwen3-30B rerun are also consistent with noise (no cell below p = 0.39).
- gfx942 (MI300-class): the kernel passes AITER's op test and the vLLM unit tests there with zero routing mismatches, is neutral to slightly positive end to end (+2.0% and +0.45% output-throughput geomean on Qwen3-30B at mbt 4096 and 2048; +1.4% to +4.7% on three Flash-Next-FP8 TP2 rows), and GSM8K is unchanged (no cell below p = 0.16). This is a lighter check than the gfx950 sweep; details below.
- Which launches change: on CDNA3 and CDNA4 (gfx942, gfx950), contiguous gating rows with T ≤ 4096 tokens, and shared experts only with sigmoid scoring and 1, 2, 4 or 8 shared experts. Everything else, and every other GPU architecture, keeps `topk_softmax`. **There is no env var to turn it on/off.**

## Validation

**Unit tests.** On one MI355X, in the candidate image (below):

```bash
pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_topk.py tests/model_executor/test_enabled_custom_ops.py -k topk
# 74 passed, 19 deselected   (at b4c61b0e0)
pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_topk.py tests/model_executor/test_enabled_custom_ops.py
# 93 passed
```

On gfx942 (MI300-class), on the nightly base with this PR's net diff and the gate change applied: 35 passed in `test_enabled_custom_ops.py -k topk` and 39 in `test_rocm_aiter_topk.py`.

`tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_topk.py` checks the shared-expert suffix against a torch reference; `test_topk_softmax_dispatch_aiter_topk_gating` pins which launcher each launch shape takes, on the enabled architectures and (monkeypatched) on another one: shared-expert sigmoid with 1/2/4/8 shared experts, an unsupported count, wrong or missing shared scoring, mismatched row strides, a narrow weights buffer, non-contiguous rows, T = 4096 versus 4097, and the kill switch (each launch shape on gfx950 and elsewhere).

**Kernel evidence.** `op_tests/test_moe_topk_gating.py` from ROCm/aiter#6306, MI355X, E=512, top-10, bf16, renorm, one shared expert. Mean kernel time per call, one run, lower is better. Every case has 0 routing mismatches against a torch reference.

| T | `topk_gating` (µs) | legacy `topk_softmax` (µs) | Δ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 5.56 | 9.76 | −43% |
| 16 | 5.87 | 10.51 | −44% |
| 64 | 5.86 | 10.86 | −46% |
| 256 | 6.05 | 11.42 | −47% |
| 1024 | 6.56 | 10.42 | −37% |
| 2048 | 10.66 | 10.60 | +0.5% |
| 4096 | 12.84 | 13.14 | −2.3% |

Above T = 1024 the kernel runs its shared-memory fallback, which is level with the legacy launcher; above T = 4096 vLLM keeps the legacy launcher (`_AITER_TOPK_GATING_MAX_TOKENS`), where an earlier measurement had `topk_gating` losing at 8K-token prefill chunks.

**End to end.** MI355X (gfx950). Both arms are the same image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-81198e97ba7eee2a22540caaa756b7fdddcb4d93`; the candidate adds only this PR's vLLM diff. Server flags in both arms: `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, `--max-num-seqs 256`, `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9`, `--trust-remote-code`, thinking off, and `--max-num-batched-tokens` as in the column. It was verified that every candidate server loaded `module_moe_topk`; no control server did. Router `T` is the decode concurrency in decode rows and `min(mbt, prompt)` per prefill chunk, so prefill chunks at mbt 8192 take the legacy launcher in both arms.

Flash-Next is `amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4` at TP2 (`--max-model-len 262144 --reasoning-parser qwen3`). Qwen3-30B-A3B is `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B` (bf16) at TP1.

**Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=1.** Output tok/s, control → candidate (Δ, higher is better).

| ISL / OSL | Conc | mbt 2048 | mbt 4096 | mbt 8192 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1k/1k | 1 | 156.3 → 161.4 (+3.2%) | 157.7 → 161.5 (+2.4%) | 157.0 → 163.3 (+4.0%) |
| 1k/1k | 32 | 2122.4 → 2147.4 (+1.2%) | 2140.1 → 2165.7 (+1.2%) | 2149.2 → 2186.5 (+1.7%) |

**Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=0.** Output tok/s, control → candidate (Δ, higher is better).

| ISL / OSL | Conc | mbt 2048 | mbt 4096 | mbt 8192 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1k/1k | 1 | 137.2 → 142.4 (+3.8%) | 138.2 → 142.3 (+3.0%) | 137.4 → 140.3 (+2.1%) |
| 1k/1k | 32 | 1841.4 → 1872.3 (+1.7%) | 1846.4 → 1870.6 (+1.3%) | 1861.5 → 1883.0 (+1.2%) |
| 1k/1k | 128 | 3588.2 → 3611.0 (+0.6%) | 3629.0 → 3653.5 (+0.7%) | 3644.9 → 3626.9 (−0.5%) |
| 8k/128 | 8 | 184.8 → 182.2 (−1.4%) | 192.3 → 193.6 (+0.7%) | 196.2 → 195.2 (−0.5%) |
| 8k/1k | 32 | 1003.1 → 1012.3 (+0.9%) | 1037.1 → 1042.1 (+0.5%) | 1046.7 → 1055.0 (+0.8%) |
| 16k/128 | 2 | 81.2 → 80.6 (−0.7%) | 85.2 → 86.0 (+0.9%) | 87.1 → 88.2 (+1.2%) |

**Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP1.** Two passes per cell, with the control and candidate cards swapped between passes. Output tok/s, candidate vs control, pass 1 / pass 2 (higher is better). 

| ISL / OSL | Conc | mbt 2048 | mbt 4096 | mbt 8192 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1k/1k | 1 | +3.5% / +3.8% | +4.4% / +4.0% | +2.0% / +3.9% |
| 1k/1k | 32 | +1.5% / +0.3% | +0.7% / +1.5% | +1.1% / +1.1% |
| 1k/1k | 128 | +0.6% / +0.8% | +0.4% / +0.8% | +1.5% / +0.9% |
| 16k/128 | 2 | +0.4% / +0.4% | +0.5% / +1.2% | +0.7% / +0.2% |

Control output tok/s at mbt 4096, pass 1: 237.6, 2782.6, 6956.8 and 115.7 for the four rows.

Geomean over these four rows, pass 1 / pass 2. Positive means the candidate is better: throughput up, mean TPOT and mean TTFT down.

| mbt | Output tok/s | Mean TPOT | Mean TTFT |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2048 | +1.5% / +1.3% | +1.5% / +1.5% | −0.4% / −0.5% |
| 4096 | +1.5% / +1.9% | +1.9% / +2.0% | −1.2% / +0.5% |

**Flash-Next geomean over the six rows per cell.** Positive means the candidate is better: throughput up, mean TPOT and mean TTFT down.

| Sweep | mbt | Output tok/s | Mean TPOT | Mean TTFT |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=1 | 2048 | +1.3% | +1.6% | −0.0% |
| Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=1 | 4096 | +1.1% | +1.4% | −1.3% |
| Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=1 | 8192 | +1.5% | +1.9% | −0.2% |
| Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=0 | 2048 | +0.8% | +1.2% | −0.3% |

| Flash-Next, TP2, FSE=0 | 8192 | +0.7% | +1.0% | −1.5% |

Reading the table:

- **Gain at small `T`, flat at large `T`.** Concurrency 1 gains +2.0% to +4.4% in every cell, while the 8k and 16k rows sit at about +0.5% to +1%: their steps are dominated by prefill chunks of 2048 tokens or more, where the kernel is level with the legacy launcher (and above 4096 the legacy launcher runs in both arms). That matches the kernel table, where the saving is about 4–5 µs per layer launch at small `T` and nothing at T ≥ 2048.
- **FSE does not change the picture.** With FSE=1 the candidate also fuses the sigmoid shared-expert scoring (the suffix from #6306); with FSE=0 `topk_gating` runs without it. The cell geomeans are +1.1% to +1.5% and +0.7% to +1.2%.
- **TTFT.** Prefill is where `topk_gating` helps least, so the TTFT geomean is flat: −1.5% to +0.0% across the six Flash-Next cells and −2.3% to +0.5% across the Qwen3-30B passes, which is the size of the run-to-run noise.

**Accuracy.** GSM8K, 5-shot, `local-chat-completions`, chat template, thinking off, `max_gen_toks 2048`, seed 4321, 1319 problems per arm, strict-match. Paired per problem with `scripts/compare_samples.py` (exact McNemar). 82–84% of Flash-Next generations and 52% of Qwen3-30B generations differ textually between arms, so the claim is "no directional change", not "identical"; there is no control-versus-control baseline for that textual churn.

| Cell | Control → candidate | Fixed / broken | Exact McNemar p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flash-Next FSE=1, mbt 2048 | 0.9629 → 0.9636 | 17 / 16 | 1.000 |
| Flash-Next FSE=1, mbt 4096 | 0.9629 → 0.9651 | 12 / 9 | 0.664 |
| Flash-Next FSE=1, mbt 8192 | 0.9666 → 0.9598 | 9 / 18 | 0.122 |

| Qwen3-30B-A3B, mbt 2048 | 0.9045 → 0.9030 | 16 / 18 | 0.864 |

| Qwen3-30B-A3B, mbt 8192 | 0.9007 → 0.9045 | 17 / 12 | 0.458 |

The lowest p (0.122, Flash-Next FSE=1 at mbt 8192, net −9 problems) is the same configuration that is +1 and +3 at mbt 2048 and 4096, and at mbt 8192 prefill chunks above 4096 tokens take the legacy launcher in both arms, so only the decode steps differ there. The flexible-extract scores move the same way. The Qwen3-30B rows above are from the first sweep. The rerun's six cells (two passes at each mbt) are also consistent with noise: strict-match 0.9014–0.9083 on both arms, exact McNemar p between 0.39 and 1.0.

**gfx942 (MI300-class).** This is a verification, not a repeat of the full gfx950 sweep. Node: 8x MI300-class (gfx942), image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-81198e97ba7eee2a22540caaa756b7fdddcb4d93` (AITER 0.1.24.post1). Candidate: this PR with the gfx942 gate plus ROCm/aiter#6306 (`15f14c767`) with `module_moe_topk` rebuilt for gfx942; the candidate server loads `module_moe_topk`, the control does not.

*Kernel.* `op_tests/test_moe_topk_gating.py` passes on gfx942: NaN/Inf, exact ties, fake-EPLB balance and the shared-expert cases, all error columns 0 (max weight error at most 3e-8). Fused `topk_gating` time for E=512, top-10, bf16, one shared expert:

**Reproduce:**

```bash
# control: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-81198e97ba7eee2a22540caaa756b7fdddcb4d93
# candidate: the same image with this PR and ROCm/aiter#6306 applied

vllm serve amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --reasoning-parser qwen3 --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'

python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend vllm --dataset-name random --request-rate inf \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 \
  --max-concurrency 32 --num-prompts 128 --warmup-requests 32 --seed 302

lm_eval --model local-chat-completions \
  --model_args model=amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4,base_url=http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions,num_concurrent=32,timeout=1200,max_retries=3,tokenized_requests=False,max_gen_toks=2048 \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --apply_chat_template --batch_size 32 --seed 4321 --log_samples

pytest -q tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_topk.py tests/model_executor/test_enabled_custom_ops.py -k topk
```

The other rows use `--random-input-len/--random-output-len/--max-concurrency/--num-prompts/--warmup-requests/--seed` of 1024/1024/1/8/1/301, 1024/1024/128/256/128/303, 8192/128/8/32/8/304, 8192/1024/32/64/32/305 and 16384/128/2/8/2/306.

## Details

**What runs before and after.** Before, every softmax top-k on ROCm with AITER (`FusedTopKRouter`, and the fused-shared-expert router) ran `topk_softmax`, AITER's legacy launcher. After, `dispatch_topk_softmax_func` takes the launch's tensors and shared-expert arguments and returns `rocm_aiter_ops.topk_gating` on CDNA3 and CDNA4 (gfx942, gfx950) when `_aiter_topk_gating_supported` accepts the launch, and `topk_softmax` otherwise (including on every other architecture). `_aiter_topk_gating_supported` accepts contiguous gating rows with at most 4096 tokens; with shared experts it also needs sigmoid scoring, 1, 2, 4 or 8 of them, `topk_weights` and `topk_indices` sharing a row stride, and `topk_weights` wide enough for the shared columns. The shared-expert ids stay as the caller prefilled them, as with the legacy launcher. `_rocm_aiter_topk_gating_impl` is a plain call into `aiter.ops.topk.topk_gating`; the router runs inside the opaque `moe_forward` custom op, so nothing here changes graph capture.

**Why the 4096-token cap.** At E=512 / top-10 the kernel is level with the legacy launcher at T = 2048 and 4096 and was slower at 8K-token prefill chunks in an earlier measurement, so above 4096 the legacy launcher keeps serving. The cap is a named constant in the router, not a magic number.

**Why no env var.** The sweep shows a small positive effect at every shape tested on gfx950 and no reproducible loss, so there is nothing to opt into, and the path is the default under the existing AITER enablement (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE`) on gfx942 and gfx950. gfx942 was verified more lightly than gfx950 (see the gfx942 section); the gate is one line (`is_topk_gating_enabled`), so another architecture can be added the same way once it is measured.

title: [DSA] Wire DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits into the DeepSeek V4.1 indexer
author: JaredforReal
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek V4.1 selects attention tokens in two levels: one indexer layer publishes the top candidate blocks of the context, and the indexer layers after it pick their top-k inside those blocks. Today the consumer layers still score the **whole** context with dense MQA logits and then mask everything outside the candidates. DeepGEMM 2.8 ships sparse MQA-logits kernels (deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#432) that score only a given list of blocks, so this PR lets the consumer layers score just the candidate blocks. Their logits work goes from O(context) to O(candidate blocks), a fixed 16K positions for V4.1-Flash, and their top-k runs in that compressed space and is mapped back to context positions.

Design:

- **A separate indexer, not a branch in the dense one.** The consumer layers use a new `SparseMQAIndexer` layer with its own backend and attention metadata (`DeepseekV41SparseIndexerBackend`, `DeepseekV41SparseIndexerMetadata`). It is a plain module rather than a custom op: V4.1 does not go through `torch.compile`, and the attention layer already runs the indexer inside its breakable-CUDA-graph eager segment. The dense `SparseAttnIndexer` op is untouched. The candidate-source layer and the indexers before it stay dense.
- **Every requirement is checked once, at engine start.** The metadata builder validates the model, the MXFP4 indexer cache, the GPU generation, the DeepGEMM version, the DeepSelect extension and the logits/top-k layout it needs, and raises a clear error instead of silently falling back per step. There is no PyTorch fallback anywhere on the path: the candidate expansion and the index remap are Triton kernels, the top-k is DeepSelect.
- **Nothing is allocated or recomputed on the hot path.** The builder owns the per-row scratch; the candidate-block expansion and the DeepGEMM schedule depend only on the candidates, which are identical for all consumer layers of a step, so the first consumer computes them and the others reuse them through the shared metadata.
- **No dtype casts on the hot path.** The sparse kernels take bf16 weights and emit bf16 logits. The fused Q RoPE-quant kernel that produces the per-head weights writes them in bf16 for this indexer (fp32 for the dense one), and DeepSelect (#56464) runs the top-k on the bf16 logits directly.
- **Opt-in** via `--attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype": "mxfp4", "indexer_sparse_logits": true}'`. Below ~16K tokens the candidates cover the whole context and the dense path is cheaper, so the default stays off; the feature is for long-context serving.
- **One KV-layout requirement.** DeepGEMM's paged kernels address pages as `base + page * stride` and need that stride 512B-aligned. In V4.1's block-major layout the stride is the whole block (all layers' pages), which is not 512-aligned. `MLAAttentionSpec` gains `block_stride_alignment`, and the block size is rounded up to it in the same place HiSparse already rounds it (`_get_kv_cache_bytes_per_block`). With the flag on this costs 0.8% of KV memory; with it off nothing changes.

## Test Plan

- `tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py`: candidate-expansion math and a randomized comparison of the Triton expansion against a PyTorch reference (including strided inputs); exact selected-value parity of the sparse path with `torch.topk` over dense bf16 logits masked to the candidates, for prefill and paged decode, including spec-decode rows, CUDA-graph capture/replay and schedule reuse by a later layer; kernel numerics vs a PyTorch fp32 reference. `tests/kernels/test_fused_indexer_q_rope_quant.py`: the bf16 weights output of the fused Q kernel (Triton and CuTeDSL) equals the fp32 result rounded once. mypy and ruff via pre-commit.
- Kernel microbenchmark of the per-layer indexer pipeline (dense logits + mask + top-k vs sparse logits + top-k + remap) with an exact selected-value parity check, GB300, CUDA-graph replay.
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP=4 on 4x GB300, MXFP4 indexer cache, greedy, prefix caching off, flag on vs off: decode and prefill throughput from 8K to 1M context, and long-context NLL.

## Test Result

Unit tests: 28 passed. The sparse kernels produce bitwise the same bf16 logits as the dense kernels on the candidate columns, so the tests assert that the sparse path selects exactly the same values per row as `torch.topk` over dense bf16 logits masked to the candidates; only tie order among equal values may differ.

**Kernel level** (GB300, speedup of the sparse indexer pipeline over the dense one per consumer layer; decode rows are one query per request, the prefill column is a chunk of query rows sharing their sequence's K. V4.1-Flash has 4 consumer layers, the first one also pays the once-per-step candidate expansion, which lowers its speedup by 20-50%):

| context | decode, batch 64 | decode, batch 256 | prefill chunk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K | 1.2x | 1.2x | 1.6x |
| 32K | 1.7x | 1.8x | 2.3x |
| 128K | 4.4x | 5.8x | 8.3x |
| 512K | 14.4x | 22.9x | |

**End to end** (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP=4, 4x GB300; decode and prefill throughput of the whole batch, from a linear fit of wall time against output length):

| batch x context | decode tok/s off | decode tok/s on | decode speedup | prefill tok/s off | prefill tok/s on | prefill speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 x 8K | 5,570 | 5,895 | 1.06x | 68,712 | 65,541 | 0.95x |
| 32 x 100K | 3,263 | 3,434 | 1.05x | 60,508 | 64,306 | 1.06x |
| 16 x 256K | 2,055 | 2,153 | 1.05x | 48,504 | 57,670 | 1.19x |
| 8 x 512K | 1,057 | 1,107 | 1.05x | 34,127 | 48,805 | 1.43x |
| 4 x 1M | 568 | 583 | 1.03x | 16,261 | 32,517 | 2.00x |

Decode gets 3-6% faster: the indexer is only a few percent of a decode step at these batch sizes. Prefill is where the O(context) cost shows: the dense indexer's fp32 logits grow with the context and are chunked, written and read back several times, while the sparse rows stay 16K wide, so prefill throughput is 1.2x at 256K, 1.4x at 512K and 2x at 1M, while at 8K it is 5% slower.

**Accuracy** (78K-token real document, mean NLL of the next token by position; the sparse kernels score in bf16, the dense path in fp32). Two runs of the same configuration differ by up to 0.002 per bucket (TP=4 run-to-run noise), and on/off differ by the same amount:

| position | 0-16K | 16K-32K | 32K-64K | 64K-78K |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| off | 0.4001 | 0.3715 | 0.3523 | 0.3735 |
| on | 0.4022 | 0.3706 | 0.3526 | 0.3755 |
| on, second run | 0.4010 | 0.3719 | 0.3534 | 0.3737 |

## Requirements and limitations

- SM100-class GPUs, DeepGEMM >= 2.8 (the repo pin is older; the flag fails at startup with a clear message on older builds), the DeepSelect extension (`vllm._deepselect_C`, built with vllm) and the MXFP4 indexer cache (the kernels take UE8M0 scales). `--sparse-indexer-topk-backend` must be `auto` or `deep_select`. Not supported with DCP/PCP.
- The sparse kernels score in bf16 with bf16 weights (no fp32 option), so the flag changes the indexer's score precision; greedy outputs are not token-identical to the dense path (see the NLL table).

AI assistance: this change was developed with an AI coding agent; the human submitter reviewed the full diff and ran the tests above.

title: [Quantization] Support packed NVFP4 Qwen4Exp PLE embeddings
author: stecasta
body:
## Purpose

Enable the `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` checkpoint to run on **1x DGX Spark without CPU or disk PLE offloading**. Its packed NVFP4 ngram table occupies 26.822 GiB and remains resident in CUDA memory. The PR's resident path was validated on one GB10 with a 4,096-token context, 2 GiB KV cache, and MTP disabled; model loading reported 97.47 GiB.

Fixes #56272.

Support `ple_embedding_dtype="nvfp4"` in Qwen4Exp ngram embeddings. The [local-inference-lab checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4/tree/ada4da32a583a78aa47299f45a70603c950490b8) stores each logical 160-value row as 80 packed E2M1 bytes and 10 E4M3 block scales, with one FP32 global scale. Upstream currently selects an unquantized table for this explicit storage format inside a ModelOpt mixed-precision checkpoint.

The change adds an embedding method to the existing device/pinned-host storage interface. Both paths keep packed weights and block scales in their original storage and decode only the requested rows. Lookup reuses the existing E2M1 decoder and produces activation-dtype rows before ETP reduction. The loader copies each checkpoint shard's overlap with the local ETP vocabulary range and validates coverage after all weight streams finish, along with the global scale, tensor shapes, and storage dtypes.

Related work was checked on September 10, 2026. [#54882](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54882) and [#55334](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55334) concern an FP8 PLE table inside a model with NVFP4 body weights. [#53899](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53899) contains an older NVFP4 PLE implementation within offload work, but its mixed-precision dispatch does not select this checkpoint's explicit NVFP4 table. [#42791](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42791) adds generic quantized vocabulary embeddings. This change targets the serialized split PLE layout through the storage interface merged in [#54371](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54371).

AI assistance was used to develop and test this change.

## Test Plan

Extend the existing PLE suite with streamed packed-weight/block-scale loading across ETP boundaries, missing row coverage, malformed storage/global scales, independent numerical decoding, compiled GPU lookup, CUDA graph replay with changing IDs, empty/padded inputs, and pinned-host prefetch. Add the NVFP4 cases to the existing H200 Qwen4Exp CI lane.

Test base: `b28c3e1568bfae930f61d4b24940e47528c85d4a`, with the matching upstream precompiled CUDA wheel, Torch `2.13.0+cu130`, and FlashInfer `0.6.18.post1`. GPUs: one isolated RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and one DGX Spark / GB10. The Spark run used the published PR commit `e251861aab69d3eb438d1a76ddec036ae45cfd4c`.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v --tb=short --timeout=300 \
  tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_config.py
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v --tb=short --timeout=600 \
  tests/compile/h100/test_startup.py::test_moe_startup
.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files \
  vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ngram_embedding.py \
  tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py .buildkite/test_areas/models_basic.yaml
.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files \
  vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ngram_embedding.py \
  tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py
```

Full-model text-generation validation used the pinned checkpoint above (image/video inputs disabled), a 4,096-token context, 512-token prefill chunks, four sequences, 2 GiB of KV cache, and full/piecewise CUDA graph capture sizes `[1, 2, 4]`. The offline harness ran with `PYTHONPATH=/opt/ngram/vllm:/run/ngram /opt/ngram/.venv/bin/python /run/ngram/model_smoke.py` on Max-Q and `model_smoke_spark.py` on Spark. Spark used `engram_config={"cpu_offload":false}` and `cpu_offload_gb=0`; Max-Q used pinned-host PLE storage. It checked selected rows from the complete table against an independent decoder, then four chat prompts and the first 32 canonical GSM8K test examples (temperature 0, thinking disabled, 768 output tokens).

## Test Result

- PLE and configuration suites: 76 passed on Max-Q and 76 passed on DGX Spark.
- Compilation startup canary on Max-Q: 2 passed.
- Actual checkpoint sample: 8 rows of width 160 matched an independent E2M1/FP8/global-scale reference exactly after BF16 conversion, through both device lookup and pinned-host prefetch with simulated ETP ownership.
- CPU PLE/configuration suites: 43 passed, 33 skipped because CUDA was unavailable.
- Pre-commit, including Python 3.10 type checks, and manual Python 3.12 type checks: passed.
- Full checkpoint loaded with 26.822 GiB of packed PLE weights/scales in CUDA memory on Spark and pinned host memory on Max-Q. On both devices, selected rows from the full table, including addresses beyond 32-bit offsets, matched the independent BF16 reference exactly.
- Full-model startup captured all six CUDA graphs on each device. All four generation checks passed on each, including a prompt requiring chunked prefill.
- GSM8K smoke evaluation: 31/32 exact numeric answers (96.875%) on each GPU. On each device, the remaining response hit the 768-token limit. This is a small smoke evaluation, not a full benchmark or comparison with the checkpoint publisher's runtime.

The checkpoint uses preview architecture names. Validation normalizes them with `hf_overrides={"model_type":"qwen4_exp","architectures":["Qwen4ExpForConditionalGeneration"]}`. PLE offload is disabled on Spark and enabled on Max-Q. It selects `kernel_config={"linear_backend":"marlin"}` because the automatic MXFP8 linear backend rejects the checkpoint's 96-output GDN projection. Real multi-GPU collectives and MTP have not been validated with this PR.

## Single-Spark reference measurements

Separate end-to-end measurements on September 10, 2026 compared the [local-inference-lab checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4/tree/ada4da32a583a78aa47299f45a70603c950490b8) using its b12x runtime with the [NVIDIA checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4/tree/fc694b54fb0174e0913e6adf86691ef85a4ead47) using upstream vLLM plus disk PLE offload patches. These measurements provide context for fitting the checkpoints on one DGX Spark. They were collected independently of this PR and do not measure its performance impact.

Workload: 32,768 shared prefix tokens, 2,048 suffix tokens, and 256 output tokens; streaming chat, temperature 0, three warmups per cell, and concurrency 1/4/8 with 10/40/80 measured requests. Both runtimes used one GB10, TP1/PP1, a 40,960-token context limit, prefix caching, chunked prefill, and MTP with four draft tokens. Latency and TTFT are means; decode throughput is aggregate active decode throughput from AIPerf.

| Checkpoint / runtime | Concurrency | Requests | Latency (s) | TTFT (s) | Decode (tok/s) | Acceptance length |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| local-inference-lab / b12x | 1 | 10 | 11.27 | 3.40 | 32.41 | 2.40 |
| local-inference-lab / b12x | 4 | 40 | 28.19 | 5.44 | 36.31 | 2.13 |
| local-inference-lab / b12x | 8 | 80 | 45.99 | 6.75 | 43.44 | 2.20 |
| NVIDIA / vLLM with disk PLE | 1 | 10 | 14.30 | 3.45 | 23.51 | 2.64 |
| NVIDIA / vLLM with disk PLE | 4 | 40 | 29.60 | 5.09 | 34.25 | 2.39 |
| NVIDIA / vLLM with disk PLE | 8 | 80 | 44.34 | 7.12 | 45.92 | 2.59 |

Each checkpoint completed all 130 measured requests with zero errors and zero preemptions. Every measured response contained 256 output tokens. Acceptance length is `1 + accepted_tokens / draft_steps`, calculated from server counters.

The local checkpoint's packed PLE payload is 26.822 GiB, held in b12x's resident managed CUDA weight storage with no explicit CPU or disk PLE offload; KV cache was 8 GiB FP8. The NVIDIA checkpoint's FP8 PLE payload is 47.684 GiB, served through disk-backed mmap and the OS page cache; KV cache was 10 GiB BF16. Quantization, backends, and prefix reuse also differ (27,216 versus 30,704 reused tokens per request), so this is a comparison of complete configurations. Each cell is a single run, and accuracy equivalence was not evaluated. Host swap activity was observed, so no swap-free claim is made.

<details>

title: [MM] Mistral vision Encoder CG support
author: NickLucche
body: Enable encoder CUDA Graphs for Mistral multimodal models using the Pixtral vision encoder, covering both `PixtralForConditionalGeneration` and `Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration` The implementation packs variable-resolution image patches into fixed-capacity graph buffers and precomputes attention metadata, rotary embeddings, and patch-merger indices. Unsupported attention configurations fall back to eager execution. It also keeps `max_seqlen` on CPU because attention backends call `.item()` on it during capture. ## Relation to existing work PR #54214 independently implements the native Pixtral path and overlaps part of this change.
