title: [ROCm][Perf] W4A16: pad gfx11 weight and activation strides
author: mgehre-amd
body:
On gfx11 (RDNA3/3.5) a W4A16 GEMM loses a large share of its achievable read bandwidth when an operand's row stride lands on a multiple of 1024 bytes. The rows alias into the same L2/DDR channels and the accesses serialize. Offsetting the stride by one 128 B cache line dodges it.

This PR nudges **both** operands off that cliff: the packed weight row (padded once at load) and the activation row (padded per call) and improves TTFT by up to 23 % and TPOT by up to 3 %.
Padding the activation (at runtime) pays for itself due to reduced GEMM time.

## The two cliffs

For weights, we pad at load time when they are a multiple of 1024 bytes. For activations,
we only pad when they are a multiple of 2048 bytes to ensure that their cost is recovered by the GEMM wins.

The following table shows how many GEMM shapes are affected by the padding in a model:

| Model | weight padded | 
|---|---|---|
| `Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16` | 4/4 (`K=4096` → 2048 B, `K=12288` → 6144 B) | 
| `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-w4a16` | 4/4 (`K=14336` → 7168 B qualifies) | 
| `gemma-3-4b-it-quantized.w4a16` | 2/3 (`K=2048`, `K=10240`) |
| `Qwen3-4B-quantized.w4a16` | 1/4 (`o_proj`, `K=4096`) |

Gated on gfx1151, where the effect was measured. This might also apply to other gfx11 parts, but we will need to measure and can enable as a follow up.

## Implementation

- `pack_skinny_int4` is the single source of truth for the skinny weight layout and applies the weight pad once at load.
- Activations are padded by an explicit copy inside the W4A16 apply op. The copy costs less than the GEMM gains by the strides. Having the activation's producer emit a padded output would make it free; that is a reasonable follow-up.
- **Activations are not padded on the decode path.** . This is why the decode win is preserved intact (see TPOT below).

## Benchmark

AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), `--output-len 128 --num-prompts 10 --max-num-seqs 1 --request-rate 0.3`, median TTFT / TPOT, n as noted. Arms differ only in the files of this PR, on the same base commit and the same build.

| Model (in/out len) | Median TTFT | Median TPOT | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16` 128/128 | 119.99 → 101.80 ms (**−15.2 %**) | 23.91 → 23.20 ms (**−3.0 %**) | 3/6 |
| `Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16` 1920/128 | 1294.82 → 1191.71 ms (**−8.0 %**) | 25.95 → 25.29 ms (**−2.5 %**) | 3/3 |
| `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-w4a16` 128/128 | 131.50 → 101.75 ms (**−22.6 %**) | 22.37 → 21.86 ms (**−2.3 %**) | 3/6 |
| `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-w4a16` 1920/128 | 1243.30 → 1162.53 ms (**−6.5 %**) | 24.27 → 23.80 ms (**−1.9 %**) | 3/3 |
| `gemma-3-4b-it-quantized.w4a16` 1920/128 | 698.16 → 657.08 ms (**−5.9 %**) | 29.59 → 29.60 ms (no effect) | 3/3 |
| `Qwen3-4B-quantized.w4a16` 1920/128 | 707.70 → 701.99 ms (**−0.8 %**) | 15.45 → 15.46 ms (no effect) | 3/3 |
| gemma-4-31B 328/256 | TTFT | 2408.500 [2405.490, 2409.240] | 2387.040 [2373.710, 2392.150] | 0.89 % |
| gemma-4-31B 328/256 | TPOT | 112.060 [111.960, 112.130] | 108.890 [108.700, 109.050] | **2.83 %** |
| gemma-4-31B 328/256 +MTP | TTFT | 2580.090 [2578.570, 2580.830] | 2545.780 [2542.360, 2549.050] | 1.33 % |
| gemma-4-31B 328/256 +MTP | TPOT | 55.790 [55.710, 55.960] | 51.450 [51.450, 51.490] | **7.78 %** |

Llama-3.1-8B is `amd/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-w4a16-llmcompressor` (compressed-tensors, g128, symmetric).

`gemma-4-31B` is `cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit` (compressed-tensors
pack-quantized, 4-bit, group_size 32, asymmetric), 328 input / 256 output tokens
with one 640x480 image per request, `--mm-encoder-attn-backend TRITON_ATTN`.
`+MTP` adds `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp",
"model":"google/gemma-4-31B-it-assistant","num_speculative_tokens":3}'`.

## Accuracy

`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 200 questions, 5-shot, greedy (temperature 0.0), `RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16` on gfx1151, n=3 per arm:

| | Accuracy | Correct | Invalid | Output tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| this PR off | 88.00 % (3/3 reps identical) | 176 / 200 | 0.0 | 23209 (3/3) |
| this PR on | 88.00 % (3/3 reps identical) | 176 / 200 | 0.0 | 23209 – 23214 |

Identical accuracy on every rep of both arms. 

`tests/kernels/quantization/test_rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py` asserts that a row-padded weight produces bit-identical output to a dense one (`rtol=0, atol=0`) through both the HIP decode kernel and the Triton prefill kernel. **95 tests pass** on gfx1151 (`pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py`). Off gfx1151 the new code paths reduce to exactly the previous behaviour. `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` is clean.

## Relation to other open PRs

This is the packed-int4 counterpart to #55090, which pads *dense* fp16/bf16 weight rows in `layers/linear.py`. Different tensors and code path, same underlying aliasing.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for this PR. Every changed line was reviewed by the submitter, and all tests, benchmarks and evals listed above were run on the hardware named.

title: [ROCm][Kernel] New "hip" GDN backend for gfx1151
author: roberteg16
body:
## Purpose

GATED_DELTA_NET prefill runs as a chain of Triton kernels that communicate through DDR. At 2048 tokens, 32 MiB are stored and loaded back per layer.

This adds the chunked delta rule (WY representation / UT transform) as a single HIP kernel for RDNA3.5. One block walks the chunks of one (head, sequence) with the state resident in registers and the per-chunk intermediates in LDS, so `h`, `w` and `u` are never formed. A chunk of 32 tokens and the identity `v_new = Tinv (V beta - (K beta exp(g_cs)) S)` keep a whole chunk inside the 64 KB LDS budget.

The kernel is also more accurate than the path it replaces: everything between the inputs and the output stays fp32, where the Triton kernels round `h`, `w`, `u`, `Tinv` and `v_new` to bf16. Against an fp64 token-by-token reference its relative RMS error is 0.53x theirs, and the final state comes out at fp32 precision.

The kernel is exposed as a new GDN prefill backend, `hip`, next to `triton`, `flashinfer`, `cutedsl` and `aiter_flydsl`:

- `auto` selects it on gfx1151, the only RDNA3.5 part run on hardware. Elsewhere `auto` keeps Triton.
- `--gdn-prefill-backend hip` enables it on gfx1150–gfx1153 and fails closed where the op is not built. `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` opts out.
- Built only for gfx1150–gfx1153. bf16 and fp16 Q/K/V/output and head dimension 128; other models resolve to Triton, and any call the kernel cannot serve falls back to Triton per call.
- The Triton/FLA path is untouched.

Also adds a single-GPU benchmark that compares the two paths correctness-first, with model presets, mixed-cache preparation and incremental JSONL output.

## Test Plan

```
python -m pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_chunked_rocm.py \
    tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_rocm_layout_dispatch.py -v

# correctness against an fp64 token-by-token reference
python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_gdn_chunk.py \
    --hv 48 --hg 16 --seqlens 32,33,64,1 --check --exact --raw-hip

# the timing grid below: four head shapes, 16 batches each
python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_gdn_chunk.py --jsonl results.jsonl

# model-level accuracy
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B --port 8765 --max-model-len 4096
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8765 \
    --num-questions 400 --num-shots 5 --temperature 0
```

<details>
<summary>What the benchmark does</summary>

**What it compares.** The Triton side calls the FLA entry point, `chunk_gated_delta_rule`; the HIP side calls the backend's wrapper, `chunk_gdn_hip_fwd`. Both are timed with their wrapper allocations, so the numbers are what each prefill backend costs per call.

**What it runs.** With no arguments it runs a fixed grid: 16 batches, from a single 32-token sequence up to 256 sequences of 256 tokens, against each of the four head shapes, which are the complete head counts of the Qwen3.5/3.6 family on one GPU. `--preset small|medium|dense|large` restricts the shapes. `--seqlens 941 --seqlens 1,4095` runs an explicit workload instead, repeatable, with `--hv`/`--hg` for its head counts and `--limit` to cut a run short. `--dtype` selects bf16 or fp16. `--dry-run` plans on CPU without importing torch, which is useful to see what a run would cover.

**How it times.** `triton.testing.do_bench` with quantiles, as elsewhere in this repository: it derives the repetition count from a first measurement and clears the L2 cache before each run, so every sample starts cold. Timing the public entry point means the samples include wrapper allocations and host launch gaps, which is what the model actually pays; `--raw-hip` additionally times the preallocated op on its own to separate that overhead from device time.

**What it checks before timing.** Output and final state are compared against the Triton path per sequence and head, with relative RMS and a finite check. `--check` skips timing entirely, and `--exact` adds an independent fp64 token-by-token recurrence, which is what decides whether the kernel is more accurate rather than merely different.

**Reading the output.** Progress goes to stdout; `--jsonl` writes one record per case with the median and the p10/p90 quantiles, the shapes, the inferred launch mode and the environment. Speedup is the Triton median over the HIP median, so above 1× is faster. Compare p10 and p90 before calling a small difference a regression: where those ranges overlap, the two paths are not conclusively different.

</details>

Hardware: one AMD Radeon 8060S (gfx1151). PyTorch `2.12.0+rocm10.1.0a20260803`, Triton `3.8.0+git4cff872c.rocm10.1.0a20260803`. Only gfx1151 has been run on hardware; the other three targets are compile-tested.

## Test Result

`tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_chunked_rocm.py`: **39 passed**. Coverage includes ratio-three heads, absent initial state, optional final state, continuation across aligned and unaligned splits, adversarial gates and fp16 inputs, all against an independent fp64 recurrence.

`tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_rocm_layout_dispatch.py`: **27 passed**. Covers backend selection (`auto` on and off gfx1151, explicit `hip`, unsupported head dims and dtypes, missing op) and, on gfx1151, the production `ChunkGatedDeltaRule` resolving to `hip` against a token-wise reference.

Every measured benchmark case passes its numerical checks.

| 16/16 | Qwen3.5-0.8B/2B | 16 | 2.19x | 0 |

| Input tokens | TTFT with kernel | TTFT with Triton | TTFT reduction | Prefill with kernel | Prefill with Triton | Speedup |

title: [Metrics] Expose cached prompt tokens by cache tier
author: cquil11
body:
## Changes

- Adds `vllm:prompt_tokens_cached_by_source_total{source}` with five values: `device`, `host`, `p2p`, `disk`, `external_unspecified`.
- Counts cache hits at admission. Source counts sum to local and external prefix-cache hits. Existing prompt-token counters are unchanged.
- Records attribution through the existing `PrefixCacheStats` path. Connectors return typed counts through `get_external_cache_hit_sources`. Incorrect totals fall back to `external_unspecified` with a one-time warning.
- Simple offload reports `host` or `disk`. NIXL, Mooncake transfer and MoRIIO report `p2p`. Mooncake Store and uninstrumented connectors report `external_unspecified`. MultiConnector delegates to the selected connector.
- Native offload uses the keys selected for loading. Mixed KV-group dependencies use the outermost required tier, so host + disk reports `disk`. Missing attribution reports `external_unspecified`. Promotion preserves the initiating request's original tier.
- Supports Python and Rust frontends.

Closes vllm-project/vllm#53368.

## Validation

[Passed Run Sweep](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/36272389390): DeepSeek-V4-Pro, one-hour AIPerf AgentX profiles, evaluations disabled. AIPerf scraped Prometheus. JSON/CSV source counts and accounting checks passed.

- B200: [DRAM c8](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/36272389390/artifacts/10917614507), [Simple NVMe c14](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/36272389390/artifacts/10919213254), [native DRAM+NVMe c14](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/36272389390/artifacts/10919342792).

Validate device/dtype/layout inputs and preserve padded page strides.

title: [Kernel][Perf][Quantization] Fix odd-row performance cliff in per-token-group quantization
author: ayush1399
body:
## Purpose

Avoid the odd-row performance cliff in per-token-group 8-bit quantization while preserving the existing launch policy for even row counts.

We identified this while investigating unexpectedly poor TPOT (time per output token) with Gemma 4 31B FP8 at TP8 on H100. The reproduction traced about 35 ms of extra time in a 13,359-token prefill forward pass to activation quantization, enough to erase the roughly 30 ms saved by FP8 GEMMs. At TP8, the down-projection input has width 2688: odd row counts launch 16-thread blocks and make quantization roughly 4× slower than the neighboring even case. The width-5376 inputs also take a roughly 2× slower path.

The current heuristic selects one group per block when the total group count is odd, launching only 16 threads. This change selects block geometry using the next even row count, then uses ceil-div and bounds checks for the actual groups. No tensors are padded or copied. All threads still participate in block and PDL synchronization, and the bounds check is compiled out for full blocks.

Quantization arithmetic and scale layouts are unchanged. The helper serves both FP8 and INT8, so both receive regression coverage. The separate packed kernel is unchanged.

### Related work

[#55330](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55330) takes a different approach: a register-resident kernel with fixed 256-thread launches for eligible inputs. This change retains the shared-memory kernel and its existing even-row policy, including support for FP32 inputs and group size 64. The approaches may be complementary, with this policy improving the shared-memory fallback.

## Performance

The H100 measurements below confirm the kernel improvement at the Gemma TP8 down-projection shape. End-to-end TP8 TPOT has not yet been remeasured with this patch.

Kernel latency in microseconds, measured with CUPTI and CUDA graphs. BF16 input, FP8 output, group size 128, column-major FP32 scales with UE8M0 rounding. Results are medians of three rounds of 30 samples; cold runs flush L2 outside the timed kernel.

| GPU | M × K | Hot before → after | Cold before → after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 32767 × 128 | 41.76 → 10.45 | 41.86 → 12.48 |
| H100 | 32768 × 128 | 10.46 → 10.43 | 12.35 → 12.35 |
| H100 | 65537 × 128 | 81.18 → 41.82 | 81.22 → 41.86 |
| H100 | 13359 × 2688 | 339.63 → 81.46 | 339.63 → 83.38 |
| GB10 | 32767 × 128 | 49.23 → 20.93 | 85.98 → 89.10 |
| GB10 | 32768 × 128 | 20.80 → 20.82 | 87.14 → 86.62 |
| GB10 | 65537 × 128 | 108.24 → 67.47 | 146.27 → 145.66 |
| GB10 | 13359 × 2688 | 517.30 → 487.12 | 541.51 → 516.96 |

**H100:** The final production-source comparison covers 18 shapes, with geometric-mean latency reductions of 39.5% hot and 38.0% cold. An earlier 259-shape policy prototype also covered the broader matrix: all 112 odd shapes were within 2.9% hot and 4.2% cold of the next-even control. That prototype always enabled the guard for odd rows; the final patch omits it when no tail exists.

**GB10:** Across 182 general shapes, the geometric-mean latency reduction is 6.7% hot and 0.2% cold. Even-row performance remains essentially unchanged. Across 91 odd/next-even pairs, geometric-mean latency differs by less than 0.4%.

Clocks were not locked on either GPU. The H100 and GB10 aggregate matrices differ, so their averages are not a direct GPU comparison. H200, B200, B300, and ROCm were not tested.

## Test Plan

Extend the existing FP8 and INT8 tests with empty inputs, odd tails, FP16/BF16/FP32 inputs, group sizes 64/128, and supported scale layouts.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v \
  tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py::test_per_token_group_quant_fp8 \
  tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py::test_per_token_group_quant_int8

.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/fp8/per_token_group_quant.cu \
  tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py
```

## Test Result

- Isolated production-source tests: **678 passed** on both H100 and GB10.
- GB10 Compute Sanitizer memcheck and synccheck: **zero errors**.
- GB10 validation reports **678 passed** with the rebuilt extension. Its command ledger names `test_utils.py` rather than the test file above; the recorded command needs reconciliation.
- Final production-source benchmarks produced byte-identical quantized outputs and identical scales against baseline on all **18 H100 shapes** and **194 GB10 shapes**.
- Repository hooks passed.
- GB10 Gemma-4-31B-it-FP8-block loaded and generated the expected response to a deterministic text prompt through the modified quantizer. This was a serving smoke test; a broader model accuracy evaluation has not been run.

title: [Core] Extensible KV cache
author: njhill
body:
## Overview

Size the KV cache from the GPU memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, instead of from a pre-capture profiling estimate. The cache's address range is reserved up front with the driver's virtual memory API, and physical memory is mapped into it only once the final size is known. Enabled by default on CUDA and ROCm with the V2 model runner.

Productization of @zhuohan123's demonstration in #47363; replaces #50779.

### Background

The KV cache has to exist before CUDA graph capture, because captured graphs bake in its addresses. So today it is sized from a profiling run that happens before capture and warmup, and everything allocated after that has to be guessed:
- **CUDA graph memory** is either ignored or estimated with a throwaway capture pass, which costs startup time.
- **Warmup and runtime transients** that profiling doesn't exercise, such as attention workspaces, sampler and logprobs buffers, and spec-decode drafts, are covered only by slack.

That slack is the `gpu_memory_utilization=0.92` default: 8% of the device, about 15 GiB of a 192 GiB GPU, left idle to absorb estimation error. When the estimate is too optimistic, the engine runs out of memory at runtime anyway.

### Extensible KV cache

The full KV cache capacity is reserved as virtual address space, with no physical memory behind it. Only the blocks that capture and warmup actually touch are backed with physical pages. After warmup, each worker measures the memory that is really free and the transient peaks it really saw. The engine then commits the final block count in one step, by mapping more physical memory into the same reserved range.

Addresses never move, so the layer views and the already-captured CUDA graphs stay valid. The cache is sized from measurement rather than from an estimate, so the default can use the whole device, keeping a measured transient reserve plus a margin.

## Claims

- **Larger KV cache by default:** 4–10% more KV cache tokens (4.9–11.3 GiB per GPU) across eight models on GB200, most of them 7–10%. The gain comes from no longer needing the 8% slack. At an explicit `gpu_memory_utilization=0.92`, the cache comes out 1–4% *smaller* than today's. It subtracts the CUDA graph and warmup memory it actually measured, which today's path leaves the slack to absorb.
- **Faster engine startup:** no throwaway CUDA graph capture pass to estimate graph memory. Engine init time, excluding weight loading, falls 21–34% (5–34 s); end-to-end startup falls 6–18%.
- **No tuning `gpu_memory_utilization` to avoid OOMs:** the cache size follows what the model, graphs and warmup actually use. The utilization setting remains a cap for sharing a GPU.
- Works with sleep mode, CUDA graphs, spec decode, hybrid models, TP/PP/DP, and the KV connectors listed under "Compatibility". Where a configuration can't use it, it falls back to today's estimate-based sizing automatically. An explicit `--enable-extensible-kv-cache` there is an error.

## Validation

- Capacity and startup benchmarks: see "Results" below.
- Unit tests:
  - `tests/utils_/test_extensible_tensor.py`
  - `tests/utils_/test_vmm_driver.py`
  - `tests/v1/worker/test_extensible_kv_cache.py`
  - `tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py`
  - `tests/v1/engine/test_engine_args.py`
  - `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker.py`
- End-to-end: greedy outputs match with the feature on and off, and before and after sleep/wake.
- NIXL P/D accuracy on GB200; on ROCm, with patched UCX and ROCr (see "Compatibility").

## Results

GB200 (189 GiB per GPU), default settings otherwise. Each start is a fresh process.
- **Variants:**
  - **off:** `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache`, i.e. today's sizing with the default `gpu_memory_utilization=0.92`.
  - **on:** this PR's defaults.
- **Method:**
  - One unmeasured warm-up start per variant, to populate the torch.compile, JIT and weight page caches.
  - Then three interleaved off/on pairs; medians are reported.
  - Weights load from a warm page cache, so end-to-end times are faster than a cold start. Weight loading is identical between variants.

**KV cache capacity per GPU**

| Model | TP | off | on | Gain | Tokens | on, at 0.92 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | 150.2 GiB | 161.6 GiB | +11.3 GiB | +7.5% | −0.6% |
| Qwen3-8B + EAGLE3 | 1 | 147.3 GiB | 157.4 GiB | +10.1 GiB | +6.8% | −1.4% |
| Qwen3-32B | 1 | 103.1 GiB | 113.0 GiB | +9.9 GiB | +9.5% | −1.9% |
| gpt-oss-20b | 1 | 150.5 GiB | 161.0 GiB | +10.5 GiB | +7.0% | −0.9% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 1 | 97.6 GiB | 106.2 GiB | +8.6 GiB | +8.8% | −2.3% |
| MiniMax-M2.7 | 4 | 109.7 GiB | 118.4 GiB | +8.7 GiB | +7.9% | −1.3% |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 | 4 | 108.1 GiB | 117.1 GiB | +9.0 GiB | +8.2% | −1.5% |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 4 | 119.9 GiB | 124.9 GiB | +4.9 GiB | +4.1% | −3.7% |

- **"on, at 0.92"** is the extensible cache at an explicit `gpu_memory_utilization=0.92`, compared with off. The cache comes out slightly smaller there because it subtracts the CUDA graph and warmup memory it measured, which today's sizing leaves to the slack.
- **DeepSeek-V4-Flash gains least** because its CUDA graphs and workspaces need about 15 GiB per GPU after warmup. Today's sizing leaves almost all of that to the 8% slack, so the slack was mostly in use already.

**Startup time** (median of 3)

| Model | TP | Engine init, off | Engine init, on | Change | End-to-end, off | End-to-end, on | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | 17.7 s | 12.5 s | −5.2 s (−29%) | 50.0 s | 40.9 s | −9.1 s (−18%) |
| Qwen3-8B + EAGLE3 | 1 | 20.1 s | 13.7 s | −6.3 s (−32%) | 51.7 s | 44.7 s | −7.0 s (−14%) |
| Qwen3-32B | 1 | 30.7 s | 21.6 s | −9.1 s (−30%) | 80.9 s | 71.4 s | −9.5 s (−12%) |
| gpt-oss-20b | 1 | 19.2 s | 13.8 s | −5.3 s (−28%) | 47.2 s | 42.2 s | −5.0 s (−11%) |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 1 | 53.3 s | 42.4 s | −11.0 s (−21%) | 119.7 s | 109.4 s | −10.4 s (−9%) |
| MiniMax-M2.7 | 4 | 55.9 s | 38.3 s | −17.6 s (−31%) | 146.9 s | 137.4 s | −9.4 s (−6%) |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 | 4 | 76.1 s | 50.1 s | −26.0 s (−34%) | 173.8 s | 144.2 s | −29.6 s (−17%) |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 4 | 112.2 s | 77.9 s | −34.2 s (−30%) | 192.2 s | 174.2 s | −18.0 s (−9%) |

- **Engine init** is the logged "init engine (profile, create kv cache, warmup model)" time, which excludes weight loading.
- **End-to-end** runs from process start until `LLM()` returns.
- **Spread:** engine init varied by about 1–2 s within a variant, and every on start was faster than every off start.
- **Where the time goes:** most of the saving is the throwaway CUDA graph capture pass that today's sizing runs to estimate graph memory. The actual capture takes the same time in both variants.
- **TP4 runs loaded checkpoints lazily** (`safetensors_load_strategy="lazy"`). The automatic background prefetch from Lustre intermittently hung multi-rank loading, independently of this change. MiniMax-M2.7's off starts used the prefetch, so its end-to-end comparison mixes the two loading modes.

<!-- TODO: H200 -->

## Details

### Implementation

- **`ExtensibleTensor`** (`vllm/utils/extensible_tensor.py`, `vllm/utils/vmm_driver.py`):
  - A tensor over a reserved virtual address range, exposed to torch through DLPack.
  - Its segments are backed with physical memory on demand, in driver-granule chunks; newly committed blocks are zeroed.
  - Uses the CUDA (`cuMem*`) and HIP (`hipMem*`) VMM APIs through ctypes.
  - A startup probe falls back to estimate-based sizing where the driver lacks VMM support, or where a HIP runtime has the `hipMemSetAccess` defect.
- **`ExtensibleKVCache`** (`vllm/v1/worker/extensible_kv_cache.py`):
  - Plugs into `allocate_kv_cache` as an allocator hook. It reserves the capacity from the profiled budget and splits it into per-layer (or per-tensor) segments, so kernels and layer views are unchanged.
  - Before capture, only the null block is backed. Warmup commits the blocks it addresses.
- **Sizing** (`gpu_worker._measure_kv_cache_blocks`, `kv_cache_planning.finalize_extensible_kv_cache`):
  - After warmup, each worker reports how many blocks fit. That is its budget less two things:
    - the measured transient peak: the larger of the profiling peak and the warmup peak;
    - a margin of `max(1 GiB, 0.75 × transient peak)`.
  - The engine takes the minimum across workers, and across DP engines, which step in lockstep. It then shrinks the configs and issues one `extend_kv_cache` RPC.
  - Warmup gains a full-budget prefill step and a prompt-logprobs chunk, so their peaks are measured rather than estimated. For MLA models it also runs a prefill over one chunked-context workspace of cached context, which measures MLA's context up-projection for prefix cache hits.
  - With the feature on and `gpu_memory_utilization` unset, the utilization defaults to 1.0; otherwise it stays 0.92. The CUDA graph memory profiling pass is skipped.
- **Sleep mode:** sleep, and `release_kv_cache_memory()`, unmap the physical pages; wake remaps them at the same addresses.
- **Weight updates** (`reload_weights`, weight-transfer sessions): a layerwise update needs transient memory that warmup can't measure, at its peak a few times the largest layer's checkpoint-format size. Before any weight changes, the worker checks free memory against that estimate:
  - If short after a pause that cleared the KV cache (the default RL weight-update flow), it releases the cache's physical memory for the update and remaps it afterwards. Nothing is reserved in normal serving.
  - Otherwise a reload fails before loading if even the largest layer can't fit, and warns if only the estimate doesn't.
- **KV connectors:**
  - The worker-side connector is created after the final extend, so it registers the final memory.
  - Under a connector, segment boundaries are aligned to the driver granule, so RDMA registrations never span physical chunks.
- **Consistency:** every worker and every DP engine agrees on whether the feature is on and on the warmup block count, so they warm up the same steps.

### Compatibility

| Not supported | Behavior | What enabling it would need |
|---|---|---|
| Platforms other than CUDA/ROCm | Off | A `VmmDriver` per platform. XPU looks feasible: Level Zero has all the VMM primitives, but the calls need PyTorch's SYCL context (a small C++ op), and PyTorch's XPU DLPack import would need to accept the mapped pointer. |
| V1 model runner | Off | Only the V2 runner is wired up. Not planned, since V1 is deprecated. |
| `kv_cache_memory_bytes`, `num_gpu_blocks_override` | Off; error if requested | Nothing: an explicit size makes measured sizing moot. |
| HiSparse | Off | HiSparse allocates its own KV cache. It would need to allocate through the extensible allocator hook. |
| Elastic EP | Off | Scale-up launches skip warmup and reuse the profiled size. New ranks would need to adopt the running engines' committed block count. |
| `LMCacheMPConnector` | Off | It shares the cache through legacy CUDA IPC, which can't export VMM memory. Needs POSIX-fd exportable allocations, LMCache's VMM IPC wrapper (`VmmCudaIPCWrapper` / `resolve_kv_wrapper_factory`) in `wrap_kv_caches`, and handling of tensors that span segments. |
| Connectors with `custom_mem_pool` (Mooncake NVLink/BAREX) | Off | The cache must come from the connector's pool. The pool would need to supply physical allocations that can be mapped into the reserved range. |
| ROCm with NIXL, Mooncake or MoRIIO | Off | UCX and ROCr can't yet register or share HIP VMM memory. Fixed upstream in openucx/ucx#12137–#12140 and ROCm/rocm-systems#13989. Once those reach the ROCm image, drop the gate and allocate exportable (POSIX-fd) memory, which is ready in a follow-up commit. |
| HIP runtimes before TheRock 7.12 | Off (probed) | Fixed upstream by ROCm/rocm-systems#2451. Nothing needed on the vLLM side. |
| Models without a KV cache | Off | Nothing to size. |
| Weight reloads without a cache-clearing pause (e.g. `reload_weights` called directly while serving) | On; the reload needs headroom from `gpu_memory_utilization`. Without it the reload warns and may run out of memory, or fails before loading when even the largest layer can't fit | Release only the cache blocks that are free: commit in finer physical chunks, and have the scheduler set aside a range of free block ids for the reload. Chunked MoE weight processing would also shrink what a reload needs. |

---

Claude was used extensively to help with this.

title: [ROCm][DSV4.1][Perf] Use AITER mHC for the delayed pre block
author: Fangzhou-Ai
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on AMD still runs its mHC block as the eager Torch reference (`vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/amd/model.py` imports `mhc_pre_delayed_torch` / `mhc_post_torch` directly). DeepSeek-V4 was moved onto the `MHCPreOp` / `MHCPostOp` dispatch layer and reaches AITER (#41946, #43950, #52737), but V4.1 was never migrated, so on MI355X it pays ~141 kernel launches per sublayer seam to Sinkhorn-normalize a 4x4 matrix.

That cost dominates decode. A per-layer census over a captured decode trace on MI355X (gfx950, TP4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash):

| launches/layer | share | source |
|---:|---:|---|
| 162 | 48.6% | mHC sinkhorn loop (4x4 comb matrix) |
| 122 | 36.6% | mHC pre/post mix + eager RMSNorm |
| 24 | 7.2% | MoE / FFN (already a fused custom op) |
| 12 | 3.6% | dtype casts/copies (bf16<->fp32) |
| 6 | 1.8% | attention + fused norm/quant |
| 4 | 1.2% | TP collective |
| 3 | 0.9% | other |

85% of the layer's 350 launches are mHC. Attributing GPU time through correlation IDs, the Sinkhorn roll-up is 37.5% of kernel time across 6,966 launches per decode step — ahead of `vllm::moe_forward_shared` at 15.4% — and `aten::sum` on `[6, 4, 4]` inputs alone is 21.5%, from 3,120 calls per step on 96-element tensors. Decode ITL on this machine degrades only 1.9x between concurrency 1 and 32 while per-GPU output throughput rises 13x, so the device is far from saturated and the per-step cost is dominated by something fixed rather than by bandwidth or compute.

## Why V4.1 cannot just reuse `MHCPreOp`

V4.1 collapses each sublayer's input with the **previous** sublayer's pre-mix, and returns the current one for the next seam. AITER's `mhc_pre` neither returns its pre-mix nor accepts an incoming one, so it cannot serve that shape as-is.

The staggering does not change the gates, though. Comparing the delayed and non-delayed formulations on identical inputs:

```
post_mix     max_abs_err = 0.000e+00   <- identical
comb_mix     max_abs_err = 0.000e+00   <- identical
layer_input  max_abs_err = 6.41e+00    <- differs (stale coefficients)
```

So the expensive part — the projection, the RMS, the gates and all 20 Sinkhorn iterations, i.e. 141 of the 142 kernels — is bit-identical between the two. Only the collapse differs.

## Approach

AITER exposes its two pre stages separately, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` consumes the unreduced split-k projection output. This PR drives those stages directly:

1. `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` — projection against `fn` plus row square-sums (1 kernel).
2. `mhc_pre_big_fuse` — post/comb gates and every Sinkhorn iteration (1 kernel). Its collapse applies the current pre-mix, which the delayed form does not want, so it is discarded.
3. New `mhc_pre_mix_triton` epilogue — recovers this seam's pre-mix from the same GEMM output and square-sums that `mhc_pre_big_fuse` already consumed, rather than repeating the projection (1 kernel).
4. `hc_collapse_triton` — the delayed collapse, with the carried coefficients (1 kernel).

New `MHCPreDelayedOp` dispatches AITER -> TileLang -> reference, mirroring `MHCPreOp`. Two cases decline AITER and fall through to TileLang: the model-entry broadcast seam (it projects a narrower operand, `x`, for which there is no AITER equivalent) and a fused RMSNorm (the composed path folds none). `hidden_size` 5120 is also outside `_AITER_MHC_FUSED_RMSNORM_SIZES`, so the fused-RMSNorm variant would not apply here regardless.

## Result

Measured on gfx950, `hidden_size=5120`, `hc_mult=4`, 20 Sinkhorn iterations, against `mhc_pre_delayed_torch`:

| tokens | launches (torch -> aiter) | worst rel err | collapse |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | 141 -> 4 | 2.4e-07 | bit-exact |
| 6 | 141 -> 4 | 5.4e-07 | bit-exact |
| 24 | 141 -> 4 | 6.6e-07 | bit-exact |
| 96 | 141 -> 4 | 8.9e-07 | bit-exact |
| 1024 | 141 -> 4 | 2.2e-06 | bit-exact |
| 16384 | 141 -> 4 | 1.2e-05 | bit-exact |

**35x fewer launches per seam**, worst relative error 1.2e-5, and the collapse is bit-exact because it is the same FP32 multiply-and-sum in both paths. `num_tokens` spans AITER's split-k choices (80 down to 2), which matters because the pre-mix is recovered from that unreduced output.

The model change also routes the three eager `(pre_mix.unsqueeze(-1) * x.float()).sum(dim=1)` collapses (including the DSpark head) through `hc_collapse_triton`, which is bit-exact for that reduction, and the `mhc_post` call sites through `MHCPostOp`.

## Test Plan

- `tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py::test_mhc_pre_delayed_rocm_aiter` — AITER vs the delayed reference over tokens 1/2/7/128/1024, both seam variants (carried and model-entry pre-mix), asserting the collapse bit-exact.
- `tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py::test_mhc_pre_delayed_rocm_aiter_declines_unsupported` — the broadcast seam and a fused norm must not silently take the AITER path. Asserted by recording which custom op runs, with a positive control so the two declines cannot pass merely because the AITER path is unavailable. (The earlier version checked this by comparing the fallback's output against a Torch reference, which fails for reasons that have nothing to do with this PR: `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_tilelang` from #56214 is broken on gfx950 with the pinned tilelang 0.1.10, reducing the RMS sum of squares inside a thread-divergent branch and recovering half of it, so `layer_input` comes out sqrt(2) high. Confirmed pre-existing by running the suite on main + #56214 with this PR reverted: the same 15 `test_deepseek_v41_mhc_pre_delayed[fused_norm=True]` cases fail there, and applying this PR leaves the count unchanged. It does not affect serving, since the AMD decoder applies `attn_norm`/`ffn_norm` separately and never passes `norm_weight` into the pre block.)
- End-to-end on MI355X (8x gfx950, TP4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), gsm8k 5-shot via lm-eval:

  | | strict-match | flexible-extract |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | baseline (eager Torch mHC) | 0.9704 ± 0.0047 | 0.9697 ± 0.0047 |
  | this PR (AITER mHC) | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 | 0.9719 ± 0.0045 |

  Within one standard error on both filters, and well clear of the 0.91 gate. The run also exercises the TileLang fallback: `hc_prenorm_gemm_tilelang` compiles 8 times on this branch and never on the baseline, which is the model-entry broadcast seam declining AITER as intended.

  Re-run on the 2026-09-11 nightly (`0.28.1rc1.dev681+ge7edf17ce` + #56214), which is main as it stands rather than the image the row above came from: **0.9719 ± 0.0045** strict-match, 0.9712 ± 0.0046 flexible-extract, 1319/1319 problems.

- Controlled A/B of the block itself, same process and identical input tensors so only the kernel choice differs, under CUDA graphs (`CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, which is how decode runs here). Microseconds per call, median of 5 x 200 iterations:

  | tokens | torch (main) | tilelang | aiter (this PR) | vs torch | vs tilelang |
  |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | 1 | 259.4 | 22.5 | **16.3** | 15.89x | 1.38x |
  | 6 | 263.7 | 23.1 | **16.6** | 15.92x | 1.39x |
  | 12 | 271.4 | 23.2 | **16.8** | 16.15x | 1.38x |
  | 24 | 282.9 | 23.4 | **16.9** | 16.74x | 1.39x |
  | 48 | 303.0 | 27.0 | **17.2** | 17.63x | 1.57x |
  | 96 | 383.3 | 31.3 | **18.0** | 21.30x | 1.74x |
  | 128 | 391.4 | 30.4 | **18.8** | 20.87x | 1.62x |

  Timed eagerly instead, the AITER path is slower than TileLang (93.4 us vs 28.8 us at 1 token): the Python wrapper in `_aiter_ops.mhc_pre_delayed` costs roughly 75 us of host time per call that a captured graph removes. It remains 7.6x-8.2x faster than the Torch reference main runs today, so eager is not a regression against the baseline this PR replaces, but trimming that host overhead is a worthwhile follow-up for `enforce_eager` users.

- The end-to-end ITL figures in the thread below are from a time-driven agentic trace and are *not* a controlled A/B; the table above is the controlled measurement.

## Notes / follow-ups

- `mhc_pre_big_fuse` still writes a collapse we discard. That redundant `[tokens, hidden_size]` bf16 store is the price of composing rather than having a native delayed kernel; it is negligible at decode shapes and ~1-2% of a prefill step. A native `mhc_pre_delayed` in AITER (have the `mhc_pre` epilogue return `pre_mix` and accept an incoming one — `pre_mix` is already computed inside the kernel as a slice of `mixes`, so no new math) would remove both it and the Triton epilogue, taking the seam to 2 launches. Happy to take that up on the AITER side as a follow-up.
- `aiter/jit/module_fused_ar_mhc.so` could additionally fuse the TP all-reduce into the mHC seam (4 collective launches per layer today). AITER already exposes `fused_allreduce_mhc_post_{only,one_stage,split}` and vLLM calls none of them. Out of scope here; tracked in the RFC below.
- Separately observed while profiling and *not* addressed by this PR: ~1,220 AITER GEMM calls per step fall back with `using torch solution:0` for the indexer shapes (`N:128,K:512` and `N:32,K:5120`), i.e. no tuned config on gfx950.

Part of a broader set of ROCm gaps for this model, collected in #56506.

title: [Perf] Fuse DSV4.1 input metadata preparation with Triton
author: WoosukKwon
body:
## Purpose

DSV4.1 prepares token-to-request mappings and flattened indexer decode metadata with chains of PyTorch operations on every model step. Replace those operations with Triton kernels that write directly into the existing buffers:

- Build token-to-request mappings from device query boundaries, including zero-length requests and padding. Device boundaries are necessary for DSpark adaptive verification, where CPU boundaries can be stale.
- Fuse SM100 varlen indexer sequence-length expansion, block-table expansion, request indices, per-request decode lengths, and padding initialization.
- Add focused correctness tests for flattened decode metadata and device token-to-request mappings, including CUDA-graph replay with stale CPU boundaries.

The replaced paths call Triton directly. No new JIT warmup-framework wrappers or registrations are added. The existing non-varlen indexer implementation is unchanged.

Duplicate-work checks: searched open PRs for `DeepSeek V4 metadata`, `indexer metadata triton`, `token_to_req_indices`, and `metadata DSpark`. No existing PR addresses this replacement. Related work is distinct: #56344 fuses attention math, #56254 changes sparse MQA-logit computation, #52628 enables ROCm fused draft-step updates, and #55692 hardens the downstream top-k block-table gather. No associated issue was supplied.

## Test Plan

Tested against `9dcf6bf344caa7793bae0b45a7896d3f8e03a01a` on four NVIDIA GB200 GPUs, with `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, TP=4, and FP8 KV cache.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/attention/test_kpool_tail_slot_mapping.py \
  tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_deepseek_v4_slot_mapping.py -q

.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/v1/attention/backend.py \
  vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py \
  vllm/v1/attention/ops/metadata.py \
  tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_deepseek_v4_slot_mapping.py
```

## Test Result

- **30 attention tests passed**, including zero-length requests, strided block tables, padding, and CUDA-graph replay with changed device boundaries and stale CPU boundaries.
- **All 24 metadata-builder cases matched baseline tensors exactly** (`rtol=atol=0`).
- Exact live metadata comparisons passed on all four ranks for ordinary decoding, DSpark, and adaptive verification, covering prefill/mixed/decode.
- Pre-commit and targeted mypy 3.12 passed; `git diff --check` passed.

### Metadata profile and microbenchmark

Measured with a local benchmark harness that is not included in this PR. CUPTI GPU timings of the five relevant builders (SWA, MLA ratios 1/2, indexer ratios 1/2), CUDA-graph replay with cold L2, batch size 16. These are metadata-only speedups.

| Case | Before (µs) | After (µs) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Prefill | 168.29 | 118.21 | 1.42× |
| Chunked prefill | 203.23 | 153.74 | 1.32× |
| Mixed | 220.42 | 72.48 | 3.04× |
| Decode | 191.10 | 46.27 | 4.13× |
| DSpark verification | 172.96 | 56.86 | 3.04× |
| DSpark adaptive verification | 167.73 | 50.37 | 3.33× |
| DSpark draft | 173.42 | 55.14 | 3.15× |
| DSpark adaptive draft | 174.75 | 58.18 | 3.00× |

Batch-16 decode GPU launches decrease from 77 to 17 per builder suite. Across three profiled iterations, CPU `aten::repeat_interleave` events decrease from 54 to zero. A full-model baseline trace also confirmed these operations occur in the input-preparation path.

### Batch-size-1 TPOT, 512 input / 128 output tokens

One repeated prompt, greedy generation, full decode CUDA graphs, compilation mode 0, FlashInfer autotuning disabled. Median of four interleaved samples per implementation on the same loaded model; engine first/last-token timestamps exclude prefill. All eight generated sequences match within each mode. The optimized adaptive run includes a retained 2.142 ms outlier.

| Mode | Before (ms/token) | After (ms/token) | Reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| No DSpark | 6.091 | 5.736 | 5.82% |
| DSpark | 1.657 | 1.407 | 15.07% |
| DSpark + adaptive | 1.781 | 1.457 | 18.20% |

### SPEED-Bench: 8K input / 1K output, DSpark adaptive enabled

NVIDIA SPEED-Bench `throughput_8k/low_entropy`, 512 source rows, normalized to exactly 8,192 DSV4.1 chat-template tokens using padding/truncation, default thinking, greedy sampling, 1,024 forced output tokens. Two runs per implementation in baseline/optimized then optimized/baseline order; `max(32, 2 × concurrency)` requests per run, identical seed and request order. At concurrency 1024, the source dataset is repeated to produce 2,048 requests per run.

Same loaded model, V2 runner, Rust frontend, Python `vllm bench serve` client, five speculative tokens, full decode graphs, compilation mode 0, FlashInfer autotuning and prefix caching disabled. Fixed server limits: `max_num_seqs=256`, `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`, `max_model_len=16384`, GPU memory utilization 0.9. GPU clocks were not locked. Metadata methods were switched outside model CUDA graphs; no profiling or validation wrappers during timing.

**Mean TTFT, including queueing**

| Concurrency | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Reduction |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 195.876 | 193.766 | 1.08% |
| 8 | 380.581 | 382.415 | -0.48% |
| 128 | 5024.837 | 4989.004 | 0.71% |
| 1024 | 128491.480 | 126614.766 | 1.46% |

**Mean TPOT, excluding TTFT**

| Concurrency | Before (ms/token) | After (ms/token) | Reduction |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 3.091 | 2.494 | 19.31% |
| 8 | 4.910 | 4.794 | 2.35% |
| 128 | 24.053 | 23.995 | 0.24% |
| 1024 | 48.804 | 48.119 | 1.40% |

**Output throughput**

| Concurrency | Before (tok/s) | After (tok/s) | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 304.9 | 373.0 | 1.223× |
| 8 | 1432.7 | 1479.2 | 1.032× |
| 128 | 4202.3 | 4224.8 | 1.005× |
| 1024 | 4898.4 | 4966.1 | 1.014× |

Latency means pool all requests across both repetitions; throughput is total output tokens / total measured duration. All 16 runs completed with exact requested token counts and zero preemptions. Concurrency-1024 TTFT includes substantial queueing behind the fixed 256 active-request limit. The concurrency-128 throughput difference is within observed run variation.

These TPOT values are not directly comparable to the earlier 512/128 test: context length, prompts, measurement boundary (streaming client vs engine), and aggregation differ. Long-prompt outputs also vary between baseline-only repetitions; universal generated-token parity is not claimed. Mean acceptance lengths before/after are 3.294/3.274, 3.177/3.153, 2.846/2.840, and 3.122/3.110 at the four concurrency levels.

### GSM8K accuracy

Optimized implementation, full 1,319-question test set, repository five-shot prompts, default thinking/high effort, greedy sampling, seed 0, maximum 16,384 output tokens, context limit 32,768. Extract answers from final text after `</think>`; unfinished reasoning is invalid.

| Mode | Correct | Accuracy | Truncated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| No DSpark | 1277 / 1319 | 96.82% | 0 |
| DSpark | 1279 / 1319 | 96.97% | 1 |
| DSpark + adaptive | 1277 / 1319 | 96.82% | 0 |

These are single-run speculative-mode evaluations of the optimized implementation, not before/after accuracy-equivalence measurements.

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex implemented the change and ran the reported checks and evaluations under the submitter's direction. This PR is a draft; human review of every changed line and human-run validation remain required before marking it ready.

title: [Perf][DSV4.1] Pad shared experts for native MegaMoE fusion
author: gcanlin
body:
## Purpose

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56217

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's 2304-wide shared expert cannot fuse with MegaMoE's routed experts padded to 2560. Pad shared weights with zeros and unit scales to enable fusion in all 40 layers, preserving checkpoint-shaped parameters and the unsupported-layout fallback.

Extends #53040. Checks of #45861 and related open PRs found no fix for this padding gap; #53567 and #54049 cover different paths.

AI assistance was used for implementation, testing, and documentation.

## Test Plan

### Deploy

Use a fresh server per arm: `VLLM_DISABLE_DSV4_MEGAMOE_SHARED_EXPERT_FUSION=1` for serial shared experts, `0` for fused. The omitted load-time hook verifies fusion state on all 8 ranks.

```bash
export MODEL=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=bond0 NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=bond0 NCCL_DEBUG=WARN
export VLLM_DISABLE_DSV4_MEGAMOE_SHARED_EXPERT_FUSION=0
uv run --active --no-project python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name dsv41-bench --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8032 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel --distributed-executor-backend mp \
  --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 128 \
  --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --seed 2026 --generation-config vllm \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_capture_sizes":[1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256],"max_cudagraph_capture_size":256}'
```

### Benchmark

Workloads follow #53040, plus 8192/1024 at C16. V4.1 uses block size 128 and FP8 indexer cache.

```bash
# Use a separate result directory for each arm.
export RESULT_DIR=results/dsv41-fused
mkdir -p "$RESULT_DIR"
bench() {
  uv run --active --no-project python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main bench serve \
    --backend vllm --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8032 --endpoint /v1/completions \
    --model dsv41-bench --tokenizer "$MODEL" --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \
    --trust-remote-code --dataset-name random \
    --random-input-len "$1" --random-output-len "$2" \
    --max-concurrency "$3" --num-prompts "$4" \
    --random-range-ratio 0 --random-prefix-len 0 --request-rate inf \
    --ignore-eos --temperature 0 --seed 42 --num-warmups 2 \
    --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,95,99 \
    --save-result --save-detailed --disable-tqdm \
    --result-dir "$RESULT_DIR" --result-filename "$5.json"
}
for repeat in 1 2 3; do bench 128 256 1 8 "decode-128-256-c1-r$repeat"; done
for repeat in 1 2 3; do bench 1024 128 1 8 "decode-1024-128-c1-r$repeat"; done
for repeat in 1 2 3; do bench 1024 128 64 128 "balanced-1024-128-c64-r$repeat"; done
for repeat in 1 2 3; do bench 8192 32 16 32 "prefill-8192-32-c16-r$repeat"; done
bench 8192 1024 16 100 kimi-8192-1024-c16-r1
```

<details>
<summary>GSM8K evaluation reproduction</summary>

Use lm-eval 0.4.12, the same fusion flag, and a fresh server per arm.

```bash
export MODEL=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=bond0 NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=bond0
export NCCL_DEBUG=WARN
export VLLM_DISABLE_DSV4_MEGAMOE_SHARED_EXPERT_FUSION=0
uv run --active --no-project python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name dsv41-gsm8k --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8031 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel --distributed-executor-backend mp \
  --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 96 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --generation-config vllm --seed 123 \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"thinking": false}'
```

Run the full test split in the lm-eval environment, with separate output directories:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=EMPTY uv run --active --no-project python -m lm_eval run \
  --model local-chat-completions \
  --model_args model=dsv41-gsm8k,base_url=http://127.0.0.1:8031/v1/chat/completions,num_concurrent=64,timeout=600,max_retries=2,max_gen_toks=1024,max_length=16384,seed=123 \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size 1 \
  --apply_chat_template --fewshot_as_multiturn \
```

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Fold the mHC post block into the delayed pre projection
author: zyongye
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1 runs an mHC post block and then the next sublayer's **delayed** pre block at every seam. Each seam therefore pays for three things: a post kernel, a split-k projection that re-reads the residual streams the post kernel just wrote, and the pre epilogue.

DSv4 already avoids the middle read: `mhc_fused_tilelang` computes the updated residual in registers and feeds the pre-norm GEMM from there. V4.1 could not reuse it, for the same reason it needed its own pre in the first place — it collapses each sublayer's input with the **previous** sublayer's pre-mix and hands the next one back, and the DSv4 fused wrapper neither accepts an incoming pre-mix nor returns one.

## Approach

`mhc_fused_post_pre_delayed_tilelang` runs the existing fused kernel and then the delayed pre epilogue (`MHC_PRE_NORM_KERNEL`, `use_pre_mix_in` / `save_pre_mix`), returning `(residual, post_mix, comb_mix, layer_input, next_pre_mix)`. Above the fused kernel's token range it falls back to exactly today's `mhc_post_tilelang` + split-k GEMM, so only the small-batch path changes shape.

Both V4.1 seams route through it, except one:

- **Attention seam** — fuses, unless Engram is injected. Engram reads the residual between the post and the pre, so the post cannot move into the projection there; that branch keeps the separate kernels.
- **FFN seam** — always fuses.
- **DSpark draft** reuses `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer`, so it inherits both.

The pre epilogue is JIT-compiled per split-k factor and warmed up from a token sweep that never produces the factors this GEMM picks, so `MHCPreNormKernel.get_warmup_keys` takes `extra_splits` and the decoder registers them. Without it the first decode step JITs inside the capture warmup.

### Tuning

The tile, split-k and block size were inherited from DSv4 unmeasured (the code carried a `TODO(gnovack): investigate autotuning these heuristics`). Sweeping all three against the separate post + split-k GEMM, on GB300 at `hc_mult=4`, CUDA-graph device time:

| tokens | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 48 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inherited config, 5120 | 8.21 | 8.01 | 8.42 | 8.82 | 10.25 | 12.73 | 13.51 | 16.81 | 19.70 |
| tuned, 5120 | **8.02** | **8.00** | 8.83 | 8.84 | **9.85** | **10.47** | **11.47** | fallback | fallback |
| unfused, 5120 | 12.74 | 12.52 | 12.72 | 12.92 | 13.32 | 13.32 | 13.37 | 13.53 | 13.49 |

Two things were wrong with the inherited constants: the 16-token cutoff was early (the fused path still wins 1.2x at 32), and one fixed tile starves the projection of parallelism as the batch grows — it is 18% off at 24-32 tokens and *slower* than the unfused path past 48. The tuned heuristic is two bands (`tile_n` 2 below 16 and 6 through 32, `n_thr` 128), within ~1-2% of the per-shape optimum for one extra compiled variant. Same bands hold at `hidden_size` 7168.

**The cutoff is 32, and it is set against a corrected baseline.** vLLM configures the TF32 projection's split count through `compute_mhc_pre_num_splits`, which buckets a good estimate into {1, 4, 16} to bound startup specializations — and that bucketing is itself 1.14-1.19x off the optimum below 128 tokens (measured: the estimator says 80 splits at one token, the bucket gives 16, the optimum is 64; rounding the estimate down to a power of two reproduces the measured best at every shape I tried). Against a GEMM given the split its own estimator computes:

| tokens | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 48 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fused | 8.44 | 8.23 | 8.83 | 9.03 | 9.85 | 10.61 | 11.29 | 13.55 |
| unfused, split as configured today | 13.13 | 12.74 | 12.76 | 13.33 | 13.35 | 13.55 | 13.56 | 13.35 |
| unfused, split=64 | 11.09 | 11.09 | 11.29 | 11.66 | 11.50 | 11.69 | 11.62 | 11.72 |
| **fused vs tuned baseline** | **1.31x** | **1.35x** | **1.28x** | **1.29x** | **1.17x** | **1.10x** | **1.03x** | 0.86x |

So the honest claim is 1.3x at decode widths, 1.17x at 16, break-even at 32. The cutoff sits at the break-even point rather than where a slow baseline would have put it (48, which is a 14% *loss* against a tuned GEMM). Fixing that split heuristic is worth 5-19% on every unfused seam — all prefill, all large-batch decode, and DSv4 as well as DSv4.1 — but it belongs in its own PR, not bundled here, since it changes a shared helper and a second model's hot path.

It is shared with the DSv4 wrapper, which uses the same kernel at the same shapes. The heuristic now also declines shapes the kernel cannot tile evenly (`mix_size % tile_n`, `hidden_size % (n_splits * n_thr)`) and falls back instead — previously those silently dropped whole tiles and k-slices.

## Relationship to the other open mHC PRs

- **#56255 (Mega-mHC from DeepGEMM)** — same two call sites, same 5-tuple refactor, same Engram carve-out. Its `mhc_shifted_post_pre` dispatches to DeepGEMM `mega_mhc` when `device_capability_family(100) and hidden_size % 1024 == 0 and hc_mult == 4`, and **falls back to the unfused pair otherwise** — which is what this PR replaces. The two are complementary and land cleanly together: benchmarked head to head below, the TileLang fusion is faster at small batch, Mega-mHC is faster at large batch. If both land, the right end state is one dispatcher picking between them by token count, and I am happy to write that as a follow-up (or fold this into #56255, author's preference).
- **#56513 (ROCm)** — same idea via AITER `mhc_fused_post_pre_gemm_sqrsum`, on `_aiter_ops.py` / `mhc/aiter.py` / `layers/mhc.py` / `amd/model.py`. No file overlap with this PR beyond the shared test file.
- **#56611** — a different optimization (overlapping the coefficient GEMM with attention/FFN), env-gated.

### Mega-mHC comparison

DeepGEMM 2.8.0 (`66081d4c`), GB300, `hc_mult=4`, `hidden_size=5120`, CUDA-graph device time per seam. Both paths are graph-capturable; `mega_mhc` lazily allocates per-stream split barriers and asserts that happens outside capture, so it must be warmed on the capture stream first (which vLLM's pre-capture warmup iteration does).

| tokens | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 48 | 64 | 128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| unfused | 13.13 | 12.84 | 13.02 | 13.54 | 13.32 | 13.54 | 13.54 | 13.55 | 13.56 | 13.97 |
| fused TileLang (this PR) | **8.43** | **8.22** | **8.83** | **8.84** | **9.65** | 10.47 | 11.28 | 13.10 | 13.54 | 13.96 |
| Mega-mHC (#56255) | 10.19 | 10.46 | 10.07 | 10.67 | 10.47 | 10.47 | **10.88** | **11.09** | **11.26** | **11.82** |

This PR is 1.08–1.27x faster than Mega-mHC at 1–16 tokens; they cross at ~24; Mega-mHC is 1.18–1.20x faster at 48+. A `torch.profiler` kernel-time breakdown agrees (at 1 token: 4.32 µs fused kernel + 5.03 µs epilogue, against a single 10.44 µs `sm100_mega_mhc_impl`).

Numerically the two differ in one place: the fused TileLang kernel projects the **FP32** post result it holds in registers, while Mega-mHC and the unfused path project its BF16 rounding. Against an FP32 reference at 8 tokens, max abs error: residual 9.77e-4 for all three; coefficients 9.25e-4 / 1.78e-3 (this PR) against 1.98e-4 / 3.46e-4 (Mega-mHC and unfused). This is inherited from the DSv4 kernel, not new — the stored residual streams are bit-identical either way.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py -v
```

New `test_deepseek_v41_mhc_fused_post_pre_delayed` (0/1/8/128 tokens x 4096/7168 hidden x carried/absent pre-mix) asserts the post-mapped residual and the collapsed layer input are **bit-identical** to `mhc_post_tilelang` + `mhc_pre_delayed_tilelang`, and the coefficients match an FP32-post torch reference to 1e-5 on the fused path. Plus a `torch.library.opcheck` case and a CUDA-graph capture/replay case, since decode replays this op from a graph. `test_deepseek_v41_decoder_mixes_match_torch` now covers both routes through the decoder.

## Test Result

```
164 passed, 23 skipped in 53.80s     # tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py, GB300
```

`pre-commit run --all-files` clean on the changed files (ruff, ruff-format, mypy-3.10).

### Model evaluation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP4 GB300, gsm8k 5-shot via `mqa-run --api-type completions --temperature 0 --max-tokens 1024`, n=1319, `num_request_errors: 0` and 0 null answers in every run:

| arm | runs | exact_match/flexible |
|---|---|---|
| this PR | 3 | 0.9242, 0.9325, 0.9204 |
| unfused baseline, same serve config | 2 | 0.9348, 0.9249 |

The baseline arm's own two runs differ by 0.99 pt, so the arms' ranges overlap and the 0.42 pt difference in means sits inside the measured noise floor for this config (batching nondeterminism at concurrency 32). Dashboard history for this model is median 0.9314, p25–p75 0.9287–0.9333.

## Second and third commits: aux hidden states for draft models

Once the post lives inside the next layer's pre, the standalone `mhc_post_tilelang` the model ran per aux-capture layer is recomputing a residual that already exists. The second commit takes `mean(dim=1)` from the fused call behind a `capture_previous_aux` flag and drops the duplicate post — the approach of **#55575** (DeepSeek-V4), which only becomes available to V4.1 once V4.1 has the fused seam.

Two seams keep the standalone post: the Engram seam captures *before* the injection (matching the post it replaces — aux consumers read the stream before Engram touches it), and the last layer on a rank has no successor to fold into, so it takes its mean from the final post that runs anyway.

I did **not** port #55575's companion change that skips the `_mtp_hidden_buffer` copy when aux hidden states are present: that depends on its `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py` edit, which is model-agnostic and would collide with #55575 in a shared file. It should follow from that PR, not this one.

### Third commit: fold the stream mean into the collapse

That leaves one pass still standing: `mean(dim=1)` over `[T, hc, H]`. The collapse in the pre epilogue already reads every one of those streams to weight them by the carried pre-mix, and the aux value is the *unweighted* mean of the same data — so the third commit accumulates it in that pass, behind a `write_aux` specialization so non-draft setups compile and run exactly what they did before. The buffer is allocated only when the caller asks.

Standalone `mean(dim=1)` is not cheap at scale (measured on GB300, `[T, 4, 5120]` bf16): 2.10 µs at 1 token, 17.9 µs at 1024, **72.1 µs at 4096**, 141.8 µs at 8192 — per capture layer, per step. Folded, the aux-capture seam costs:

| tokens | 1 | 8 | 32 | 128 | 1024 | 4096 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| seam + separate mean | 10.55 | 11.50 | 13.94 | 17.65 | 60.25 | 209.32 |
| seam + folded mean | **8.43** | **9.04** | **11.50** | **13.74** | **40.88** | **140.63** |
| saved (µs) | 2.13 | 2.46 | 2.45 | 3.90 | 19.38 | 68.70 |

Both epilogues carry the path — the one that applies RMSNorm and the plain one — so no caller falls back to a torch mean. Bit-exact against `torch.mean` on both, at 1/8/33/128/1024 tokens and 5120/7168 hidden, with every other output of the op unchanged when capturing is on. The Engram seam still uses a separate mean, since its aux is the *pre*-injection post and the epilogue runs after Engram.

### DSpark verification

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP4 GB300, `{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":3,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}` with **real** verification (not `synthetic`), 8 fixed prompts at `temperature 0`, same branch with and without the commit:

| | drafts | draft tokens | accepted | rate | length | per position |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| neither commit | 106 | 318 | 204 | 0.6415 | 2.9245 | 92 / 64 / 48 |
| harvest | 106 | 318 | 204 | 0.6415 | 2.9245 | 92 / 64 / 48 |
| harvest + folded mean | 106 | 318 | 204 | 0.6415 | 2.9245 | 92 / 64 / 48 |

Byte-identical generated text (sha256 of the concatenated completions matches) and identical acceptance counters, which is the end-to-end statement that the harvested tensor is the one the draft model used to get. `test_deepseek_v41_capture_previous_aux` pins the same thing at the unit level with `atol=0`, for both the fused and Engram seams.

That probe pins the tensor exactly but is only 8 prompts, so both arms were also run through **GPQA-Diamond at full size** — 198 questions x 4 epochs = 792 samples per arm, chat path with thinking on, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, `max_tokens` 57344, concurrency 128, same TP4 GB300 node:

| arm | headline | answered-only | pass@4 | request errors | truncated | null answers | empty@stop |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DSpark k=5, real verification | 0.9104 | 0.9138 | 0.9545 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| no spec decode | 0.9129 | 0.9163 | 0.9495 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 0 |

Acceptance over that run, from the engine's own counters rather than a synthetic profile: **1,467,764 drafts, 7,338,820 draft tokens, 3,207,521 accepted — rate 0.4371, acceptance length 3.185** of a possible 6.

**Both arms are this branch**, so this is not a before/after for the PR; the before/after is the gsm8k table above. What it establishes is that the code these two commits touch carries 1.47M drafts at an accuracy indistinguishable from the no-draft arm: 2 questions of 792, where one question is 0.126 pt and the sign flips between exact_match and pass@4. Finished generations ran to a median of 2239 tokens with a p90 of 16232 and a max of 56320 against the 57344 cap, so the three truncations per arm are a genuine budget limit rather than a loop — identical in both arms, so they do not move the comparison.

## AI assistance

This change was written with AI assistance (Claude Code). I reviewed every changed line, ran the tests and benchmarks above myself, and can defend the change end to end.

title: [ROCm][DSv4.1][Perf] Replace the Torch prefill combine with the shared combine_topk_swa_indices kernel
author: JohnQin-llm
body:
## Purpose

ROCm's V4.1 sparse prefill combines the top-k and sliding-window indices with ordinary Torch indexing, about ninety small ops per call. This sends it to the shared `combine_topk_swa_indices` kernel the CUDA path already uses: one launch, and it brings the SWA bounded-replay bound, the SWA-only guard and the JIT warmup with it. The ROCm-only Triton kernel and the Torch path are removed.

## What changes

- `amd/rocm.py`: prefill calls `combine_topk_swa_indices` from `common/ops/cache_utils.py`.
- The shared kernel gains two guards that leave well-formed input untouched:
  - both lengths clamp at 0. Warmup batches reach it with a negative position, and the Torch path had `clamp_min(0)` for that;
  - a negative top-k index stays -1 instead of becoming `M * b - 1`, a row of the previous request.

## Tests

`tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_triton_attn_dsv4.py` compares the kernel against the Torch path it replaces, copied over unchanged so the reference cannot drift toward the kernel: `seq_len` below `query_len`, `seq_len == 0`, `compress_ratio == 0`, a non-zero `query_start_loc[0]`, -1 candidates, and windows 64/128/256. It also checks that ROCm dispatches to the shared kernel. `test_v41_combine_topk_swa_stops_at_replay_start` covers the replay bound on that kernel. It runs on ROCm as well, and now includes the shorter replay chunk from #59136 (co-authored by @yuzhouo7), so #59136 is no longer needed.

```bash
pytest -q tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_triton_attn_dsv4.py
pytest -q tests/v1/attention/test_deepseek_v4_swa_visible.py -k stops_at_replay_start
```

title: [Bugfix][NIXL] Report a full prefix cache hit as finished
author: jyizheng
body:
Reopens #54714 (accidentally closed by a bad force-push that orphaned the branch history; GitHub would not let it reopen). Same single commit, with @njhill's review addressed: `awaiting_kvs` gating with tests for the abort seed and `num_external_tokens == 0` readback, plus the cosmetic comments (condensed comments, collapsed tuple assignment).

## Purpose

`_read_blocks` returns early when the local block list is empty — D already holds the KV, so only the producer needs telling — and it returns without recording anything. `get_finished` builds `done_recving` from `_recving_transfers` and `_failed_recv_reqs`, so the request is named in neither.

The scheduler has no other way to release it:

```python
if request.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS:
    if request.request_id not in self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids:
        return False
```

There is no timeout. The request stays in `skipped_waiting` — a queue counted in neither `num_running_reqs` nor `num_waiting_reqs` — holding the blocks it was allocated, for the life of the process.

Recording an empty transfer list is enough: `_pop_done_transfers` already treats a request with no outstanding handles as complete. This does it whether or not the notification lands, since the KV is local either way and a failed notification only costs the producer a timeout before it frees its own blocks, which is what the existing message says.

## How it showed up

A 10-prefill/3-decode deployment under saturation. Restarting peers made `send_notif` fail 122 times in half an hour, and each of those requests was abandoned. The three decode workers ended up holding 73–85% of their KV cache with zero running and zero waiting requests and no traffic anywhere on the deployment, until their liveness probes killed them. Only a restart cleared it.

The state is hard to see from outside: with the requests parked in `skipped_waiting`, both queue-depth gauges read zero while most of the cache is spoken for.

## Test Plan

`test_full_prefix_cache_hit_is_reported_finished`, parametrised over the notification succeeding and failing, asserts the request reaches `done_recving`.

## Test Result

Against the unpatched worker the request is reported in neither case; patched, in both.

title: [Perf] Parallelize mHC pre-norm JIT warmup
author: WoosukKwon
body:
## Purpose

Compile independent mHC pre-norm warmup variants concurrently. Add a `compile_many()` hook to `VllmJitKernel`, retain sequential compilation by default, and use TileLang's `par_compile()` for missing `MHCPreNormKernel` variants with at most four compiler workers per process. Cached variants are retained and duplicate keys are removed. TileLang elaborates the modules serially before compiling them in parallel.

The existing open PRs #51802 and #49707 address mHC warmup coverage. This change preserves the existing registered keys and runtime dispatch, and changes how those keys are compiled. Searches for parallel JIT compilation and `par_compile` found no open PR implementing the same change. This PR is independent of the dummy-initialization change in #56682.

## Test Plan

```bash
PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/test_jit_warmup.py tests/kernels/test_mhc_jit_warmup.py -q
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files vllm/model_executor/warmup/jit_warmup.py vllm/model_executor/kernels/mhc/warmup.py
```

Also exercised the existing `test_deepseek_v41_mhc_pre_delayed` reference and CUDA graph replay assertions after batch warmup, for broadcast, identity, and carried pre-mix (33 tokens, fused normalization, DeepGEMM enabled, 20 Sinkhorn iterations).

## Test Result

60 existing warmup tests passed in 18.86 seconds. All three GPU reference/CUDA graph replay cases passed on GB200 after batch warmup. Applicable pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed. No test additions are included.

On GB200, nine cold-cache DSV4.1 pre-norm variants (hidden size 5120, hc_mult 4, three input/pre-mix configurations and split counts 1/4/16) compiled in:

| Compilation | Wall time |
|---|---:|
| Sequential | 95.03s |
| Four compiler workers | 43.39s |

This is a 2.19x speedup for the isolated compilation stage. These are single-run measurements excluding imports/key enumeration, with separate empty TileLang caches; host-side engine initialization was concurrent, so they are exploratory measurements rather than a controlled end-to-end startup comparison. Generated CUDA source sets matched between the two runs.

A later TP4 real-weight DSV4.1 startup and greedy completion succeeded with this change. Its registry mHC phase had five variants already compiled by profiling and compiled the remaining four in parallel in approximately 14 seconds. No model-quality benchmark was run; this changes compilation scheduling, not kernel math. Full-engine startup speedup is not claimed.

AI assistance was used for diagnosis, implementation, and validation.

title: [Feature][Humming] Humming feature integration
author: jinzhen-lin
body:
This PR expands Humming quantization support and integrates a unified input processing kernel.

#### 1. Hadamard transforms for online quantization

Enable Hadamard transforms by setting `hadamard_block_size` in `VLLM_HUMMING_ONLINE_QUANT_CONFIG`.

#### 2. SM120/SM121 support

Add support for NVFP4, MXFP4, and MXFP8, including the non-public `float4e0m3` and `float8e3m4` data types, see https://github.com/vllm-project/humming/pull/41 .

#### 3. Additional input quantization modes

Support `static_per_tensor`, `static_tensor_dynamic_group`, and `dynamic_group_tensor`. The latter two primarily serve NVFP4 quantization.

#### 4. Checkpoint quantization and input schema fallback

Honor checkpoint input quantization settings and automatically fall back to a higher-precision input schema when the device does not support the configured activation quantization type.

To retain the original WNA16 behavior, set:

```bash
export VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype":"bfloat16"}'
```

Input schemas explicitly specified through `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` disable fallback by default. Unsupported configurations raise an error unless `"allow_fallback": true` is explicitly specified.

#### 5. Unified `process_input` kernel

Support fused combinations of optional activation function, Hadamard transforms, and input quantization across multiple layouts.

Custom activations support `unary`, `binary_split`, and `binary_interleaved` modes, with implementations supplied as CUDA C++ expressions.

| Path | Gemm Type | Fused operations | Padding handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dense | `dense` | Optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | — |
| MoE gate/up | `indexed` | Optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | — |
| MoE gate/up | `grouped_contiguous` | MoE permutation, optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | Skip invalid padding tokens in EP |
| MoE gate/up | `grouped_mask` | Optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | Skip invalid padding tokens |
| MoE down | `indexed` | Activation, optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | Skip invalid padding tokens in EP |
| MoE down | `grouped_contiguous` | Activation, optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | Skip invalid padding tokens in EP |
| MoE down | `grouped_mask` | Activation, optional Hadamard transform and input quantization | Skip invalid padding tokens |

#### 6. Additional scatter indices

Extend `moe_permute` and `moe_align_block_size` to return the `scatter_idx` required by `process_input`.

#### 7. Humming mxfp6 backend

Add `HummingMxFp6LinearKernel`.

#### 8. Humming utility refactoring

Refactor `humming_utils.py`, moving some validation and conversion logic into the Humming library.

#### 9. Type annotations

Add type annotations to `vllm/utils/humming.py`.

title: [watermark] compatibility validation
author: TQCB
body:
## Summary

- centralize engine and request compatibility policy in `VllmConfig._check_supports_watermarking(config) -> bool`
- treat omitted or `true` request watermarking as enabled by default, with `false` as the sole explicit opt-out
- warn once and fall back to unwatermarked generation when the engine or request mode cannot apply watermarking
- cover missing engine configuration, greedy decoding, trace replay, and beam search with the same warning-and-fallback policy
- centralize request-time resolution in engine admission, applying the result only to the request-local copy so reused caller parameters cannot carry a decision across requests or engines
- validate supported speculative-decoding methods and reject incompatible draft, rejection, parallel-drafting, and custom-sampler configurations
- keep explicit seeds and parallel sampling (`n > 1`) supported, with documented caveats for plain Gumbel diversity and seeded fallback sampling
- preserve the optional request value across OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, speech, realtime, batch, beam-search, and direct engine paths until centralized admission resolves it
- explicitly opt internal bookkeeping requests out: language detection, generative scoring, KV-transfer cleanup, and mixed prefill/decode warmup
- add CPU contract tests plus accelerator smoke tests for seeded parallel sampling, prefix caching, grammars, tool calling, TP/PP/DP, mixed batches, API propagation, and internal request paths

## Request behavior

- `watermarking=None`: request watermarking by default
- `watermarking=True`: request watermarking explicitly
- `watermarking=False`: opt out

If watermarking cannot be applied, vLLM warns once for that incompatibility and continues with the request unwatermarked. Transcription, translation, and realtime requests therefore warn once and continue unwatermarked with their default greedy decoding.

## Test plan

- focused impacted suite excluding the unavailable optional Cohere SDK: `139 passed, 15 skipped, 412 deselected`
- all pre-commit hooks for touched files pass, including Ruff, markdownlint, and mypy
- Cohere conversion tests were not collected locally because the optional `cohere` SDK is not installed
- accelerator smoke modules collect successfully; CUDA/GPU execution remains pending

title: [watermarking] add context deduplication support to speculative decoding
author: TQCB
body:
## Purpose

Extend generation-side watermark context deduplication to speculative decoding.

- Build target verification contexts from committed and proposed draft tokens.
- Detect repeated contexts in committed history and earlier positions of the same speculative block while respecting `deduplicate_contexts_max_history`.
- Use the ordinary draft proposal at repeated contexts before running the unchanged acceptance test.
- Use the ordinary draw from the existing residual or target distribution for repeated rejection-recovery and bonus contexts.
- Leave disabled and greedy requests on their existing paths.
- Fuse committed-history and speculative-local context checks to avoid launch-heavy PyTorch bookkeeping.
- Fuse ordinary and watermarked draft sampling into one vocabulary reduction while preserving the pre-temperature draft-logit cache.

This keeps the standard `min(1, q/p)` acceptance rule and does not force rejection at repeated contexts.

## Test Plan

- Run the focused CPU watermark/configuration tests.
- Run all pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed files.
- Run the watermark suite and CPU/Triton parity tests on an H100.
- Microbenchmark draft, target-mask, rejection-resampling, and fused draft-sampling overhead separately.

## Test Result

- `python -m pytest -q tests/watermarking/test_watermarking.py`: 51 passed, 18 skipped locally.
- Watermarking and Gumbel suites on an H100: 95 passed.
- Fused draft sampling exactly matches the previous ordinary/watermarked selection, including draft-specific RNG streams and bit-exact pre-temperature logits caching.
- Applicable Ruff, formatting, syntax, mypy, configuration, accelerator API, and sign-off checks: passed.

### H100 microbenchmark

The new fused draft-sampling path was compared with the previous sequence—ordinary draft sampling with cache write, watermarked sampling, then `torch.where`. Both paths include temperature preprocessing and draft-logit cache writes, use float16 logits with vocabulary size 32768, and report the median of five 1000-iteration measurements.

| Batch size | Previous two-pass path | Fused mixed path | Time saved per draft step | Sampling-section speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 91.31 us | 57.40 us | 33.91 us | 1.59x |
| 8 | 92.96 us | 58.14 us | 34.82 us | 1.60x |
| 32 | 92.62 us | 58.13 us | 34.49 us | 1.59x |

These are isolated eager-execution microbenchmark timings, not end-to-end inference throughput measurements.
