title: [ROCm][Perf] Enable HCA dual-stream overlap for DeepSeek-V4
author: shen-shanshan
body:
## Purpose #51794 enabled multi-stream overlap for CSA layers on ROCm but left HCA layers (main compressor present, no indexer) single-stream, because the ROCm attention subclass dropped its aux streams whenever no indexer exists. On `gfx950` the HCA main compressor is a large fraction of the attention-layer decode time and is fully independent of the query/KV chain: both branches only read the layer input (`hidden_states`) plus their own weights and state, and nothing on the default-stream chain consumes the compressor's outputs until the sparse attention. For HCA layers the attention forward now forks inside the gated region: - **Default stream:** fused wqa/wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert. - **Aux stream 0:** HCA main compressor (fused wkv/wgate score GEMM + DeepseekCompressor). The streams join before the sparse MLA attention, which reads the compressed KV cache and the SWA window. The serial MHC fused post+pre prelude keeps running on the default stream ahead of the fork; the fork's start event orders the aux chain after it. ## Trace Comparison (take `conc=4` as an example) Before: After (**7.47%** faster for HCA layer): ## Test Plan Benchmark with SA InferenceX `8k1k` workload with server launch commands below: ```bash export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1 export AITER_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \ --port 8333 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --max-model-len 9472 \ --max-num-seqs 512 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --async-scheduling \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --moe-backend aiter \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \ --compilation-config '{"mode":3,"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' ``` Accuracy test with `gsm8k` dataset using `lm_eval`: ```bash lm_eval \ --model local-completions \ --model_args model=/shared/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro,base_url=http://0.0.0.0:8333/v1/completions,num_concurrent=64,max_retries=10,max_gen_toks=2048,timeout=60000 \ --batch_size auto \ --tasks gsm8k \ --num_fewshot 5 \ --output_path . 2>&1 | tee -a eval.log lm_eval \ --model local-completions \ --model_args model=/shared/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro,base_url=http://0.0.0.0:8333/v1/completions,num_concurrent=256,max_retries=10,max_gen_toks=2048,timeout=60000 \ --batch_size auto \ --tasks gsm8k \ --num_fewshot 30 \ --output_path . 2>&1 | tee -a eval.log ``` > [!NOTE] > All tests based on latest `nightly-rocm100` image. ## Test Result ### Benchmark | Conc | Version | Output token throughput (tok/s) | Change | Mean TTFT (ms) | Change | Mean TPOT (ms) | Change | | ---: | :------ | ------------------------------: | :-----: | -------------: | :------: | -------------: | :-----: | | 1 | Main | 69.61 | — | 429.89 | — | 13.92 | — | | 1 | This PR | 72.00 | 3.43% ↑ | 365.36 | 15.01% ↓ | 13.51 | 2.95% ↓ | | 4 | Main | 229.96 | — | 454.21 | — | 16.50 | — | | 4 | This PR | 236.13 | 2.68% ↑ | 445.49 | 1.92% ↓ | 16.07 | 2.61% ↓ | | 16 | Main | 642.98 | — | 711.37 | — | 23.36 | — | | 16 | This PR | 653.01 | 1.56% ↑ | 708.66 | 0.38% ↓ | 22.99 | 1.58% ↓ | | 64 | Main | 1298.06 | — | 1600.01 | — | 46.73 | — | | 64 | This PR | 1310.56 | 0.96% ↑ | 1601.33 | 0.08% ↑ | 46.28 | 0.96% ↓ | In summary, the PR provides a positive overall performance impact, primarily through higher output token throughput and lower TPOT. The improvements are particularly noticeable at low concurrency, while at high concurrency the throughput and TPOT gains remain positive but become smaller. The TTFT results at high concurrency are essentially neutral, with no meaningful regression. ### Accuracy Test Conc=64, numshot=5 (default): |Tasks|Version| Filter |n-shot| Metric | |Value | |Stderr| |-----|------:|----------------|-----:|-----------|---|-----:|---|-----:| |gsm8k| 3|flexible-extract| 5|exact_match|↑ |0.9477|± |0.0061| | | |strict-match | 5|exact_match|↑ |0.9484|± |0.0061| Conc=256, numshot=30: |Tasks|Version| Filter |n-shot| Metric | |Value | |Stderr| |-----|------:|----------------|-----:|-----------|---|-----:|---|-----:| |gsm8k| 3|flexible-extract| 30|exact_match|↑ |0.9515|± |0.0059| | | |strict-match | 30|exact_match|↑ |0.9522|± |0.0059| Full GSM8K evaluation on this change (1,319 examples) and both results exceed the required 94% threshold. ---

title: [Metrics][KV Offload] Add vllm:kv_offload_config_info - generic info metrics for offloading the offloading connector
author: amirfr3
body:
## Purpose

An offloading spec holds static configuration that no metric reports. The CPU cache
exports usage only (`vllm:kv_offload_cpu_cache_usage_perc` and the read/write
variants). A secondary tier exports nothing. So an operator cannot read the capacity,
the mount path, or the eviction policy of a tier from `/metrics`. Every spec that
adds such a fact today must also add its own metric, its own label list, and its own
emission call.

This adds `vllm:kv_offload_config_info`, a gauge with the constant value `1`, and two
hooks. The spec declares the label names. The manager fills the values.

```python
class OffloadingSpec(ABC):
    @classmethod
    def config_info_keys(cls, extra_config: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return ()


class OffloadingManager(ABC):
    def config_info(self) -> Sequence[Mapping[str, str | int | float | bool]]:
        return [{}]
```

`SecondaryTierManager` carries both methods, with the same defaults. Its
`config_info()` returns one mapping, because one tier gives one series.

### One series for each tier

The metric name carries no tier identity. One `tier` label tells the series apart. The
label value comes from `TieringMetricsTracker.tier_label()`, so it equals the `tier`
label that the tiering counters and histograms already carry. An operator joins the
two metrics on that label.

| Source | Name the tier declares and fills | Series in `/metrics` |
|---|---|---|
| a standalone CPU manager | `cpu_num_chunks` | one series, no `tier` label |
| the primary tier of a tiering manager | `cpu_num_chunks` | `tier="0:primary"` |
| secondary tier 0, tier type `example` | `example_info` | `tier="1:example"` |
| secondary tier 1, tier type `example` | `example_info` | `tier="2:example"` |

Two tiers of one type add a series. They add no label name. A new tier keeps the label
set of the other tiers, so an existing query survives.

A tier cannot know its own index, so a tier declares and fills its own names only.
`TieringOffloadingSpec.config_info_keys()` declares the union of the names of every
configured tier, plus `tier`. `TieringOffloadingManager.config_info()` adds the `tier`
label to each mapping. The label name is the constant `TIER_LABEL` in
`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`, and the tiering metrics use the same
constant. The manager also writes an empty value for each name that another tier
owns, because every series of one metric carries every label.

This shape replaces the earlier revision of this pull request, which put the tier
index in the label name, as `tier1_fs_path`. The helper `config_info_prefix()` that
built such a name is gone.

The gauge is per-engine, like the other offloading gauges. Each engine reports its own
managers, not the instance total.

**This pull request publishes two facts, as a start.** `CPUOffloadingManager`
publishes `cpu_num_chunks`, the number of chunk slots in the CPU tier. The in-tree
`example` secondary tier publishes `example_info`, the value of its `custom_param`, as
a worked example for a tier author. #53902 adds the other CPU facts. The tiering
compose is here, so an out-of-tree secondary tier gets its series today.

A `ConfigInfo` dataclass in `vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py` holds the facts of one
manager. Each field name is a label name, so one class gives both the declared names
and the filled values. `CPUOffloadingInfo` and `ExampleTierInfo` use it.

### Why the spec declares and the manager fills

`OffloadPromMetrics` runs in the API-server process. That process holds the spec
class and the `kv_connector_extra_config` dict. It never builds a spec, and it never
holds a manager. So `config_info_keys()` is a classmethod, and it takes the same dict
that the spec itself receives. The manager holds the built configuration, so it owns
every value. A new fact costs one dict entry there.

Notes:

1. The gauge exists from `__init__`, next to every other offloading metric, so the
   metric never appears late. A labelled gauge makes no child until `.labels()` runs,
   so an engine that never reports exposes no series.
2. `_observe_info()` cannot raise on a disagreement. It builds the value tuple from
   the declared names alone, so the arity always matches. An exception in
   `_get_prometheus_metric()` ends the output handler. Every in-flight request then
   waits forever while the process stays up.
3. `_observe_info()` renders each value with `str()`, so a `bool` reads `True`. That
   matches `CacheConfig.metrics_info()` in `vllm/config/cache.py`.

### The spec is the authority

The two sides need not agree on the order, because the frontend reads each declared
name out of the payload. On a name disagreement:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| the spec declares a name, and no tier fills it | the label value is `""` |
| a tier fills a name that the spec never declared | the frontend drops it |
| either case | one `warning_once` line for each engine |

The check runs once for each payload, and not once for each tier, because the
declaration holds the names of every tier. A name that one tier owns reads empty on
the other tiers by design. So the check cannot see a name that one tier declares and
then leaves unfilled. The docstrings of `OffloadingManager.config_info()` and
`SecondaryTierManager.config_info()` tell an implementer to assert the agreement in a
test, which catches that case in CI.

### How the info reaches the API-server process

1. `OffloadingConnectorScheduler.get_stats()` calls `manager.config_info()` one time.
   It writes the result to the stats payload under `_StatsKey.INFO`. A `_info_sent`
   flag stops a repeat. A Prometheus child keeps the values it received, so one send
   is enough.
2. `is_empty()` counts `INFO`. `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` drops an empty
   scheduler payload, and the first payload usually carries no observation.
3. `aggregate()` copies `INFO` from `other`. The scheduler payload is the `other` in
   `kv_connector_stats.aggregate(scheduler_kv_connector_stats)`. Without this copy
   the info dies on every step that also transfers, and `_info_sent` blocks a second
   try.
4. `reduce()` ignores `INFO`, because the info belongs to Prometheus alone.
   `KVConnectorLogging.log()` now skips an empty summary, so an info-only payload
   adds no bare `KV Transfer metrics: ` line to the interval log.
5. `_observe_info()` aligns each tier mapping with the declared names, under the rules
   in **The spec is the authority**. It reports one series for each mapping.

`INFO` holds label names, not metric names, so it is no metric section. A tier that
rewrites its own metric names now walks the new `OffloadingConnectorStats.metric_sections()`,
and not `stats.data.values()`. `KVCRSecondaryTierManager` is the one such tier in tree.

### `multiprocess_mode="mostrecent"`

`_create_metric` never passed `multiprocess_mode`, so every offloading gauge took
`Gauge`'s default `sum`. Stats attach to one client's outputs per step, so `sum`
multiplies a per-engine constant by the number of frontends under
`--api-server-count > 1`. The default now lives on `OffloadingGaugeMetadata`, which is
`Gauge`-only, so a counter or a histogram cannot set it. Counters and histograms stay
as they are, because their deltas reach exactly one frontend per step. This also
corrects the seven offloading gauges that exist today, all of them per-engine
snapshots.

### Relation to #53902

#53902 adds three fields to `CPUOffloadingInfo`: `cpu_blocks_per_chunk`,
`cpu_kv_bytes_per_chunk`, and `cpu_capacity_tokens_at_max_len`.

## Test Plan

- **Unit tests** - 26 new tests, over five sections of the change.

  - **The declaration in `OffloadPromMetrics.__init__`** - the spec keys become the
    gauge label names, and only a gauge takes `multiprocess_mode`.
  - **`_observe_info()`** - the frontend reads the payload by name, reports one series
    for each mapping and each engine, blanks a declared name that no tier fills, and
    drops a name that the spec never declared.
  - **The transport to the frontend** - `is_empty()` passes an info-only payload,
    `aggregate()` keeps the info, `metric_sections()` leaves the info out, an
    info-only payload writes no log line, and the real scheduler sends the info once.
  - **The CPU manager** - `CPUOffloadingManager` fills the names that
    `CPUOffloadingSpec` declares.
  - **The tiering compose** - the spec declares the union of the tier names, the
    manager fills one mapping for each tier under the `tier` label, each tier reads
    its own config dict, and a tier cannot declare the reserved `tier` label.

  Files: `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_metrics.py` holds 17,
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_tiering_offloading.py` holds 8, and
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_manager.py` holds 1.

- **Full offloading suites** - every test under `tests/v1/kv_offload` and
  `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector`, on macOS and on Linux. Each
  failure also occurs on `main`, or needs a GPU.

- **Real server** - one NVIDIA H100 80GB, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, and
  `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a CPU primary tier plus one `example` secondary tier.
  The run scrapes `/metrics` after three completion requests.

- **Data-parallel run** - two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, which also starts
  two API server processes. The scrape returns one series for each engine. This run
  covers an earlier revision of the branch.

- **Model evaluations: not applicable.** Metrics only. `get_stats()` writes one
  constant mapping to a payload that the scheduler already emits on every step. No
  scheduling decision, no KV-cache placement, no transfer path, and no model output
  changes. Nobody ran an evaluation, because no output can differ.

- **Not verified.** No run of the unit tests used a GPU. The 32 tests in
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_gpu_worker.py` need CUDA or XPU, so they fail on both
  CPU-only hosts. This pull request does not change the GPU worker.

## Test Result

Full offloading suites:

```
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_offload \
    tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector \
    --ignore-glob='*test_swa_eviction*' -q -rs
```

| Host | Revision | Result |
|---|---|---|
| macOS, no GPU | `e358020cd5`, on `main` `8cc9aa5ad3` | `1056 passed, 74 failed, 15 skipped` |
| macOS, no GPU | `main` `ccfd1cea75` | the same 74 test ids fail |
| Linux pod, no GPU, `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu` | `ae199eedc2`, an earlier revision | `1088 passed, 32 failed, 25 skipped` |

- **macOS, 74 failures.** 32 are in `cpu/test_gpu_worker.py`, and 42 are in
  `cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py`. The same 74 test ids fail on `main`, so the
  platform causes them, and this pull request does not.
- **Linux, 32 failures.** All 32 are in `cpu/test_gpu_worker.py`, and each one stops
  at `assert gpu_tensor.is_cuda or gpu_tensor.is_xpu`. On Linux,
  `cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py` passes 51 of 51.
- **Linux, 25 skips.** The host has no CUDA, ROCm, or Triton (11), no `fs_io_C` (11),
  and no `kvcr` backend (1). Two more skips come from an empty backend parameter.
- **Revisions.** After `ae199eedc2`, the branch changed only docstrings and added
  the `TIER_LABEL` constant.

**Real server.** One NVIDIA H100 80GB, an earlier revision without `TIER_LABEL`:

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --gpu-memory-utilization 0.2 --max-model-len 2048 \
    --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
    "kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use":2147483648,"block_size":16,"eviction_policy":"lru",
    "secondary_tiers":[{"type":"example","custom_param":67}]}}'
```

The scrape after three completion requests:

```
vllm:kv_offload_config_info{cpu_num_chunks="1170",engine="0",example_info="",model_name="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",tier="0:primary"} 1.0
vllm:kv_offload_config_info{cpu_num_chunks="",engine="0",example_info="67",model_name="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",tier="1:example"} 1.0
```

- The two tiers give two series, and the `tier` label tells them apart.
- `cpu_num_chunks="1170"` is on the primary tier, and `example_info="67"` is the
  `custom_param` of the `example` tier.
- A name that the other tier owns reads `""`, because every series of one metric
  carries every label.
- No series appears before the first request, because the info travels with the
  first scheduler payload.

**Two engines**, two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, which also starts two API
server processes. This scrape covers an earlier revision of the branch:

```
vllm:kv_offload_config_info{...,cpu_num_chunks="910",engine="0",
  model_name="facebook/opt-125m"} 1.0
vllm:kv_offload_config_info{...,cpu_num_chunks="910",engine="1",
  model_name="facebook/opt-125m"} 1.0
```

The `engine` label makes the two label sets different, so the `mostrecent` multiprocess
mode keeps both instead of one engine overwriting the other. Twelve concurrent requests

title: [Model][DSv4.1] FlashMLA mega attention and the NVFP4 compressed KV cache
author: zyongye
body:
## Purpose

Supersedes #56344, which closed when its base branch `dsv41-optimized` was deleted.

FlashMLA's mega-attention kernel does Q RoPE, sparse attention, the output's inverse RoPE and its FP8 cast in one launch, writing straight into the buffer `wo_a` consumes. It arrives as `FlashMLAMegaAttnBackend` (`FLASHMLA_MEGA_ATTN_DSV41`) with its own attention layer, plus the V4.1 NVFP4 compressed KV record that only this kernel can read — and, as of this revision, **it is the SM100 default** rather than an opt-in backend.

Rebased onto current `main`, which now includes #56441 (KV-only DSpark context insertion); that PR touched the same translation unit and its interaction with this one is described under *Rebase onto #56441* below.

## The interface capability the base layer acts on

`accepts_unnormed_unroped_query` — the attention kernel applies the Q norm and RoPE itself and reads Q in its own chunk-interleaved layout, so the layer's fused KV insert reduces to a zero-pad of Q to the kernel's head count, and to nothing at all once the shard is already that wide.

The output side needs no flag: the mega layer's `_alloc_attn_out` / `_o_proj` pair speaks `QuantizedActivation` where every other layer speaks bf16 and rotates in `_o_proj`. An earlier revision of this PR declared a second capability, `produces_inv_roped_quantized_output`; it had no reader — the dispatch is the override pair — so it is gone.

## Q reaches the kernel through the existing fused op, not a new one

Rather than a separate Triton pad kernel, `fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_rope_quant_insert` gains two independent knobs:

- `apply_q_rope` — rotate Q as well; KV is always rotated. A runtime argument, on the `kv_mxfp8` precedent.
- `is_q_interleaved` — read and write Q in the mega layout (32 chunks of `[heads, 16]` per token), which moves the padding heads to the tail of every head-dim chunk. A template parameter, because it selects the address arithmetic.

They are orthogonal, and that is tested. A lane owns dims `[16l, 16l+16)` of its head in **either** layout — only the address differs — so the per-head RMSNorm and the GPT-J RoPE are equally valid interleaved. `test_q_interleaved_is_orthogonal_to_norm_and_rope` pins it over all eight of (16, 64 heads) × (norm on/off) × (RoPE on/off): the head-major result permuted into the interleaved layout must equal the interleaved path on a permuted input, bit for bit, with the KV cache byte-identical so the Q layout cannot leak into the KV half. An earlier revision conflated the two into one flag on the mistaken belief that the layout made RoPE ill-defined; that test fails against the conflated form.

`q_head_padded = 0` additionally asks for the KV insert alone, which is what TP1 wants — its 64 live heads are already the kernel's head count, so no Q pass is scheduled at all.

## One buffer pair per step

The output travels as a `QuantizedActivation` (`kMxfp8Dynamic`: fp8 e4m3 data, packed-ue8m0 MN-major scales). FlashMLA's fused ops take caller-provided `out_fp8` / `out_sf`, so a single buffer pair covers a whole step: the prefill chunks and the decode segment fill disjoint token ranges, and one `fp8_einsum` over all N tokens replaces one call per segment. The scale buffer's head-dim stride is `ceil4(N)` — both what the kernel requires of a caller buffer and what DeepGEMM expects for that N.

`wq_b` rows and `wo_a` columns are permuted once at load into the kernel's chunk-interleaved layouts, so the surrounding GEMMs speak them directly rather than shuffling per step. DSpark's draft layers are ordinary `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer`s and therefore take the engine-wide backend, so they owe the same post-load permutation; `DSparkDeepseekV4ForCausalLM.process_weights_after_loading` now runs it, where before it finalized only MoE weights and every draft forward hit the layer's own guard.

## NVFP4 compressed cache

`nvfp4_ds_mla` now means the V4.1 MXFP8 sliding-window record beside a 288 B NVFP4 compressed record (256 B of e2m1 pairs, then 32 e4m3 scales of 16 dims). It rides the byte-width dispatch the fp8 records already use, so `rope_quant_insert` and `dequantize_and_gather_k_cache` pick it up with no call-site change; CuteDSL has no fp4 gather, so that record takes Triton.

This is the format the reference implementation itself stores: `inference/model.py` quantizes the compressed latent with `fp4_act_quant(latent, 16, True, scale_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)` — group 16, e4m3 scales. `fp8_ds_mla` is *more* precise than the reference on that cache, not less.

Each layer declares the packed record its kernel prefers, and an unspecific `--kv-cache-dtype` resolves to it:

| layer | `auto` / `fp8` | explicit `fp8_ds_mla` | explicit `nvfp4_ds_mla` |
|---|---|---|---|
| mega attention | `nvfp4_ds_mla` | `fp8_ds_mla` | `nvfp4_ds_mla` |
| `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` | `fp8_ds_mla` | `fp8_ds_mla` | rejected by the backend |
| plain-row (FlashInfer) | `fp8` | — | `ValueError` |

## Default backend on SM100

An unspecified `--attention_config.backend` now resolves to `FLASHMLA_MEGA_ATTN_DSV41` on SM100. The layer answers `is_available_for()` rather than letting the selector guess, because `__init__` raises on topologies the kernel cannot serve — it is SM100 only, it needs `WV_GROUP_SIZE` heads per `wo_a` group, and a build may not carry the kernel at all. On a 64-head model that admits TP1 through TP8 and declines TP16 (4 local heads), which falls through to `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` instead of failing at startup.

The default is chosen for TP1's win plus the 45%-smaller compressed record, **not** for a uniform speedup — see the table below, where TP2 through TP8 are a wash. Set `--attention_config.backend=FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` to get the previous path.

## Performance

`benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_dsv41_mega_attn.py`, one GB300, CUDA graphs on, counting every per-step op each path runs (topk_swa=128, topk_extra=512, NVFP4 compressed cache), as mega / `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` microseconds on a 64-head model:

```
  s_q                    1      32     128     256     512
  TP1 (64 live heads)  29/29   31/31   31/40   53/72   96/140    up to 1.45x
  TP2 (32 live)        29/29   31/30   35/35   61/63  110/119
  TP4 (16 live)        29/29   31/29   34/34   59/58  109/109
  TP8 (8 live)         29/29   31/29   33/33   59/57  107/104
```

The decisive variable is live heads over padded heads, not batch size: the kernel absorbs the inverse RoPE and the FP8 cast, whose cost scales with *live* heads, while its own cost scales with *padded* heads — always 64, since FlashMLA's FP8 decode takes only `h_q` in {64, 128}. So TP1 wins and TP2 down cancel to within a few percent. There is no batch size at which falling back pays, so there is no minimum-token threshold and no fallback path to maintain.

An earlier revision of this table also charged the mega arm for a separate Q-pad kernel "that the split-KV path gets for free"; that is no longer true — the pad is now inside the same fused insert both paths run, and at TP1 it is skipped entirely.

These are decode numbers; **prefill is unmeasured**. Measure under CUDA graphs — in eager mode launch overhead swamps both paths and overstates the fused one several-fold.

## Accuracy: measured end to end, with DSpark

The earlier revision listed accuracy as not covered. It now is. Both arms on one GB300, TP4, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` at pinned snapshot `517ef625`, identical eval config, DSpark k=5 with **real** rejection sampling (`rejection_sample_method=synthetic` deliberately absent, so acceptance measures the draft rather than echoing the config). The two recipes differ by exactly one engine flag.

| | mega attention (NVFP4) | `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` (fp8_ds_mla) | history band |
|---|---|---|---|
| gsm8k flexible / strict | **0.9318** / 0.9318 | 0.9265 / 0.9265 | median 0.9287, IQR 0.9265–0.9318 |
| gpqa_diamond exact / pass@4 | **0.9053** / 0.9545 | 0.9066 / 0.9545 | median 0.9040, IQR 0.8990–0.9141 |
| draft acceptance gpqa | 0.4376 (len 3.188) | 0.4341 (len 3.171) | |
| draft acceptance gsm8k | 0.4957 (len 3.479) | 0.4945 (len 3.473) | |

All four scores land inside their interquartile range, and the two arms agree within sampling noise (gsm8k 0.53 pt, gpqa 0.13 pt; gpqa is n=198 at temperature 1.0, so one question is ~0.5 pt). **The fused kernel and the 45%-smaller compressed record cost nothing measurable in accuracy.**

Draft acceptance is the more sensitive check, because it reads draft-versus-target agreement directly: all four figures span 0.4341–0.4376 on gpqa and 0.4945–0.4957 on gsm8k, and they also reproduce the pre-rebase run to three decimals.

Scores were validated before being quoted: `num_request_errors: 0` on every eval, step durations plausible (530/114 s and 519/113 s), gsm8k > gpqa cross-task ordering, flexible − strict gap exactly 0.0000, and truncation of 3/792 gpqa and 1/1319 gsm8k rows so that answered-only accuracy tracks the headline (mega 0.9087 / 0.9332; sparse 0.9100 / 0.9279). GSM8K runs `api_type: completions` 5-shot greedy, so it bypasses the chat template and is not the deployed serving path; GPQA runs the deployed chat path with thinking on and the `deepseek_v41` reasoning parser.

## Rebase onto #56441

#56441 added a KV-only context-insert op to the same translation unit. Two of its call sites needed updating for this series and **git reported no conflict on either**, because neither side edited those lines — they would have surfaced only at compile time: `launchFusedDeepseekV4Templated` gains a template parameter (`is_q_interleaved`) and a runtime one (`apply_q_rope`), and the KV-only op calls it. Both are fixed at the call site, with a comment noting that zero query heads means no Q slot is scheduled so neither knob is reachable there.

The two series had also independently arrived at the same `kNumHeadsQPadded == 0` grid fix (I contributed it to #56441 during review); it collapsed to one.

## Test Plan & Result

```
pytest tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_insert.py \
       tests/kernels/test_compressor_kv_cache.py \
       tests/kernels/test_dsv41_mega_attn_layouts.py \
       tests/kernels/test_fused_indexer_q_rope_quant.py \
       tests/kernels/test_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant.py     # 522 passed, 17 skipped
pre-commit run --files <changed files>                    # all hooks pass
```

The last two suites are there because the op this PR changes is also called by the **DSv4.0** paths (`deepseek_v4/attention.py`, its dspark, xpu); the two new parameters are defaulted so those call sites still bind, which is worth testing rather than assuming.

New tests cover the NVFP4 record byte-exactly against a reference quantizer derived from FlashMLA's `tests/quant.py` (scales exact, values within half an e2m1 step, untouched rows and page padding preserved), an insert→gather round trip, the `wq_b` / `wo_a` permutations against a reference that permutes the activation instead, the interleaved Q pad (live elements bit-exact, padding heads zero, both grid variants, and the KV-insert-only launch), the norm/RoPE orthogonality described above, and graph-replay coverage that a captured insert refills its allocated Q buffer over changed input.

## Not duplicating

#56893 (merged) landed the V4.1 MXFP8 KV record this builds on. #56344 is the earlier flag-gated form of this same integration and is closed. #56441 (merged) added a KV-only wrapper op in the same files; disjoint in intent, and the interaction is described above.

## Not yet covered

- **Prefill perf is unmeasured** — every number above is decode.
- **Non-SM100 arches** are untouched by design; the kernel has no SM90 instantiation and the default declines there.
- Two commits in this series do not build standalone (a call-site fix landed one commit later than the parameter it fixes), which matters only for `git bisect` across the series, not for the tip or a squash-merge.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). The backend, the interface capability, the NVFP4 record, the default-backend selection, the tests, the benchmark and the accuracy runs above were produced in that session and reviewed by me.

title: [ROCm][Perf] W4A16: widen skinny GEMM LDS activation loads to b128
author: roberteg16
body:
## Summary

The `wvSplitK` int4 skinny GEMM stages activations into LDS as `s[k_ + K * n]` and reads them back per row. `K` is a runtime value, so the compiler cannot prove the per-row offset `K*n` is 16-element aligned and falls back to paired `ds_load_2addr_b32`/`b64` for the higher rows. But `K` is a multiple of `A_CHUNK` and so is `k_`, so `s[k_ + K * n]` is in fact `sizeof(bigTypeA)`-aligned for every row — annotating the read lets the compiler widen all activation rows to `ds_load_b128`.

That invariant was implicit: `A_CHUNK` is a template argument pinned to 16 by the launch macro, and the host only checks `K % 16 == 0`. The k-loop already relies on it too, since it consumes whole `A_CHUNK` chunks. The host check now uses a shared `kInt4KAlign` constant, each kernel does `static_assert(kInt4KAlign % A_CHUNK == 0)`, and the LDS buffer is declared `alignas(sizeof(bigTypeA))`, so raising `A_CHUNK` fails to build until `kInt4KAlign` is raised with it.

This is a compiler-visibility argument rather than an architectural one, so it is not gated on a specific gfx target. The global fallback read in the medium kernel is deliberately left untouched: `A[]`'s base alignment is not guaranteed there.

LDS load instructions across all int4 instantiations, gfx1151 with ROCm 10.2, counted by disassembling the gfx1151 device image out of the built `_rocm_C.abi3.so`:

| | `ds_load_b128` | `ds_load_2addr_b32` | `ds_load_2addr_b64` | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 6864 | 3744 | 624 | 11232 |
| after | 9360 | 0 | 0 | 9360 |

`N=1` and `N=2` were already fully widened by this compiler and come out byte-identical; the change is confined to `N=3,4,5`.

## Measurements

`benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_rdna_hybrid_w4a16_gemm.py`, `--group-size 128`, batch 4, median of 3 passes, TFLOP/s, symmetric / asymmetric:

| K x N | before | after | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2048x2048 | 2.501 / 2.020 | 2.929 / 2.316 | **+17.1% / +14.6%** |
| 2560x2560 | 3.040 / 2.853 | 3.392 / 3.038 | **+11.6% / +6.5%** |
| 8192x2048 | 2.218 / 1.645 | 2.276 / 1.743 | +2.6% / +6.0% |
| 2560x3840 | 3.834 / 3.402 | 3.877 / 3.510 | +1.1% / +3.2% |
| 2048x6144 | 3.301 / 3.122 | 3.275 / 3.077 | -0.8% / -1.4% |
| 2048x16384 | 3.258 / 3.162 | 3.272 / 3.164 | +0.4% / +0.1% |
| 2560x19456 | 3.361 / 3.334 | 3.369 / 3.321 | +0.2% / -0.4% |

The win concentrates on small `out_features`, where the kernel is bound by the LDS read rather than by the weight stream. Batch 1 and 2 are flat everywhere, which is exactly what the instruction counts predict. Only shapes that actually reach the HIP skinny path (`M <= 5` and `K*M <= 32768`) are listed; the rest route to Triton and are unaffected.

Reproducing the asymmetric column needs #57004, without which the benchmark's `hybrid-w4a16-zp` provider raises.

## Model evaluation

GSM8K on gfx1151, full 1319 questions, 5-shot, greedy, seed 42. `max_num_seqs=4` so every decode step runs the `N=3,4` instantiations this change touches (`max_num_seqs=1` would only exercise the unchanged `N=1` path):

```bash
lm_eval --model vllm \
  --model_args pretrained=<model>,max_model_len=4096,max_num_seqs=4,dtype=float16,gpu_memory_utilization=0.75,enforce_eager=False,seed=42 \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size auto --seed 42
```

| model | filter | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ` | strict-match | 0.8582 ± 0.0096 | 0.8590 ± 0.0096 |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ` | flexible-extract | 0.8613 ± 0.0095 | 0.8620 ± 0.0095 |

Qwen3-8B-AWQ differs by a single question, well inside one stderr. Average output throughput over the eval run is flat (20.9 vs 20.6 tok/s).

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py` on gfx1151: 84 passed.
- [x] `pre-commit run --files csrc/rocm/skinny_gemms_int4.cu` passes, clang-format included.
- [x] ISA verified by disassembling the built device image and counting LDS opcodes per instantiation; the `static_assert`/`alignas` hardening leaves it byte-identical.
- [x] With the launch macro set to `A_CHUNK=32`, the build fails on the `static_assert` in both kernels, and succeeds again once `kInt4KAlign` is raised to 32.
- [x] GSM8K 5-shot on `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ`: accuracy matches the baseline (see above).

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for this change, as required by `AGENTS.md`. Not a duplicate: the only other open PR touching `csrc/rocm/skinny_gemms_int4.cu` is #56301, which changes host-side weight row-stride padding and does not touch the LDS activation reads.

title: [Bugfix][MRV2][Spec Decode] Honor dynamic K in autoregressive speculators, 1.2~1.3x kernel perf improvement
author: yewentao256
body:
## Purpose

MRV2 did not propagate `SchedulerOutput.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule` to autoregressive speculators, causing unnecessary draft forwards and stale draft tokens.

This PR fixes the issue

## Test

Acc covered in current unit test

Perf can be seen in this AI generated script

```py
from functools import partial
from types import SimpleNamespace

import torch
import triton

from vllm.v1.spec_decode.dynamic.utils import build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup
from vllm.v1.worker.gpu.input_batch import InputBatch, InputBuffers
from vllm.v1.worker.gpu.spec_decode.autoregressive.speculator import (
    AutoRegressiveSpeculator,
)

MAX_K = 5
MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 48
HIDDEN_SIZE = 4096
NUM_REQS = (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48)
DYNAMIC_K_SCHEDULE = [(1, MAX_BATCH_SIZE, 3)]


class SyntheticSpeculator(AutoRegressiveSpeculator):
    """MRV2 proposer whose model forward is replaced by a matmul."""

    def load_draft_model(self, target_model, target_attn_layer_names):
        raise NotImplementedError("This benchmark does not load a model")

    def __init__(self, device: torch.device) -> None:
        # Deliberately skip the real constructor: it allocates model-related state.
        self.num_speculative_steps = MAX_K
        self.max_num_reqs = MAX_BATCH_SIZE
        self.max_model_len = 8192
        self.dp_size = 1
        self.dp_rank = 0
        self.pcp_manager = None
        self.eplb_state = None
        self.use_fused_multi_step_decode = True
        self.prefill_cudagraph_manager = None
        self.decode_cudagraph_manager = None
        self.speculative_config = SimpleNamespace(
            uses_dynamic_speculative_decoding=lambda: True,
        )

        self.input_buffers = InputBuffers(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, MAX_BATCH_SIZE, device)
        self.hidden_states = torch.zeros(
            MAX_BATCH_SIZE, HIDDEN_SIZE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device
        )
        self.last_token_indices = torch.zeros(
            MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int64, device=device
        )
        self.current_draft_step = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
        self.sample_src_positions = torch.zeros(
            MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int64, device=device
        )
        self.idx_mapping = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
        self.temperature = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, device=device)
        self.seeds = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
        self.draft_tokens = torch.zeros(
            MAX_BATCH_SIZE, MAX_K, dtype=torch.int64, device=device
        )

        self.weight = torch.randn(
            HIDDEN_SIZE, HIDDEN_SIZE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device
        )
        self.src = torch.randn(
            MAX_BATCH_SIZE, HIDDEN_SIZE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device
        )
        self.dst = torch.empty_like(self.src)
        self.count_steps = False
        self.steps = 0

    def _synthetic_forward(self, num_tokens: int) -> None:
        torch.mm(self.src[:num_tokens], self.weight, out=self.dst[:num_tokens])
        self.src, self.dst = self.dst, self.src
        if self.count_steps:
            self.steps += 1

    def _prefill(self, num_reqs: int, num_tokens: int, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        self._synthetic_forward(num_tokens)
        self.draft_tokens[:num_reqs, 0].zero_()

    def _generate_draft(
        self, num_reqs: int, num_tokens_padded: int, *args, **kwargs
    ) -> None:
        self._synthetic_forward(num_tokens_padded)


def count_forwards(speculator: SyntheticSpeculator, run) -> int:
    speculator.steps = 0
    speculator.count_steps = True
    run()
    speculator.count_steps = False
    return speculator.steps


def main() -> None:
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        raise RuntimeError("CUDA is required")

    device = torch.device("cuda")
    speculator = SyntheticSpeculator(device)
    target_buffers = InputBuffers(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, MAX_BATCH_SIZE, device)
    target_hidden_states = torch.randn_like(speculator.hidden_states)
    temperature = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, device=device)
    seeds = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
    last_sampled = torch.zeros(MAX_BATCH_SIZE, dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
    dense_schedule = build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup(
        DYNAMIC_K_SCHEDULE,
        vllm_max_batch_size=MAX_BATCH_SIZE,
        vllm_num_speculative_tokens=MAX_K,
    )

    print("batch  sched_k  buggy_ms  fixed_ms  speedup  forwards(buggy->fixed)")
    for num_reqs in NUM_REQS:
        batch = InputBatch.make_dummy(num_reqs, num_reqs, target_buffers)
        common_args = dict(
            input_batch=batch,
            attn_metadata={},
            slot_mappings={},
            last_hidden_states=target_hidden_states[:num_reqs],
            aux_hidden_states=None,
            num_sampled=torch.ones(num_reqs, dtype=torch.int32, device=device),
            num_rejected=torch.zeros(num_reqs, dtype=torch.int32, device=device),
            last_sampled=last_sampled,
            next_prefill_tokens=target_buffers.input_ids,
            temperature=temperature,
            seeds=seeds,
            dummy_run=True,
            skip_attn_for_dummy_run=True,
            is_profile=True,
        )
        dynamic_k = dense_schedule[num_reqs]

        # Buggy: model_runner omitted runtime K, so propose() used max K=5.
        buggy = partial(speculator.propose, **common_args)
        # Fixed: model_runner passes the scheduler-selected runtime K=3.
        fixed = partial(
            speculator.propose,
            **common_args,
            num_speculative_tokens=dynamic_k,
        )

        buggy_steps = count_forwards(speculator, buggy)
        fixed_steps = count_forwards(speculator, fixed)
        assert dynamic_k == 3
        assert buggy_steps == MAX_K
        assert fixed_steps == dynamic_k

        buggy_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(buggy)
        fixed_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fixed)
        print(
            f"{num_reqs:>5}  {dynamic_k:>7}  {buggy_ms:>8.3f}  "
            f"{fixed_ms:>8.3f}  {buggy_ms / fixed_ms:>7.3f}x  "
            f"{buggy_steps}->{fixed_steps}"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

And we can get

```bash
batch  sched_k  buggy_ms  fixed_ms  speedup  forwards(buggy->fixed)

    2        3     0.148     0.115    1.286x  5->3
    4        3     0.149     0.115    1.298x  5->3
    8        3     0.148     0.115    1.282x  5->3
   16        3     0.151     0.115    1.315x  5->3
   32        3     0.150     0.114    1.306x  5->3
   48        3     0.149     0.115    1.287x  5->3
```

title: [Attention] Add UltraQuant 4-bit KV cache backend (FlyDSL D=256)
author: aditi-amd
body: ## Purpose Adds an `ultraquant_4bit` KV-cache dtype for long-context / agentic serving, where the KV cache is the limiter. UltraQuant stores the cache at 4 bits, FP4 E2M1 codes with UE8M0 (power-of-two) per-group-32 scales, and Hadamard-rotated keys, giving **~2× KV density over fp8**, so more concurrency fits before eviction and decode stays memory-efficient under load. Decode runs on a FlyDSL `D=256` kernel for GQA group sizes **{6, 8, 16}**, with a Triton unified-attention fallback and numerical reference paths. ## Design - New `UltraQuantAttentionImpl`, a standalone subclass of `TurboQuantAttentionImpl`. - `TurboQuantAttentionBackend.get_impl_cls()` dispatches to the UQ impl on the `ultraquant_4bit` cache dtype. - New ops under `vllm/v1/attention/ops/ultraquant/` (FP4/UE8M0 format, Hadamard store, dequant, Triton unified attention, reference) and the FlyDSL D=256 decode kernel/launcher. ## Test Plan - **Unit tests** (`tests/kernels/ultraquant/`): store, dequant, decode, and FlyDSL-vs-reference numerical checks, plus config. - **Serve smokes**: Qwen3.8 (GQA-16, TP=8) and Qwen3.6-27B (GQA-6, TP=2), confirming FlyDSL dispatch (no Triton fallback) and coherent output. - **Accuracy** (KV format is the only variable; sampling fixed): GPQA-Diamond. - **Performance**: SemiAnalysis-style 262K-token agentic replay, throughput/latency and peak KV utilization across concurrency. ## Usage Enable the 4-bit KV cache with `--kv-cache-dtype ultraquant_4bit` (D=256, GQA {6,8,16}): vllm serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-MXFP4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN \ --kv-cache-dtype ultraquant_4bit \ --max-model-len 163840 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --trust-remote-code The 4-bit KV cache composes with MXFP4 weights. Decode auto-dispatches to the FlyDSL D=256 kernel (gfx950), otherwise it falls back to Triton unified attention. All accuracy/perf runs use the sampling settings recommended in the model's Hugging Face card (Qwen3.8: `temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20`). ## Test Results **Accuracy — GPQA-Diamond, mean over multiple seeds.** UltraQuant is at parity with the fp8 (KV8) baseline — in fact marginally ahead on the mean. The decode kernel is numerically exact, so per-seed differences are sampling variance (the arms trade places seed to seed). | Model | UltraQuant 4-bit (mean) | KV8 fp8 (mean) | |---|---|---| | Qwen3.8 | **93.27%** | 92.42% | | Qwen3.6-27B | **86.87%** | 85.61% | **Performance: throughput–latency Pareto (262K-token requests, MI355X):** Qwen3.8 (GQA-16, TP=8). UQ and KV8 track together at low concurrency; UQ pulls ahead from **C=32** onward. KV8 saturates its cache at **C=38 (100%, evicting)** and throughput collapses, while UQ is still at ~44% cache and keeps scaling. | Concurrency | UQ tok/s | KV8 tok/s | Δ | UQ peak KV | KV8 peak KV | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 8 | 193.9 | 199.4 | −2.7% | 8.2% | 14.1% | | 16 | 280.2 | 288.0 | −2.7% | 17.4% | 32.0% | | 32 | 374.0 | 363.1 | +3.0% | 35.1% | 66.3% | | 36 | 398.9 | 299.6 | +33.1% | 39.7% | 82.4% | | 38 | 414.6 | 225.4 | +84.0% | 44.2% | **100.0%** | | 42 | 430.7 | 114.7 | +275% | 45.4% | 99.9% | --- UQ first wins at **C=32 before any eviction** (KV8 only 66% cache), and the gap widens sharply once KV8 hits the eviction wall at C=38. Qwen3.6-27B (GQA-6, TP=2). Same shape; UQ wins even before KV8 evicts at C=42 UQ delivers +9% throughput at lower ITL while KV8 is only ~39% cache. UQ peak KV is ~half of KV8 at every point. | Concurrency | UQ tok/s | KV8 tok/s | Δ | UQ peak KV | KV8 peak KV | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 8 | 268.3 | 271.8 | −1.3% | 4.8% | 8.4% | | 16 | 383.3 | 391.4 | −2.1% | 9.7% | 15.2% | | 32 | 519.9 | 529.5 | −1.8% | 17.6% | 32.1% | | 34 | 545.1 | 537.6 | +1.4% | 19.0% | 31.8% | | 42 | 592.0 | 543.1 | +9.0% | 22.6% | 38.7% | ## Notes - Requires a FlyDSL-capable ROCm build (gfx950) for the D=256 decode kernel; falls back to Triton unified attention otherwise. - Benchmark figures were measured across differing vLLM / AITER / FlyDSL bases, so absolute throughput/latency (and the 8-bit baseline) are indicative rather than bit-identical across environments; the accuracy and relative UQ-vs-KV8 trends are the takeaway. ## References [UltraQuant 4bit KV](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.20474)

title: [Bugfix] Make online FP8 MoE experts batch-invariant under VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT
author: ybwbqg9379
body:
Fixes #57016

## Purpose

With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, a MoE model served with `--quantization fp8` (online per-tensor FP8, Triton experts) still produces output that depends on which other requests share its batch: greedy tokens flip within the first ~10 positions and prefix-cached K/V differs depending on who wrote it. Dense layers are invariant; only the experts are not.

Two things were wrong:

1. `Fp8PerTensorOnlineMoEMethod` (and `Fp8MoEMethod` for FP8-serialized per-tensor checkpoints with dynamic activations) quantize the expert inputs with one dynamic scale over the whole activation tensor (`kFp8DynamicTensorSym`), i.e. the max over every token of every co-batched request. Under batch-invariant mode this PR selects `kFp8DynamicTokenSym` and passes `per_act_token_quant=True`, mirroring what `Fp8LinearMethod` already does for dense layers.
2. Switching to per-token activations exposed a latent launcher bug: `invoke_fused_moe_triton_kernel` passed `stride_bse=0` for 1-D `[E]` weight scales (and `stride_bsn=1` for the singleton dim of `[E, 1, 1]`), so the kernel's `per_channel_quant` branch read expert 0's scale for every expert or indexed past the buffer. The combination tests already skipped "per-tensor weights + per-token activations" for the Triton experts as NYI, although `TritonExperts._supports_quant_scheme` advertises the pair. This PR passes the expert stride unconditionally and broadcasts singleton scale dims, and narrows the NYI gate to the still-unsupported "per-channel weights + per-tensor activations" case so the combination suite covers the fixed pair.

The bf16 Triton expert path is already invariant on `main` (`get_default_config`/`get_moe_configs` pin the tile config under the flag); the reporter's bf16 mismatch was on 0.27.1.

## Test Plan

- New `tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py::test_online_fp8_moe_logprobs_bitwise_bs1_vs_bsN` (granite-3.1-1b-a400m-instruct, `--quantization fp8_per_tensor`, greedy, BS=1 vs BS=8 bitwise tokens+logprobs). Fails on `main`, passes with this PR.
- `tests/kernels/moe/test_modular_kernel_combinations.py`: the per-tensor-weight + per-token-activation FP8 config is no longer skipped for `TritonExperts` / `BatchedTritonExperts` / `TritonOrDeepGemmExperts`.
- Reporter's reproducer (co-batch and writer-suffix modes) against a running server.
- Kernel check: `fused_experts` vs `tests.kernels.utils.torch_experts`, E=32, N=1024, K=2048, M=128, topk=4, per-tensor `[E,1,1]` weight scales: max abs err 0.010 with per-tensor activations, 0.003 with per-token activations (before the launcher fix the per-token case returned values in the thousands).
- Existing suites: `tests/kernels/moe/test_block_fp8.py`, `tests/kernels/moe/test_moe.py::test_fused_moe`, pre-commit, `mypy-3.12`.

Hardware: RTX 5090 (sm_120), WSL2, torch 2.13.0+cu130. The modular kernel combination suite itself does not run on this WSL2 machine (spawned worker fails with `CUDA error: invalid resource handle` on unmodified `main` too), so that part relies on CI and on the independent H20 run linked below.

## Test Result

- Reporter's probe, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 --quantization fp8`, before: A-alone vs A-with-B first token flip at 11 (logprob gap 0.166), warm-vs-cold flip at 11 (gap 0.347). After: every comparison identical, both rounds.
- gsm8k 5-shot, 1319 questions, granite-3.1-1b-a400m-instruct `--quantization fp8 --enforce-eager` (tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py): default (no flag) 34.1%, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` on `main` 34.3%, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` with this PR 32.7%. Per-token activation quantization is strictly finer than per-tensor, and the kernel-level error is lower, so the small delta is sampling noise from a 1B model.
- New e2e test: PASS with the PR, FAIL on `main` ("logprobs are not bitwise equal between BS=1 and BS=8; max abs diff 2.2e-01").
- Independent cross-architecture validation by @CarrotSwordsman on H20 (sm_90, real Linux GPU, driver 535), [comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57092#issuecomment-5730213177): the same e2e test FAILS on a clean 0.28.0+cu129 wheel (max abs diff 2.8e-01) and PASSES with this PR's files applied, reproducing and eliminating the #57016 symptom on Hopper. Their `test_modular_kernel_combinations.py` run on the patched wheel was 8 passed / 2 failed / 1 skipped, the two failures being `deep_gemm`'s `NVCC >= 12.3` assert in a container pinned to 12.1. As they note, that suite does not discriminate against a release wheel (the pre-PR NYI skip is not present there to be removed), so the e2e pair is the evidence in that setup.
- `tests/kernels/moe/test_block_fp8.py` (non-DeepGEMM): 164 passed, 20 skipped. `tests/kernels/moe/test_moe.py -k test_fused_moe`: 241 passed. pre-commit and `mypy-3.12` clean on all changed files.

> Note: since #53585, online per-tensor FP8 is selected with `--quantization fp8_per_tensor`; commands above that use `--quantization fp8` predate that change.

Not a duplicate: no open PR references #57016 (checked with `gh pr list --search "57016 in:body"` and by searching open PRs for "batch invariant moe"); #55881 is the XPU MoE variant and does not touch the CUDA Triton path or FP8 activation quantization.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the investigation and drafting; every line was reviewed and every test run by the submitter.

title: [Perf] Optimize Molmo2 pooling preparation
author: Levius-Fubuki
body:
### Purpose

Molmo2 pooling currently materializes a tiled batch-index tensor and uses
multi-dimensional advanced indexing before masking invalid patches and reducing
the attention query.

This change keeps the implementation in native PyTorch while reducing that
overhead. It flattens the batch-local patch indices into global row indices,
uses `torch.index_select` for the gather, masks invalid entries in place, and
performs the existing sum/mean query reduction without changing the subsequent
attention, projection, or token filtering behavior.

No Triton kernel or custom-op dispatch is added, so there is no extra JIT
startup cost or platform-specific fallback path.

### Tests and validation

Pooling coverage is consolidated into the existing
`tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_molmo2.py` suite. Two parametrized
cases exercise `Molmo2VisionBackbone.forward` with lightweight substitutes
for the encoder and learned layers, checking masked and ordinary means,
partially/all-invalid groups, repeated indices, cross-batch indexing, attention
masks, and invalid-group filtering against explicit expected values.

The standalone 228-line pooling test file and benchmark script have been
removed. The pooling implementation is unchanged by this review follow-up.

Agent-run on macOS 15.1 ARM64, Python 3.12.13 and PyTorch 2.14.0, from the
PR worktree using the parent checkout's virtual environment:

```bash
PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 ../../.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_molmo2.py
# 7 passed; one existing warning about missing vllm._version

../../.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_molmo2.py \
  vllm/model_executor/models/molmo2.py
# All applicable hooks passed, including Ruff and mypy

git diff --check
# Passed
```

The suite uses the existing `skip_global_cleanup` marker because these CPU
unit tests do not initialize distributed or accelerator state. Without it,
the existing processing tests triggered a macOS/PyTorch
`empty_host_cache` teardown crash in the local environment.

### RTX 4090 Microbenchmark (historical)

The script is preserved at [the pre-follow-up commit](https://github.com/Levius-Fubuki/vllm/blob/e26ed1564398652949f446d78fa252eac26b40a2/benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_molmo2_pooling.py); the command below refers to that version. These measurements were not rerun for this test-only follow-up.

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_molmo2_pooling.py \
  --batch-sizes 1 2 \
  --dtypes float16 bfloat16 \
  --warmup 50 --repeats 200 --trials 10
```

Hardware/software: NVIDIA RTX 4090, PyTorch 2.12.1+cu130, Triton 3.7.1.

The benchmark compares the exact upstream native preparation path against the
optimized native helper. Across 24 image/video rows, every measured case
improved. The geometric-mean speedup was 1.29x, with a range of 1.06x--1.50x.

| B | kind | dtype | groups | Upstream median / IQR (us) | Optimized median / IQR (us) | Speedup |
|---:|:---|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | image K=4 | FP16 | 550 | 165.55 / 0.17 | 118.42 / 0.34 | 1.40x |
| 1 | video K=9 | FP16 | 256 | 175.82 / 13.33 | 117.49 / 0.82 | 1.50x |
| 1 | video K=9 | BF16 | 4096 | 991.10 / 0.44 | 927.38 / 0.53 | 1.07x |
| 2 | video K=9 | FP16 | 4096 | 1954.28 / 5.32 | 1830.80 / 0.18 | 1.07x |


### Limitations

The performance measurements isolate pooling preparation rather than full-model
end-to-end latency. This follow-up was validated against the PR source with local
Python dependencies and no built vLLM native extensions. CUDA tests, full-model
evaluation and benchmarks were not rerun; GPU evidence above is historical.
The new validation results are agent-run, not human-run.

### AI assistance

AI assistance was used during implementation, testing, benchmarking, review,
and PR drafting. I reviewed and take responsibility for the change and
evidence.

title: [MM][Mistral] Add compile support for Pixtral vision encoders
author: jzakrzew
body:
## Purpose
Add `compile_mm_encoder` support for both Pixtral vision encoder implementations:

- `PixtralForConditionalGeneration`, including Mistral-format Mistral 3 models.
- The Hugging Face Pixtral encoder used by `Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration`.

The change applies `support_torch_compile` to the transformer blocks in both implementations and marks the token, rotary embedding, and packed-sequence dimensions as dynamic.

The feature remains gated behind `compile_mm_encoder`, which is disabled by default.

### Performance results
Note: the results are only about GPU kernel time. Total E2E runtime improves much less, even with Cuda graphs from #56277, because apply_hf_processor is the main bottleneck now.

Profiling was performed on an NVIDIA GB200 system using the same 16-image BF16 capture before and after enabling compilation. 
Total GPU kernel time decreased by **42%**, from **1173.6 ms to 676.8 ms**, corresponding to a **1.73x speedup**.

The improvement came from eliminating or fusing much of execution overhead:

| Kernel category | Before | After | Reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FlashAttention | 273 ms | 273 ms | 0% |
| GEMM | 272 ms | 272 ms | 0% |
| Elementwise operations | 368 ms | 11 ms | 97% |
| SiLU | 121 ms | 44 ms | 64% |
| Concat | 96 ms | 0.3 ms | >99% |


  ### CUDA-graph compatibility

  This work is complementary to #56277, which adds Pixtral encoder CUDA-graph support. It does not duplicate or modify that implementation.

  The CUDA-graph PR’s pixtral.py and mistral3.py changes apply cleanly over this change. Its packed encoder forwards continue to use the unchanged transformer interface. Encoder CUDA-graph capture also performs an eager warmup before capture,
  allowing the transformer blocks to compile first.

  A combined compile_mm_encoder=True plus cudagraph_mm_encoder=True integration test should be added once #56277 is merged.

## Test Plan
Exercise both encoder implementations with compilation enabled and disabled:

- Mistral-format `PixtralForConditionalGeneration`
- Hugging Face `Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration`

The test uses dummy weights and verifies that the compilation counter increases only when `compile_mm_encoder` is enabled.

## Test Result

```console

  tests/compile/fullgraph/test_multimodal_compile.py \
  -k pixtral_compilation -vv -s

4 passed, 4 deselected
```

title: [KV Cache] GLM-5.3-Flash: use the generic packed KV layout; CircularBufferSpec tail with speculative ring slots
author: andakai
body:
## Purpose

Move kernel block splitting from the block table into each attention group. Previously `BlockTable` split every manager block for the whole KV cache group (`kernel_block_sizes`). All backends in a group had to share one kernel block size, block tables and slot mappings were at kernel granularity, and packed (block-outermost) caches could not be split at all, since other layers' pages sit between a layer's blocks. Now block tables stay at manager granularity, and each `AttentionGroup` maps manager blocks to the kernel blocks its own backend needs.

On top of this, GLM-5.3-Flash moves to the generic packed KV layout, and its model-specific KV code is removed.

## Design

### Kernel block mapping

**Choosing the kernel block size**
- `prepare_kernel_block_sizes` picks a size per KV cache group with `select_common_block_size(manager, backends, specs)`. Packed groups keep the manager block size and are never split group-wide.
- Each `AttentionGroup` then picks its own size for its backend and spec. It sets `kernel_block_size` only when that is smaller than the manager block.

**Mapping block tables**
- The group maps manager block `b` to kernel blocks `b * stride + j` (`j < block_size / kernel_block_size`).
  - `stride` is the number of kernel blocks per manager block.
  - For packed caches it is the packed block stride in kernel blocks.
- The mapped table is persistent and preallocated per ubatch, so CUDA graphs capture a stable buffer.
- Mapping happens inside `build_metadata`, `build_metadata_for_cudagraph_capture` and `build_metadata_for_drafting`. All runners and drafters (V1/MRv2, EAGLE, Gemma4, Step3.5, DFlash) go through these. Fused multi-step draft decode re-maps before replaying a FULL graph.
- `BlockTable`/`InputBatch` (V1 and MRv2) drop `kernel_block_sizes`. Slot mappings, CP and DFlash stay at manager granularity.

**Mapping KV views**
- When KV caches are bound, each group views its cache in kernel blocks. Packed caches use `as_strided` with the packed block stride.
- Only compressed caches (`tokens_per_state > 1`) may be split this way, because their write slots come from the mapped block table. Token and pooled caches are written through manager-block slot mappings, so they are rejected.
- The KV block zeroer maps the views back to manager blocks.

**Alignment**
- `block_stride_alignment` accepts `MultipleOf(n)`, meaning whole kernel blocks of up to `n` tokens, so a packed block always splits into whole kernel blocks.
- Fixed-size backends get it automatically; sparse MLA backends set their own in `customize_spec`.
- Bytes per block: block-outermost layouts round to the lcm of all alignments; layer-outermost layouts pad each layer's page separately.

**Consumers:** NIXL, Mooncake and HiSparse pick kernel block sizes the same way as the worker.

### GLM-5.3-Flash

- Uses the packed `BLHNC` layout. Removed its custom groups, byte layout, `KpoolTailSpec` and `storage_block_size`.
- The kpool indexer is a compressed spec whose backend declares DeepGEMM page sizes (32/64; 64 on SM120). The tail is a `CircularBufferSpec` ring of `kpool + num_speculative_tokens`.
- FlashMLA fp8 on SM90 reads 64-token pages over flat rows, so packed blocks need not be split.

**Example** (GLM-5.3-Flash on H200, manager block = 640 tokens, `index_kpool = 4`):

| Attention group | States per manager block | Kernel block | Kernel blocks per manager block |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sparse MLA (`FLASHMLA_SPARSE`) | 640 | 640 (no split) | 1 |
| kpool indexer (`tokens_per_state = 4`) | 160 | 32 (DeepGEMM page) | 5 |

For a request with manager block table `[7, 2]`:
- **Sparse MLA** builds its metadata from `[7, 2]` unchanged.
- **The indexer group** maps it to `[7·S, …, 7·S+4, 2·S, …, 2·S+4]`, where `S` is the stride between manager blocks in kernel blocks:
  - In a plain (layer-outermost) cache, `S = 5`, giving `[35..39, 10..14]`.
  - In the packed `BLHNC` cache, each manager block also holds the other layers' pages, so `S` is the packed block size divided by the indexer's 32-state page. `MultipleOf` alignment keeps that an integer.

The scheduler, slot mappings and other groups never see kernel blocks. On main, the whole group had to share one kernel block size, so the indexer needed the GLM-only `storage_block_size` workaround instead.

## Test Result

Each cell is GSM8K / GPQA Diamond / acceptance length; no request errors.

| Platform | Model / backend | main | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| GB200 | GLM `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE`, MTP5 | 0.9280 / 0.7323 / 4.73 | 0.9333 / 0.7374 / 4.73 |
| GB200 | DSv4.1 default, DSpark5 | 0.9257 / 0.8384 / 4.08 | 0.9261 / 0.8460 / 4.01 |
| H200 | GLM `FLASHMLA_SPARSE` | — | 0.9386 / 0.7323 / 4.78 |
| H200 | GLM `FLASHMLA_SPARSE` + `fp8_ds_mla` (GSM8K / accept) | 0.9325 / 3.937 | 0.9348 / 3.930 |
| H200 | DSv4.1 default | — | 0.9272 / 0.8535 / 4.05 |
| MI350X | GLM `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` | 0.9211 / 0.6768 / 3.33 | 0.9191 / 0.6835 / 4.82 |
| MI350X | DSv4.1 default | 0.9272 / 0.8333 / 4.03 | 0.9303 / 0.8535 / 3.94 |

- **Prefix caching:** mid-block hits give byte-identical outputs to main.
- **NIXL 1P1D:** GLM 0.9401, DSv4.1 0.9265, 0 failed transfers.
- **Mooncake P/D:** GLM 0.9136.

Performance, PR vs main (medians, concurrency 1 / 16 / 64):

| GB200 | GLM 4K/1K | −0.1% / +3.5% / +0.3% | −3.4% / −4.6% / +0.7% | −1.9% / +0.7% / −1.5% |

| H200 | GLM sonnet | +11.2% / −1.6% / +1.2% | −3.6% / −2.4% / −1.5% | −2.0% / +6.4% / −0.6% |

title: [XPU] Dispatch nn.LayerNorm to fused SYCL kernel via CustomOp
author: mganczarenko
body:
## Purpose

  vllm-xpu-kernels exposes fused SYCL kernels for standard (non-RMS) LayerNorm ([vllm-xpu-kernels#577](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-xpu-kernels/pull/577)) - `layer_norm`, `fused_add_layer_norm`, `nemotron_layer_norm`, `fused_add_nemotron_layer_norm` - but nothing in vLLM dispatched to them yet. Every model with a bare
  `nn.LayerNorm` fell back to torch-xpu-ops' generic kernel on XPU.

  - Adds `StandardLayerNorm`, a `CustomOp` (registered `"layer_norm"`) - drop-in for a bare `nn.LayerNorm`, dispatching via `forward_native`/`forward_cuda`/`forward_xpu`, matching `RMSNorm`/`GemmaRMSNorm` in the same file.
  - Reworks `NemotronLayerNorm1P` (Nemotron's "+1 to weights" variant) from an `nn.LayerNorm` subclass into a `CustomOp` sibling (`"nemotron_layer_norm"`); its XPU path also dispatches the fused-residual-add kernel when a residual is present.
  - Wires both into GPT-2, GPT-J, OPT, SigLIP (PaliGemma's vision tower), and Nemotron.
  - Adds `replace_layernorm_class` (`transformers/utils.py`), matching `replace_linear_class`/`replace_conv_class`/`replace_embedding_class`, so the Transformers modeling backend's generic recursive module-replace picks this up too - covers StarCoder2-style models with no dedicated vLLM model file.
  - Kernel calls are wrapped as real `torch.ops.vllm.xpu_*` custom ops (`_xpu_ops.py`, via `direct_register_custom_op`), the same way `GemmaRMSNorm` wraps its kernel - compile-safe by construction, gated only by the standard `CustomOp` `+`/`-custom_ops` toggle.
  - Every dispatch path is `hasattr(torch.ops._C, ...)`-guarded and falls back to native `F.layer_norm` when the op isn't present - currently a no-op everywhere, since no `vllm-xpu-kernels` release yet contains #577 (just merged) and `requirements/xpu.txt`'s pin predates it.

  ## Test Plan

  - `ruff check`, `ruff format`, full `pre-commit` (incl. `mypy`) on every touched file.
  - Kernel correctness on Intel B70 hardware: parametrized cases across hidden sizes (incl. non-power-of-2), bf16/fp16, weight/bias/weight_bias combinations, plus fused-add cases, for both `layer_norm` and `nemotron_layer_norm`/`fused_add_nemotron_layer_norm`, checked against a plain-PyTorch fp32 reference.
  - End-to-end serve (`--enforce-eager`) on the same hardware, per affected model.
  - End-to-end performance via the official `vllm bench serve`/`throughput`/`latency`, baseline vs patched, N=3 median.
  - Not yet added: a correctness test in the repo (`tests/kernels/core/test_layernorm.py` covers `RMSNorm`/`GemmaRMSNorm`, nothing exercised plain LayerNorm before this PR). Not yet done: lm_eval accuracy check for any affected model. A reproducible kernel-level benchmark (`benchmark/benchmark_layer_norm.py`) is already
  committed on the vllm-xpu-kernels PR itself.

  ## Test Result

  **Correctness:** 64 parametrized cases + 2 fused-add cases, all pass vs plain-PyTorch fp32 reference.

  **Kernel microbenchmark** (native `F.layer_norm` vs SYCL, bf16, hidden_size=4096):

  | tokens | native | SYCL | speedup |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1 | 8.35us | 3.60us | 2.32x |
  | 128 | 9.63us | 3.70us | 2.60x |
  | 512 | 28.20us | 5.90us | 4.78x |
  | 1024 | 51.73us | 10.83us | 4.78x (peak) |
  | 2048 | 103.91us | 56.61us | 1.84x |

  **End-to-end serve:** GPT-J, GPT-2, OPT-125m, Nemotron/Minitron-8B, PaliGemma (SigLIP), and StarCoder2-3B all served and generated correctly with `--enforce-eager`; SYCL dispatch confirmed firing inside the real engine, not just via a direct standalone op call.

  **End-to-end performance:**

  | Model | Path | Throughput | Latency | Serve |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | GPT-2-124M | direct swap | **+9.1%** | -9.5% (faster) | **+5.3%** |
  | OPT-125M | direct swap | **+9.2%** | -1.2% (faster) | **+9.4%** |
  | GPT-J-405M | direct swap | **+6.1%** | -4.4% (faster) | **+9.2%** |
  | StarCoder2-3B | generic swap | +1.0% | -1.2% (faster) | +1.3% |
  | Minitron-8B (Nemotron) | direct swap | +0.8% | -0.9% (faster) | +0.5% |


  **Caveat:** the above was measured against an earlier revision of this dispatch code (direct `torch.ops._C.*` calls, gated by `torch.compiler.is_compiling()`). This PR wraps those same calls through `torch.ops.vllm.xpu_*` instead, for `torch.compile` safety - a thin pass-through to the identical kernel call, so behavior should
  be unchanged, but hasn't itself been re-run on hardware.

title: [Core] Model console logging as CLI configuration
author: markmc
body:
Addresses #57200.

Adds a typed `LoggingConfig` to `VllmConfig` with three initial fields:

- `configure_logging`
- `log_level`
- `pylogging_config_file`

The complete object can be supplied as `--logging-config` JSON or with dotted arguments such as `--logging-config.log_level DEBUG`. `--log-level` is a convenience override for `log_level`, while the pre-existing `--log-config-file` is retained as a legacy override for `pylogging_config_file`.

The same model is available through serve YAML and Python configuration. `VLLM_CONFIGURE_LOGGING`, `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL`, and `VLLM_LOGGING_CONFIG_PATH` remain as compatibility defaults. Explicit CLI and YAML configuration takes precedence, and the convenience/legacy CLI arguments override their matching `--logging-config` fields.

The resolved configuration is applied after argument parsing and propagated through `VllmConfig` to Uvicorn and API, engine, coordinator, and worker processes. This fixes the asymmetry where a CLI-supplied `--log-config-file` configured Uvicorn but arrived too late for vLLM's already-initialized root logger. Code that previously inspected `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL` directly now uses the effective logger level.

The existing default text output and custom Python `dictConfig` behavior are preserved. Tests cover JSON and dotted CLI forms, CLI/YAML/environment precedence, post-import reconfiguration, custom configuration files, and spawned-process propagation.

Co-authored-by: AI Assistant <noreply@openai.com>

title: [Perf][Pooling] Avoid blocking seq_lens GPU-to-CPU copy for pooling in FlashInfer metadata builder
author: frankwang28
body:
## Purpose
FlashInfer's metadata builder needs per-request sequence lengths on the CPU to plan paged KV metadata. For V2 model runner, `seq_lens` live on the GPU, so the builder fetches them with `common_attn_metadata.seq_lens.cpu()`. For pooling models this copy is avoidable; pooling models have no speculative tokens, so `seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound` maintained by the model runner is exact, not optimistic. The pooling runner already relies on this (`pooling_runner.py`: ["Pooling has no speculative tokens, so this CPU upper bound is exact"](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.29.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pool/pooling_runner.py#L142)). 

This results in a measured performance boost of about 1.35%.

AI assistance (locally hosted GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 as well as GPT-6 Astra) was used for implementation and analysis. All changed lines were reviewed and validated end-to-end.

title: [Core] structured generation mode for DiffusionGemma model (Jev-like)
author: mmastrac
body:
## Prerequisite PRs A few PRs that can go in on their own merits were split out: - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57414: hand out stashed logprobs only on the committing step (bug fix) - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57416: give a prefill-only batch the model state's number of logit rows (perf) - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57417: honor logprob_token_ids on the converging step (feature parity w/autoregressive) - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57462: type cast error if dynamo falls back to eager mid-run (bugfix) - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57589: fix multimodal support in DiffusionGemma (bugfix) ## Purpose DiffusionGemma (and likely other models in vLLM) contains all of the necessary components to build a Jev-like model that provides structured answers with bounded choices. By fixing canvas positions in the given structured output format, you can ask the model to provide a token and logprobs (from which a client derives entropy) that can be used to determine the models most likely answer and its confidence in that answer. If entropy does not pass a given threshold, you can perform additional sampling to determine agreement between runs and therefore the actual confidence of the model's answer. This PR contains a prototype example server for serving the `/v1/systemone` endpoint. It does not implement a standard endpoint in vLLM. The model is sufficiently powerful to work with _any_ structured output that follows one limitation: the token choices _must_ be a single token, so that the canvas itself does not shift. The requesting client can always translate multi-token options into single token options, however (ie: "moderation_spam" -> "A"). The choices are always laid out in a system prompt and the model correctly diffuses single-token-slot answers (or makes a guess and flags it with uncertainty). Why do we require the token IDs in the request? Currently we provide the token slot positions that are unfixed for the model to choose and this allows the two to be matched more accurately. A followup PR will likely add a template syntax. The model, using this framework, can answer yes/no ("noul" in Jev parlance), scale, or multiple choice questions, and provides its certainty and error bars with the answer. The only missing pieces for this to work in vLLM today are in this PR: - A way to pre-seed the canvas with the fixed tokens - A way to send read-only requests that emit the argmax canvas on the converging step and skip the commit forward (logprobs come from that step at temperature 1) - A way to limit the number of steps run (we only want the first step) - A bugfix for two parallel DiffusionGemma generations that stomp on each other in lockstep: two concurrent requests with logprobs on where one converges in the same step another commits loses its stash and the request fails with HTTP 500 "list index out of range". This PR currently contains the machinery to make this model work and a sample interposer server is included to demonstrate end-to-end functionality that is sufficient to serve traffic at reasonable scale. | field | type | validation | effect | |---|---|---|---| | `diffusion_seed_canvas` | `list[int]`, exactly the request's canvas width | ids in `[0, vocab)`, length checked against `diffusion_canvas_length`, else the served `--diffusion-config` | replaces the random canvas after prefill | | `diffusion_max_steps` | `int >= 1` | clamped to `max_denoising_steps` | denoise steps before the canvas is emitted | | `diffusion_pinned` | `list[int]` of canvas positions | needs a `diffusion_seed_canvas`; positions must lie inside the request's canvas | held at their seed value on every denoise step, and their self-conditioning soft embed is zeroed, so a read past one step denoises the canvas the request seeded instead of one the model rewrote | | `diffusion_read_only` | `bool` (the OpenAI server delivers JSON booleans in `vllm_xargs` as 0/1, which is accepted) | caps `max_tokens` at the canvas, sets `ignore_eos` | emit on the converging step, skip the commit forward, temperature-1 logprobs | | `diffusion_canvas_length` | `int`, 1 to the served `canvas_length` | validated in `verify`; the seed must be this long | the request runs on a canvas this wide: the scheduler schedules this many draft tokens and the sampler tiles the read at this width, so a short schema on a wide server costs the same as on a server of its own width | | `logprob_token_ids` (a request field, not in `vllm_xargs`) | `list[int]`, up to 128 | existing vLLM validation | exact logprobs for those ids at every canvas position. The sampler now honors it on the converging step, so a read asks for its label ids instead of hoping they rank in the top-k (with 26 options only 1-8 did) | Example request: ``` { "model": "dgemma", "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Answer a fixed set of questions about the state ... Question urgent: ...\n yes\n no\n..."}, {"role": "user", "content": "{\"ticket\": \"Since this morning the dashboard shows a blank page after login...\"}"} ], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}, "max_tokens": 17, "logprobs": true, "top_logprobs": 20, "return_tokens_as_token_ids": true, "vllm_xargs": { "diffusion_seed_canvas": [100, 45518, 107, 101, 148436, 236787, 71203, 107, 36164, 236787, 9950, 107, 66387, 236787, 236743, 189012, 106, 0, 0, "... 64 ids total"], "diffusion_max_steps": 1, "diffusion_read_only": true } } ``` ## Example Queries These are _raw_ example queries passed to the model: ``` Answer a fixed set of questions about the state the user provides. Each question lists its allowed answers; reply with exactly one label per question. You are reviewing a user post on a community forum. Question violates: Does the post break the community rules? yes no Question category: Which rule does it come closest to breaking? A: none B: spam (unsolicited promotion) C: harassment (targets a person or group) D: self_harm Question severity: How severe is it? 1: none 2: mild 3: serious 4: critical Reply with one line per question, in this order, formatted as "id: label". ``` Answer template (@ standing in for a noised slot): ``` <|channel>thought\nviolates: @\ncategory: @\nseverity: @ ``` Seeded canvas: ``` [100, 45518, 107, 101, 51584, 1090, 236787, 58369, 107, 10618, 236787, 13112, 107, 127243, 236787, 236743, 144194, 106, 0, 0, ... 0] pos 7: violates <- 58369 (' Mell') pos 11: category <- 13112 (' laugh') pos 16: severity <- 144194 ('اهرة') ``` ## Test Plan Run locally on a DGX spark, with a concurrency sweep to ensure it scales and does not corrupt parallel generations. ``` pytest tests/test_sampling_params.py tests/v1/sample/test_diffusion_gemma_reads.py ``` Run with: ``` vllm serve nvidia/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it-NVFP4 --diffusion-config '{"canvas_length": 32}' --max-logprobs 32 --enable-prefix-caching --async-scheduling --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN --max-num-seqs 32 python examples/features/structured_diffusion/structured_server.py --upstream http://127.0.0.1:8000 --tokenizer nvidia/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it-NVFP4 --canvas 32 ``` ## Test Result Hardware: 1 DGX Spark, sole active GPU process. Setup: read-only single reads, 32-row canvas, three decisions per request, cache-busted state with the schema prefix cached Results: 1-way 8.7 req/s at 0.12 s, 32-way 54.0 req/s at 0.58 s, about 162 decisions/s. Using a sample request/response corpus to determine, from a mock support request, the urgency, tone and routing of an outage report, we get the correct variable number of samples per request (the auto policy re-reads only when the first read is uncertain): H1: is the first read's entropy per question over the top-20 logprobs (note that reads=4 when H1>0.1) ``` == samples=auto outage 527ms reads=4
