title: [ROCm][Perf] Restore 32-bit buffer addressing for TRITON_ATTN KV cache views
author: umarkovi-amd
body:
## Overview



On ROCm, give the K/V cache views used by `TRITON_ATTN` a Triton `ptr_range()` bounded by their layer's region. This lets Triton's AMD backend keep 32-bit buffer addressing for them, fixing a ~16% throughput regression on RDNA3 introduced by #51718, which moved the KV cache into one backing allocation.

## Claims



- `TRITON_ATTN` throughput on Radeon Pro W7900 (gfx1100):
  - **+18%** for Whisper-large-v3: 5.34 → 6.31 req/s, back to the pre-#51718 level of 6.40.
  - **+18%** for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 2.70 → 3.19 req/s.
- No accuracy change:
  - Whisper transcripts are token-identical on all 2,703 LibriSpeech validation-clean clips.
  - lm-eval GSM8K is within run-to-run noise.
- No change to KV-cache allocation, layouts, KV connectors/offloading or non-ROCm platforms, and no new configuration.

## Validation



W7900 (gfx1100) Base = this PR's parent, using the same build (the change is Python-only). Base and PR ran back to back on the same GPU.

| `vllm bench throughput` | base (3 runs) | this PR (3 runs) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper-large-v3, fp16, eager, LibriSpeech, 100 prompts × 200 tokens | 5.33 / 5.35 / 5.34 | 6.32 / 6.31 / 6.31 | **+18.2%** |
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, bf16, `TRITON_ATTN`, CUDA graphs + compile, random 1024 / 256, 500 prompts | 2.698 / 2.698 / 2.700 | 3.191 / 3.197 / 3.196 | **+18.4%** |

| Accuracy | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Whisper, LibriSpeech validation-clean (2,703 clips), greedy, identical outputs | — | 2,703 / 2,703 |
| Whisper WER (simple normalization) | 4.410% | 4.410% |
| GSM8K, Qwen2.5-7B, `TRITON_ATTN`, 5-shot (strict / flexible) | 79.98 / 83.32 (repeat: 80.14 / 83.47) | 79.76 / 83.85 |

The GSM8K stderr is ±1.1. Base-vs-base differences are the same size as base-vs-PR.

<details>
<summary>Profile, code generation and lint</summary>

- **rocprofv3 kernel trace:** Whisper cross-attention, about 63% of GPU time, goes from 1,843 µs to 1,379 µs median per `kernel_unified_attention` call.
- **Code generation** (compiled into an empty `TRITON_CACHE_DIR`): with this PR, `key_cache_ptr`/`value_cache_ptr` carry `tt.pointer_range = 32` in `kernel_unified_attention` (VGPRs 256 → 205) and in `reshape_and_cache_kernel_flash`.
- **Lint:** `pre-commit run --from-ref main --to-ref HEAD` and `pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual` pass.
- **No new tests:** the change only affects code generation, and CI has no RDNA runners.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Reproduce</summary>

```bash
export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=0 FLASH_ATTENTION_TRITON_AMD_ENABLE=TRUE
vllm bench throughput --model openai/whisper-large-v3 --trust-remote-code \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --dtype float16 --max-model-len 448 \
  --dataset-name hf --dataset-path openslr/librispeech_asr --hf-subset clean --hf-split validation \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":1}' --num-prompts 100 --backend vllm --output-len 200
vllm bench throughput --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --max-model-len 4096 --attention-config.backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts 500 --seed 0
# GSM8K: lm_eval.simple_evaluate(model=VLLM(pretrained="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", dtype="bfloat16",
#   max_model_len=4096, attention_config={"backend": "TRITON_ATTN"}), tasks=["gsm8k"], num_fewshot=5)
```
</details>

## Details



**Root cause.**
- Triton's AMD backend marks a pointer argument `tt.pointer_range = 32`, which enables buffer loads with 32-bit offsets, only if `arg.ptr_range()` or else `arg.untyped_storage().size()` is ≤ 2 GiB (`is_within_2gb`).
- Since #51718, each layer's KV cache is a view into one allocation (~36.6 GiB here), so the storage check fails.
- `kernel_unified_attention` therefore uses 64-bit addressing: 205 → 256 VGPRs, and occupancy on gfx1100 drops from 7 to 5 waves/SIMD.
- Bisected with only vLLM changing: #51718 measures 5.40 req/s, its parent 6.40.

**Change.**
- `set_triton_ptr_range(region, *views)` sets each view's `ptr_range()` to the bytes from its `data_ptr()` to the end of `region`, computed from shape and strides.
- `TritonAttentionImpl` calls it on ROCm for the K/V views in `forward` and in `do_kv_cache_update`.

**Safety.**
- The bound is the view's real extent, and Triton still checks it against 2 GiB at every launch. Layers above 2 GiB, or block-outermost layouts, keep 64-bit addressing.
- Both kernels only address within the view: through block-table indices or slot mappings, with padding slots skipped. This is the assumption Triton already made before #51718.
- Views are rebuilt every forward, and only host-side metadata is read, so there is no GPU synchronization.

**Duplicates.** I searched open and closed PRs and issues for `ptr_range`, `pointer_range`, buffer ops/addressing, 2 GiB, and #51718 regressions; none overlap.

title: [Model][MoE] Load MegaMoE experts directly into the DeepGEMM layout
author: aoshen02
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

DeepSeek-V4 MegaMoE (also used by Kimi-K3) loads the routed experts into loader-side parameters, then `finalize_weights` asks the `DeepGemmMegaMoEBackend` (#58053) to transform them into DeepGEMM's layout and drops the loaded parameters, so any later `load_weights` has nowhere to write. The fused shared expert is built the same way, from a shared MLP whose weights the fusion then takes over.

This PR moves the layout into load time. The backend is selected when the experts are constructed, registers the kernel-layout tensors as the parameters (`create_weights`), and writes each checkpoint shard straight into them (`load_weight`). Whether the shared expert is fused is also decided at construction. Loading, reloading and updating weights then write into the tensors the kernel reads, and there is no MegaMoE post-load step left: `finalize_weights`, `finalize_mega_moe_weights` and the post-load hooks that only called them are removed (DeepSeek-V4 keeps its mHC hook).

## Claims

- `reload_weights` works with MegaMoE. DeepSeek-V4-Flash GSM8K after a reload: `main` 0.948 → 0.008, this PR 0.951 → 0.948.
- DeepSeek-V4.1 (MXFP8 shared expert) keeps its fused shared expert across a reload: `main` 0.898 → 0.010, this PR 0.904 → 0.901.
- An identity reload changes no parameter and moves no storage (0 of 1588 per-rank checksums, DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP2).
- The shared expert has no second copy: its four kernel tensors are the parameters (DeepSeek-V4-Flash TP2: 76.6 GiB, same as `main`).
- Kimi-K3 drops its `finalize_weights` override and the `_mega_l*` buffers.

## Validation

GB200, real weights, `vllm serve`, `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe`, EP. GSM8K: 1319 questions, 5-shot, greedy.

| model, parallelism | `main`: GSM8K → `reload_weights` → GSM8K | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP2, MTP k=2 | 0.948 → **0.008** | 0.951 → 0.948 |
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP4 | 0.898 → **0.010** | 0.904 → 0.901 |
| Kimi-K3 (1.5T MXFP4), 4 nodes, TP4 × DP4, EP16 | 0.944 → 0.950, 137.52 GiB | 0.949 → 0.937 and 0.945 → 0.954 (two runs), 137.52 GiB |

The `main` column was measured before #58053; #58053 moved the transform into the backend but kept the post-load transform that drops the loaded parameters. On `main`, Kimi-K3 survives this reload only because the checkpoint is the same: its `finalize_weights` returns early once transformed experts exist, so reloaded expert weights never reach the kernels.

Neither DeepSeek run logs the shared-expert fusion fallback warning, so both keep the fused shared expert.

`tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_mega_moe.py` (68 passed on GB200):
- Shuffled, per-shard routed loads (with EPLB replicas) are compared against DeepGEMM's batched transform, including the real DeepGEMM CUDA transform.
- A second routed load updates the kernel tensors in place.
- Shared-expert shards (gate, up, down; weights and 1x32 scales, both `.w2.` and `.down_proj.` names) land where DeepGEMM's transform puts them; reloading one shard overwrites in place and leaves the other half alone; the returned names are the registered parameters (for `enable_weights_track`).
- The fusion decision at construction: fused for DeepSeek-V4-Flash (e8m0 128x128) and V4.1 (uint8 1x32) scales; not fused for an older DeepGEMM, BF16 shared experts, non-UE8M0 scales or scales that do not tile to 1x32.

`tests/models/kimi_k3/test_weight_loading.py` is removed: it only checked that the removed Kimi-K3 finalize ran once.

`pre-commit` passes.

Setup: the vLLM image `nightly-dev-arm64-cu130-ac9126e58aa7` plus this change, overlaid file by file with SHA-256 gates.

Reviews: Codex (gpt-6-astra), Kimi K3 and Claude Fable 5.1 audited this change. The two Codex should-fix findings (backend chosen for GPU 0 when the model is built on `meta` under `ipc_cache`; fused shared parameters reported under checkpoint names to weight tracking) are fixed and re-verified by Codex.

## Details

**Backend interface.** #58053's `transform_weights` / `transform_shared_expert_weights` / `supports_shared_experts(deep_gemm)` become:
- `create_weights(layer, ...)`: register the routed (and fused shared) parameters in the kernel layout, indexed by local expert on dim 0 (EPLB moves experts along it);
- `load_weight(dst, src, shard_id, is_scale)`: write one checkpoint shard into one expert slice or a shared parameter;
- `supports_shared_experts(shared_experts)`: decide fusion at construction.

A post-load transform cannot coexist with in-place weight updates, because it replaces the storage the loaders write into. A backend with a different layout (e.g. an SM90 plugin) expresses it in `create_weights` and `load_weight`. Out-of-tree backends written against #58053 need this migration.

**SM100 layout.** DeepGEMM's `transform_weights_for_mega_moe` interleaves gate/up rows in groups of 8 and permutes scale rows for UTCCP; the L2 weight is unchanged. Each row of each shard lands at a fixed position, so `load_weight` copies a shard into a strided view of its final location:
- L1 gate row `r` → `(r // 8) * 16 + r % 8`, up row `r` → `(r // 8) * 16 + 8 + r % 8`.
- Scales are the UE8M0 bytes expanded to one per 1x32 block, packed four along K per int32, stored MN-major, with the UTCCP row map `128b + 32j + i → 128b + 4i + j`.

Routed FP4 parameters are int8 (the kernel's dtype) instead of uint8; loads reinterpret the bytes.

**Shared expert.** Fusion requires FP8 shared weights with UE8M0 scales that tile to 1x32 (checked on the shared MLP's parameters, which its quant method creates at init) and a DeepGEMM with the shared-expert API. Otherwise it warns once and keeps the separate shared MLP, as on `main`, but at construction instead of after loading, so the layout never changes after load. When fused, `DeepseekV4MoE.shared_experts` is `None` and `load_weights` routes `shared_experts.*` tensors to the experts' four kernel-layout parameters.

**Backend selection.** The backend is selected for the device the model is built on, or for the worker's current GPU when that is `meta` (`--load-format ipc_cache`).

**Scope.** EPLB with a reload after a rebalance is broken on `main` and is not addressed. XPU keeps its own implementation.

**Not a duplicate.** #59003 (draft, stacked on #53509) also targets MegaMoE reload, but by staging new checkpoint sources and re-packing into buffers through a reload lifecycle. This PR removes the packed copy: the parameters are the kernel tensors, so there is nothing to stage or rebuild.

**AI assistance.** Written with Claude Code. The submitter reviewed every changed line and ran the tests and GPU checks above.

title: [ROCm][DSv4.1][Perf] Route gfx942 sparse MLA prefill to AITER pa_prefill_sparse
author: frida-andersson
body:
## Summary

On gfx942, fp16/bf16 sparse MLA prefill with at least 512 query rows goes to AITER `pa_prefill_sparse`. Shorter calls stay on the in-tree kernel. The import and the `Using AITER pa_prefill_sparse for sparse MLA prefill on gfx942` log happen only when that kernel launches.

## What changed

- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py`: after the gfx950 OPUS attempt, call `pa_prefill_sparse` when the gfx942 gate passes. One KV pool. The caller output is passed as `out` when it matches `q`; a narrower output is copied from the kernel result.
- `tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_triton_attn_dsv4.py`: the dense Triton fallback test stubs the getter, so that case stays in-tree.

## Gating

gfx942, AITER enabled, `q` fp16 or bf16, `kv.dtype == q.dtype`, and `q.shape[0] >= 512` (`_GFX942_AITER_PA_PREFILL_SPARSE_MIN_QUERIES`).

The long-BF16 test still patches `on_gfx942()` so other ROCm devices take that routing decision. It pins `get_cdna_version()` to the physical chip first, so `pa_prefill_sparse` runs only on real CDNA3.

`pa_prefill_sparse` does not split the KV. Under 512 rows the call stays on the in-tree ragged prefill, which also does not. DeepSeek-V4.1 decode uses `rocm_sparse_attn_decode` and does not enter this function. The 2-row and 16-row shapes stay off `pa_prefill_sparse`. On this branch that is the in-tree kernel, not Gluon split-K.

## Depends on

[ROCm/aiter#6002](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/6002). The symbol is imported only after the gate. A missing symbol raises on an eligible call. A short call does not import it.

## Performance

### DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Nightly `0.31.1rc1.dev1+gbb87d227d`, 4× MI325X, TP4, spec off, no FlyDSL QuickReduce, no decoder replay. Seed 7. This table is the Oct 7 run, when the gate was 1024. It was not rerun for this commit. Every length below is also above 512, so the prefill kernel is the same. The on arm logged the AITER line.

| 65536 | 128 | 2 | 7966.74 → 7082.31 | −11.1% | 21.30 → 23.56 | +10.6% |
| 65536 | 1024 | 2 | 7950.64 → 7081.32 | −10.9% | 91.54 → 96.61 | +5.5% |

title: [Perf][HiSparse] Fuse per-layer slot invalidation and shorten the all-resident resolver path
author: MatthewBonanni
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Cut HiSparse's per-layer decode overhead in GPU time and launches: fuse per-layer slot invalidation into one launch per step, mask CUDA-graph padding rows inside the resolver, and cheapen resolver arithmetic.

## Claims

- Slot invalidation: one launch per step instead of one per leader layer. On B200 with 78 index groups, each step drops from 374–759 µs to 3.5–162 µs.
- Resolver: 1.16×–3.69× faster per layer than main at every swept shape on B200, with bit-identical outputs.
- GLM-5.3-NVFP4, TP8 B200, 16k/1k: mean TPOT −1.8% at c=16 and −0.5% at c=64.

## Validation

#### Microbenchmarks (B200, main vs PR kernels in one process, CUPTI device time)

Outputs are bit-identical between main and PR at every point.

**Slot invalidation per step** (78 = GLM-5.3 index groups):

| groups × tokens | main | PR |
|---|---|---|
| 61 × 64 | 367 µs (61 launches) | 9.9 µs (1) |
| 78 × 8 | 374 µs (78 launches) | 3.5 µs (1) |
| 78 × 64 | 634 µs | 13.0 µs |
| 78 × 256 | 759 µs | 59.1 µs |

**Resolver per layer** (top-k 2048, CUDA graph; main includes the padding `copy_` + `masked_fill_`):

| requests (rows/graph rows) | pages on host | main | PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 (64/64) | 0% | 9.2 µs | 4.6 µs | 2.00× |
| 64 (64/64) | 10% | 18.8 µs | 14.0 µs | 1.34× |
| 100 (100/128) | 0% | 15.3 µs | 4.8 µs | 3.19× |
| 64, MTP3 (256/256) | 0% | 20.0 µs | 11.4 µs | 1.76× |
| 100, MTP3 (400/512) | 0% | 48.8 µs | 13.2 µs | 3.69× |
| 128, MTP3 (512/512) | 100% | 54.7 µs | 47.2 µs | 1.16× |

PR is faster at all 36 swept points (1–128 requests, q=1/4, 0/10/100% host pages): 1.16×–3.69×.

#### End to end (GLM-5.3-NVFP4, 8×B200, TP8, 16k in / 1k out)

Main and PR were run back to back on one node, interleaved, with 2 reps each and a server restart per point. Both have the same KV capacity (1.49M GPU + host tokens).

| concurrency | variant | output tok/s | mean TPOT (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | main | 802 / 809 | 15.84 / 15.67 |
| 16 | PR | 816 / 817 | 15.47 / 15.46 |
| 64 | main | 1265 / 1262 | 40.23 / 40.35 |
| 64 | PR | 1267 / 1270 | 40.12 / 40.02 |
| 64 | no HiSparse | 1327 | 38.27 |

Summary: −1.8% TPOT at c=16, −0.5% at c=64. That closes about 11% of HiSparse's remaining 2.0 ms TPOT gap to no-HiSparse at c=64; the rest is outside these kernels.

```bash
vllm serve RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 -tp 8 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 64 \
  --max-model-len 18432 --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"HiSparseConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"host_pool_gib":128}}'
vllm bench serve --model RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 16384 --random-output-len 1024 \
  --num-prompts $((2*C)) --max-concurrency $C --ignore-eos --seed 42
```

Benchmarks compare main at `d0c20bb840` with this PR at `ab5afbdab6`. The later merge of main only routes the op calls through the HiSparse platform backend (#62592), and the unit tests were rerun on it.

**Tests**

- [x] `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py -k hisparse tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_connector.py tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py` → 103 passed on B200. New test: `test_hisparse_invalidation_covers_every_index_group`.
- [x] `pytest tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py` → 5 passed on B200.
- [x] GLM-5.3-NVFP4 serve A/B on B200 (above).

## Details

Cut HiSparse's per-layer decode overhead on the GPU and in launches:

- **One slot-invalidation launch per step.** Today it's one eager launch per leader layer after the forward graph. The kernel now runs over (written tokens × index groups) using a cached device table of each group's `device_global_indices`. `HiSparseRuntime.invalidate_written_slots` is replaced by `HiSparseSlotInvalidator`.
- **Resolver masks CUDA-graph padding rows itself** from `num_valid_rows`, one block per padding row. This removes the per-layer `copy_` + `masked_fill_` and the `request_ids`/`row_indices` buffers. On main, one block masks the whole padding run serially, which dominates the launch on padded batches.
- **Cheaper resolver arithmetic.** Power-of-two block math uses shift/mask (compile-time for 64-row blocks), and the first row's top-k is loaded before the request lookups resolve.

- `HiSparseSlotInvalidator` caches one device table of `device_global_indices` addresses per leader set. It is built on first use, so steady-state steps do no H2D copy. All index groups must share one hot layout (checked).
- Remaining HiSparse TPOT overhead at c=64 (~1.8 ms vs no HiSparse) is outside these kernels.

Not a duplicate: no open PR touches these kernels.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Use native merge_attn_states kernel on gfx942/gfx950
author: amd-mghanimi
body:
## Overview

Use the native `merge_attn_states` kernel on CDNA3 and newer (gfx942, gfx950, gfx1250) instead of the Triton fallback. The kernel is already built and registered on ROCm. The Python dispatch in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/merge_attn_states.py` is gated on `get_cdna_version() >= 3`, so gfx90a stays on Triton. The kernel was introduced for CUDA in #16173.

## Claims

- On gfx942 and gfx950, the native kernel is faster than the Triton kernel in every case of `tests/kernels/attention/test_merge_attn_states.py`: 2592 timed cases per GPU, median 2.4x, minimum 1.1x.
- The native output matches Triton on both architectures, including FP8 output (`float8_e4m3fnuz` on gfx942, `float8_e4m3fn` on gfx950).
- In end-to-end serving of an MLA model, the merge kernel time drops about 4x. Serving metrics are unchanged within run-to-run noise, because merge is a small share of prefill.
- gfx90a (CDNA2) and RDNA stay on Triton. `get_cdna_version() >= 3` also selects gfx1250 (CDNA5); that GPU was not part of the runs below.

## Validation

### Unit test

`pytest -s tests/kernels/attention/test_merge_attn_states.py`, unmodified, on one GPU at vLLM 92044241:

| GPU | arch | result | native vs Triton, 2592 timed cases |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MI325X | gfx942 | 2598 passed | min 1.10x, median 2.39x, max 8.58x, 0 slower |
| MI355X | gfx950 | 2598 passed | min 1.64x, median 2.36x, max 8.30x, 0 slower |

The test calls the native op and the Triton op directly, so these numbers do not depend on this change. The smallest gains on both GPUs are fp32 inputs at head size 256.

The rows from #16173 (16 query heads per rank, head size 128, i.e. an MLA model at TP=8):

| tokens | dtype | MI325X triton | MI325X native | MI325X speedup | MI355X triton | MI355X native | MI355X speedup |

| 4096 | float32 | 0.06322ms | 0.03733ms | 1.6936x | 0.06578ms | 0.02589ms | 2.5406x |

| 1024 | float16 | 0.03403ms | 0.01482ms | 2.2957x | 0.03294ms | 0.01368ms | 2.4078x |
| 1536 | float16 | 0.03905ms | 0.01515ms | 2.5777x | 0.03676ms | 0.01455ms | 2.5260x |
| 4096 | float16 | 0.06068ms | 0.02637ms | 2.3013x | 0.06493ms | 0.01966ms | 3.3030x |

| 512 | bfloat16 | 0.03024ms | 0.01357ms | 2.2284x | 0.02903ms | 0.01269ms | 2.2876x |

With FP8 output (same rows, bf16/fp16/fp32 input to FP8), native is 2.1x to 2.9x faster on MI325X and 2.2x to 3.5x faster on MI355X.

### End-to-end

Kimi-K3, 8x MI355X, TP=8, FP8 KV cache, `--load-format dummy`, concurrency 16. Each configuration was run once without and once with this change; nothing else differs between the two runs. All numbers are from the profiled runs. Merge launches and merge kernel time come from the rank-0 torch profiler trace over the same window of steps, which covers one full request. TTFT, TPOT and throughput are from the same runs, with the profiler active for that window.

| input/output | merge kernel | merge launches | merge kernel time | mean TTFT (ms) | median TTFT (ms) | mean TPOT (ms) | output tok/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 60k/600 | Triton | 1176 | 118.90 ms | 7280.80 | 3337.37 | 89.97 | 152.49 |
| 60k/600 | native | 1176 | 29.30 ms | 7291.12 | 3231.90 | 89.54 | 153.09 |
| 128k/1k | Triton | 3744 | 424.50 ms | 17272.42 | 9884.53 | 111.25 | 122.19 |
| 128k/1k | native | 3792 | 98.31 ms | 17312.48 | 10211.05 | 110.82 | 122.54 |

The merge kernel is 4.1x faster at 60k and 4.3x faster at 128k. Over the profiled window it is 0.26% (60k) and 0.42% (128k) of total kernel time under Triton, so the serving metrics move within noise.

```bash
vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3 --load-format dummy --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --trust-remote-code --max-model-len 131072 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-num-seqs 256 --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --async-scheduling \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}'
```

</details>

title: [KV Connector][NIXL] Register HiSparse host pool under single TP Rank
author: praveingk
body:
When HiSparse uses its **shared host pool**, all local TP ranks share one `/dev/shm` mmap per DP rank. Even so, every TP rank registers the whole pool with NIXL, and every TP rank READs the same host-pool KV into the same pages. With UCX this means `ibv_reg_mr` of the full pool on every NIC, twice per NIC when relaxed ordering is on. At TP8 with 8 NICs, the pool is registered **128 times per node**, and each request's host-pool KV is pulled **8 times** into identical memory.

This PR adds an opt-in flag, `VLLM_NIXL_HISPARSE_DRAM_RANK0_ONLY=1`, which makes TP rank 0 the only rank that registers the shared pool and pulls into it. The other ranks:

- keep the DRAM regions in their metadata, so the prefill handshake still sees identical region lists;
- skip the DRAM `register_memory`;
- skip the DRAM transfer dlist;
- skip the DRAM part of each READ.

The GPU-resident part (the indexer cache) is still read by every rank, and every rank still notifies the producer.

Completion and ordering need nothing new:

- A request finishes only when all TP ranks report it done.
- HiSparse restores from the shared pool on the next step.
- The `cudaHostRegister` pin of the pool on every rank is unchanged, because each rank's GPU still reads from it.

### Changes

- `vllm/envs.py`: adds `VLLM_NIXL_HISPARSE_DRAM_RANK0_ONLY` (default off).
- `nixl/base_worker.py`:
  - `_leaves_dram_xfer_to_rank0()` decides whether a rank skips. That requires the flag, mixed DRAM/VRAM regions, `tp_rank != 0`, and `use_shared_hisparse_host_pool()`. Private (non-shared) pools are never affected.
  - Skipping ranks:
    - do not register DRAM ranges;
    - store `None` instead of preparing DRAM dlists, in both the local path and the split path;
    - leave zeroing of clipped shared-pool pages to rank 0.
  - Shutdown ignores the `None` handles.
- `nixl/pull_worker.py`: `_read_blocks_mixed()` drops the DRAM descriptors on skipping ranks and keeps the device part. It registers the request even when nothing is left to read, so it still completes and notifies.
- `NixlPushConnector` already rejects mixed-memory KV caches, so it is unchanged.
- Tests (`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py`):
  - **The rank decision:** flag on/off × rank 0 vs non-zero × shared vs private pool.
  - **No DRAM dlist on skipping ranks:** descriptor positions still cover the DRAM regions, so ids stay aligned with the remote side.
  - **A READ that keeps only the device part** still notifies.
  - **A READ left with no descriptors** still completes and notifies.
  - Existing `object.__new__` fixtures initialise the new attribute.

### Why: VM freezes on cloud RoCE VFs

On Cloud VPC instances (QEMU/KVM guests with ConnectX-7 SR-IOV VFs over RoCE, UCX 1.21 via NIXL 1.3.2), a GLM-5.3 HiSparse decode froze **both VMs** during NIXL registration with a 384 GiB pool. There was no guest panic, no guest log and no watchdog output; the nodes had to be reprovisioned. The same configuration passes on bare-metal H200 with InfiniBand.

Guest-side sampling explains the scale of the problem:

- **Pins per page:** `nr_foll_pin_acquired − released` measured exactly **8 + ranks × NICs × 2** (relaxed ordering) per page of pool.
- **Registration metadata:** the VFs' `fw_pages_total` stayed flat at 4 per VF throughout, so the registration metadata is not taken from guest memory.
- **Freeze point:** the freeze appeared between 36.9 TiB (passed) and 49.2 TiB (froze) of NIC-registered memory per VM.

### Results (llmd-roce cluster, GLM-5.3, DeepEP LL decode, 8 NICs, relaxed ordering on unless noted)

**Registration footprint per VM**, from a 2-node decode (DP2 × TP8). These numbers are measured with a startup patch equivalent to this PR on vLLM `87ecf7dbb`.

| Host pool | Stock: pins/page | Stock: NIC-registered | This PR: pins/page | This PR: NIC-registered | This PR: rank-0 registration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 GiB | 136.1x | 12.5 TiB | **24.2x** | **1.58 TiB** | ~28 s (ranks 1–7 < 1 s) |
| 288 GiB | 136x | 36.9 TiB | **24.05x** | **4.51 TiB** | ~80 s |
| 384 GiB | 136x | 49.2 TiB, **both VMs froze** | **24.04x** | **6.01 TiB, passes** | 43–52 s |
| 384 GiB, relaxed ordering off | — | — | 16.02x | 3.01 TiB, passes | 21 s |

Startup is not faster per node: rank 0 does the same per-rank work as before. What drops 8x is the number of registrations, the pinned memory and the NIC metadata.

**P/D correctness**, using a separate prefill and greedy decoding:

- **Results:** P/D output matched the prefill-only reference for 18-, 28.7k- and 250k-token prompts, at pool sizes 100, 288 and 384 GiB. The short prompt shows the usual small numerical divergence between prefill and decode kernels; the 28.7k answer is identical; the 250k answer is the same sentence, differing in one word ("at" vs "in").
- **Transfer count:** each request takes **9** NIXL transfers (rank 0 host + 8 device) instead of 16.
- **Failures:** 0 failed transfers.

**End-to-end benchmark**, 4P/4D, 64 H100:

- **Prefill:** DP4 × PCP8/DCP8.
- **Decode:** DP4 × TP8 with a 288 GiB shared pool.
- **Load:** cc_traces 256k, constant load, 900 s per level.
- **Fairness:** both arms ran on the same 8 nodes, and both roles were re-created between arms.

| Concurrency | Out tok/s (PR vs stock) | TTFT p99 | ITL p50 | ITL p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | **602 vs 503 (+19.7%)** | **21.6 vs 89.0 s** | 20.9 vs 23.3 ms | 116 vs 167 ms |
| 64 | 547 vs 563 | 98.2 vs 87.5 s | 19.2 vs 21.6 ms | 33.3 vs 46.6 ms |
| 128 | 482 vs 520 | 194 vs 183 s | 18.2 vs 20.7 ms | 36.5 vs 65.6 ms |

- **ITL improves at every level:** p50 by 10–12%, p99 by 28–44%.
- **At c64 and c128 both arms are prefill-bound:** request rate is equal within 2%, and the tok/s gap follows output length.

**Transfer totals over the sweep:**

| Metric | This PR | Stock |
|---|---|---|
| NIXL bytes pulled | 5.35 TB | 31.3 TB |
| Average transfer time | 30.8 ms | 122 ms |
| p90 transfer time | 63.7 ms | 318 ms |
| CPU time posting transfers | 472 s | 3,657 s |
speedup_claims: ITL improves at every level:** p50 by 10–12%

speedup_evidence.claim: ITL improves at every level:** p50 by 10–12%

title: [Spec Decode][GLM-5.3-Flash] Support adaptive verification
author: jonahsamost
body:
## Motivation

Adaptive verification chooses on the GPU how many draft tokens to verify for each request. During full CUDA graph replay, the physical token buffer and captured control flow remain fixed, while the live request boundaries can change. GLM-5.3-Flash previously made two assumptions that were incompatible with this behavior:

- GDN captured the ordinary one-token decode path, even though replay could group those token rows into fewer requests with multiple verification tokens.
- The k-pool scatter path assumed every physical token row belonged to a live request, but a replayed graph can contain additional padding rows.

This PR updates both paths to handle GPU-selected request lengths and graph padding.

## Changes

- Allow the GDN backend to replay CUDA graphs whose per-request query lengths are chosen on the GPU.
- Capture GDN’s speculative path and the k-pool indexer at the maximum configured verification width.
- Update the k-pool scatter path to safely discard CUDA graph padding without synchronizing lengths back to the CPU.
- Add tests for variable verification lengths, graph padding, and sparse-indexer alignment.

## Testing

Added and ran focused tests covering:

- Mixed per-request GDN verification lengths
- CUDA graph padding in the k-pool scatter path
- Sparse-indexer sequence-length alignment
- Capture-time and replay-time request partition differences

## Throughput results

I benchmarked GLM-5.3-Flash with MTP on four B300 GPUs (TEP4). The sweep covered:

- Speculative depths `kmax = 1...5`
- 18 batch sizes from `B = 1` through `B = 256`
- Prefix lengths `S = 512, 8192, 32768`

The table reports decode throughput for adaptive verification relative to fixed verification at the same maximum depth. Each value is the unweighted mean over the `(B, S)` at that speculative depth.

| Maximum depth | Adaptive / fixed at same depth |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.965× |
| 2 | 0.958× |
| 3 | 0.965× |
| 4 | 1.065× |
| 5 | 1.127× |

---

title: [Spec Decode][MRV2] Suffix decoding speculator for Model Runner V2
author: nishantrevur
body:
## Overview `method="suffix"` today needs Arctic Inference, runs on the CPU, forces Model Runner V1 and disables async scheduling. With this PR it runs on Model Runner V2 with a GPU speculator, with async scheduling and without Arctic; V1 keeps using Arctic. This is the "suffix" item in #47172. The speculator builds on `ngram_gpu` (#40704) and borrows from #52097 (thanks @zip95297). Related fix on main: #61509 (adaptive verification's startup profiling was counted as CUDA graph memory). @njhill rebased this onto the speculator config refactor and simplified it: seeded requests are no longer special-cased, and the runner hooks are `BaseSpeculator` methods. ## Claims - `method="suffix"` runs on Model Runner V2: GPU-resident, no host sync on the propose path, async scheduling, no Arctic dependency. V1 is unchanged except for the default `num_speculative_tokens` (below). - Acceptance is on par with Arctic: 1.937 tokens per step vs Arctic's 1.923 (k=8) and 1.948 (k=24) on a 21K-request replay. - With adaptive verification, throughput matches or beats Arctic on V1 at every concurrency for Qwen2.5-7B (offline and online serving) and for Qwen2.5-1.5B from concurrency 64 up; at 1.5B concurrency 8 and 32 Arctic is ahead (below). Without adaptive verification, verifying every slot loses from concurrency 32 up, as with `ngram_gpu`. - GSM8K accuracy matches no speculation. - `num_speculative_tokens` now defaults to 8 for suffix decoding (was `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth`, 24), because V2 verifies every slot. ## Validation The results below were measured before @njhill's rebase and simplification. That change only affects requests with an explicit `seed`, and none of these benchmarks send per-request seeds, so they still apply. #61509 has since merged, so the "with #61509" figures are what adaptive verification gets on current main. **Tests** ```bash pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_suffix_speculator.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py # 49 passed pytest tests/test_config.py -k "speculative or suffix or heterogeneous or model_runner" # 68 passed pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_ngram_gpu.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_custom_speculator.py # 58 passed pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/ngram_suffix/test_ngram_suffix.py -k suffix # 3 passed ``` The e2e tests ran with the CI model's weights (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on one L4, before the simplification (which doesn't touch greedy decoding): - The V2 GSM8K correctness test passes (76.3%). At the old default k=24 it ran out of memory: V2 profiles one logits row per request, while every step computes 1 + k. - The V2 cross-request test gives 0.74 → 4.47 accepted tokens per draft on the repeated pass. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it's 1.32 → 5.12, and 1.28 → 1.28 with the corpus off, which the test's `second > 2 * first` check rejects. - The Arctic acceptance test (V1) passes. **Runtime checks** - **No new host syncs:** `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` with and without adaptive verification, including ingestion. - **TP=2:** corpus, index, statistics and drafts are identical on both ranks after 312 requests, with and without adaptive verification, on the default ring and on a 2,048-token ring where bursts of up to 48 finished requests wrap over themselves. **Acceptance.** Replay of 21,299 greedy Qwen2.5-1.5B requests with 5.1M output tokens (UltraChat, Alpaca, GSM8K, Spec-Bench, code edit, rewrite and templated JSON), in waves of 64, with a 1M-token corpus and k=8. Mean tokens per step. Arctic runs via `arctic_inference` and also sees responses still being generated. The kernel matches the replay on all 1,280 sampled drafts. | Drafter | All | Code edit | Rewrite | Templated JSON | |---|---|---|---|---| | Own history only | 1.651 | 5.50 | 4.74 | 1.65 | | **This PR** | **1.937** | 5.45 | 4.69 | 4.25 | | Exact corpus search + same vote (upper bound) | 1.956 | 5.45 | 4.69 | 4.28 | | Arctic (V1), k=8 | 1.923 | 5.12 | 4.07 | 3.89 | | Arctic (V1), k=24 | 1.948 | 5.89 | 4.37 | 4.11 | **Throughput.** Offline `LLM.generate` on this PR's final code. Output tokens/s relative to no speculation. - **Setup:** concurrency = `max_num_seqs`; prompts from a pinned pool with the replay's category mix (its GSM8K and Spec-Bench prompts also appear in the replay); greedy, `max_tokens=256`, k=8. - **Backends:** FlashAttention 2, except adaptive verification on `TRITON_ATTN`, which is compared against no speculation on `TRITON_ATTN`. - **Runs:** one per point; runs with another process on the GPU were discarded and rerun. | Model | Concurrency | `ngram_gpu` | Arctic (V1) | This PR | This PR + adaptive verification | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Qwen2.5-7B | 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 | 1.28 / 1.14 / 0.73 / 0.52x | 1.31 / 1.29 / 1.24 / 1.03x | 1.46 / 1.32 / 0.82 / 0.59x | **1.39 / 1.36 / 1.24 / 1.18x** | | Qwen2.5-1.5B | 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 / 128 / 256 | 1.45 / 1.25 / 0.84 / 0.55 / 0.50 / 0.44x | 1.41 / 1.43 / 1.17 / 1.00 / 0.91 / 0.82x | 1.66 / 1.47 / 0.97 / 0.64 / 0.56 / 0.52x | **1.56 / 1.29 / 1.15 / 1.05 / 0.99 / 0.91x** | - **Where Arctic wins:** 1.5B at concurrency 8 and 32, by 11% and 5% in absolute tok/s. Adaptive verification trims too much there (open question 2). - **Backend difference:** at 1.5B concurrency 128 / 256, `TRITON_ATTN` without speculation is 1.13 / 1.21x faster than FA2. Against the FA2 baseline the other columns use, adaptive verification is 1.12 / 1.10x. - **With #61509:** the 7B KV cache with adaptive verification grows from 21–46K to 50–70K tokens. 7B throughput becomes 1.38 / 1.32 / 1.30 / 1.15x, within run-to-run noise except at concurrency 32. **Online serving** (`vllm bench serve`, Qwen2.5-7B, prompts not in the 256-request warm-up, up to 256 output tokens, `--generation-config vllm`). Output throughput vs no speculation: | Config | Concurrency 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 | |---|---| | `ngram_gpu` | 1.26 / 1.11 / 0.73 / 0.53x | | Arctic (V1) | 1.42 / 1.37 / 1.24 / 1.10x | | This PR | 1.49 / 1.35 / 0.87 / 0.65x | | **This PR + adaptive verification** (vs no-spec on `TRITON_ATTN`) | **1.44 / 1.44 / 1.30 / 1.23x** | Median TTFT at concurrency 1 is 125 ms with this PR (with or without adaptive verification) and with `ngram_gpu`, vs 73 ms without speculation and 74 ms for Arctic on V1, which runs without async scheduling. That is about one decode step, so it's a V2 spec-decode cost rather than a suffix one.
GSM8K, workloads and correctness checks **GSM8K** (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all 1,319 questions, 5-shot, `max_num_seqs=128`). Accuracy matches within noise (binomial SE about 1 point); at this load speculation doesn't speed it up: | Config | Greedy | Temperature 0.7 | Wall time (greedy) | |---|---|---|---| | No speculation (FA2) | 83.0% | 81.7% | 193 s | | No speculation (`TRITON_ATTN`) | 83.4% | 82.3% | 156 s | | Arctic (V1) | 83.4% | 83.2% | 252 s | | This PR | 82.8% | 83.6% | 387 s | | This PR + adaptive verification (`TRITON_ATTN`) | 82.9% | 81.6% | 157 s | **Workloads.** Offline, throughput vs no speculation (adaptive verification vs no-spec on `TRITON_ATTN`). Concurrency 32, except long context: | Workload | This PR | + adaptive verification | Arctic (V1) | |---|---|---|---| | VLM: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, 360 distinct camera frames, templated JSON reports and captions | 1.38x (3.18 tok/step) | 1.50x | 1.56x | | RL rollouts: Qwen2.5-1.5B, GSM8K, n=8, temperature 1 | 0.94x | 1.40x | 1.16x | | Multi-turn chat: Qwen2.5-7B, UltraChat history | 0.78x | 1.15x | 1.03x | | RAG + summarization: Qwen2.5-7B, Spec-Bench | 0.86x | 1.16x | 1.10x | | Long-context decode: 24K-token prompts, concurrency 3 | 1.38x | 0.29x; **1.46x with #61509** | 1.19x | At long context, adaptive verification's startup profiling cost the KV cache 1.9 GiB (43K instead of 80K tokens), so prefixes were evicted and re-prefilled. #61509 fixes that accounting on main. **Correctness** (this PR's final code; greedy outputs vs no speculation, 48 distinct prompts; fp32 Qwen2.5-0.5B on `TRITON_ATTN`, since FA2 has no fp32): | Check | This PR | + adaptive verification | `ngram_gpu` | |---|---|---|---| | Plain greedy | 45/48 | 45/48 | 46/48 | | Repetition/frequency/presence penalties | 43/48 | 44/48 | 43/48 | | Structured outputs (JSON schema, regex, choice), `max_tokens=2`, logprobs | identical | identical | regex 11/12, rest identical | | Stop strings with `min_tokens`; `ignore_eos` to 300 tokens | 48/48; 45/48 | 47/48; 45/48 | 47/48; 45/48 | | 24 distinct 800–1,800-word prompts with chunked prefill (`max_num_batched_tokens=512`); 8 prompts ending 40 tokens before `max_model_len` | 24/24, 8/8 | 24/24, 8/8 | 24/24, 8/8 | | Preemption (small KV cache, 144 requests, 355–509 preemptions) | 128/144 | 125/144 | 126/144 | - **Baseline noise:** two no-spec runs, async vs sync scheduling, differ on 1/48 plain prompts. - **Logprobs:** deltas on identical outputs are at most 5e-3, the same as `ngram_gpu`. - **Sampling** (Qwen2.5-1.5B bf16, temperature 1, top-p, top-k, n=16, each method with its own seed): total-variation distance of per-position token marginals vs a no-spec run is 0.153 / 0.079 / 0.131. A second no-spec run gives 0.161 / 0.059 / 0.128, `ngram_gpu` 0.148 / 0.056 / 0.131. - **Aborts** (`vllm serve`, 48 streams aborted mid-generation): the server stays healthy. Greedy requests sent afterwards match those sent before 8/8 without adaptive verification. With it, 7/8 in fp32 (one flip at a 0.0004-nat near-tie) and 2/8 in bf16 7B: the number of verified slots changes the batch shapes.
## Details **How it works** - **Own history:** the longest suffix match within the request's prompt and output, up to `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth`. Same kernel layout as `ngram_gpu`. - **Cross-request corpus:** finished responses go into a GPU token ring (`suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens`, default 1M). A hash index on each request's last 2 and last 4 tokens returns up to 16 candidate positions. Each is verified and extended to its full suffix match, so the index is only an entry point for suffix matching, and hash collisions or overwritten documents only cost a candidate. - **Frequency vote:** for each candidate match length, the candidates matching at least that long vote on the continuation, as in SuffixDecoding. The highest-scoring chain wins, ties going to the longer match; then the longer of the own-history and corpus matches wins. - **Adaptive verification** (`enable_adaptive_verification`): per-slot confidences, learned online by source, match length and position, let the runner trim slots that aren't worth verifying. - **Ingestion:** one GPU program per (document, block). Each program replays the batch's placement to find its offset and skips positions that a later document of the same batch overwrites. Every position is written by exactly one program, so the result is exact and order-independent even when a burst is larger than the ring. A 256 × 4,096-token burst at the default 1M ring takes 0.58 ms. - **TP consistency without collectives:** finished ids are ingested in sorted order, index inserts use `atomic_max` over `(document << 32 | position)`, and the statistics are integer counters. - **Memory at the defaults:** 36 MB (4 MB corpus plus a 32 MB index). Suffix decoding also keeps the runner's token history on the GPU (`max_num_seqs × max_model_len × 4` bytes, e.g. 32 MiB at 256 × 32K).
How a corpus lookup works (diagram) ``` Request history: ... "report" "the" "camera" "at" "the" "north" "gate" └──── last 4 ────┘ └─ last 2 ┘ 1) LOOK UP hash(last 4), hash(last 2) -> buckets, 8 slots each (slot = newest occurrence in each of the last 8 documents) 2) EXTEND BACKWARDS each candidate against the request (up to 24 tokens): request: report the camera at the north gate corpus: log: the camera at the north gate -> match length 6 stale or colliding candidate -> length 0, dropped 3) VOTE + DRAFT candidates matching >= L tokens vote on the next k tokens; the chain with the highest summed probability wins 4) COMPARE with the longest match in the request's own history; the longer match wins, empty slots get the last token ``` Ingestion when a request finishes: `[last 3 prompt tokens | response]` is appended to the ring, and each position with at least 2 (4) tokens before it in the document is indexed under them: `table[hash][doc % 8] = max(existing, (doc, pos))`.
**Why a hash index** | Index | Propose cost (L4) | Notes | |---|---|---| | Suffix tree (Arctic, V1) | CPU, per request | Host sync, so no MRV2 or async scheduling | | Suffix array (#52097) | 1.3–4.5 ms as an eager library call (prototype measurement on a shared L4); #52097 reports 0.4–1.9 ms with its CUDA-graph path (L20, k=16) | Background rebuilds, epochs and a CPU collective for TP | | Brute-force GPU scan | 0.3–1.2 ms at batch 128 (prototype measurement) | Exact; cost grows with batch × corpus | | **Hash index + vote (this PR)** | **11–35 µs** GPU time for batch 1–256 (CUDA-graph microbenchmark), the same at 1M and 4M corpus tokens. As the engine runs it (eagerly): 89–95 µs per step at 4K context for batch 1–256, 231 µs at 128K context with 32 requests (`ngram_gpu`: 75–78 and 111 µs) | No rebuilds. The index alone is within 0.4% of an exact longest-match search; with the vote, about 1% below exact search + vote | One difference from Arctic: corpus matches need at least 2 tokens (so `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth` must be at least 2 for the corpus), while own-history matches can be 1. Storing the last 3 prompt tokens with each response lets a response's first tokens be drafted from the corpus. **Taken from #52097 and @zip95297's MRV2 port** (`zip95297/vllm-dev`, branch `zip95297/suffix-gpu-mrv2`): GPU cross-request matching with no host sync; an `on_requests_finished` hook in `finish_requests` that ingests from `RequestState` and skips preempted requests (from the MRV2 port); sorting finished ids for TP consistency; the replay-based acceptance evaluation. **Changes outside the speculator** - `SuffixSpeculatorConfig` (`suffix/config.py`): suffix's default `num_speculative_tokens` is `min(8, suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth)` on both runners. On V1 it caps Arctic's dynamic draft length; set 24 for the previous V1 behavior. - `BaseSpeculator`: new no-op `add_request`, `on_requests_finished` and `reset_state` methods, which the runner and MRV2's kernel warmup call directly. The suffix speculator uses them to reset per-slot stats, ingest finished requests, and drop the warmup requests from the corpus. Dense `all_token_ids` for suffix. **Limitations** - Seeded sampling isn't reproducible with suffix decoding: drafts come from previously finished requests, and with adaptive verification the number of verified slots depends on the batch. The same seeded request sent alone twice gave identical output 0/4 (fp32; 4/4 without speculation). With `suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens: 0` and adaptive verification off it's 4/4. - The corpus is shared across requests regardless of `cache_salt` or LoRA adapter, like Arctic's global tree on V1 (documented; set `suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens: 0` to isolate). - Adaptive verification needs full CUDA graphs and an attention backend that replays variable-length decode batches. On L4 that is `TRITON_ATTN`: vLLM's FA2 backend declares uniform-batch support only. Until #61509 lands, its startup profiling also costs KV capacity, which matters at long context. - Under async scheduling a finished request can carry up to about 2k+1 tokens past the stop point into the corpus. ## Open questions 1. **Adaptive verification by default?** It is what makes suffix decoding pay off from concurrency 32 up. It isn't on by default here because it fails at startup on backends that can't replay variable-length decode graphs (FA2, the pre-Hopper default), so a default needs a fallback to off. Happy to add that here, or in a follow-up. 2. **Low-concurrency trimming.** Adaptive verification trims too much at low concurrency on small models: Qwen2.5-1.5B at concurrency 8 is 1.29x with it vs 1.47x verifying every slot (7B: 1.36x vs 1.32x). Tune it here (for example with a more optimistic prior) or later? 3. **Corpus default.** 4M tokens adds about 2–3% acceptance, but the index grows from 32 MB to 128 MB. 4. **Tokens past the stop point.** Pass the scheduler's final length down to ingestion? 5. **Arctic-only options** (`max_spec_factor`, `min_token_prob`) are ignored on V2 (documented). Warn as well? ## Follow-ups - Exclude filler slots from spec-decode metrics for GPU drafters (as #52097 does on V1 and its MRV2 branch does; see also #44056 and #50518). With adaptive verification, trimmed slots are still counted as drafted. - Index responses while they're still being generated. That may be why Arctic is ahead on the templated VLM workload. - CUDA-graph the propose path (@zip95297's bucketized draft graphs). - aarch64 benchmarks. ---

(Mandatory for agents, optional for humans). - [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR. - [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity. - [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI. - [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples. - [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
**Not duplicating existing work:** the only other suffix decoding drafter PR is #52097 (`suffix_gpu` on V1), whose author is collaborating here; searches for "suffix decoding", "suffix_gpu" and "SuffixSpeculator" find no other MRV2 implementation. AI assistance (Claude) was used to investigate, prototype, write and test this change. cc @njhill @zip95297 @benchislett @TheEpicDolphin

title: [Perf] Support minimum KV splits configuration for TokenSpeed MLA decode
author: wzhao18
body:
## Overview

The TokenSpeed MLA decode kernel supports passing an optional flag `min_split_kv` to force a minimum number of KV splits, which can accelerate performance by up to 4x speedup under certain workloads, see https://github.com/lightseekorg/tokenspeed/pull/1693.

Expose the split floor through `AttentionConfig`:

```bash
--attention-config '{"tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv": 8}'
```

The default is `1`, preserving automatic scheduling. Values are validated in `[1, 256]`; the setting only applies to TokenSpeed MLA decode.

## Claims

- Configure the decode split floor per engine through the existing attention configuration API.
- Reserve workspace for the configured floor and pass `min_split_kv` directly to the decode kernel; `1` preserves automatic scheduling.

## Validation

Configuration-interface update (October 9, 2026):

- `pre-commit run --files vllm/config/attention.py vllm/envs.py vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/tokenspeed_mla.py tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py`: passed.
- `pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <changed files>`: passed.
- Isolated source validation with `.venv/bin/python /private/tmp/pr60345_validate.py`: passed actual `AttentionConfig` default/boundary validation, invalid-value rejection, hash differentiation, and JSON/dotted argument parsing; all 12 existing CPU decode contract cases passed using the actual forward method, including direct forwarding of `min_split_kv` at both `1` and `8`. GPU backend imports were isolated for macOS.
- Added coverage to the existing CLI suite and updated decode tests for the workspace interface. Full pytest collection (`pytest tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py -k test_attention_config -q`) stopped at the unavailable `tblib` dependency in `tests/conftest.py`.
- CUDA/DCP kernel tests and model evaluations were not rerun on this macOS host. The following benchmark and accuracy results are prior validation of the same kernel setting, before the configuration-interface change.


### E2E agentic benchmark result
Kimi K3 nvfp4 2xDCP8 + 1xDEP16 c320: **1.64x e2e speedup**

```
baseline: Throughput per GPU: 11942 tok/s
decode with min_split=8: Throughput per GPU: 19678 tok/s
```

### Accuracy Eval
Tested Kimi K3 nvfp4 DCP8 + DEP16 GSM8k:
```
Num questions: 1319
Num shots: 5
Max tokens: 256
Temperature: 0.0
Seed: 42
Accuracy: 0.935
Invalid responses: 0.001
Total latency: 45.735 s
Questions per second: 28.840
Total output tokens: 140154
Output tokens per second: 3064.495
```

## Details

This updates the existing PR rather than opening a duplicate. `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv` follows the other backend-specific split controls in `AttentionConfig`. The backend reads it once during initialization for both kernel dispatch and workspace sizing, and passes `min_split_kv=self._min_split_kv` directly; the proposed env var is removed. The pinned `tokenspeed-mla==0.2.15` supports this keyword, including the default value `1`. Changes to `tests/test_config.py` were removed. Increasing the floor may increase workspace memory.

AI assistance was used for this change. The repository's `/pr-checklist` skill was applied.

title: [Kernel] Integrate FA4 SM90 FP8 MMA for Gemma-4 full attention
author: katec846
body:
## Overview

Enable FP8 MMA in the SM90 FA4 full-attention kernel ([PR199](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/199)) for Gemma-4 while retaining FP8 KV-cache storage.

Gemma-4 uses head dimension 512 for full attention and 256 for sliding-window attention. This change compares FP8 MMA against the existing path that reads FP8 KV, dequantizes it, and performs FP16 MMA.

On H200, FP8 full attention uses FA4, while FP8 sliding-window attention continues to use FA3. FA4 FP8 sliding-window attention with head dimension 256 is currently unsupported.

## Claims

- Integrate the SM90 d512 FP8-MMA kernel while preserving native FP16/BF16 queries and supported FA3 sliding-window routing.
- Gate unsupported kernel combinations and normalize descale layouts.
- Allow FA4 full-attention layers to select splits automatically, removing the previous CUDA-graph cap of 32 for these layers; retain the cap for FA3.
- Report measured gains over the KV-dequantization baseline and the remaining regression against BF16 KV/MMA.

## Validation
The MMA labels describe the **full-attention path**. Both FP8-KV configurations use FA3 FP8 sliding-window attention; the BF16-KV reference uses FA4 BF16 sliding-window attention.

Serving setup:

- Gemma-4-31B-it-FP8 weights for all configurations.
- Four H200 GPUs on one node; TP4.
- Approximately 25K shared prefix plus 3K unique input tokens.
- 128 requests, 200 output tokens per request.
- MTP enabled with three speculative tokens.
- Prefix-cache reuse enabled.
- Concurrency 1–64; median of three rounds.

### Serving performance
The `8k-in-1k-out` benchmark of [`gemma_4_31b_it_h200`](https://github.com/vllm-project/perf-eval/blob/main/workloads/gemma_4_31b_it_h200.yaml) on one H200 at TP=1, with GPU clocks locked. Each number is the median of 3 repetitions, as perf-eval aggregates them; no request failed.

| | Output tok/s | Mean TPOT (ms) | Median ITL (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before (`5d35ce3934` + FA `b273a02`) | 796.5 | 126.5 | 75.1 |
| This PR + vllm-project/flash-attention#199 | **831.1 (1.04x)** | **123.2** | **69.3** |
| Delta | +4.3% | -2.6% | -7.8% |

<details><summary>Reproduce</summary>

- Before is this PR's base, `5d35ce3934`, with FlashAttention at vllm-project/flash-attention#199's base, `b273a02`. After is this PR's head, `237043eee6`, with #199's head, `2648f1b`.
- Neither PR changes C++. Both runs use one editable build of `237043eee6` with `VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_SRC_DIR` set to the FlashAttention checkout, and differ only in Python sources.
- The model is a local copy of `RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-FP8-dynamic`. Server and benchmark match perf-eval@5f4e445 (`lib/server.sh`, `lib/run_vllm_bench.sh`, `lib/aggregate_perf.py`).

```bash
VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 \
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --enable-auto-tool-choice

# 3 repetitions against the same server; median of each metric
vllm bench serve --backend openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --model $MODEL \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 --ignore-eos \
  --num-prompts 512 --max-concurrency 128 --num-warmups 128
```

</details>

### Model evaluation
Accuracy scores are percentages. **87.19% for AIME 2025, 85.73% for GPQA Diamond (avg@16), and 86.86% for MMLU-Pro are measured in this PR; the two reference columns are reported baselines from [PR #48666](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48666).**

| Benchmark | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA ([PR199](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/199)) | FP8 KV + FP16 MMA (reference FA4) | 	BF16 TRITON |
|---|---|---|---|
| AIME 2025 (avg@64) | 87.19 | 86.88 | 87.29 |
| GPQA Diamond (avg@16) | 85.73* | 86.55 | 85.42 |
| MMLU-Pro | 86.86  | 86.64 | 86.44 |

\* Note that in a paird GPQA Diamond comparison using the same 198 questions and 16 seeds, FP8 MMA scored 85.73% versus 85.32% for the FP8 KV + FP16 MMA. The difference was +0.41 percentage points, with a paired question-bootstrap 95% interval of [−0.51, +1.36] points. Both runs had zero invalid or truncated answers. The table’s 86.55% reference is imported from PR [#48666](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48666) and is separate from this matched control.

### MTP speculative decoding

Mean acceptance length (**AL**), median of three rounds, from the same sweep as the serving-performance table above. All configurations use FP8 model weights, TP4 on four H200 GPUs, three speculative tokens, and prefix-cache reuse enabled. Each measurement completed **128/128 requests without errors**. AL includes the bonus token emitted per speculative step.

| Configuration | cc1 | cc2 | cc4 | cc8 | cc16 | cc32 | cc64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | 2.9830 | 2.9932 | 3.0002 | 2.9640 | 2.9849 | 2.9860 | 2.9793 |
| FP8 KV + FP16 MMA | 2.9924 | 2.9691 | 3.0130 | 2.9995 | 2.9993 | 2.9857 | 2.9979 |
| BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | 3.0053 | 2.9823 | 2.9940 | 2.9935 | 2.9995 | 3.0002 | 2.9982 |

## Reproduction commands
The Hopper FP8 MMA path supports text-only workloads. The commands use --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' to disable Gemma-4’s bidirectional/mm-prefix attention. Multimodal Gemma-4 with FP8 KV uses Triton instead of this kernel. FP8 sliding-window layers use FA3, so do not force FA4 globally.

Serve and benchmark: 25K shared prefix, TP4, MTP3, cache reuse on

* FP8 KV + FP8 MMA (this PR):

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

* FP8 KV + FP16 MMA (PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) baseline kernel environment):
(The two FP8-KV serving commands are identical because MMA selection depends on the FlashAttention kernel source, not a CLI flag. For the control, we kept the same vLLM integration but replaced its vendored CuTe sources with the PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) dequantizing kernel, including the baseline safety fixes, then restarted the server. --kv-cache-dtype fp8 selects FP8 cache storage in both cases)

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

* BF16 KV + BF16 MMA:

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

These recorded runs left the FA version unset. The dequantized control uses the PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) baseline kernel environment.

Benchmark:

```bash
aiperf profile \
  --model "$MODEL" --tokenizer "$MODEL" --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --endpoint-type chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --streaming \
  --use-legacy-max-tokens --url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --input-file "$DATASET" \
  --extra-inputs max_tokens:200 --extra-inputs min_tokens:200 \
  --extra-inputs ignore_eos:true --extra-inputs skip_special_tokens:false \
  --random-seed 1234 --use-server-token-count \
  --concurrency 16 --request-count 128 --num-dataset-entries 128
```

Run at concurrency 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64; report the median of three rounds.

<details>
<summary>Evaluation commands</summary>

Evaluation server on four H200 GPUs. AIME and GPQA use `--max-num-seqs 16`; MMLU-Pro uses `32`. No MTP.

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" --served-model-name gemma \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 4 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --kv-cache-memory-bytes 101716968203 --enforce-eager \
  --trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --attention-config.flash_attn_version=3 --block-size 64 \
  --kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune=false \
  --kernel-config.enable_cutedsl_warmup=false \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}'
```

**AIME 2025, avg@64**

Use `aime.yaml` with 64 samples per problem, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and the GPT-4.1 judge configuration. Export `INFERENCE_API_KEY`.

```bash
docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=100g \
  -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e INFERENCE_API_KEY \
  -v "$PWD/aime.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/aime-results:/results" \
  --entrypoint bash nvcr.io/nvidia/eval-factory/simple-evals:26.03 \
  -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml'
```

**GPQA Diamond, avg@16**

Use `gpqa.yaml` with all 198 questions, the `eval/aai/mcq-4choices` prompt, temperature 1.0, and top-p 0.95. Run seeds 0–15.

```bash
pids=()
for seed in $(seq 0 15); do
  docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=4g \
    -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e HF_TOKEN \
    -e NEMO_EVALUATOR_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=0 -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
    -v "$PWD/gpqa.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
    -v "$PWD/gpqa-results/seed-$seed:/results" \
    --entrypoint bash "$EVAL_IMAGE" \
    -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml "$@"' \
    -- --overrides "config.params.extra.args=++prompt_config=eval/aai/mcq-4choices ++inference.random_seed=$seed" &
  pids+=("$!")
done

status=0
for pid in "${pids[@]}"; do
  wait "$pid" || status=1
done
test "$status" -eq 0
```

**MMLU-Pro**

Restart the evaluation server with `--max-num-seqs 32`. Use `mmlu.yaml` with all 12,032 questions, one sample per question, the `eval/aai/mcq-10choices-boxed` prompt, temperature 1.0, and top-p 0.95.

```bash
mkdir -p mmlu-results
chmod 777 mmlu-results

docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=4g \
  -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e HF_TOKEN \
  -e NEMO_EVALUATOR_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=0 -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  -v "$PWD/mmlu.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/mmlu-results:/results" \
  --entrypoint bash "$EVAL_IMAGE" \
  -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml'
```

</details>

## Details

### Why FP8 is slower than BF16

Nsight shows that faster FP8 full attention does not necessarily produce faster end-to-end execution.

#### Sliding-window attention and KV-cache operations offset full-attention gains

The profiling setup uses 25K inputs, TP4, MTP enabled, prefix reuse enabled, and offered concurrency 64.

| Target-model kernel work | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | FP8 time reduction vs. BF16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | **6.681 ms** | 7.584 ms | **+11.9%** |
| Sliding-window attention | 5.482 ms | **4.206 ms** | −30.3% |
| KV-cache writes | 0.261 ms | **0.157 ms** | −66.2% |
| Attention preparation | 0.105 ms | 0 | N/A |
| Whole-cycle GPU span | 29.879 ms | **29.391 ms** | −1.7% |

Time reduction is `100 × (BF16 time − FP8 time) / BF16 time`, calculated from the displayed times. Positive values mean less time (faster); negative values mean more time (slower). 

Full attention is approximately **12% faster**, but sliding-window attention is approximately **30% slower**, with additional KV-write, preparation, and combine work.

KV-write overhead refers to the kernels that reshape and write newly generated keys and values into the paged cache, including the FP8 conversion/quantization path. Attention reads and prefix-cache reuse accounting are separate from this kernel category.

Reuse-off profiles show the same pattern.
The following comparison uses **cc16**, 25K inputs, TP4, MTP enabled, and prefix-cache reuse disabled. These matched pure-decode cycles process **16 active requests per target step**. Values are medians across four GPU ranks of each rank's per-cycle medians, with 69 matched cycles per rank for BF16 and 87 for FP8.

| Target-model kernel work | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | FP8 time reduction vs. BF16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | **1.9670 ms** | 2.4358 ms | **+19.2%** |
| Sliding-window attention | 1.9593 ms | **1.3867 ms** | −41.3% |
| KV-cache writes | 0.2551 ms | **0.1413 ms** | −80.5% |
| Attention preparation | 0.1098 ms | 0 | N/A |
| Whole-cycle GPU span | 14.6594 ms | **14.2903 ms** | −2.6% |

Full attention is faster, but SWA, KV-cache writes, and attention preparation/combine offset the gain. The whole-cycle GPU span is **2.6% longer** for FP8. This is a profiling comparison, not an unprofiled end-to-end throughput measurement.

---

title: [ROCm][Perf][DSv4.1] Mono decode layer for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on MI355X
author: Fangzhou-Ai
body:
## Purpose

Opt-in (`VLLM_ROCM_MONO_DECODE=1`, meant as the one switch for every model's mono decode kernels) fast path for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode on MI355X (gfx950). Every backbone layer of a decode step runs on persistent FlyDSL launches:

| Launch | Layers | Stages |
|---|---|---|
| K1 | 30 standard layers | the mHC attention seam, then the attention front: wqkv, q/kv norms, the KV insert, wq_b |
| K2 | 30 standard layers | the attention back (split attention, combine, wo_a, wo_b), the attention TP all-reduce, the FFN seam, the MoE (router, top-6, shared expert, MXFP4 experts) and its TP all-reduce |
| FFN | the other 10 | after vLLM's attention seam and attention: the attention TP all-reduce (wo_b's unreduced output pushed to every rank), then K2's FFN seam and MoE |

All TP all-reduces run in-kernel over symmetric peer memory. K1 + K2 replace the ~40 kernels this path launches per standard layer today; the FFN launch replaces the attention all-reduce, the FFN seam and the MoE's kernels on the others.

**Scope**
- **Layers:** K1 + K2 on the 30 backbone layers with the standard mHC seam and no compressor or indexer of their own: 3–7, 9–13, 15–19, 21–23, 25–27, 29–31, 33–35, 37–39. The FFN launch on the other 10: layer 0 (embedding-broadcast seam), the Engram layer 1, and the compressor/indexer layers 2, 8, 14 (also Engram), 20, 24, 28, 32, 36.
- **Steps:** decode only, ≤ 48 rows (8 requests × 1 + 5 DSpark drafts), TP2 or TP4, eager or a FULL CUDA graph. K1 + K2 also need causal SWA windows and `fp8_ds_mla` KV records.
- **Everything else** runs as before: the DSpark draft layers, and prefill, mixed or larger steps. The paths take and return the same tensors at the layer boundary, so they interleave freely.

### Layout

```
vllm/models/deepseek_v41/amd/mono_decode.py   eligibility per layer / per step, vLLM tensors -> kernel inputs
vllm/models/deepseek_v41/amd/mono/
    runner.py     DSV41MonoLayer: scratch, epoch, peer memory, the launches
    layer.py      K1 / K2 and the FFN launch, composed from the stages below
    attention/    attention stages
    stages/       seam.py (mHC seams, attention reduce), moe.py, moe_shape.py, moe_plan.py, router.py, gemv.py, dims.py
    common/       tagged mailbox, device ops, MX helpers, build keys, peer memory
```

`stages/` and `common/` are adapted from ROCm/ATOM's DeepSeek-V4.1 mono decode (MIT License, commit 97359d6). Each adapted file names its origin and keeps AMD's copyright notice. The changes from ATOM:
- the seams are specialized to these layers;
- vLLM's numerics: f32 router logits, the shared expert reading vLLM's row-major FP8 weights, vLLM's `mxfp8_e4m3_quantize` and `silu_and_mul_with_clamp`;
- hand-offs carry epoch tags instead of per-step mailbox clears, so no host step hook and the launches are graph-safe. ATOM's clears also wiped what another step width had laid out differently; without them each width gets a scratch of its own;
- ATOM's engine-side modules are dropped.

### Design

- **Weights** are read in place, with no second copy. The attention linears stay vLLM's row-major MXFP8 (32×32 E8M0 scales). The routed experts stay in AITER's shuffled MXFP4 layout.
- **Path selection.** The model is not torch.compiled, so the per-step decision is plain Python. It runs when a FULL graph is captured (uniform decode) and on every eager step. PIECEWISE (breakable) captures are always declined, because they are replayed for mixed batches.
- **wo_b's reduce on the FFN-launch layers.** Their `wo_b` is built with `reduce_results=False`, as the sequence-parallel path already does. A decode step hands the partial to the FFN launch; any other step reduces it in the decoder layer with the same `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce`. ROCm's preshuffled-FP8 `wo_b` path now honors `reduce_results` as the linear does. This also fixes a bug on main: with sequence parallelism and an FP8-block checkpoint, `wo_b` was all-reduced and then reduce-scattered.
- **TP ranks stay in lockstep.** Every rank must take the same path at every layer, since the kernels wait on each other's pushes. The conditions read only metadata that all ranks hold alike.
- **Failure modes.** An explicit opt-in that cannot run raises: a CDNA version outside the kernels' (`get_cdna_version()` in `CDNA_VERSIONS`, CDNA4 / gfx950 today, so a later generation is one entry once ported), TP other than 2 or 4, FlyDSL missing, expert / data parallelism or EPLB, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE_A4W4_DSV4`, a routed-expert backend other than `AITER_MXFP4_BF16`, or fewer than 256 compute units (a partitioned GPU: every CTA of a launch must stay resident). The MoE and shared-expert tensors are checked for the kernels' shapes and dtypes at the first step, as the attention ones are. A layer outside the kernels' scope is logged once.
- **All-reduces are exact:** fp32 sum in rank order, then bf16. At ≤ 48 rows vLLM's own decode all-reduces are below the INT4 quick-reduce threshold, so the current path runs them exact too.
- **A scratch per step width.** Hand-offs between CTAs are tagged mailbox pairs in a scratch laid out per step width. Each width has its own scratch, allocated at its first (eager) step: 3–16 MB, and at most 8 widths under DSpark. So a word one width polls as a tag only ever holds tags. The MoE's task counters outlive a width and live in the epoch buffer.
- **Dependencies:** the `flydsl` wheel, plus two small AITER helpers that path already depends on: `aiter.ops.flydsl.kernels.buffer_ops` (FlyDSL's wheel no longer ships it) and `UncachedIpcHeap` for peer memory.

## Duplicate check

- No open PR targets DeepSeek-V4.1 mono decode. Searched "dsv41 mono", "DeepSeek V4.1 mono", "mono decode layer" and "dsv41_mono".
- The sibling mono-decode PRs are for other models: #59705 (MiniMax-M3) and #60216 (GLM-5).
- This PR hooks per decoder layer rather than replacing the model forward, because only 30 of DSv4.1's 40 layers are eligible.

## Test Plan

- `pytest tests/models/test_dsv41_mono_decode.py` (CPU, wired into the MI355 Basic Models job): a decode step takes the mono path and hands the kernels `[blocks, block, 584]` cache views. A padded FULL-graph step takes it too (the kernels skip pad rows, whose slot is -1). PIECEWISE steps, prefill or mixed steps, more decode tokens than rows, non-causal windows, missing metadata, more than 48 rows and the first layer all take the original path. Deployments the kernels cannot run raise.
- `pytest tests/models/test_dsv41_mono_numerics.py` (4 × MI355, its own CI step). One layer with random weights in the checkpoint's formats, at TP2 and TP4: the kernels against the ops vLLM runs for the same decode step (the mHC seams, the ROCm attention chain, the all-reduce, `DeepseekV4MoE`). Each stage is checked on its own input, by cosine and relative error, for the whole layer and the FFN launch, at 1×6 and 8×6 rows. Then both widths' launches are captured in one graph and replayed 300 times, bit for bit against the first run.
- `pytest tests/models/test_dsv41_mono_layers.py` (same CI step). A five-layer DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP2 and TP4 holding both layer kinds the mono path takes: the whole layer at a ratio-2 and a ratio-1 consumer, and the FFN launch at the sliding-window and KV / index-source layers. It is served with mono on and off on the same random weights, and every decoder layer's outputs at every decode token must match. It runs `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer.forward` as the engine does, so a change to the layer that the kernels do not follow fails it.
- Race stress: the whole layer and the FFN launch in one HIP graph, 48-row and 6-row steps alternating, every intermediate compared bit for bit with the first run. 100K replays each on layers 3 and 9 (ratio 2) and 21 (ratio 1).
- Compile-only build (`COMPILE_ONLY=1`) of the in-tree kernels: K1 and K2 at TP2 and TP4, M = 6 and 48, both layer types.
- No regression of K1 + K2: K2's FFN half is factored out and shared with the FFN launch. K2 disassembles instruction-identical to the first commit's (TP2 M=6 ratio 1, TP4 M=48 ratio 2), and the whole-layer accuracy check reproduces its earlier numbers exactly.
- FFN launch, kernel level: against vLLM's FFN half (the attention all-reduce, `MHCPreDelayedOp`, `DeepseekV4MoE` with its all-reduce) on the real weights of the 10 layers, with the attention partial from a real ROCm attention chain. 48 points: TP2/TP4 × concurrency 1/2/4/8 × 1–6 tokens per request; the 10 layers chained in one HIP graph, cold weights.
- Kernel level (MI355X): the layer against vLLM's own modules (`DeepseekV4MoE`, the mHC seams, the ROCm attention chain, the all-reduce) in a TP process group, with real checkpoint weights. 96 points: TP2/TP4 × concurrency 1–8 × 1–6 tokens per request × the two layer types. Timing: 8 layers chained in one HIP graph, cold weights, vLLM's path captured under `graph_capture`.
- GSM8K: InferenceX's task, 5-shot, full 1,319, temperature 0, concurrency 8, DSpark block rejection; TP2 for K1 + K2 alone, TP2 and TP4 with the FFN launch.
- AgentX e2e with the InferenceX#3690 recipe (this tree's image, a8w4 MoE, INT4 quick reduce), golden DSpark acceptance 3.51, 3600 s per point, c1/c2/c4/c8 at TP2 and TP4.
- Accuracy, per RFC #59665: GPQA-Diamond and AIME25 at TP2, thinking on with `reasoning_effort` high, 8 requests in flight a server (every decode step within 48 rows), against the same build with `VLLM_ROCM_MONO_DECODE=0`. Long context: RULER NIAH (single, multikey 2 and 3) at 32K, 128K and 256K.

## Test Result

**Unit:** 33 passed. **Compile-only:** all K1 / K2 / FFN builds compile.

**Numerics test (GPU):** passed at TP2 and TP4: every token's output cosine ≥ 0.9993 against vLLM's chain, relative errors 0.3–0.5% (bounds 1–1.5%; a routed scale off by 3% fails), 300 replays bit-exact. **Race stress:** no mismatch in 100K replays on each layer. Before the per-width scratch, layer 3 diverged at replay 13 on every run. **Model-level test:** passed at TP2 and TP4 (9 of 9 local runs of the final version; 40 of 41 of the TP2-only one before it, the failure not recurring and its log not kept). A routed scale off by 3% fails it at both sizes.

**Accuracy**, TP2, per RFC #59665 ([details](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60397#issuecomment-6051909168)):

- ± is the standard error across questions; Δ is paired by question.

**FFN launch, kernel level, µs per layer** (vLLM's FFN half → the FFN launch, at 6 tokens per request). Every point is faster or at parity: TP2 1.01–2.14×, TP4 1.12–2.32×. The residual and the MoE input match vLLM's bit for bit at every point; the layer output's cosine is ≥ 0.99999, and every token's ≥ 0.9999.

**Kernel level, µs per layer.** Every one of 96 points is faster, 1.10–2.18×. Accuracy: residual cosine ≥ 0.99999. MoE output: 1,234 of 1,260 tokens at cosine ≥ 0.999. Each of the other 26 is a top-6 routing near-tie: the reference's own 6th/7th expert score gap is ≤ 3.2e-3, against medians near 1e-2. On the same FFN input the MoE matches vLLM's at cosine 0.99999.
