<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's PR checklist.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation and review of this PR.
- [x] This is the ROCm counterpart to #61727, not a duplicate implementation for the same platform.
- [x] **Design Fit:** Reuses the existing KV-cache lifecycle and shared Step-5 sparse components without scheduler changes.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Covers BF16/FP8 K/V, prefill, chunked prefill, decode, MTP, the head-wise gate, warmup, and connector page geometry, with model validation on real gfx942 and gfx950 hardware.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps the platform-specific model code under `amd/` and shares platform-independent code through `common/`
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Documents the current implementation, commands, limitations, and validation results.

</details>

title: [ROCm][Perf] Triton port of the fused GDN MTP decode kernel
author: iseeyuan
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->
## Overview

GDN layers with the flat qkvz layout (Qwen3.5 family) fall back to the unfused speculative-decode path on ROCm because `fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp` (#51674) only builds for CUDA. This adds a Triton port with the same signature and uses it on ROCm: a state-update kernel tiled over the value dimension like `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update` (tile size chosen from the grid size) plus a small gated-RMSNorm epilogue. It covers every model built on `QwenGatedDeltaNetAttention` with the flat layout: the Qwen3.5 family, Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (table below). Qwen3-Next (interleaved layout) stays ineligible, as on CUDA.

## Claims

- Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, MTP k=3, 1x MI350X, one request at a time: decode 2.39 -> 2.08 ms/token (-13%), E2E 544 -> 488 ms (-10%), on vLLM main (nightly `77154ca`) with aiter main. The first version of this PR (one program per value head, no V tiling) gave 2.19 ms/token in the same side-by-side run.
- Per decode step on MI350X: copy/fill/cat kernels 1.56 -> 0.31 ms, kernel launches 1008 -> 768, GPU kernel time 7.74 -> 6.71 ms.
- Faster at higher concurrency too: per-step time (median ITL) -12% at 1, -6% at 8 and -6% at 32 concurrent requests, output throughput +14% / +16% / +10% (`vllm bench serve`, 2K/256).
- Numerics match the unfused path: the existing MTP kernel test, parametrized over CUDA op / Triton port, passes for the Triton port on MI350X and MI300X (22/22 each); states are bit-identical to the first version at every tile size, and outputs are too or differ only in the rounding of the norm's sum; MTP acceptance unchanged (2.85-2.87 accepted tokens per step).
- Accuracy unchanged: GPQA Diamond 0.821 (main) vs 0.826 (this PR), needle-in-a-haystack 100% for both at 4K-64K tokens.
- Long context (64K in / 1K out): decode step (median ITL) -12% / -6% / -3% at 1 / 8 / 32 concurrent requests; prefill unchanged.
- MI300X (gfx942): per call, 49-60% faster than the unfused path at 1 request and 25-44% at 32 (table below).
- GSM8K unchanged within run-to-run variation (base 0.854-0.861 over 4 runs, this PR 0.848-0.862 over 3 runs), above the 0.84 threshold in `tests/evals/gsm8k/configs/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-DEP2.yaml`.
- CUDA unchanged: the CUDA op is still used wherever it is built.

## Validation

Kernel test (MI350X and MI300X, ROCm 7.2.3; the CUDA-op cases skip because the op is not built on ROCm):

```
pytest tests/kernels/fla/test_fused_gdn_post_conv.py -k mtp
22 passed, 22 skipped
```

End to end: Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (BF16), 1x MI350X, `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_FA --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' --async-scheduling`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1`. Workload: 104 image-to-video prompt-rewriting requests (one image + 9.5K-token system prompt, ~180 output tokens, temperature 0.6 / top_p 0.95 / top_k 3), one at a time, first pass on a fresh server.

| vLLM | GDN MTP decode | Decode ms/token | Accepted tokens/step | TTFT median ms | E2E mean ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main (nightly 77154ca) + aiter main | unfused fallback | 2.39 | 2.86 | 107 | 544 |
| main (nightly 77154ca) + aiter main | first version of this PR (no V tiling) | 2.19 | 2.85 | 112 | 510 |
| main (nightly 77154ca) + aiter main | **this PR** | **2.08** | 2.87 | 111 | **488** |

The three servers ran side by side on three GPUs of the same host. The I2V, profile, GSM8K, GPQA and NIAH runs predate the tile-size rule; at one request it picks the same 32-row tiles, and it leaves states and outputs unchanged in the checks above.

aiter main is used because aiter <= v0.1.25 sends the multi-token verify batch to an unsplit gfx950 attention kernel (fixed by ROCm/aiter#6336, not yet released); without it attention dominates the step and hides this change.

Per decode step GPU time (torch profiler, 39 steps, same servers):

| | unfused fallback | first version | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDN kernels | 0.48 ms | 0.78 ms | 0.62 ms (includes the gated RMSNorm) |
| copies / fills / cat | 1.56 ms | 0.31 ms | 0.31 ms |
| other elementwise | 0.48 ms | 0.53 ms | 0.53 ms |
| kernel launches per step | 1008 | 738 | 768 |
| total GPU kernel time | 7.74 ms | 6.86 ms | 6.71 ms |

`vllm bench serve` (base and PR servers side by side; random dataset, 2048 input / 256 output tokens, `--ignore-eos`, 4x concurrency prompts, min 32). Acceptance differs between runs because the outputs differ. With MTP each streamed chunk is one decode step, so median ITL is the per-step time independent of acceptance; TPOT x acceptance is shown too:

| Concurrency | Base TPOT ms / acceptance | PR TPOT ms / acceptance | Median ITL (step) | TPOT x acceptance | Output tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.90 / 2.32 | 2.49 / 2.38 | 6.75 -> 5.93 ms (-12%) | -12% | 314.0 -> 359.2 |
| 8 | 6.75 / 1.89 | 5.66 / 2.25 | 10.92 -> 10.31 ms (-6%) | -0.2% | 971.7 -> 1126.8 |
| 32 | 12.46 / 2.24 | 11.48 / 2.26 | 18.74 -> 17.55 ms (-6%) | -7% | 2150.1 -> 2354.9 |

Long context, `vllm bench serve` with 64K input / 1K output tokens (random dataset, `--ignore-eos`, 8 / 32 / 64 prompts at concurrency 1 / 8 / 32, both servers with `--max-model-len 69632` and prompts neither had cached):

| Concurrency | Median TTFT | Median ITL (step) | Base TPOT ms / acceptance | PR TPOT ms / acceptance | Output tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1834 -> 1833 ms | 7.26 -> 6.42 ms (-12%) | 2.49 / 2.89 | 2.33 / 2.71 | 233.9 -> 242.3 |
| 8 | 1917 -> 1886 ms | 14.65 -> 13.79 ms (-6%) | 12.37 / 2.89 | 13.38 / 2.49 | 524.2 -> 512.5 |
| 32 | 2746 -> 3073 ms | 31.43 -> 30.64 ms (-3%) | 34.51 / 2.78 | 34.18 / 2.75 | 782.1 -> 801.9 |

The 64K prefill dominates these runs, and acceptance on random prompts varied from 2.49 to 2.89, which moves throughput more than this change does. The decode step itself is 3-12% faster and prefill is unchanged; at 32 concurrent requests, time to first token mostly reflects queueing behind other prefills and varied by about 30% between passes. A pass with another prompt seed gave -12% / -7% / -6% median ITL.

GSM8K (`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 1319 questions, 5-shot, greedy, `--max-concurrency 16`, so MTP verify batches of up to 16 requests go through the new kernel):

| | Run 1 | Run 2 | Run 3 | Run 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 0.861 | 0.861 | 0.854 | 0.858 |
| this PR | 0.855 | 0.862 | 0.848 | |

GPQA Diamond and needle-in-a-haystack, main vs this PR side by side (both servers with `--max-model-len 69632`):

| | GPQA Diamond accuracy | per repeat | mean output tokens | NIAH 4K / 8K / 16K / 32K / 64K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 0.821 | 0.808 / 0.833 | 8105 | 33/33 each |
| this PR | 0.826 | 0.828 / 0.823 | 8087 | 33/33 each |

GPQA Diamond uses the OpenAI simple-evals prompt and answer pattern: 198 questions x 2 repeats with shuffled choices, thinking on, temperature 0.6 / top_p 0.95 / top_k 20, up to 24K output tokens, 64 concurrent requests. NIAH follows RULER's `niah_single_1`: a 7-digit number hidden at 11 depths (0-100%) in the noise haystack, 3 samples per depth, thinking off, greedy.

Reproduce (on a ROCm image, from the vLLM repo root):

```
pytest tests/kernels/fla/test_fused_gdn_post_conv.py -k mtp
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B --port 8100 \
  --max-model-len 32768 --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_FA --async-scheduling \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8100 --max-concurrency 16
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B --port 8100 --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2048 \
  --random-output-len 256 --ignore-eos --num-prompts 32 --max-concurrency 1
```

## Details

Models that take the fused path on ROCm with this change (eligibility is unchanged from the CUDA op: flat qkvz layout, K = V = 128, value/key head ratio 1/2/3/4/8, BF16 activations, at most 8 tokens per verify):

| Model | vLLM model code | GDN K/V heads (ratio) | GDN layers | Validated |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5-397B-A17B | `qwen3_5.py` | 16/64 (4) | 45 | kernel test |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | `qwen3_5.py` | 16/64 (4) | 36 | kernel test |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B | `qwen3_5.py` | 16/32 (2) | 30 | end to end (this PR) |
| Qwen3.5-27B / 9B / 2B | `qwen3_5.py` | 16/48 (3) / 16/32 (2) / 16/16 (1) | 48 / 24 / 18 | kernel test |
| Qwen3.8-27B | `qwen3_5.py` (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) | 16/48 (3) | 48 | kernel test |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (incl. FP8) | `vllm/models/qwen4_exp` (same GDN layer, flat layout) | 16/48 (3) | 36 | kernel test |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B | `qwen3_next.py` (interleaved layout) | 16/32 (2) | - | not eligible (unchanged) |


- **Root cause.** On ROCm the layer logs `Falling back to the Triton GDN spec decode path: torch.ops._C.fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp is not built`. The AITER fused GDN path only covers non-speculative decode, so every GDN layer's verify step runs ~8 small kernels around the recurrent kernel: contiguous copies of `a`/`b`, three copies plus a `cat` to unpack q/k/v, a zero-fill, an output copy, and the gated RMSNorm.
- **Kernels.** Two launches. The update kernel runs one program per (request, value head, tile of the value dimension). It reads q/k/v and `a`/`b` in place from the projections and runs the gated delta-rule update over the request's tokens with the same state reads and writes as `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update`: start from the state at the last accepted token, store the state after every token, slot index <= 0 means no state. Each tile writes its rows of the output and their sum of squares per token. The epilogue, one program per (request, value head, token), adds the partial sums and applies the gated RMSNorm, the only step that needs the whole value dimension, then writes the `out_proj` input. Recurrent state layout is `[slot, HV, V, K]`, BF16 or FP32.
- **Tile size.** 32 rows per program while there are fewer (request, value head) pairs than CUs, 64 up to 4x the CUs, else one tile per value head. A sweep of 32/64/128 rows on MI300X and MI350X (both head shapes, both state dtypes, 1-32 requests) put this rule within 8% of the best tile size everywhere; a fixed 32 was up to 36% slower at 16-32 requests on MI300X.
- **Wiring.** Same keyword signature as the CUDA op; the layer picks the Triton port on ROCm. `forward_hip` routes speculative-decode configs to the packed fused-norm path (`forward_cuda`); non-speculative ROCm decode keeps the AITER path. Opt out with the existing `VLLM_GDN_DECODE_KERNEL=triton`.
- **Per call.** Qwen3.5-35B-A3B shape (16/32 K/V heads), 4 tokens per request, CUDA-graph replay, current ROCm nightly image; "first version" is this PR before the review (one program per value head):

  | GPU | State | Requests | unfused | first version | this PR |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | MI350X | FP32 | 1 | 30.0 us | 18.7 us | 11.5 us |
  | MI350X | FP32 | 8 | 46.7 us | 26.8 us | 21.8 us |
  | MI350X | FP32 | 32 | 91.4 us | 71.9 us | 64.3 us |
  | MI350X | BF16 | 1 | 28.3 us | 12.5 us | 10.2 us |
  | MI350X | BF16 | 32 | 68.1 us | 36.5 us | 39.6 us |
  | MI300X | FP32 | 1 | 30.2 us | 21.7 us | 13.3 us |
  | MI300X | FP32 | 8 | 56.7 us | 38.5 us | 33.3 us |
  | MI300X | FP32 | 32 | 145.7 us | 96.8 us | 88.8 us |
  | MI300X | BF16 | 1 | 28.5 us | 16.3 us | 11.3 us |
  | MI300X | BF16 | 32 | 117.0 us | 66.5 us | 65.2 us |

  With FP32 state, the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 default (`mamba_ssm_dtype: float32`), this PR is faster than the first version at every batch size on both GPUs. With BF16 state at 32 requests on MI350X it is 8-9% slower than the first version (one tile per head plus the epilogue launch), still well ahead of the unfused path. The 16/48 head shape behaves the same way.
- **Coverage.** End to end this was run on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B only. The other models in the table are covered by the kernel test, which runs every eligible head ratio (1/2/3/4/8) at TP 1-16, but were not run end to end.
- **CI.** The parametrized test runs the Triton port on any GPU (NVIDIA too), so existing CUDA CI covers its numerics; AMD CI covers the ROCm path where it runs `tests/kernels/fla`.
- **Related open PRs (not duplicates).**
  - #61675 adds an opt-in (`VLLM_ROCM_QWEN_MTP_GDN`), shape-specialized ROCm kernel that also fuses the conv. It accepts only 16/48 K/V heads (Qwen3.8-27B), TP=1 and verify widths up to 4, and raises for any other shape, including Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (16/32). This PR makes the default ROCm path fused under the same contract and eligibility as the upstream CUDA op (head ratios 1/2/3/4/8, any TP, up to 8 tokens). The two can coexist, with #61675 taking over when it is enabled.
  - #61434 defers state stores inside the unfused Triton spec-decode kernel (FP32 state, `mamba_cache_mode="none"`). On ROCm this PR replaces that path whenever the fused path is eligible; the deferred-store idea could be applied to this kernel in a follow-up.
  - #59366 adds a separate CUDA replay op for RecoverSSM and leaves the op ported here unchanged.
  - #60833 / #61325 (Qwen3.8 mono decode on MI355X) run vLLM's GDN core for verify steps, so this change applies there too.
- **Provenance.** The first version of the kernel was written and validated in Meta's internal vLLM fork; the V tiling was added in this PR after review.
- **AI assistance.** Drafted with Claude Code (port, V tiling and tile-size rule after review, test parametrization, benchmarks); reviewed and run by the submitter.

---

<details>
<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill. (Mandatory for agents, optional for humans).
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

- [ ] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.
- [ ] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI.
- [ ] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples.
- [ ] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.

title: [Perf] Kimi K3 Specialized Decode: CuTeDSL Optimized GB300 (1.5-2x)
author: benchislett
body:
## Overview (this PR description was manually written by me) This is an NVIDIA-developed specialized implementation of Kimi K3 for GB300 that achieves 1.5-2x decode speedups. It supports: - TP8 and TP16 on GB300 - NoSpec (up to B64) and DSpark verification with 3-7 draft tokens (up to 64 tokens -- B8 for DL7, B16 for DL3) - Decode context parallelism with DCP=TP (DCP-off also supported) It is enabled opt-in via `--additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}'`. All changes are localized to `vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/`. ## Claims With FP8 KV Cache, FP32 SSM Cache, and model-provider weights: - TP16, ISL 1, no speculation: decode step **1.79-1.92x faster than stock at B1-B8** (3.90 vs 7.38 ms at B1). - TP16, DSpark DL7, synthetic acceptance 6: **1.53-1.71x decode tok/s at B1-B8**. - DL7, ISL 32k, DCP on: **1.36-1.50x (TP8)** and **1.53-1.75x (TP16)** decode tok/s. - AIME25, GPQA-Diamond and MRCR v2 8-needle match stock within about one standard error, with and without speculation. ## Validation ### Correctness Testing Evals for this branch ran with DCP = TP (TP8+DCP8 and TP16+DCP16); stock ran on TP8 without DCP, C2 and C8 pooled. Spec on = DSpark DL7 with probabilistic drafting and standard rejection sampling (no forced acceptance). Score ± standard error, n samples per cell; pooling ours' C2 and C8 cells gives AIME25 avg@4, GPQA-Diamond avg@2, GSM8k avg@2. MRCR v2: 8-needle, (128k, 256k] contexts, thinking on, 32k output cap. | Task | Spec | Stock TP8 | Ours TP8+DCP8 C2 | Ours TP8+DCP8 C8 | Ours TP16+DCP16 C2 | Ours TP16+DCP16 C8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | AIME25 | off | 0.867 ± 0.033 (n=120) | 0.867 ± 0.048 | 0.917 ± 0.035 | 0.900 ± 0.037 | 0.900 ± 0.037 | | AIME25 | DL7 | 0.892 ± 0.032 (n=120) | 0.917 ± 0.042 | 0.900 ± 0.037 | 0.883 ± 0.052 | 0.950 ± 0.037 | | GPQA-D | off | 0.924 ± 0.011 (n=594) | 0.919 ± 0.019 | 0.914 ± 0.020 | 0.919 ± 0.019 | 0.929 ± 0.018 | | GPQA-D | DL7 | 0.916 ± 0.011 (n=594) | 0.939 ± 0.017 | 0.929 ± 0.018 | 0.919 ± 0.019 | 0.955 ± 0.015 | | GSM8k | off | 0.867 ± 0.009 (n=1319) | 0.856 ± 0.010 | 0.860 ± 0.010 | 0.864 ± 0.009 | 0.873 ± 0.009 | | GSM8k | DL7 | 0.863 ± 0.005 (n=5276) | 0.853 ± 0.010 | 0.854 ± 0.010 | 0.868 ± 0.009 | 0.865 ± 0.009 | | MRCR v2 | off | 0.282 ± 0.039 (n=100) | 0.334 ± 0.042 | 0.226 ± 0.036 | – | – | | MRCR v2 | DL7 | 0.343 ± 0.042 (n=100) | 0.339 ± 0.042 | 0.320 ± 0.042 | – | – | Sample counts: AIME25 n=60, GPQA-D n=198, GSM8k n=1319, MRCR n=100. Single MRCR runs swing by ~0.1 between repeats; a larger TP8 C8 matrix ({ours, stock} x {DCP on, off} x {spec off, DL7}, 750–900 samples per build) gives **0.296 (ours) vs 0.290 (stock)**.
Numerical validation and the MRCR output-length study - **Greedy logprobs, spec vs no-spec on the same build** (up to and including the first divergence): TP8 drift ≤ 0.50 vs stock's own 0.38, divergences only at near-ties (top-1/top-2 margin ≤ 0.50); TP8+DCP8 (~8k context) drift ≤ 0.38, margins ≤ 0.375, inside stock's B1-vs-B4 noise of 0.875. :heavy_check_mark: - **Greedy probes at 128k–256k context vs stock** (32 MRCR prompts, 4096 tokens, top-10 logprobs): every divergence is at an exact BF16 top-1/top-2 tie; ours-vs-stock |Δ logprob| (0.007–0.009, first divergence ~step 50–80) matches stock DCP-on vs DCP-off (0.014, ~59); no growth with position. Same with DL7. :heavy_check_mark: - **Per-step error vs a 1-ulp noise floor** (stock re-run with 1-ulp-perturbed embeddings on the same state), out to 245k context with and without DCP: KL, top-1 agreement, hidden-state, KDA-state and KV differences all equal the floor; accumulated drift over 1536 consecutive decodes equals the accumulated floor. Prefill is bit-identical to stock. :heavy_check_mark: - **Decode vs prefill rescoring** (CUDA graphs, sampling, 8192 tokens; the same server then rescores the text via prefill logprobs): per-token decode-minus-prefill logprob, stratified by confidence, is identical to stock's in all configs and flat with depth. :heavy_check_mark: - **Output length:** At low cap (32k), we see many truncations and slightly more for ours than baseline. This remains unclear, as there is very high variance and the mean OSL at 32k is a bit higher. With a 64k cap (100 samples per config), we see very few truncations and mean output length is comparable. : | build | config | mean | std | capped at 64k | |---|---|---|---|---| | ours | DCP, spec off | 8757 | 13515 | 3 | | ours | DCP, DL7 | 7540 | 12612 | 2 | | ours | no DCP, spec off | 6987 | 9577 | 0 | | ours | no DCP, DL7 | 11891 | 19250 | 9 | | stock | DCP, spec off | 9458 | 12858 | 1 | | stock | DCP, DL7 | 10634 | 16039 | 5 | | stock | no DCP, spec off | 9083 | 14634 | 4 | | stock | no DCP, DL7 | 10526 | 16881 | 5 |

Decode tok/s excludes prefill; output tok/s and TPOT include the other requests' 16k prefill chunks, so their gains are smaller. TTFT is at parity. | B | TP8+DCP8 decode tok/s, ours / stock | output tok/s | TPOT ms, ours / stock | TP16+DCP16 decode tok/s, ours / stock | output tok/s | TPOT ms, ours / stock | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 374 / 249 (**1.50x**) | 1.32x | 2.68 / 4.02 | 483 / 276 (**1.75x**) | 1.49x | 2.08 / 3.63 | | 2 | 625 / 420 (**1.49x**) | 1.16x | 3.87 / 5.41 | 775 / 473 (**1.64x**) | 1.35x | 3.10 / 4.72 | | 4 | 875 / 625 (**1.40x**) | 1.18x | 7.14 / 8.91 | 1156 / 750 (**1.54x**) | 1.24x | 5.45 / 7.28 | | 8 | 1233 / 904 (**1.36x**) | 1.14x | 11.92 / 13.91 | 1667 / 1088 (**1.53x**) | 1.20x | 9.70 / 12.30 | ### Full matrix (nsys decode step, stock / ours) SPEED-Bench mixed prompts at ISL 8k / 32k / 100k; DSpark DL3 at forced acceptance 2.87, DL7 at 3.78.

## Details ### vLLM Integration No weight changes were made in this model implementation: it is fully compatible with Aggregated vLLM serving, and falls back to the default implementation for prefills, mixed batches, and large batches. The specialized decode runtime is implemented via _composition_: a SpecializedDecode object owned by the Kimi LLM model, built when supported (see `unsupported(...)`), and called during forward(). The runtime can opt-out of a batch (e.g. when it has too many tokens) by checking `decode.plan(...) is None`, and fall back to stock forward. I considered a few alternate designs but ultimately feel like this is the cleanest integration. It uses the ModelState protocol to build the runtime object and hook into initialize_kv_cache(). The rest of the integration is organized into subfolders, e.g. `vllm/models/kimi_k3/specialized_decode/nvidia/cutedsl/kda/` with the specialized implementation(s) for each component. ---

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode on GB300
author: yaoyaoding
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

This PR adds an NVIDIA specialized decode for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, for the small decode batches that agentic serving runs. It supports:
- one GB300 tray at TP4;
- DSpark speculative decoding with 5 draft tokens;
- FULL-graph decode steps of up to 384 rows (64 requests × 6 tokens). Prefill, mixed batches and larger batches fall back to the stock forward.

It is opt-in via `--additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}'`, the same switch as #61867. With the default (`auto`), the model runs exactly as on upstream `main`. The model changes are all under `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/`; outside it, the PR only adds tests and a CI step.

The integration follows #61867: the model owns a decode executor that takes over FULL-graph decode steps. The stacked follow-up #61869 puts the DSpark draft model on the same executor. Both follow the RFC #59665 fast-track process. Related: #57448 (DeepSeek-V4.1 tracking), #59725 (Cake kernels).

## Claims

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray with DSpark, the same build with the switch on and off:
- Decode step (one speculative step, including the draft): **18.3% faster at batch 1** (5,355 → 4,375 µs), 13.7% at batch 8 and 11.3% at batch 32.
- InferenceX AgentX traces: **P90 interactivity up 16–24%** at every concurrency from 1 to 64, with throughput per GPU up 1–6% and TTFT unchanged.
- GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, AIME25 and RULER NIAH stay within one point of the switch-off model, and the DSpark acceptance length does not change.

## Validation

### Correctness

The reference is the same build with the switch off. GPQA-Diamond and AIME25 use reasoning effort high and temperature 0.6.

| Task | Samples | Switch off | Switch on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K, strict match (c1 / c8 / c32) | 1,319 per cell | 0.973 / 0.972 / 0.973 | 0.974 / 0.970 / 0.975 |
| GPQA-Diamond | 198 × 16 | 0.796 | 0.788 |
| AIME25 | 30 × 16 | 0.994 | 0.990 |
| RULER NIAH single / multikey-2 / multikey-3, 32K / 128K / 256K (c1 and c8) | | 1.0 in every cell | 1.0 in every cell |
| DSpark acceptance length on GSM8K (c1 / c8 / c32) | | 3.93 / 3.95 / 3.93 | 3.93 / 3.96 / 3.97 |

- **GPQA-Diamond.** Paired by question over the 16 repeats, on − off is −0.79 ± 0.56 points (bootstrap 95% interval −2.2 to +0.6). The first eight repeats gave −1.6 points, mostly answers that ran past the 16,384-token limit without a final answer; the second eight gave +0.06.
- **Later revisions.** GSM8K at c8 was rerun after each later change, with its mean acceptance length: 0.972 and 3.92 on `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1), 0.975 and 3.95 on `011fa68c`, 0.971 and 3.97 after the move into the executor, 0.976 and 3.96 with the CuTe DSL kernels, 0.972 and 3.99 after the rebase onto `main` `03ee2e13` (FlashInfer 0.7.2), 0.975 and 3.92 after the rebase onto `main` `aa3564ce`, and 0.972 and 3.91 after the rebase onto `main` `3b518982`. Both rebases also changed compiled code in `main` (the first DeepGEMM's build and the top-k kernels, the second the top-k softmax and DCP kernels), so the decode step was timed across each on one GB300 tray (old `main` wheel and branch against new, blocks old-new-new-old, two repeats each): B1 +0.1%, B8 +0.8%, B32 +0.4% across the first, and B1 −0.2%, B8 −0.1%, B32 −0.1% across the second, all within noise (|t| < 2), so the performance numbers in this description still stand. After each rebase the kernel, numerics and layers tests pass again (run at the tip of #61869, which contains this PR).

The tests check each kernel against the stock op it replaces, the TP4 collectives bitwise against the unfused path, and a five-layer model served with the switch on and off:

<details><summary>Tests, sanitizers and CI</summary>

```bash
# One SM100-family GPU: each kernel against the stock op it replaces
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_kernels.py -v
# Four GPUs: TP4 collectives bitwise against the unfused reference, and graph replays
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_numerics.py -v
.venv/bin/python -m tests.models.deepseek_v41.nvidia.specialized_decode.test_numerics --replays 100000  # race stress
# Four GB300: five-layer model on random weights at TP4 with DSpark, switch on vs off
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_layers.py -v
```

| Check | What it covers | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kernel tests | Each kernel against the stock op it replaces, at every supported row count, eagerly and replayed from a CUDA graph | 90 passed |
| Numerics (TP4) | The fused collectives bitwise against the unfused reference over 1,000 graph replays; the indexer top-k equal up to boundary ties | Passed |
| Race stress | 100,000 graph replays: collectives bitwise, top-k sets equal throughout | Passed before the restructure, which changed no kernel |
| Layers test (4× GB300) | A five-layer model at TP4 with DSpark, served with the switch on and off; the activations of every layer are compared within tolerance. The test checks which paths each layer took, that the executor ran on the switch-on steps and that it never ran with the switch off | Passed |
| compute-sanitizer (CUDA 13.0.2) over the kernel tests | memcheck, synccheck, racecheck | memcheck: no errors. synccheck: no report in this PR's kernels. Kernels that are not this PR's are left uninstrumented, because synccheck aborts every kernel it reports: FlashInfer's TRT-LLM-gen kernels and CuTe DSL dense GEMMs, and vLLM's `LLBf16SplitK`, which this PR calls ("Divergent thread(s) in block"). racecheck: FlashInfer's CuTe DSL split-K `mm_bf16`, which the LM head calls, reports shared-memory hazards; upstream calls the same kernel from its BF16 linear backend. No other test reports a hazard: cooperative top-k, the sparse-MLA KV counters, the MXFP8 projections, the index key store, Engram, the side-stream table builds and the metadata graphs are racecheck-clean. Those were run over the DSpark PR's kernel tests, which include all of this PR's, before the restructure, which changed none of them. The CuTe DSL routed-expert kernels were checked with all three tools at this revision: no memcheck error, no synccheck report and no race hazard. |
| pre-commit | All hooks | Passes on every changed file |

**CI.** A new 4×B200 step runs the kernel, numerics and layers tests. Like the other 4×B200 steps, it is optional, so it runs nightly rather than on every PR. No CI agent has four GB300, so the layers test skips there; it and the end-to-end results were run on GB300 outside CI.

</details>

### Performance

All runs use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray (TP4) with DSpark (5 draft tokens), Model Runner V2 and FULL CUDA graphs for decode. The switch-off arm is upstream `main` at the same base. These numbers were measured before the code moved into the executor and before the routed-expert kernels were ported to CuTe DSL; both changes were then compared with the revision before them and moved the decode step by at most 1.3% (see "Since these measurements" below).

AgentX throughput per GPU against P90 interactivity, upstream (switch off) and this PR (switch on), with the InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash GB300 vLLM curve for reference:

![AgentX throughput against interactivity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yaoyaoding/vllm/75c4f9b4c668f368921bf802ff83875b83d7f337/agentx_frontier_main.svg)

**Decode step.** The speculative step with its draft, timed from the client over long-context decodes, in ABBA blocks on one tray (one server per block), on `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1). Every switch-on block beats every switch-off block.

| Batch | Switch off (µs) | Switch on (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 5,355 | 4,375 | −18.3% |
| 8 | 10,598 | 9,151 | −13.7% |
| 32 | 17,483 | 15,516 | −11.3% |

On the older base `2c74fd1`, the same ABBA gave −20.5%, −17.4% and −13.1%. The switch-on step is the same there (4,371 µs at batch 1); `main` has since made the switch-off step faster.

**AgentX.** The InferenceX AgentX trace corpus for 3,600 s per concurrency, upstream `main` `2c74fd1` against this PR on that base. Each cell reads switch off → switch on.

| Conc | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | Change | Total tok/s/GPU | TPOT p50 (ms) | TTFT p50 (s) | E2E p50 (s) | Requests |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 655.2 → 811.3 | +23.8% | 7,402 → 7,861 (+6.2%) | 1.46 → 1.14 | 0.81 → 0.93 | 2.1 → 2.0 | 326 → 341 |
| 4 | 557.7 → 681.7 | +22.2% | 9,590 → 10,055 (+4.9%) | 1.50 → 1.17 | 0.36 → 0.43 | 1.2 → 1.1 | 735 → 759 |
| 8 | 478.3 → 560.9 | +17.3% | 16,443 → 16,985 (+3.3%) | 1.52 → 1.27 | 0.37 → 0.39 | 1.2 → 1.2 | 1,431 → 1,449 |
| 16 | 365.5 → 452.6 | +23.8% | 29,444 → 29,727 (+1.0%) | 1.95 → 1.54 | 0.37 → 0.37 | 1.3 → 1.1 | 2,720 → 2,737 |
| 32 | 256.8 → 297.0 | +15.7% | 61,732 → 62,969 (+2.0%) | 2.68 → 2.03 | 0.72 → 0.84 | 2.3 → 2.2 | 4,867 → 4,951 |
| 64 | 175.8 → 211.5 | +20.3% | 100,638 → 101,811 (+1.2%) | 4.30 → 3.53 | 4.90 → 5.55 | 8.3 → 8.6 | 10,410 → 10,463 |

The TTFT column compares two trays, and the difference is the trays', not this PR's; a same-tray run shows TTFT unchanged:

<details><summary>TTFT on one tray</summary>

Each arm in the table above ran on its own tray. AgentX TTFT is mostly the API server's single-threaded work before the engine sees the request: chat-template rendering and tokenization of the whole conversation. Its speed differs between trays and over time by up to 15% (2.3–3.3 s of API-server CPU per million prompt tokens). aiperf's per-request `request_ack_ns` separates that work from the engine, and the cross-tray TTFT differences above are all in it; the engine part is equal. This PR changes only worker-side code.

To take the tray out of the comparison, three AgentX blocks ran on one tray, one server each, in the order upstream → this PR → upstream, at c4 for 1,200 s each:

| Block | TTFT p50 / p90 (s) | API-server CPU per M prompt tokens (s) | TPOT p50 (ms) | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Upstream | 0.229 / 1.179 | 2.72 | 1.46 | 545.2 |
| This PR | 0.233 / 1.157 | 2.69 | 1.13 | 702.6 |
| Upstream | 0.224 / 1.177 | 2.73 | 1.46 | 553.8 |

Paired over the same 272 requests, this PR's TTFT is 2.5 and 3.2 ms below the two upstream blocks. The two upstream blocks differ from each other by 0.6 ms.

</details>

<details><summary>Since these measurements: the executor restructure, the CuTe DSL port, and the switch-off check</summary>

**Restructure.** Following #61867, the paths moved from the stock layers into the executor, with no kernel change. Both revisions were measured with the switch on, on `main` `d6f0b7a4`, on one tray with one server each (each value the mean of two blocks):

| Batch | Before (µs) | Executor (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,344 | 4,347 | +0.1% |
| 8 | 9,061 | 9,096 | +0.4% |
| 32 | 15,545 | 15,464 | −0.5% |

On AgentX at c16 (two 1,200 s runs per revision, same tray), P90 interactivity is 405.9 before and 399.4 tok/s/user with the executor, and total throughput 20,924 and 20,957 tok/s/GPU. Runs of the same revision differ by up to 3% in P90 interactivity, so neither metric moves beyond run-to-run noise.

**CuTe DSL kernels.** The routed-expert front, route and GEMM kernels were first written in CUDA and compiled with NVRTC at run time. They are now CuTe DSL kernels with the same schedule and arithmetic, and their outputs are bitwise those of the CUDA versions. Kernel time (CUPTI, cold L2, median, µs), CUDA → CuTe DSL:

| Kernel | 1 row | 6 rows | 8 rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Front | 3.46 → 3.04 | 4.51 → 4.06 | 5.06 → 4.64 |
| Route | 2.32 → 2.18 | 2.18 → 1.95 | 2.37 → 2.30 |
| GEMM1 | 10.06 → 9.76 | 18.62 → 17.60 | 18.91 → 17.76 |
| GEMM2 | 7.30 → 6.24 | 11.23 → 10.37 | 11.49 → 10.62 |

The decode step with the CUDA and the CuTe DSL kernels, in the same-tray ABBA (switch on in both, each value the mean of two blocks):

| Batch | CUDA (µs) | CuTe DSL (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,356 | 4,298 | −1.3% |
| 8 | 9,113 | 9,178 | +0.7% |
| 32 | 15,483 | 15,430 | −0.3% |

Both CuTe DSL blocks are faster at batch 1. These kernels take up to 8 rows, so at batch 8 and 32 (48 and 192 rows per step with DSpark) both arms run the same code, and the differences are block-to-block spread: the two CUDA blocks differ by 0.8% at batch 8.

**Switch off.** With the switch off, this branch matches upstream at the base (measured against `2c74fd1`): the decode step stays within ±0.5% at batch 1 and 32 and is 1.3–1.8% faster at batch 8 (two same-tray ABBA halves); GSM8K at c8 is 0.971 (upstream 0.972); AgentX c1 gives P90 interactivity 657.2 against upstream's 655.2, with TPOT p50 1.46 ms in both.

</details>

## Details

### Where the time goes

Agentic workloads such as AgentX send long multi-turn conversations (median 350K tokens of context, almost all prefix-cached) and wait for each reply before sending the next turn. Each server therefore decodes only 1 to 64 requests at a time, and users see the time per output token.

At batch 1, stock vLLM's speculative step takes about 5.4 ms: one target forward that verifies six tokens, plus the DSpark draft. There is no single hotspot.

- **GPU.** A step runs about 1,600 kernels, most of them a few microseconds long. One target layer without an indexer is a serial chain of about 105 µs: about 50 µs of attention (quantize, `wq_a`/`wkv`, norm-quant, `wq_b`, KV insert, index build, `q_lens` and counter fixes, FMHA, `wo`, publish, all-reduce) and about 53 µs of MoE (front 14, GEMM1 19, GEMM2 12, finalize and all-reduce 6). The GEMMs see 1 to 48 rows but run kernels tuned for larger batches; the all-reduce + mHC at each of the 80 sublayer boundaries is fused only up to 16 rows; and layers with the sparse-attention indexer add their own chain of small kernels (logits, top-k and index tables).
- **Host.** The host loop is busy about 4.95 ms of the 5.37 ms step, and about 2.2 ms of that builds attention metadata for the target's and the draft's KV-cache groups. A GPU-only speed-up beyond about 0.4 ms would just expose the host.

So the executor removes kernels and launch gaps, uses kernels sized for 1 to 8 rows, moves independent work onto side streams, and takes host work out of the step loop.

### What changed

Each row is one optimization and the saving we measured when it was added, as a batch-1 decode-step ABBA on one tray unless a batch is named. They were measured one at a time on a development branch, so they do not add up exactly to the end-to-end figure. The full list of paths and their gates is in `nvidia/specialized_decode/AGENTS.md`.

| Optimization | Why | Saving when added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fused all-reduce + mHC** | | |
| One fused Lamport all-reduce + mHC kernel at every sublayer boundary up to 384 rows (stock: 16). The next layer's mHC coefficients are computed on a side stream up to 48 rows. | Above 16 rows, the stock path runs a separate all-reduce, mHC and copies at each boundary. | −11.4% at batch 8 (48-row cap); −4.5% at batch 32 (384-row cap) |
| The fused kernel also writes the next attention input as MXFP8. | That removes a separate quantize kernel per layer. | −54 µs |
| `wo_b`'s GEMM epilogue stores straight into the fused kernel's mailbox. | That removes a copy kernel; the fused kernel then only collects. | −41 µs |
| The MoE finalize is deferred into the fused kernel at the Engram and final boundaries too, in a residual-only variant. | These boundaries previously ran the finalize and all-reduce separately. | −36 µs |
| The aux hidden-state means for DSpark are computed on the mHC side stream. | They were on the critical path. | −23 µs |
| **GEMMs for 1–8 rows** | | |
| Routed experts: one fused front kernel (routing, MXFP8 quantization, permutation) and two `tcgen05` GEMM kernels, all in CuTe DSL. The top-k reduction is left to the next boundary's fused kernel. | FlashInfer's TRT-LLM-gen MoE path is tuned for larger M and launches more kernels. | −192 µs (GEMMs), −114 µs (front and finalize) |
| `fused_wqa_wkv`, `wq_b` and `wo_b` on FlashInfer's low-latency CuTe DSL MXFP8 GEMM, with tactics pinned per shape. | The stock MXFP8 GEMM is a persistent kernel sized for larger batches. Pinning keeps the fastest measured tactic per shape instead of the autotuner's pick. | −53 µs, then −62 µs from pinning |
| Compressor, indexer-weight and indexer `wk` projections on vLLM's low-batch BF16 split-K GEMM. The index key store reads `wk`'s FP32 output. | At 1–8 rows these skinny GEMMs give cuBLAS few output tiles; split-K spreads the long K over the SMs. | −60 µs |
| LM head on FlashInfer's CuTe DSL BF16 GEMM, and logits gathered with the custom all-gather. | The stock path uses cuBLAS plus an NCCL all-gather. | −15 µs, −27 µs |
| **Sparse-attention indexer and attention** | | |
| Compressed layers that share an index source reuse one sparse-index table. Sparse-MLA decode launches on a KV-counter buffer that is zeroed once. | Each layer rebuilt the same table and zeroed counters before every launch. | −207 µs (1,578 → 1,486 kernels per step) |
| The tables of every KV-cache group are built once per key, on a side stream. | Each group rebuilt its tables serially. | −103 µs |
| Candidate blocks are selected with `cooperative_topk` over the valid columns. | The stock top-k scans the padded width. | −86 µs |
| Indexer query, compressor and index-key work, and candidate expansion with its MQA-logits schedule, run on side streams. Each joins at its first reader. | They are independent of the attention chain until then. | −50 µs, −33 µs |
| Dense indexer rows are sharded over the TP ranks and all-gathered, on pure-decode steps of at least 8 requests. | The indexer is replicated on every rank, and its cost grows with batch and context. | −1.9% at batch 8, −7.6% at batch 32 |
| **Host and launch overhead** | | |
| Attention-metadata builds are recorded into CUDA graphs at capture, one per decode batch shape and KV-cache group, and replayed. | These Python and Triton builds were about 2 ms of the host loop. | −86 µs, then −27 µs |
| Each Engram layer's KV projection chain (table-row lookup, all-gather, MXFP8 quantize, `wkv` GEMM) runs ahead of the layer on the Engram prefetch stream. | It reads only table rows looked up from the token IDs, so it need not wait for the layer's input. Each Engram layer's main-stream span drops from 70 to 6 µs. | −90 µs |
| Decode steps skip the per-request replay-start upload when the device already holds zeros. | Decode steps only ever upload zeros. | −24 µs |

### vLLM integration

As in #61867, the model owns a decode executor (`specialized_decode/runtime/decode.py`). With the switch on, the model returns a model state subclass (`specialized_decode/runtime/model_state.py`) that builds the executor once the weights are loaded, then tunes and compiles its kernels before memory profiling. For each forward, the model asks the executor for a step (`plan()`). Only FULL-graph captures of pure decode steps of up to 384 rows get one. The backbone runs its embedding and Engram hashing as usual, then hands its decoder layers to the step (`run()`). Every other forward runs the stock layers, which the executor does not modify.

| Package (`nvidia/specialized_decode/`) | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `__init__.py` | The opt-in, and `unsupported()`, which lists every requirement the deployment misses |
| `runtime/` | The executor and its per-step gates, the model state, warm-up, attention-metadata CUDA graphs |
| `boundary/` | The mHC between sublayers on the fused all-reduce + mHC kernel, and the publishing `wo_b` GEMM |
| `attention/` | Low-batch MXFP8 and BF16 projections, the row-sharded indexer, candidate overlap, shared sparse-index tables and the sparse-MLA decode |
| `moe/` | The MoE step with a deferred finalize, and the low-batch routed-expert kernels in CuTe DSL |
| `engram/` | The Engram KV projection ahead of the decoder layers |
| `logits/` | The low-batch LM head and the logits gather |

**Scope.** The switch is validated on one deployment:
- GB300 (SM103), MRV2, TP=4, with no PP, DP, EP or CP and no micro-batching;
- DSpark without adaptive verification;
- `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41` with an fp8 KV cache and the MXFP4 indexer with sparse logits;
- FULL graphs for decode only;
- no `torch.compile` of the model (the executor runs inside the forward), and no sleep mode (the routed-expert GEMMs and the publishing `wo_b` bind weight addresses);
- DeepGEMM and NVLink multicast;
- no LoRA, KV transfer or batch invariance.

Any other deployment raises at start-up on every TP rank, listing every missing requirement. Eligibility is combined across ranks with a MIN all-reduce, so ranks always agree. We made it an opt-in because the set is validated end to end on this one deployment; within it, each path still dispatches at run time on host state that every rank shares, as #59665 asks. It can become the default on that deployment in a follow-up.

**Rank lockstep.** The paths contain cross-rank collectives, so a rank that diverged would hang rather than fall back. Every per-step gate therefore reads only host state that all TP ranks share: row and request counts, and the graph mode. Nothing is read back from the GPU in steady state. For example, the row-sharded indexer runs only on even row slices, because DeepGEMM's paged MQA logits need 8-byte-aligned indices on every rank.

**With the switch off.** Inside `nvidia/`, the shared files take small seams with the same behavior:
- `model.py`: the backbone hands its decoder layers to the executor's step when it gets one, and the model picks the model state class;
- `model_state.py`: the replay-start upload and the attention-metadata build become methods, which the executor's model state overrides;
- `vl_model.py`: takes the model state class from the language model;
- `ops/o_proj.py`: a `wo_b_proj` keyword for the publishing `wo_b`;
- `ops/cute_dsl/all_reduce_mhc.py`: the fused all-reduce + mHC source is parameterized by its row count and variants, and built at 16 rows as before when the switch is off.

**FlashInfer version.** Three paths use FlashInfer internals: the publishing `wo_b` GEMM, the fused kernel's MXFP8 layer input, and the pinned MXFP8 GEMM tactics. They run only on `flashinfer-python==0.7.2`, the version `main` pins; the internals they use are unchanged from 0.7.1, where they were first checked. On any other version, each warns once and takes the stock path, so a FlashInfer bump should recheck them.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Any-shape low-latency MoE router GEMM on MI355
author: AndreasKaratzas
body:
## Overview

On MI355 (gfx950), the MoE router GEMM now has a low-latency kernel for **any** router shape (fp32 or bf16 weights, fp32 output, M ≤ 32), matching the CuTeDSL `ll_fp32w` / `ll_bf16` router kernels from #44343 and #50174. Previously only five hard-coded `(hidden_size, num_experts)` shapes had a fast path; every other model paid 9–13 µs per MoE layer per decode step in `F.linear` / hipBLASLt.

## Claims

- **Decode 1–14% faster** on all 8 tested MoE models whose router path changes, largest at low concurrency.
- **No accuracy change**: GSM8K matches `main` on every model (paired McNemar p = 1.0 and 0.34 where runs varied most).
- **No regressions**: prefill, an unchanged-path control (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and the 5 previously tuned shapes stay flat; shapes where the kernel would lose keep today's path.
- **New MI355 CI job** mirroring `(B200) Gate Linear CuTeDSL Kernels`.

Changes:

- Generalize `rocm_fp32_router_gemm` to any shape: masked K tail, MI355-swept launch rule, bf16 weights, size guards
- `GateLinear`: enable the fp32 router tier on gfx950 for any shape and route bf16-weight fp32-logit gates (tier 6) through the same dispatch op
- Extend `test_rocm_fp32_router_gemm.py` and fix the now-outdated rejection test in `test_gate_linear_rocm_dispatch.py`
- Add `:amd: (MI355) Gate Linear Router Kernels` (B200 mirror + optional `test-amd.yaml` entry) and move the 3 ROCm router test files there from MI355 Misc

## Validation

`main` vs this PR, end to end on MI355 (decode TPOT Δ, + is faster; median of 5 reps):

| Model | Router | Decode Δ C1 / C8 / C32 | GSM8K main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| ERNIE-4.5-21B-A3B | fp32 2560×64 | **+14.1 / +3.4 / +2.1%** | 86.58 → 86.28 |
| Trinity-Nano | fp32 1024×128 | **+9.6 / +4.9 / +4.0%** | 79.08 → 79.00 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8 | fp32 2688×128 | **+9.4 / +5.4 / +2.2%** | 90.96 / 90.69 (A/A) → 90.83 |
| Ling-mini-2.0 | fp32 2048×256 | **+7.7 / +4.6 / +2.5%** | 88.02 → 88.10 |
| GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 (TP2) | fp32 4096×128 | **+5.0 / +5.0 / +2.9%** | 72.33 → 72.02 |
| Step-3.5-Flash-FP8 (TP2) | fp32 4096×288 | **+4.7 / +3.1 / +2.7%** | 89.61 → 89.31 |
| Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it | bf16 2816×128 | **+8.9 / +5.5 / +3.5%** | 94.31 → 94.39 |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (TP2) | bf16 4096×256 | **+2.0 / +1.2 / +1.0%** | 95.80 → 95.86 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (control) | unchanged | −0.2 / 0.0 / +0.2% | 91.66 → 91.58 |

8K prefill TTFT is flat on every model (within ±0.7%).

<details>
<summary>Methodology and accuracy details</summary>

- `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, prefix caching off, 1–8 input / 256–512 output tokens. `main` and the PR were served at the same time on separate GPUs, alternating every run, with GPU load logged each rep.
- GSM8K: lm_eval 5-shot chat, median of 3+ runs.
- Nemotron and DeepSeek-V4 were re-run with `--log_samples` for a paired per-question test. Nemotron PR vs `main`: 9 / 9 discordant, McNemar p = 1.0; `main` vs `main` A/A: 9 / 6, p = 0.61. DeepSeek-V4: 3 / 7 in the PR's favor, p = 0.34. An earlier DeepSeek-V4 round read 96.06 → 95.53; the repeat did not reproduce it.
- ERNIE's −0.7% prefill is within the 0.3–0.5% spread between GPUs, which a GPU-swap A/B confirmed. Trinity's prefill TTFT ranges overlap.
- **Why decode improves:** one router GEMM per MoE layer per step drops from 9–13 µs (`F.linear`) or 5–11 µs (hipBLASLt) to 1.9–4.9 µs at ≤ 8 tokens, saving 0.2–0.6 ms per step. Prefill and large batches never reach the kernel.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Kernel benchmark</summary>

MI355, one idle GPU, median of 30 graph replays, 2 runs with ≤5% drift. M = 1–32.

| | Shapes | vs today's path |
|---|---|---|
| fp32, the 5 old shapes | 5 | 0.97–1.30× vs old tuned configs (median 1.07×) |
| fp32, new shapes (DeepSeek-V3, Kimi-K2, Qwen3, Qwen3.8, gpt-oss, Llama4) | 7 | **1.2–6.8×** vs `F.linear` (median 4.1×) |
| fp32, held out from the sweep (GLM-4.5, Ernie, 1000×100, 1024 experts, …) | 10 | **1.1–7.0×**; two 1024-expert M=32 cases keep `F.linear` |
| bf16 | 9 | **1.7–5.4×** vs hipBLASLt at M ≤ 8, 1.04–2.9× at 16–32; never slower |

Max relative error vs float64: 1.3e-7 (fp32 weights), 8.9e-8 (bf16 weights).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Tests</summary>

- New CI command `pytest -v -s tests/kernels/test_rocm_fp32_router_gemm.py tests/kernels/test_gate_linear_rocm_dispatch.py tests/kernels/test_bf16x3_router_gemm_rocm.py`: 847 passed, 10/10 loops, ~5 min each.
- Each new test fails against a mutated kernel or dispatcher: no K-tail mask, the old shape list, a bypassed dispatcher, no bf16 cutoff, or no gfx950 tier-6 routing.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design details, scope and related PRs</summary>

- **Launch rule:** one program computes `BLOCK_M` tokens for one expert. Narrow routers (< 64 experts) keep `BLOCK_M = 1`; wide routers grow it with the token count. Fitted on 12 shapes, checked on 10 held-out shapes: within 1.11× of the per-shape best and faster than the fallback everywhere.
- **Size guards:** at M·N·K ≥ 2^27 (fp32) or tokens × experts > 8192 (bf16) the fallback is faster, so the kernel declines and today's path runs.
- **Compile safety:** runtime branching stays inside the existing `fp32_router_gemm_dispatch` custom op.
- **Scope:** gfx950 only; gfx942, CUDA, biased/quantized gates and batch-invariant mode are unchanged.
- **Not covered end to end:** MiniMax-M2.5-MXFP4 decodes at ~196 ms/token on both `main` and the PR, so the difference is unmeasurable. Kimi-Linear-48B and LongCat-Flash-Lite-FP8 crash on unmodified `main`, unrelated to this change. Their router shapes are covered by the kernel tests.
- **Related PRs:** #59023 does the bf16 extension for Kimi-K3's 7168×896 gate only (this PR gives the same M ≤ 9 limit there, for any shape). #57626 forces fp32 weights for the 5 listed shapes instead; this PR runs bf16 weights directly with no fp32 copy. #61687 targets a separate AITER tier and is orthogonal.

</details>

title: [Perf][Kernel] Add a CuteDSL BF16x3 router GEMM for fp32 router weights on Hopper
author: ischencheng
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

On H100/H200, `GateLinear` runs fp32 router weights above 32 tokens as `F.linear(x.float(), w)`, an fp32 SGEMM on CUDA cores. SM100 has the CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for this (#47973, #55899) and gfx950 has a hipBLASLt one (#52668). SM90 had nothing. This PR adds a CuteDSL BF16x3 kernel for SM90 behind the existing BF16x3 tier.

Models on main that hit this path on SM90 (fp32 router weight, bf16 activations): MiniMax-M2/M2.5/M3, GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7 and GLM-4.5-Air, Hunyuan-V3/V4, Step-3.5-Flash, ERNIE-4.5, Ling 2.0 (`router_dtype: fp32`), and others. The new models are on it too. Beam-1.0 (#62074) keeps fp32 router weights `(5120, 256)`, and Muse Spark Open (#61879) keeps `(8192, 256)`. Both shapes are in the fp32 GEMV table since #62042 and #62126, so on H200 every batch above its limit runs the fp32 SGEMM.

The first revision of this PR used Triton. It is now CuteDSL, like the other router GEMMs in the tree, and uses the `VllmJitKernel` warmup contract.

## Claims

- Router GEMM on 1xH200, inside CUDA graphs with cold L2, over 10 router shapes: 1.6-3.8x faster at 33-512 tokens and 3.3-7.7x faster at 1024-16384 tokens.
- MAE against an fp64 reference is 0.16-0.73x that of the fp32 SGEMM it replaces, at every shape and token count measured.
- MiniMax-M2.5 FP8, TP2 on 2xH200, with main and PR alternating in one container: TTFT 3-5% lower for 8K and 32K prompts, prefill throughput 4-6% higher, and on a mixed 1K-in/128-out workload 4.6% more output tokens/s and 4% lower TPOT. GSM8K accuracy is unchanged and its wall time is 2.5% lower.
- In eager mode one router call costs 17-18 µs of host time, against 21-36 µs on main.
- Beam-1.0 FP8 on one H200, as one TP8 rank (all 52 layers, dummy weights, main and PR alternating): an 8K prefill chunk takes 14.0% less time (155.3 to 133.5 ms), and a decode step at 64 and 128 requests takes 7.4% and 10.9% less.
- On SM90 the fp32 GEMV now runs up to 24 tokens instead of 32, where the new kernel is faster. The GB200 rule for `(5120, 256)` from #62042 and the B300 rule for `(4096, 352)` from #61727 stay Blackwell-only.
- No change for 24 or fewer tokens on the fp32 GEMV shapes, under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`, or on other architectures.

## Validation

### Unit tests

```bash
pytest -v tests/kernels/test_bf16x3_router_gemm_cutedsl.py tests/kernels/test_fp32_router_gemm.py tests/kernels/test_ll_fp32w_gemm.py
```

1xH200: 662 passed, 83 skipped with this head. 76 of them are the SM90 tests in `test_bf16x3_router_gemm_cutedsl.py`. The skips are the SM100-only tests: the 5 SM100 cases in that file and `test_router_retains_fp32_weights_and_logits`.

1xB200, after the rename (`test_bf16x3_router_gemm_cutedsl.py` and `test_fp32_router_gemm.py`): 485 passed, 76 skipped (the SM90 cases).

The SM90 tests check:
- MAE against fp64 is not above the fp32 SGEMM's, for 9 router shapes (with Beam-1.0 and Muse Spark Open) and 7 token counts (8 to 8192);
- partial K and expert tiles, and a K with fewer tiles than the largest split;
- the weight split is bit-exact (one-hot activations);
- `GateLinear` dispatch: the fp32 GEMV runs up to 24 tokens for `(5120, 256)` and `(4096, 352)`, so the GB200 and B300 rules stay off Hopper, and this kernel runs above that and for a generic shape.

The file runs in the new `(H100) BF16x3 Router GEMM Kernels` Buildkite step, and in `Kernels (B200)` as before.

| Step-5 (4096, 352) | 8.0e-07 → 3.7e-07 | 9.0e-07 → 3.7e-07 | 9.4e-07 → 4.0e-07 | 1.3e-06 → 4.0e-07 | 1.1e-06 → 4.4e-07 | 1.3e-06 → 4.4e-07 |

</details>

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```python
"""PR component benchmark: SM90 router GEMM for fp32 gate weights, main vs this PR (1xH200).

main: F.linear(x.float(), W) for M > 32 (fp32 SGEMM). PR: torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm.
Each number is the per-call time inside one CUDA graph that replays the op on N rotating copies of
(x, W) whose footprint is >= 4x L2, so every call starts with cold weights. MAE is against fp64.
"""

import json
import os
import statistics

import torch

import vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.router.bf16x3_router_gemm_sm90  # noqa: F401

torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")
dev = torch.device("cuda")
L2_BYTES = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(dev).L2_cache_size
print("device", torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch", torch.__version__, flush=True)

SHAPES = {
    "MiniMax-M2/M2.5": (3072, 256),
    "MiniMax-M3": (6144, 128),
    "GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7": (5120, 160),
    "GLM-4.5-Air": (4096, 128),
    "Hunyuan-V3": (4096, 192),
    "Hunyuan-V4": (2816, 256),
    "Step-3.5-Flash": (4096, 288),
    "Ling-flash-2.0": (4096, 256),
    "ERNIE-4.5-300B": (8192, 64),
    "Step-5": (4096, 352),
}
MS = [int(m) for m in os.environ.get("MS", "33,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192,16384").split(",")]
SCALE = 0.053


def graph_time_us(fns, reps=7):
    for f in fns:
        f()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(g):
        for f in fns:
            f()
    g.replay()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        s = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        t = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        s.record()
        g.replay()
        t.record()
        t.synchronize()
        times.append(s.elapsed_time(t) * 1000 / len(fns))
    return statistics.median(times)


def mae(out, ref):
    return (out.double() - ref).abs().mean().item()


def main_path(x, w):
    return torch.nn.functional.linear(x.float(), w)


def pr_path(x, w):
    return torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm(x, w)


rows = []
for name, (k, e) in SHAPES.items():
    gen = torch.Generator(device=dev).manual_seed(0)
    for m in MS:
        nc = int(min(64, max(4, -(-4 * L2_BYTES // (m * k * 2 + e * k * 4)))))
        xs = [torch.randn(m, k, generator=gen, device=dev).to(torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(nc)]
        ws = [torch.randn(e, k, generator=gen, device=dev) * SCALE for _ in range(nc)]
        ref = xs[0].double() @ ws[0].double().T
        row = {"model": name, "K": k, "E": e, "M": m}
        for label, fn in (("main", main_path), ("pr", pr_path)):
            row[f"{label}_us"] = round(graph_time_us([lambda i=i: fn(xs[i], ws[i]) for i in range(nc)]), 2)
            row[f"{label}_mae"] = mae(fn(xs[0], ws[0]), ref)
        row["speedup"] = round(row["main_us"] / row["pr_us"], 2)
        rows.append(row)
        print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
        del xs, ws
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

os.makedirs("control/artifacts", exist_ok=True)
with open("control/artifacts/pr_component.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(), "torch": torch.__version__, "rows": rows}, f, indent=1)
```

</details>

### SM90 cutoff for the fp32 GEMV (1xH200)

Same timing method, per call in µs, fp32 GEMV / this kernel. The new kernel is almost flat up to 96 tokens. The fp32 GEMV grows with the token count.

| (K, E) | M=16 | M=24 | M=25 | M=32 | M=40 | M=48 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Beam-1.0 (5120, 256) | 5.79 / 7.52 | 7.47 / 7.52 | 7.58 / 7.53 | 9.70 / 7.56 | 11.86 / 7.62 | 13.82 / 7.59 |
| Muse Spark Open (8192, 256) | 7.80 / 9.87 | 10.79 / 9.91 | 11.12 / 9.93 | 14.11 / 9.97 | - | - |
| Step-5 (4096, 352) | 6.38 / 6.87 | 8.42 / 6.92 | 8.80 / 6.92 | 8.59 / 6.91 | - | - |
| MiniMax-M2/M2.5 (3072, 256) | 4.09 / 5.94 | 4.99 / 5.93 | 5.19 / 5.96 | 6.97 / 5.94 | - | - |
| MiniMax-M3 (6144, 128) | 5.78 / 8.07 | 8.05 / 8.10 | 8.02 / 8.10 | 10.36 / 8.11 | - | - |

The crossover is at 18-28 tokens depending on the shape. With 24 for all shapes, each shape stays within 1.5 µs of the faster kernel. The GB200 rule from #62042 (fp32 GEMV up to 48 tokens for multiples of 8, else 16) would cost up to 6.2 µs per call here (48 tokens: 13.82 vs 7.59), so it now applies only on Blackwell. Two rounds; the spread is within 0.2 µs.

At 25-32 tokens the new kernel's MAE is 0.89-1.15x the fp32 GEMV's (for example Beam at 25 tokens: 4.2e-7 vs 4.1e-7), and well below the fp32 SGEMM's that main runs from 33 tokens. Neither kernel picks a different top-8 than fp64 at any measured point; the fp32 SGEMM does in 1 of 16384 rows for Beam-1.0 and MiniMax-M3.

### Beam-1.0 FP8, one TP8 rank on 1xH200

#62074 is not merged, so this runs its model code on top of this branch. The model is one TP8 rank of Beam-1.0 FP8: all 52 layers and 256 experts, so the router is the real `(5120, 256)` fp32 GEMM; attention heads and MLP widths are one rank's share (6 Q heads, 1 KV head, expert width 320). Weights are dummy, with `--moe-backend triton` and `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` as in the H200 recipe. There is no all-reduce. The main arm keeps this branch but turns the SM90 tier off in `GateLinear`, which is what main runs. Arms ran in one container in the order main, PR, PR, main, 3 runs each. The PR arm was the merge commit before the 24-token cutoff; no step here has 25-48 router rows.

| | main | PR | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K prefill chunk (ms) | 155.08-155.57 | 133.39-133.99 | -14.0% |
| 64 x 512-token prompts, prefill (s) | 0.626-0.627 | 0.538-0.542 | -14.0% |
| Decode step, 64 requests (ms) | 8.120-8.133 | 7.519-7.528 | -7.4% |
| Decode step, 128 requests (ms) | 9.377-9.385 | 8.360-8.378 | -10.9% |

The savings match the kernel numbers. At 8192 tokens one router call drops by 432 µs, and 49 MoE layers give 21.2 ms per chunk; measured is 21.8 ms. At 128 tokens it is 19.3 µs x 49 = 0.95 ms per step; measured is 1.02 ms. On a real TP8 deployment every rank still runs the full router, so the time saved per step is the same, but the step also includes all-reduce, so the relative gain will be smaller than here.

### End-to-end: MiniMax-M2.5 FP8, TP2, 2xH200

`vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.5 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --trust-remote-code --max-model-len 40960 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --no-enable-prefix-caching --jit-monitor-mode warn --jit-monitor-verbose`, with the default 8192 batched tokens and CUDA graphs. All runs were in one container, in the order main, PR, main, PR. Before each arm, its files were copied over the installed package and the server was restarted, with `VLLM_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1`. Each `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-range-ratio 0 --ignore-eos` workload ran twice per arm, so 4 runs per side.

| Workload | main (4 runs) | PR (4 runs) | Change of the means |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K prompt, 1 at a time: median TTFT (ms) | 328 / 332 / 332 / 331 | 317 / 318 / 314 / 313 | -4.6% |
| 32K prompt, 1 at a time: median TTFT (ms) | 1808 / 1812 / 1812 / 1816 | 1761 / 1757 / 1746 / 1750 | -3.2% |
| 8K prompts, concurrency 16: req/s | 3.56 / 3.56 / 3.57 / 3.56 | 3.77 / 3.77 / 3.78 / 3.77 | +5.8% |
| 32K prompts, concurrency 4: req/s | 0.601 / 0.602 / 0.602 / 0.601 | 0.625 / 0.625 / 0.625 / 0.625 | +3.9% |
| 1K in / 128 out, concurrency 64: output tok/s | 1422 / 1472 / 1461 / 1467 | 1518 / 1525 / 1523 / 1522 | +4.6% |
| same: mean TPOT (ms) | 39.0 / 37.8 / 38.1 / 38.0 | 36.8 / 36.7 / 36.6 / 36.7 | -4.0% |

The prefill rows are GPU-bound 8K chunks, so the router speedup shows directly (62 layers). Decode at 32 or fewer requests is unchanged by design.

GSM8K (`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 1319 questions, 5-shot, concurrency 128), twice per arm:

| | main | PR |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.9287 / 0.9378 / 0.9333 / 0.9310 (mean 0.9327) | 0.9356 / 0.9340 / 0.9303 / 0.9356 (mean 0.9339) |
| Wall time (s) | 94.9 / 92.0 / 90.9 / 90.3 | 90.4 / 92.4 / 88.1 / 88.0 |

GSM8K at concurrency 128 mostly runs mixed steps above the CUDA graph sizes, so they run eagerly. With the Triton revision its wall time was slower than main in 3 of 4 containers, from the host time per router call. This version takes less host time per call than main (see Host overhead).

## Details

**Kernel.** The MMA runs swapped: 64 experts form the wgmma M dimension and tokens the N dimension (32 to 128 per CTA), so small batches still fill the instruction. One TMA warp brings fp32 weight tiles and bf16 token tiles into shared memory. The MMA warpgroup reads each k16 slice of its weight fragment as fp32 and splits it in registers into three bf16 terms. Each term keeps the top 16 bits of what is left, so the three terms sum back to the weight bit for bit. It then issues register-A wgmma against the token tile, and splits the next slice while the current one runs. Products with bf16 activations are exact in fp32, so all error comes from accumulation:
- The first-term products go to a tensor-core partial that starts from zero every K-tile (64 or 128 wide). It is then added into an fp32 register accumulator.
- The second and third terms are about 2^-8 of the output. They keep their own partial across K, as the SM100 kernel does. This is the one numerical change from the Triton revision, which promoted all three terms every K-tile. It makes the largest tiles up to 9% faster. The worst MAE in my checks is 0.87x of the fp32 SGEMM's (GLM-4.7 shape, 7 tokens).

Split-K uses a thread-block cluster of up to 8 CTAs. Each CTA writes its partial tile to its own shared memory, reusing the weight stages, and after a cluster barrier sums one slice of the tile over all peers through DSMEM, in rank order. Results are deterministic, and there is no workspace and no second kernel. There is no host sync and no data-dependent shape, so the op is safe to capture in CUDA graphs.

**Configs.** There is no autotuning. `_pick_config` scores 4 tiles x 4 splits with a fixed cost model: waves times per-CTA time. A wave is one CTA per SM, and clusters of 4 or 8 only fill 15/16 of the SMs (120 of 132; at one CTA per SM, `cuOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` gives 30 clusters of 4 and 15 of 8 on H200). The per-tile costs were fitted to H200 timings. Over 10 shapes and 14 token counts, the rule is within 0.1% (geomean) of the fastest of the 16 configs per cell, and at most 4% slower. Each of the 10 shapes reaches 9-13 configs between 1 and 16384 tokens, at about 1 s of compile each.

**Warmup.** The kernel is a `VllmCuTeDSLJitKernel`. `GateLinear` registers it with its `(K, E)` and `max_num_batched_tokens`, as it does for `ll_fp32w` and as #50177 does for SM100. Warmup traces `dispatch` over 1..max tokens and compiles each key from fake tensors, with no launch. In the end-to-end runs above, the PR arm warmed 13 keys in about 10.5 s at startup. The JIT monitor logged no compile of this kernel while serving; it logged two `fused_moe_kernel` Triton compiles on both arms.

**Host overhead.** Outside CUDA graphs (mixed prefill/decode batches above the capture sizes), the host cost per call matters as much as the kernel. `_pick_config` is cached, and the launch is one TVM-FFI call. Eager host time per call on an idle H200 host:

| | M=64 | M=930 | M=4096 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main, fp32-GEMV dispatch op (MiniMax-M2.5 shape) | 26.3 µs | 29.2 µs | 28.9 µs |
| PR, same op | 18.1 µs | 18.4 µs | 18.3 µs |
| main, `F.linear(x.float(), w)` (GLM-4.7 shape) | 21.7 µs | 24.1 µs | 36.3 µs |
| PR, `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm` | 17.1 µs | 17.5 µs | 17.1 µs |

The Triton revision took about 31 µs here. Its GSM8K runs (mostly eager mixed steps) were slower than main by a few percent in some containers.

**Integration.**
- `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is now also true on SM90, with the same `K % 8 == 0` condition as SM100. `bf16x3_router_gemm_module()` returns the SM90 module on SM90 and the SM100 module otherwise. The fp32-GEMV dispatch op and tier 4 use it.
- In the fp32-GEMV dispatch op, SM90 bf16 inputs use the fp32 GEMV up to 24 tokens. The `(5120, 256)` GB200 rule from #62042 and the `(4096, 352)` B300 rule from #61727 are in the non-SM90 branch unchanged.
- `bf16x3_router_gemm_cutedsl.py` is renamed to `bf16x3_router_gemm_sm100.py`, next to `bf16x3_router_gemm_sm90.py`.
- The kernel is the custom op `torch.ops.vllm.sm90_bf16x3_router_gemm`, as #55899 does for SM100. The fp32-GEMV shapes keep dispatching on the runtime token count inside `fp32_router_gemm_dispatch`.
- PDL is always on. SM90 supports it.

**Alternatives measured on H200.**
- The Triton revision of this PR. This kernel is 1.25x faster (geomean over 10 shapes and 15 token counts). It is slower only for ERNIE-4.5 (E=64) at 128 or fewer tokens, where 9.6 µs vs 7.2 µs: one 64-expert tile and at most 8 splits leave most SMs idle. It is still 1.55x faster than main there.
- One cuBLAS GEMM over the stacked `(3E, K)` bf16 weight, which is what gfx950 does: MAE 1.4e-6 to 4.3e-6 for the Step-5 shape, worse than the fp32 SGEMM's 3-5e-7.
- A round-to-nearest split, like the SM100 kernel's but without `sub.rn.f32x2` (sm_100 only): 0.5-4% slower than the truncating split at 64-8192 tokens on the Step-5, Beam-1.0, MiniMax-M2.5 and Muse shapes. Both MAEs are well below the fp32 SGEMM's. The other way round, the truncating split in the SM100 kernel on B200 is 0.1-2.3% slower than its own split on the same shapes, so each kernel keeps its own.
- Two bf16 terms (BF16x2): 16 of fp32's 24 significand bits. Even with exact accumulation, that alone gives an MAE of 5.7e-6 to 7.4e-6 at 1024 tokens on the Step-5, Beam-1.0 and MiniMax-M2.5 shapes, against 0.8e-6 to 1.4e-6 for the fp32 SGEMM.
- A pre-split weight kept in memory: needs 1.5x the fp32 router weight per layer (about 760 MB per rank for 88 layers of Step-5). The in-register split needs no extra memory.
- One promoted partial for all three terms per k16 slice, instead of keeping the small terms apart: MAE rose above the fp32 SGEMM's at 33 tokens.
- Two MMA warpgroups per CTA, along the experts or along the tokens (up to 4): not faster than the selected configs in my sweeps.

**Limitations.**
- With one token, cuBLAS's fp32 GEMV is more accurate than this kernel for 3 of the 10 shapes (for example MiniMax-M3: MAE 3.1e-7 vs 4.7e-7). From 2 tokens up, all 10 shapes beat it. In eager mode those batches stay on the fp32 GEMV or `ll_fp32w`. The test starts at 8 tokens.
- As on SM100, generic shapes reach tier 4 through tier 3's Python check on `x.shape[0]`. Under vLLM's guard-free `torch.compile`, that branch can be fixed at the first traced size, the issue #60681 fixes for tier 1. Small batches of those shapes may then run this kernel, which is still faster than the `F.linear` path main would freeze.
- The cost model was fitted on H200 (132 SMs). Other SM90 parts get correct results and an SM-count-aware choice, but the choice may not be the fastest.
- #61727 lowers the fp32 GEMV cutoff for Step-5 to 11 tokens when `allow_bf16x3_router_gemm` is set, based on B300. On H200 the fp32 GEMV is still faster at 16 tokens for that shape, so that rule belongs in the non-SM90 branch next to the GB200 one.
- The Beam-1.0 numbers come from a one-rank proxy with dummy weights. A full TP8 run needs #62074 merged and 8xH200.

**Not a duplicate.** I listed every open PR that touches `gate_linear.py`, `fused_moe/router/`, `fp32_router_gemm*` or `ll_fp32w*`, or that has router/gate/bf16x3 in its title. Most are for other hardware or other tiers: #60376 (SM100 large batch), #60681 (tier 1 custom op), #61727 (Step-5), #50177 and #49627 (warmup), #50535, #61687, #61895, #59023 and #57626 (ROCm), #59486 (quantization), #59925 (deterministic MoE), #37306 (Llama4), #57848 (SM103) and #61463 (ll_bf16 split-K fix).

Merged since this PR opened: #62042 (`(5120, 256)` fp32 GEMV up to 48 tokens and its GB200 rule) and #62126 (Step-5 and Muse Spark Open shapes in the fp32 GEMV). Neither adds an SM90 path above the GEMV's limit. I merged main into this branch and moved the GB200 rule behind the SM90 check.

#49312 (for #49277) also targets SM90 fp32 router weights. It adds an opt-in path (`VLLM_ENABLE_HPC_ROUTER_GEMM=1`) through the external hpc-ops library, with a cached bf16 high/low copy of the weight. This PR is on by default, adds no dependency, keeps no extra weight copy, and its error stays below the fp32 SGEMM's.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write the kernel and tests, run the benchmarks above and draft this description.

title: [Perf][Sampler] Speed up the small-batch split top-p pipeline
author: abmfy
body:
## Overview

The small-batch split top-p pipeline (#54651) caps its grid at one program per SM (`S * B <= num_SMs`), and at that occupancy its step kernels are latency-bound. On a 148-SM GPU S drops to 2 at 38 rows, so a top-p call at 38-64 rows (e.g. 8 requests x 8 spec-decode verify tokens) takes about twice as long as at 37 rows. This PR makes two changes:

1. It keeps splitting rows past one wave while each slice still spans at least 7168 vocab entries.
2. It lets MRV2 skip the split pipeline when no row is top-p-only. Today the pipeline is still launched in that case, as 7 kernels whose programs all exit immediately.

cc @njhill

## Claims

- With the `has_topp_only_rows` hint that MRV2 passes, `apply_top_k_top_p` on <= 64 rows is as fast or faster for every row mix measured: all top-p-only, half and half, and all top-k on both GPUs, plus 1, 10% and 25% top-p-only rows on B300. This holds on B300 (148 SMs) and H200 (132 SMs), across the vocab sizes of current models (120K-262K, plus 32K). Main -> this PR:
  - Top-p-only rows, where main is at S=2: 1.22-2.16x on B300 and 1.05-1.90x on H200.
  - Batches that mix top-k rows with top-p-only rows, B >= 32, V >= 120K: 1.43-2.70x. At 32K, where S changes only from B=38 on B300 and B=34 on H200, it is 1.00-1.62x. The fewer top-p-only rows, the bigger the win: with a single top-p-only row, up to 3.7x at V=151936 and 4.4x at V=262144 (B300).
  - Batches where every row has top-k (e.g. the Qwen3.8 and Gemma 4 defaults): 1.00-1.21x. MRV2 no longer launches the split pipeline for them.
  - The worst ratio, 0.97x, is in configs where nothing changes, within the A/A noise. Callers that do not pass the hint get the same gains, except that all-top-k batches run at 0.90-0.98x (see Change 2).
- Real MiMo-V2.6 spec-decode verify rows (top_p 0.95) on B300: 561 -> 219 us at B=38 (2.56x) and 565 -> 318 us at B=64 (1.78x).
- End to end on the Triton sampler path (B300):
  - Llama-3-8B-Instruct, seeded top-p, c=48: median ITL -5.1%.
  - MiMo-V2.6-Pro TP4 with DFlash K=7, c=8: top-p goes from 558 to 301 us per step, and GPU busy time excluding MoE GEMMs drops by 0.27 ms of a 22.7 ms decode step.

## Validation

**Tests**, on fa75d3456d + this PR:
- B300: `pytest tests/v1/sample/test_topk_topp_sampler.py tests/v1/sample/test_sampler.py tests/v1/sample/test_rejection_sampler.py tests/v1/sample/test_sampling_params_e2e.py tests/model_executor/test_watermark_sample_warmup.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_sampler_flags.py`: 287 passed, 1 skipped (ROCm only).
- B300: `cd tests && pytest watermarking`, in its own session as CI runs it: 191 passed, 3 skipped. In a shared session, the default device that `test_topk_topp_sampler.py` sets leaks into these CPU tests; that is unrelated to this PR.
- H200: `pytest tests/v1/sample/test_topk_topp_sampler.py`: 140 passed, 1 skipped. This ran on the revision before the new test gained its monkeypatch; the kernel code is the same.
- New tests:
  - B=48 in `test_topp_only` and `test_topk_and_topp`. On 128-152-SM GPUs this is the only tested size where main uses S=2.
  - `test_skip_split_without_topp_only_rows`: with `has_topp_only_rows=False` the split pipeline is not launched, and the result is bitwise identical, including for a grammar-masked row.
  - `test_has_topp_only_rows`: covers MRV2 `SamplingStates`, including top_k values that disable top-k.
- CI runs `tests/v1/sample` on H200 MIG and MI355.

**Microbenchmark setup.** Calls are to `apply_top_k_top_p_triton`, one CUDA graph per variant, with variants interleaved and capture order alternated between configs. Each number is the median of 100 replays with L2 hot. On an earlier revision without the hint, cold L2 agreed within 0.07x.
- "main" is this tree with `_topp_split_count` patched back and no hint.
- "PR" passes `has_topp_only_rows` computed from k and p, as MRV2 does.
- A second capture of "PR" (A/A) gives the noise floor: 95% of configs fall within +-1.5%, the worst at 0.96x/1.05x.
- Logits are randn x 3; p=0.95 and k=50 unless stated. The script is below.

V=151936, main -> PR:

| rows | GPU | B=16 | B=32 | B=38 | B=48 | B=64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| top-p only | B300 | 1.09x | 1.01x | 1.93x | 1.52x | 1.29x |
| | H200 | 1.16x | 1.06x | 1.69x | 1.38x | 1.05x |
| half top-k, half top-p only | B300 | 1.09x | 1.50x | 2.44x | 2.16x | 1.86x |
| | H200 | 1.08x | 1.51x | 2.06x | 1.92x | 1.66x |
| all top-k + top-p | B300 | 1.08x | 1.09x | 1.07x | 1.07x | 1.05x |
| | H200 | 1.06x | 1.07x | 1.04x | 1.07x | 1.07x |

S goes 8->16 at B=16 and 4->16 at B=32. It goes 2->16 from B=38 on B300 and from B=34 on H200; at B=34 the H200 speedups are 1.74x for top-p only and 2.13x for half top-k.
