As concurrency grows the router becomes a smaller share of the step and the difference shrinks into the noise. The four negative points (-0.21% at most) all overlap with the base runs. Nothing regresses outside the same-arm drift.

Accuracy on the same build, lm-eval 0.4.9 `gsm8k` (1319 questions, 5-shot, greedy) through `/v1/completions`:

| model | base | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 92.12% ± 0.74 | 92.04% ± 0.75 |
| Kimi-K2.6 | 93.48% ± 0.68 | 93.71% ± 0.67 |

One question apart on GLM, three on Kimi-K2.6, both inside the standard error. MiniMax-M3.1-Flash routes through a group count `FusedTopKBiasRouter` synthesises (128 experts, top-4, 4/4); at that shape the kernel selects the same experts as AITER on all 17040 rows of a randomised check (fp32 and bf16 gating and bias, 1-128 rows), max weight difference 7.45e-08.

An earlier A/B on Kimi-Linear, taken before the graph-capture fix, measured +0.07% to +0.16%; the probe shows that run never substituted, so it is not used.

### Accuracy on MI300X (gfx942)

A/B on Moonlight through the served endpoint, lm-eval 0.4.13.

**NIAH** (RULER, 4096): the three reported task scores match between arms — `niah_multikey_1` 1.00/1.00, `niah_single_2` 0.94/0.94, `niah_single_1` 0.00/0.00. The subtask scoring zero on both arms is inconclusive; this is task-level agreement, not per-sample output agreement.

**GPQA** (`gpqa_diamond_zeroshot`, 198 questions, loglikelihood). A first single-run A/B looked like +2.0 points for this PR. Three interleaved runs per arm show the difference changes sign:

| run | AITER | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.3131 | 0.3333 |
| 2 | 0.3384 | 0.3182 |
| 3 | 0.3485 | 0.3283 |

AITER alone spans 0.3131–0.3485 across its own three runs.

Repeated on Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B, three interleaved runs per arm:

| run | AITER | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.3889 | 0.4040 |
| 2 | 0.3990 | 0.4192 |
| 3 | 0.3990 | 0.4091 |
| median | 0.3990 | 0.4091 |

Here this PR is nominally higher in all three runs, by 1.0 point. **That is not claimed as an accuracy improvement**: 1.0 point is 2 questions out of 198, well inside the ±3.4 point standard error, and a routing difference confined to 0.15% of calls has no mechanism by which it could make a model more accurate. Taken with the Moonlight runs, these results show no regression, but are not sufficient to establish accuracy equivalence.

### Bias dtype

`rocm_aiter_ops.biased_grouped_topk` casts `correction_bias` to the gating dtype before dispatching, because AITER raises on a mismatch. A bf16 gating output next to an fp32 correction bias is a common router layout, so without the same cast the new path would score experts at a precision the replaced path never uses, and could select different experts. `sigmoid_bias_flat_topk` therefore makes the same cast at its own entry; Removing the cast fails 4 of the 6 cases in `test_flat_topk_casts_bias_like_aiter`; the other two shapes happen not to be sensitive to the bias precision.

### Known behavioural differences

| input | result |
|---|---|
| well-formed gating | weights agree to 2e-3 in unit tests; selected ids match on 4571 of 4576 live routing calls across two models |
| near-ties in the biased score | weights agree to 1.19e-07; the index chosen among near-equal experts may differ |
| NaN in gating output | **materially different from AITER** (6/10 synthetic configs, max weight delta 0.93) |

If maintainers would rather the gate reject non-finite input, that is a small addition to `can_use_sigmoid_bias_flat_topk`.

## Details

### Why the substitution sits at the wrapper

Review asked whether a model with no grouping should simply not be routed to `GroupedTopKRouter`. Two things make the wrapper the better place.

First, the advertised routing method is not a label. `layer.py:378` takes it from `router.kernel_routing_method_type` and stores it on the MoE config, where the AITER mxfp4 expert kernels consume it: `_supports_routing_method` lists `[Renormalize, RenormalizeNaive, DeepseekV4, DeepSeekV3]`, `self.renormalize` is derived from the same tuple, and the apply path branches on `DeepSeekV3` to pick `score_mode="sigmoid"`. `MiniMax2` is in none of them, so degenerating `num_expert_group` 1 → None would make those backends refuse these models and would flip `renormalize` to False for a checkpoint whose config says `norm_topk_prob: true`.

Second, and more decisively, changing the router would not remove the op. Calling `fused_topk_bias` directly — the routine `FusedTopKBiasRouter` uses — with a 64-expert, top-6 sigmoid+bias router on ROCm with AITER enabled:

```
synthesised group count for 64 experts: 2
biased_grouped_topk CALLED 1x with (num_expert_group, topk_group) = (2, 2)
```

`_aiter_get_num_expert_group` picks a divisor AITER has a kernel for, with `topk_group == num_expert_group` so the grouping is a no-op. A model moved off `GroupedTopKRouter` would still reach the grouped kernel, with a fabricated two-group configuration in place of its real single group.

Specialising at `rocm_aiter_ops.biased_grouped_topk` covers both callers, needs no routing-metadata change, and generalises the condition from "one group" to "no group is eliminated".

### Relation to #49870

[#49870](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49870) short-circuits the same degenerate shape for the case where AITER fused MoE is **not** enabled, which this PR does not touch.

### Scope and bounds

`can_use_sigmoid_bias_flat_topk` requires `topk_group >= num_expert_group`, a contiguous bias of exactly `num_experts`, and bounded token/expert/topk counts. The scoring function is not checked: at this call site the op is AITER's biased (sigmoid) top-k by construction, so matching that op is the contract. `_MAX_EXPERTS = 512` and `_MAX_TOPK = 8` are where the gfx950 measurements above stop showing a win: up to there the mean per shape is 1.16×–1.57× and no launch falls below 0.92×, even with a forced tie; at top-16 single tied rows pull launches to 0.62×–0.78×. An earlier revision of this PR accepted up to 1024 experts and top-32, set to cover the widest router in this family without having measured it there; the gfx950 sweep showed that was wrong, and those routers, Kimi-K3 (896 / top-16) among them, now keep AITER. `_MAX_TOKENS = 1` restricts it to single-token batches, one request decoding without speculation, where the end-to-end sweep shows a gain on every model; at larger batches the gain was within noise, so those keep AITER.

### Limitations

- Micro and unit tests on gfx942 and gfx950. The MI355X e2e and GSM8K runs are on current `main`; the gfx942 e2e, NIAH and GPQA runs are on an older build, see the next point.
- The e2e and accuracy comparisons used the container's own older vLLM build for both arms, because today's `main` cannot start against this image's AITER (`aiter.ops.flydsl.moe_common` missing, `fused_moe()` without `swiglu_limit`). Both arms are that same build differing only in this kernel. Unit and micro results are against `db3b0f0fa`.

title: [ROCm][Spec Decode] Enable fused multi-step draft decode for ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN
author: fengshaoyi-amd
body:
## Overview

#46849 runs all MRV2 autoregressive draft decode steps from one metadata build in one CUDA graph when every draft attention backend sets `supports_draft_decode_metadata_update`. `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` does not, so EAGLE and MTP drafters on it log

```
Attention backend(s) ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN cannot update draft decode metadata in place; falling back to rebuilding attention metadata eagerly.
```

and rebuild the metadata on the host and replay one draft graph for each of the k−1 draft decode steps. Its metadata holds only views of buffers the fused loop keeps current plus step-invariant values, so this PR opts it in with a no-op `update_draft_decode_metadata`, as the Triton backend and FlashInfer trtllm-gen (#58371) do.

## Claims

- With `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN`, multi-step drafters run the fused draft decode loop, and the fallback line is no longer logged.
- On MI355X the draft decode loop, timed in isolation, takes 16–19% less time at k=3 (571 → 463 µs at batch 1, 697 → 585 µs at batch 8, 678 → 559 µs at batch 32) and 6–8% less at k=7 (1197 → 1108 µs, 1623 → 1530 µs, 1559 → 1464 µs). The saving per loop, 90–120 µs, does not grow with k.
- No end-to-end throughput gain is claimed. At k=3 serving throughput moves by +0.1% and +0.2% at concurrency 1 and 8, and by −0.6% at concurrency 32 (see Details for what the profiler shows there); at k=7 by +1.9%, −0.1% and −0.2%, within the variation between server instances.
- Output quality is unchanged: GSM8K accuracy at k=3 and k=7, GPQA accuracy of gpt-oss-20b at k=4, and acceptance length match main within run-to-run variation.

## Validation

MI355X (gfx950), `rocm/vllm-dev:ci_base` (torch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, HIP 7.15), `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`. Measured on `main` at `124501da`, then rebased onto `f9b0a11f`; the touched files are unchanged in between.

**Unit tests.** The unified builder is added to the two draft decode tests in `tests/v1/attention/test_triton_attn_metadata_builder.py` and is collected only on ROCm. Before review moved them there, the same two checks ran on MI355X from a separate file, with each tree applied in place and `vllm.__file__` checked:

| tree | result |
|---|---|
| this PR | 2 passed |
| main + this test | 2 failed: the flag is `False`, and the base `update_draft_decode_metadata` raises `NotImplementedError` |
| `build()` stages `seq_lens` in a builder-owned tensor | 2 failed: a builder-owned tensor is written, and the update leaves stale `seq_lens` |

The shared file has not been run on ROCm outside CI.

**Draft loop.** Wall time of `_multi_step_decode` (main) and `_fused_multi_step_decode` (this PR), synchronized before and after, in an in-process `LLM` serving 1024-token prompts with the configuration below; 1151 calls per arm, 4 rounds per batch size, first discarded, median of round medians (spread ≤ 0.54%).

**Serving.** Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with `RedHatAI/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-speculator.eagle3`, k=3. Synthetic rejection sampling fixes the acceptance length at 2.78, so both arms do the same work. One fresh server per run, 4 runs per arm, first discarded, median of 3, total tok/s:

```bash
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --max-model-len 8192 --block-size 64 --num-gpu-blocks-override 6144 --max-num-seqs 64 \
  --speculative-config '{"method": "eagle3", "model": "RedHatAI/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-speculator.eagle3", "num_speculative_tokens": 3, "attention_backend": "ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN", "rejection_sample_method": "synthetic", "synthetic_acceptance_length": 2.78}'
vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 512 --ignore-eos \
  --max-concurrency 32 --num-prompts 256   # concurrency 1 and 8 use 32 and 128 prompts
```

`--num-gpu-blocks-override 6144` keeps each layer's KV cache at 1.5 GiB, below the 2–4 GiB range where unified attention is wrong on gfx950 (ROCm/aiter#6661).

| concurrency | main | this PR | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1804 | 1807 | +0.1% |
| 8 | 10854 | 10875 | +0.2% |
| 32 | 27741 | 27572 | −0.6% |
| 32, arms run in reverse order | 27556 | 27387 | −0.6% |

**Accuracy.** GSM8K, 5-shot, greedy, all 1319 questions, real rejection sampling. Responses are as often identical between main and this PR (67.8%) as between the two main runs (66.3%).

| | main | main (rerun) | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| strict-match | 0.7020 | 0.7043 | 0.7028 |
| flexible-extract | 0.7763 | 0.7726 | 0.7703 |
| acceptance length | 2.343 | 2.345 | 2.344 |

**Syncs.** `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=warn` at concurrency 32 reports no synchronizing call and no implicit-sync copy in either arm.

**k=7.** Measured at this PR's head (`ade35875`), main being the head with this change reverted, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same drafter at `"num_speculative_tokens": 7`. gpt-oss-20b with `nebius/EAGLE3-gpt-oss-20b` is not used at k=7: on main its greedy output already differs from non-speculative decoding at k ≥ 5 (#65611), with or without this change and with `TRITON_ATTN` as well. Draft loop as above, 849 calls per arm, spread ≤ 0.4%:

| batch | main | this PR | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1197 µs | 1108 µs | −7.5% |
| 8 | 1623 µs | 1530 µs | −5.8% |
| 32 | 1559 µs | 1464 µs | −6.1% |

Serving as above with the synthetic acceptance length at 3.78, the value measured on GSM8K below. Two rounds, main then this PR and then the reverse, one fresh server per run and the same prompts within a round; mean of the two rounds, total tok/s:

| concurrency | main | this PR | Δ (round 1, round 2) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1916 | 1953 | +1.9% (+0.5%, +3.3%) |
| 8 | 12011 | 11996 | −0.1% (−0.5%, +0.3%) |
| 32 | 28041 | 27998 | −0.2% (0.0%, −0.3%) |

Main's three server instances at concurrency 1 alone span 3% (1937, 1895 and 1876 tok/s).

GSM8K on the same setup: zero-shot greedy chat completions over all 1319 questions, the last number in the reply compared with the reference, real rejection sampling. Extracted answers agree between main and this PR (93.3%) as often as between the two main runs (92.7%).

| | main | main (rerun) | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| accuracy | 0.8681 | 0.8787 | 0.8749 |
| acceptance length | 3.773 | 3.774 | 3.785 |

**GPQA.** gpt-oss-20b with `nebius/EAGLE3-gpt-oss-20b` at k=4, the largest k whose output is correct, with real rejection sampling, run through `tests/evals/gpt_oss/run_gpqa_eval.py` at the CI settings (low effort, 8 repeats of 198 questions); two rounds per arm with the GPUs swapped between rounds. Without speculative decoding the same build scores 0.4905 and 0.4912 on one GPU here, so the gap to the CI threshold (0.568) does not come from speculative decoding; we have not isolated where this setup loses it.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| round 1 | 0.4735 | 0.4792 |
| round 2 | 0.4855 | 0.4729 |
| acceptance length | 2.229 | 2.232 |

## Details

**Audit.** The builder inherits `RocmAttentionMetadataBuilder.build()`. Its metadata references the persistent buffers the fused loop keeps current (`seq_lens`, advanced in place, plus `block_table`, `slot_mapping` and `query_start_loc`), and its scalars do not change across draft steps: `max_seq_len` is fixed once per `propose()` to cover every draft step, and `max_query_len` is 1. It has no host plan (`scheduler_metadata` is `None`) and writes no builder-owned tensor; `build_for_cudagraph_capture` only fills the persistent `seq_lens` for capture. The draft decode tests check both properties: `build()` leaves every builder-owned tensor byte-identical, and after the in-place update the metadata equals a fresh build of the replayed batch.

**Scope.** Only `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` changes; it is opt-in through `--attention-backend` on MI300/MI355 and the default on RDNA with AITER. `ROCM_ATTN` shares `build()` but runs different decode kernels that were not validated here, so it keeps the fallback. Draft-model speculation (`method=draft_model`) does not use this loop. #62749 adds a separate flag for the target model's decode build and composes with this change.

**Concurrency 32.** The serving runs above are blocked by arm, so the state of each server instance is confounded with the arm. Torch profiler runs with the arms interleaved and the order balanced (five servers per arm, 60 steady decode steps each) show no per-step difference:

| per step, median over servers | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| step | 7432 µs | 7431 µs |
| draft decode segment | 588 µs | 583 µs |
| idle gaps between draft steps | 4.4 µs | 0 µs |
| target `lm_head` GEMM | 241 µs (237–284) | 241 µs (231–292) |

The draft decode segment is faster in every run because the gaps between draft steps disappear. The only kernel whose time moves is the target model's `lm_head` GEMM, which nothing in this change runs alongside; its time varies between server instances by up to 25% in both arms. The −0.6% at concurrency 32 is within that instance-to-instance variation, and the profiles show nothing in this change that costs time. We have not isolated the cause of the `lm_head` variation.

**CI.** `:amd: (MI300) V1 Attention` runs `tests/v1/attention`, which collects the unified builder's cases; elsewhere only the Triton cases run.

Not a duplicate: searched for `supports_draft_decode_metadata_update`, `update_draft_decode_metadata`, the fallback string and "draft decode metadata". #54790, #58371 and #58449 opt in other backends, and #62749 adds a separate target-side flag.

title: [Perf][MXFP4] Optimize activation quant for mxfp4. 3x kernel speedup, 5% throughput improvement
author: ilmarkov
body:
## Overview

Pass optional `sorted_expert_ids` through Cutlass MXFP4 MoE activation quantization so each sorted token row uses a direct expert index instead of searching expert offset tables.

## Claims


- Kernel: sorted_expert_id path is bitwise identical to offset_search on microbenchmark cases; up to ~3.3× lower median latency at 256 experts for representative input / intermediate_fused shapes.
- E2E: On RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-MXFP4 (TP=4, no spec), ~+5.7% output tok/s vs main.
- API change: Optional sorted_expert_ids on mxfp4_experts_quant, silu_and_mul_mxfp4_experts_quant, and get_cutlass_moe_mm_data; wired from Cutlass MXFP4 MoE when routing metadata exists.
## Validation

### Microbenchmark

title: [ROCm] Fuse tiny-M MXFP8 quant into the block32 GEMM; guard lm_head skinny-GEMM by weight size
author: alexm-redhat
body:
## Overview

Two decode-time fastpaths for DeepSeek-V4.x block32 MXFP8 linears on MI355X (gfx950): fuse the tiny-M activation quant into the block32 GEMM (one launch instead of two), and guard the lm_head skinny-GEMM dispatch by weight size (weights far larger than L2 stay on the generic GEMM fall-through).

Part of the DSV4.1-Flash MI355X serving fastpath series — four **independent** PRs on `main`@90c4a1a73e, each reviewable and mergeable separately, in any order. Siblings: #63180 (fused shared experts), #63181 (fused draft sampling), #63182 (draft-prepare fastpaths). The four series PRs all register kill switches in `vllm/envs.py` at the same anchor and therefore conflict textually with each other there; the resolution is to keep both sides. This branch trial-merges cleanly into current `main`.

## Claims

- **Fused quant+GEMM** (`rocm_block32_gemm.py`): at M ≤ 8 (decode shapes) the block32 linear path launched `_mxfp8_quant_triton_kernel` solely to produce the e4m3 tiles + E8M0 scales the packed GEMM immediately re-reads. The fused kernel computes that quant inside the GEMM's K loop, in registers, with the same arithmetic — one launch instead of two, no activation round trip. Bit-exact against the stock two-launch path at all eligible shapes (tuned tiers, masked K tail, in-launch split-K); ineligible inputs (non-contiguous x, fp32 x, M > 8) fall back bit-identically. Kill switch `VLLM_DEBUG_DISABLE_FUSED_MXFP8_QUANT_GEMM`.
- **lm_head skinny-GEMM guard** (`layers/utils.py`): `wvSplitK_hf_sml` re-reads the weight matrix once per K-shard, so its effective bandwidth collapses on weights far larger than L2 — at TP=4 the DSpark draft vocab-parallel lm_head shard ([32320, 5120] bf16, ~315 MiB, one call per decode step) hit this collapse. Weights above `VLLM_SKINNY_GEMM_MAX_WEIGHT_BYTES` (default 256 MiB) stay on the generic hipBLASLt fall-through at 1 < n ≤ 5; n = 1 (no pathology) is unchanged. Kill switch `VLLM_DEBUG_DISABLE_LMHEAD_SKINNY_GEMM_GUARD`.
- **−117 µs median decode ITL (−2.1%) on the current base** (`main`@`717cf84342`) — official DSV4.1-Flash serving command at TP=4 on MI355X, every paired run faster (rebase re-check under Validation). The submission-base study measured **−2.45% (−177/−188 µs)** over 12 position-balanced A/B cycles, and the win holds at the same magnitude across bases and images (−127 µs on the nightly ROCm-10 re-verification, −117 µs on the rebased tip). TTFT unchanged within noise.

## Validation

**Benchmark** — official serving command (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, DSpark k=5, `--monokernel`, MI355X), measured at TP=4; both fastpaths key on batch/weight shapes, not TP size. Both arms run this branch's tip; the OFF arm disables only this PR's two levers. 12 position-balanced A/B cycles (blocked AAA BBB, then BAB, then ABA), fresh server per arm per cycle, 2 sampled + 1 greedy client run per cycle (16 prompts, ISL 16 / OSL 2048, concurrency 1); arm statistic = median of per-run mean ITL; every lever's engagement asserted from the server log before the client runs.

| metric | ON median | OFF median | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| ITL t>0 | 7.065 ms | 7.243 ms | −177 µs (−2.45%) |
| ITL t0 | 6.977 ms | 7.165 ms | −188 µs |
| TTFT t>0 | 24.70 ms | 25.01 ms | −0.31 ms |
| TTFT t0 | 24.74 ms | 25.68 ms | −0.94 ms |

11 of 12 sampled cycles faster (one boundary overlap: ON max 7.148 ms vs OFF min 7.120 ms).

**Nightly ROCm-10 re-verification** — re-measured on the current nightly ROCm-10 image (`vllm/vllm-openai-rocm` nightly, TP=4, same command and protocol; one fresh boot per arm, 2 sampled + 1 greedy run each): ON 5.498 ms vs OFF 5.625 ms median mean-ITL → **−127 µs (−2.27%)**, fully disjoint per-run ranges (ON 5.438–5.510, OFF 5.550–5.636), spec-decode acceptance parity (sampled-run means 3.29 vs 3.34).

**Rebase re-check** — rebased onto the latest `main`; the runtime diff is unchanged, with one added test-only commit hardening the skinny-GEMM guard tests against dropped ROCTracer captures (the profiler flake behind the `amd-mi300-model-executor` CI failure). Full local CI-equivalent suites on this tip: model_executor 1313 passed, benchmarks 219 passed. Same A/B protocol: ON 5.510 ms vs OFF 5.627 ms median mean-ITL → **−117 µs (−2.09%)**; every paired run is faster (sampled −133/−92 µs, greedy −169 µs), and both arms' censuses assert the fused path engaged / disabled respectively.

**Accuracy** — gsm8k, 5-shot, strict match, 1319 samples, one run per arm: ON 0.9325, OFF 0.9242. Both inside the 0.9196–0.9340 band observed across repeated draws of this build; across the series the paired on/off deltas scatter on both sides of zero (engine run-to-run scatter) and no arm falls outside the band.

**Tests** — the fused-quant tests live in `tests/kernels/quantization/test_rocm_mxfp8_linear.py` next to the other `RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel` tests (the standalone file from the first revision is gone). Beyond the bit-exactness-vs-stock comparison, the serving-shape test now also checks the fused output against a high-precision QDQ reference — dequantize both MXFP8 operands and contract in fp32, independent of the block32 GEMM kernel under test (rel err < 5e-3) — so a regression in the GEMM itself cannot hide behind the bit-exact comparison. All tests pass locally on MI355X (gfx950):

```
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rocm_mxfp8_linear.py \
       tests/model_executor/layers/test_lmhead_skinny_gemm_guard.py -q
111 passed, 15 warnings in 47.26s
```

Of the 111, the tests added by this PR are 28 items — 21 fused-quant tests (~1.8 s) and 7 skinny-GEMM-guard tests (~1.4 s); the rest of the wall time is interpreter/import startup and the pre-existing MXFP8 suite. Single MI355X GPU, nightly ROCm-10 image.

CI notes: the fused-quant tests are CDNA4-gated (`current_platform.is_rocm() and supports_mx()`) and skip on MI300 CI pools — they are validated locally above; the skinny-GEMM guard test runs on any ROCm GPU (needs the `wvSplitK` custom op). The full pre-commit suite passes on the changed files (ruff, typos, mypy, check-torch-cuda-call, check-test-tethering, check-forbidden-imports, ...), and every commit is DCO-signed.

The tip adds review-driven changes over the benchmarked tree — tests centralized into the existing file, the QDQ reference, the kill switches renamed to `VLLM_DEBUG_DISABLE_*`, and the long docstrings trimmed to the dispatch rules (benchmark details now in this description) — plus two earlier lint-level fixes (`torch.accelerator.synchronize()` for pre-commit `check-torch-cuda-call`, a local `args: tuple` annotation in `rocm_block32_gemm.py` for mypy). No serving-path semantics change: the renamed kill switches are the only env-facing difference.

<details><summary>Reproduction</summary>

Server (ON arm) — official serving command, as measured at TP=4 (the fastpaths are not TP=4-specific):

```
VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 AITER_TRITON_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR \
VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1 \
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1 \
VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 \
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --port 8123 \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --moe-backend aiter \
  --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true}' \
  --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4","indexer_sparse_logits":true}' \
  --block-size 128 --monokernel \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":false}'
```

OFF arm: identical, plus `VLLM_DEBUG_DISABLE_FUSED_MXFP8_QUANT_GEMM=1 VLLM_DEBUG_DISABLE_LMHEAD_SKINNY_GEMM_GUARD=1`.

Load (after a 4-prompt warmup; add `--temperature 0` for the greedy run):

```
vllm bench serve --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 \
  --port 8123 --backend openai --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 16 --random-output-len 2048 \
  --num-prompts 16 --max-concurrency 1 --ignore-eos \
  --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 90,95,99 \
  --save-result
```

Accuracy (same engine config; `max_model_len 16384` and no `cpu_offload` are the only harness deviations):

```
python -c '
import lm_eval
lm_eval.simple_evaluate(
    model="vllm",
    model_args=dict(
        pretrained="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017",
        max_model_len=16384, tensor_parallel_size=4,
        tokenizer_mode="deepseek_v41", gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,
        block_size=128, moe_backend="aiter", monokernel=True,
        attention_config={"indexer_kv_dtype": "mxfp4",
                          "indexer_sparse_logits": True},
        compilation_config={"cudagraph_capture_sizes": [1, 2, 4, 6, 8]},
        speculative_config={"method": "dspark",
                            "num_speculative_tokens": 5,
                            "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic",
                            "rejection_sample_method": "block",
                            "enable_adaptive_verification": False}),
    tasks=["gsm8k"], num_fewshot=5, batch_size=8)'
```

</details>

## Details

**Fused quant+GEMM.** At M ≤ 8 the block32 linear path pays a full `_mxfp8_quant_triton_kernel` launch just to produce the e4m3 tiles + E8M0 scales the packed GEMM immediately re-reads; the fused kernel computes that quant inside the GEMM's K loop, in registers, with the exact same arithmetic. Eligibility is a shape-table hit (serving shapes at TP=4 covering the K-structure variety: multi-band K=5120 with the in-launch split-K tier, the masked-K-tail K=1280, a small-K tile, and the default-config tier); degenerate activation blocks (all-zero, denormal, huge, negative-mirror) quantize identically, and CUDA-graph capture/replay is bit-exact in both counter states. The per-row-scale dispatch branch of the linear kernel is unaffected.

**lm_head skinny-GEMM guard.** The guard is a byte-size predicate on the weight at the skinny dispatch site: above the cap, at 1 < n ≤ 5, the call goes to the generic hipBLASLt GEMM (the same kernel class the n=6 path uses); below the cap, or at n=1, or with the kill switch, dispatch is stock. The swap is not bit-exact (different GEMM kernel, different accumulation order) — numerics are checked within bf16 GEMM tolerance, and the decision table, dispatch selection, env behavior and one-shot-per-site census warning are pinned by tests.

Both paths log their engagement as WARNINGs (one line per site/state), so ON/OFF arms can be asserted from the server log before benchmarking.

<details><summary>MI355X measurements behind the skinny-GEMM guard</summary>

Measured on MI355X (gfx950), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP=4, vocab-parallel `[32320, K]` bf16 lm_head shards, from serving traces and isolated microbenches:

- The DSpark draft lm_head `[32320, 5120]` (315.5 MiB, n=5, once per decode step) ran `wvSplitK_hf_sml<..., 2, 5>` at **1.55 TB/s** (213.8 µs/call in-graph), while the generic fall-through class runs the same GEMM at **~6.5 TB/s** (~51–73 µs).
- The n=6 target-verify lm_head `[32320, 7168]` (442 MiB) already dispatches to hipBLASLt `Cijk MT64x16x512` (56.2 µs/call in-graph, 7.9 TB/s), i.e. the fall-through kernel is fast and CUDA-graph-capture-safe in this exact serving configuration.
- Isolated microbench on the target-shape shard at n=5: wvSplitK 313.3 µs vs `torch.linear` 71.2 µs (4.4×).
- The n=1 variant (`wvSplitK_hf_sml<..., 2, 1>`) shows no pathology on large weights (6.9 TB/s on the 442 MiB shard); its fall-through (LLMM1) would be a numerics change with no speed win, so n=1 keeps stock dispatch.

The mechanism is weight re-reads: `wvSplitK_hf_sml` streams the weight once per K-shard, so above L2-sized weights the effective bandwidth collapses. This is orthogonal to VGPR-spill fixes in the skinny kernel itself (#63015, #62846) — see the related-PRs note below.

</details>

**Related PRs.**

- #63015 / #62846 (skinny-GEMM tile/spill fixes): the guard here addresses a different mechanism — weight re-reads vs L2 bandwidth on very large weights — not VGPR spills, so the two are orthogonal and compose. The spill fixes should recover `wvSplitK` throughput on shapes that spill; the re-read cost on weights far above L2 remains. Once either lands we can re-measure the `[32320, 5120]` n=5 shard on top of it and revisit the guard's byte cap / n-window if the fixed `wvSplitK` wins there.
- #59782 (fused MXFP8 quant, draft): same fused-quant idea, per-shape cutoffs and keeps the fusion past M=8 on some shapes, where this PR caps every shape at M=8 with a bit-exactness contract against the stock path. In our measurements the fusion works well at M ≤ 8; we have not measured beyond that and are happy to coordinate on which approach to keep.

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Per-request draft retention for structured output under PP
author: yzong-rh
body:
Co-authors: @michael-gpu, @tomasruizt 
cc @ArcheyChen 

## Overview

Revert https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54442, which introduces a performance regression under PP + spec decode with structured outputs, and re-fix https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54437 by addressing the root cause in `DraftTokensHandler`.

Rework of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61348, rebased, with remaining comments addressed, pre-commit fixed, and simplified implementation + tests.

## Claims

#54442 patched the issue in #54437 by masking out the draft tokens after a handoff race in `DraftTokensHandler`. This fixes #61348 but effectively shortens the draft sequence, causing an acceptance-length (and performance) regression under PP + spec decode with structured outputs.

This PR addresses the `DraftTokensHandler` handoff race directly, fixing the original issue #54437 while maintaining acceptance length.

This PR also adds an E2E repro for #54437 and acceptance length regression.

## Validation

Correctness:

Case | Main avg [95% CI] | PR avg [95% CI] | Change
-- | -- | -- | --
broad / c1 | 673.6 [668.3, 678.9] | 675.7 [666.5, 684.9] | +0.32%
broad / c96 | 9,835.7 [9,749.2, 9,922.2] | 9,785.8 [9,690.9, 9,880.7] | −0.51%
tight / c1 | 1,057.8 [1,047.7, 1,067.9] | 1,062.4 [1,051.7, 1,073.1] | +0.43%
tight / c96 | 18,582.1 [18,469.9, 18,694.3] | 18,565.3 [18,389.4, 18,741.2] | −0.09%

</body></html>

Recover performance regression on PP=2

Case | Main avg [95% CI] | PR avg [95% CI] | Change
-- | -- | -- | --
broad / c1 | 661.45 [660.82, 662.08] | 662.79 [662.39, 663.19] | +0.20%
broad / c96 | 3,951.12 [3,822.93, 4,079.30] | 12,038.09 [11,768.25, 12,307.93] | +204.68%
tight / c1 | 1,021.45 [1,020.70, 1,022.19] | 1,024.63 [1,023.00, 1,026.26] | +0.31%
tight / c96 | 3,865.53 [3,771.94, 3,959.13] | 21,029.32 [20,574.89, 21,483.75] | +444.02%

</body></html>

## Details

### Background

`DraftTokensHandler` allows workers to asynchronously send draft tokens back to the scheduler / structured output manager for processing.

With async scheduling, it works roughly like:
```
Scheduler-side                          Worker-side
--------------------------------------------------
schedule step N
sample step N
                                        execute step N
schedule step N+1
wait for step N
                                        sample step N
                                        DraftTokensHandler.set_draft_tokens
                                        execute step N+1
DraftTokensHandler.get_draft_tokens
generate sampling bitmasks
sample step N+1
                                        sample step N+1
...
```

On main, `DraftTokensHandler` holds the latest batch set by the worker. This works fine for PP=1, but when PP>=2, this can occur:
```
Scheduler-side          Worker-side
----------------------------------
                        set_draft_tokens(micro-batch A)
                        set_draft_tokens(micro-batch B)
get_draft_tokens
```

Micro-batch B replaces micro-batch A in the handler. Scheduler-side cannot recover A's drafts and generates incorrect grammar bitmasks, leading to #54437.

#54442 fixes this by effectively truncating the worker-side draft sequence, reducing acceptance length.

This PR fixes this by making `DraftTokensHandler` track draft tokens by request ID. So micro-batch B cannot override micro-batch A.

Final notes:
- Suggest reviewing commits independently
  - `e3595db629d88881e74eafc357e471924b4d9c1f`: revert #54442, could be a separate PR
  - `c67afdec130ca06c6beb5e286a5b83b91fdae3a2`: track draft tokens by request ID.
  - `bb3694db86066ea2d272051b0495bad3ae09d026`: E2E repro
- Alternative #61348 includes adding a debug flag to catch the handoff race, this is not included in this PR in favor of the E2E repro.

title: [Spec Decode] Support trace replay with speculative decoding
author: aoshen02
body:
## Overview

Allow `trace_decode_token_ids` (MRv2 trace replay) together with speculative decoding. A draft is accepted only if it equals the trace token at its position, and the verified tokens are replaced by the trace, so the replay emits the trace and scores it on the decode path while skipping target forward passes for drafts that match.

## Claims

- Trace replay works with ngram, EAGLE3 and MTP speculators; emitted token ids equal the trace for every request.
- With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, the returned raw logprobs (trace token and top-5) are bitwise equal to trace replay without spec decode.
- Replay speedup with a good drafter: 1.47x–2.03x (EAGLE3, Qwen3-8B), 1.64x–1.88x (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8).

## Validation

### Experiments

GB300, one GPU per run, nightly `8e2beaa3bf` with this patch overlaid (the three source files), MRv2. 64 traces per model, up to 512 tokens, 3/4 sampled at temperature 1.0 with a seed and 1/4 greedy, generated by the target model without spec decode. Each replay uses `trace_decode_token_ids=trace, max_tokens=len(trace), logprobs=5`. Arms: A = replay without spec, A2 = A with reversed request order (numerical floor), B = replay with spec (k=3), `*1` = batch size 1 on 16 traces, `*bi` = `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. All arms returned every request with ids equal to the trace and a logprob entry per token.

| model / speculator | comparison | speedup | acceptance | trace-token logprob bitwise equal | top-5 logprobs bitwise equal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B / EAGLE3 (RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-speculator.eagle3) | A vs A2 (floor) | - | - | 86.0% | 82.4% |
| | A vs B | 1.47x | 46% | 39.4% | 24.8% |
| | A1 vs B1 | 2.03x | 47% | 100% | 100% |
| | Abi vs Bbi | 1.82x | 46% | 100% | 100% |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8 / MTP | A vs A2 (floor) | - | - | 10.7% | 5.6% |
| | A vs B | 1.64x | 66% | 9.3% | 4.4% |
| | A1 vs B1 | 1.88x | 66% | 9.4% | 4.6% |
| Qwen3-0.6B / ngram | A vs A2 (floor) | - | - | 99.7% | 99.7% |
| | A vs B | 0.82x | 3.5% | 97.7% | 97.7% |
| | A1 vs B1 | 0.91x | 3.7% | 100% | 100% |
| | Abi vs Bbi | 1.05x | 3.5% | 100% | 100% |

Without batch invariance, the spec arm changes batch shapes, so logprobs differ at the same order as reordering requests. With batch invariance they are bitwise equal. The FP8 MoE model is not batch invariant even run-to-run, so for MTP the evidence is exact token match plus differences at the reorder floor. ngram accepts few drafts on these chat traces and is slower; that is a drafter-quality effect.

Sampling parameters and off-distribution traces (Qwen3-8B / EAGLE3, replay with `temperature=0.5, top_p=0.95`, `logprobs_mode=processed_logprobs`; "random" traces replace every trace token with a uniformly random id, so drafts almost never match):

| traces | comparison | speedup | acceptance | trace-token logprob bitwise equal | top-5 ids equal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| model-generated | Abi vs Bbi | 2.14x | 46% | 99.99% | 98.97% |
| model-generated | A vs B | 2.32x | 46% | 92.1% | 97.1% |
| random | Abi vs Bbi | 0.89x | 0% | 99.36% | 99.99% |
| random | A vs B | 0.68x | 0% | 99.19% | 82.9% |

Emitted ids equal the trace in every arm. Raw logits are bitwise equal under batch invariance (table above), so the remaining processed-logprob differences come from top-p masking: `apply_top_k_top_p_triton` uses the split top-p pipeline for at most 64 rows (`_SPLIT_MAX_BATCH`) and the monolithic kernel above that, and the two can place the nucleus boundary differently. Verification expands each request to k+1 rows, so the two arms land on different paths. This is an existing batch-invariance gap of top-p masking (non-spec decoding hits it too when the batch crosses 64 rows), not specific to trace replay.

### Tests

Old = image vLLM, new = image vLLM with the patched files, same test tree.

| test | old | new |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_trace_replay.py` (new `TestApplyTraceToVerified`) | collection error (missing function) | pass |
| `tests/v1/sample/test_trace_replay_params.py` | 1 failed (spec decode rejected) | pass |
| `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py::test_trace_replay_with_spec_decode` | fail (spec decode rejected) | pass |
| `tests/v1/spec_decode`, `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_*.py`, `tests/v1/engine/test_input_processor_trace_replay.py` | 1122 passed, 18 failed (the 16 below plus the 2 changed trace replay params tests) | 1140 passed, 16 failed, all also failing on old |

The 16 failures shared by old and new are environment or baseline failures unrelated to this change: `test_acceptance_length.py::test_eagle3_acceptance_length` (11 cases), `test_gpu_model_runner.py` mamba cases (2), `test_gpu_pcp_manager.py::test_parallel_config_manages_decode_sharding` (3). No test fails only on new.

## Details

`RejectionSampler._verify` runs the usual rejection sampling, then for requests with a trace `TraceReplayState.apply_trace_to_verified` rewrites the verified tokens: starting from the current trace step, it writes trace tokens while each draft equals the trace token at its position, stopping at the first mismatch, at the bonus position, or at the end of the trace, and sets `num_sampled` accordingly. Logprobs, rejection counts, the committed tokens and the drafter's next-step inputs all read the rewritten `sampled`/`num_sampled`, so no other path changes. The hook is a single kernel launch per verify step with no host synchronization, and requests without a trace return immediately in the kernel.

Penalties stay consistent with non-spec replay: row i of the verify step folds in drafts 0..i-1, and a row is emitted only if all of those drafts matched the trace, so the history of every emitted row is the trace prefix.

Limitations:
- Bitwise equality with non-spec replay requires batch invariance, and for processed logprobs under top-k/top-p it is limited by the top-p masking path switch described above.
- Not covered by tests or experiments: preemption/resume mid-trace, prefix caching, TP/DP, non-neutral penalties. Code reading shows the trace step comes from `total_len - prompt_len`, which these paths keep consistent.

title: [Perf][Kimi K3] Opt-in KV-balanced FP8 MLA decode for agentic workloads
author: wzhao18
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Adds an opt-in MLA attention backend for Kimi-K3 on Blackwell, `--attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA`. Its decode splits each request's KV by its own length, so the decode stays balanced across the GPU when the context lengths in one batch differ a lot, as they do in agentic workloads. It is a standalone backend built on the common MLA backend classes (`MLACommonBackend`, `MLACommonImpl`, `MLACommonMetadataBuilder`); it does not depend on `TOKENSPEED_MLA`. The code lives in `vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kv_balanced_mla/`. Outside it, the PR only adds the backend's entry to `AttentionBackendEnum` (as the DeepSeek V4, MiniMax M3 and Step5 backends in `vllm/models/` have).

## Claims

- **Decode attention, AgentX context lengths on GB300:** 1.34–1.59x faster than `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`, and 1.91–2.67x faster than its default (geometric mean over batch sizes, DEP16 and DCP8, target verify and draft).
- **End-to-end, AgentX on GB300:**
  - DEP16 decode (3P1D c336): +7.8% TPS/GPU and +20% p90 interactivity.
  - DCP8 decode: +4.6% TPS/GPU and +10% p90 interactivity at 3P4D c240, and +2.7% / +13% at the prefill-bound 2P3D c240.
  - The baseline is `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`, the setting these recipes already use.
- **Accuracy:** gsm8k with real speculative rejection on the latest revision is 0.961 (DEP16) and 0.967 (DCP8).
- **Opt-in.** The backend is never selected automatically; without `--attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` nothing changes.

## Validation

**Unit tests** (`tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kv_balanced_mla.py`, 12 tests, passing on GB300). They check the kernel against an FP32 reference for:
- unequal lengths and an empty request;
- the DSpark draft block (non-causal);
- a DCP8 shard on rank 0, and on rank 5 with interleave 64. The rank-5 lengths end inside that rank's chunks, so the causal mask cuts its last keys. Passing the wrong rank or interleave gives about 80% error, versus 2% when correct.
- a peaked softmax that fails without the P prescale;
- plan plus decode captured in a CUDA graph and replayed with KV lengths changed in place;
- a shared workspace larger than 2 GiB.

The backend tests check that `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` resolves to this backend, its builder and its base-2 LSE convention, and is in no platform's priority list; that selection rejects an FP16 model, a non-FP8 KV cache, a non-SM10x GPU and a `kv_lora_rank` other than 512; and that `forward_mqa` only runs the kernel. The decode tests check one plan per forward, the DCP path with the LSE, and that a step the kernel can't run raises a `ValueError`.

**Microbenchmark.** Time per decode step on one rank, from CUDA-graph replays, mean of 5 random batches per N. Context lengths are sampled from the AgentX trace (median about 98K tokens, p90 about 284K). Every variant decodes the same requests and was checked against an FP32 reference.
- `ts1` is `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with the default `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=1`.
- `ts8` is the same with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`.
- `kvb` is this PR's decode, excluding its plan. The plan takes 4–13 µs, runs once per forward and is shared by all MLA layers.

| Decode | Step | kvb vs ts1 | kvb vs ts8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| DEP16: 96 heads, full KV | verify (q=5, causal) | 2.63x (1.93–3.30) | 1.37x (1.25–1.54) |
| DEP16 | draft (64 heads, q=4) | 2.67x (1.17–4.39) | 1.34x (1.17–1.47) |
| DCP8: 96 gathered heads, 1/8 KV shard, LSE | verify | 1.91x (1.34–3.33) | 1.52x (1.41–1.70) |
| DCP8 | draft | 2.46x (1.78–3.32) | 1.59x (1.48–1.82) |

<details>
<summary>Per batch size (µs)</summary>

| Decode | Step | N | ts1 | ts8 | kvb | kvb vs ts1 | kvb vs ts8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DEP16 | verify | 4 | 402.1 | 308.7 | 208.5 | 1.93x | 1.48x |
| DEP16 | verify | 8 | 928.3 | 433.6 | 281.1 | 3.30x | 1.54x |
| DEP16 | verify | 16 | 2335.6 | 1017.3 | 759.1 | 3.08x | 1.34x |
| DEP16 | verify | 24 | 2744.4 | 1341.3 | 1045.3 | 2.63x | 1.28x |
| DEP16 | verify | 32 | 4374.5 | 2223.9 | 1783.0 | 2.45x | 1.25x |
| DEP16 | draft | 4 | 189.5 | 189.5 | 161.4 | 1.17x | 1.17x |
| DEP16 | draft | 8 | 470.6 | 295.2 | 203.7 | 2.31x | 1.45x |
| DEP16 | draft | 16 | 1175.5 | 593.9 | 403.6 | 2.91x | 1.47x |
| DEP16 | draft | 24 | 2473.4 | 764.9 | 563.3 | 4.39x | 1.36x |
| DEP16 | draft | 32 | 3778.6 | 1245.7 | 964.9 | 3.92x | 1.29x |
| DCP8 | verify | 16 | 295.5 | 151.3 | 88.7 | 3.33x | 1.70x |
| DCP8 | verify | 32 | 413.3 | 293.1 | 189.1 | 2.19x | 1.55x |
| DCP8 | verify | 64 | 763.2 | 640.3 | 430.8 | 1.77x | 1.49x |
| DCP8 | verify | 96 | 984.9 | 971.1 | 662.0 | 1.49x | 1.47x |
| DCP8 | verify | 128 | 1189.6 | 1251.3 | 888.6 | 1.34x | 1.41x |
| DCP8 | draft | 16 | 159.5 | 91.9 | 50.5 | 3.16x | 1.82x |
| DCP8 | draft | 32 | 340.5 | 168.1 | 102.7 | 3.32x | 1.64x |
| DCP8 | draft | 64 | 561.5 | 350.5 | 228.6 | 2.46x | 1.53x |
| DCP8 | draft | 96 | 668.0 | 508.4 | 339.1 | 1.97x | 1.50x |
| DCP8 | draft | 128 | 780.4 | 649.2 | 438.4 | 1.78x | 1.48x |

</details>

**End-to-end.**
- **Setup:** Kimi-K3 MXFP4 on GB300 NVL72, using the InferenceX AgentX agentic-coding replay with Dynamo disaggregated serving, Mooncake KV offload, and DSpark speculative decoding with 4 tokens (synthetic acceptance, as the recipes use).
- **Builds:** both sides run the same vLLM main build. The only difference is the decode workers' decode kernel. These runs used this PR's earlier revision, which selected the same kernel and dispatch through `additional_config` instead of the attention backend name. A rerun of the DEP16 point on the latest revision gave the same result.
- **Baseline:** the decode workers use `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`.
- **Runs:** one run per side for each point. A repeat of the DEP16 pair gave +8.6% TPS/GPU.

| Config | TPS/GPU | Interactivity p50 / p90 (tok/s) | E2E latency p90 | TTFT mean / p90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3P1D, TP8 prefill + DEP16 decode, c336: baseline | 27,267 | 38.1 / 35.2 | 60.6 s | 3.14 / 5.82 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **29,402 (+7.8%)** | 45.8 / 42.4 (+20% / +20%) | 53.9 s (−11%) | 4.22 / 9.69 s |
| 3P4D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode, c240: baseline | 20,421 | 75.7 / 68.9 | 33.3 s | 1.89 / 3.03 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **21,370 (+4.6%)** | 83.1 / 75.9 (+10% / +10%) | 30.8 s (−7%) | 1.84 / 2.94 s |
| 2P3D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode, c240: baseline | 24,503 | 63.7 / 58.0 | 43.9 s | 5.21 / 10.74 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **25,162 (+2.7%)** | 72.6 / 65.3 (+14% / +13%) | 40.7 s (−7%) | 5.83 / 12.41 s |

- **Why TTFT rises at 3P1D and 2P3D:** a faster decode lets more requests through, which puts more load on the prefill workers that limit those points. At 3P4D, with more prefill capacity, TTFT improves slightly.
- **Why DCP8 gains less:** with DCP8, MLA attention is a smaller share of each decode step than with DEP16.

**Accuracy.** gsm8k (5-shot, lm-eval) with real speculative rejection, `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` on the decode workers (latest revision). Every decode step ran on the kernel.

| Config | strict-match | flexible-extract | Acceptance length |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1P1D, TP8 prefill + DEP16 decode | 0.961 | 0.961 | 3.61 |
| 1P1D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode | 0.967 | 0.967 | 3.27 |

**CI.** The B200 Kimi K3 step (`models/kimi_k3`) runs the new tests. They were validated on GB300 (SM103) and not run on B200 (SM100). On the MI355 step the tests are skipped, and the test module imports without the CuTe kernel.

## Details

**KV imbalance in agentic decode.** An agentic decode batch mixes very different context lengths, for example 5K, 20K, 98K and 300K tokens. To spread one request's attention over the GPU, the decode cuts its KV into splits; clusters process the splits in parallel and a reduction merges them. `TOKENSPEED_MLA`, the existing FP8 MLA decode for this model, uses one split count for the whole batch: it's chosen from the batch size and SM count, with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv` as a floor. With a skewed batch, any single count is wrong for most requests:
- **Too many splits for short requests.** Short requests are cut into tiny splits that each pay the per-split setup and the reduction.
- **Too few splits for long requests.** The longest requests leave a tail in which a few clusters stream hundreds of thousands of keys while the rest of the GPU is idle.

`min_split_kv=8` helps the long requests and hurts the short ones; at DCP8 N=128 it is slower than the default (see `ts8` vs `ts1`).

**What the KV-balanced decode does:**
1. **Plan.** A Triton planner gives each request its own split count from its KV length: 1 to 8 splits of at least 1024 tokens, sized to fill at most 8 waves of the GPU's clusters. It writes the planned (query tile, request, split) entries as a device work list. It reads nothing on the host, so it is captured in the decode CUDA graph. It runs once per forward, and every MLA layer reuses it.
2. **Execute.** One wave of persistent 2-CTA clusters walks the work list, so every cluster gets about the same amount of KV.
3. **Skip the merge where possible.** A request planned as a single split stores its final output directly, and the reduction skips it.
4. **Keep small probabilities.** Long splits can make probabilities small enough to flush to zero in E4M3, so P is stored scaled by 2^6 and the LSE removes the factor.

**Code layout** (`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kv_balanced_mla/`):
- `kernel.py` and `helpers.py`: TokenSpeed MLA 2.0.3's FP8 decode kernel (MIT), vendored with the changes above. Compared with the release, the kernel adds 347 lines (including renames and casts so it passes `typos` and mypy) and drops its 1,252-line benchmark harness; the helpers add 59 lines, the work-list tile scheduler. They do not import the `tokenspeed_mla` package at runtime.
- `core.py`: the planner and the compiled kernel.
- `decode.py`: the per-layer dispatch: the once-per-forward plan, the DCP arguments and the shape checks.
- `backend.py`: `KimiK3KvBalancedMLABackend`, `KimiK3KvBalancedMLAMetadataBuilder` and `KimiK3KvBalancedMLAImpl`. The impl's `forward_mqa` runs the kernel.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py`: the `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` entry.

Kimi-K3's MLA layer (`mla.py`) is unchanged: it calls the selected backend's `forward_mqa`.

**Why a standalone backend.** The backend is about 190 lines on the common MLA classes, and it states everything the kernel relies on itself, so a later change to `TOKENSPEED_MLA` can't silently change what this backend runs:
- the FP8 KV cache layout (576 values per token, pages of 32 or 64);
- the decode metadata (`seq_lens`, `block_table`, `dcp_tot_seq_lens`) with uniform query lengths and `UNIFORM_BATCH` CUDA graphs;
- the packed FP8 query from the common MLA impl;
- the base-2 LSE convention of the DCP combine (`lse_base_on_e=False`);
- non-causal multi-token decode for the DSpark draft, with and without DCP.

Prefill uses the configured MLA prefill backend, as in the other MLA backends.

**Supported configurations.** An FP8 E4M3 KV cache, an SM10x GPU, a BF16 model and MLA dimensions (`qk_nope_head_dim`, `qk_rope_head_dim`, `v_head_dim`, `kv_lora_rank`) = (128, 64, 128, 512); backend selection rejects anything else with the reason. Alibi, sliding window, soft cap and non-decoder attention raise a `ValueError` when the layer is built. The kernel also needs more than 64 query rows per request (heads × query tokens) and at most as many requests as it plans for; the head count isn't known at selection, so these fail at model build with a `ValueError`. There is no fallback decode: a decode step the kernel can't run raises a `ValueError` with the reason. In the end-to-end runs every decode shape (target verify q=1–5, draft q=4) ran on the kernel. `cp_kv_cache_interleave_size` is read from the parallel config on every call, since NIXL P/D sets it after the model is built. The DSpark draft takes its backend from the speculative config's `attention_backend`.

**Tradeoffs and limitations:**
- **Size:** the vendored kernel adds about 4.9K lines. Integrating through the `tokenspeed_mla` package instead (reusing its compiled kernel with planned per-request splits) gave about 20% less speedup in our microbenchmarks. The work-list scheduler, direct output and P prescale need kernel changes.
- **Memory:** the split-KV scratch is sized as requests × query tiles × 8 splits of FP16 partial outputs. That's about 0.5 GB for 128 requests at heads=96, q=5, versus about 0.23 GB for TokenSpeed's SM-based bound; it's logged at startup.
- **Host syncs:** by inspection, the decode path adds none. Planning is a device kernel, and the once-per-forward check compares the forward context and a data pointer. This was not checked with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Make MXFP4 the default indexer K cache dtype for DeepSeek-V4
author: shen-shanshan
body:
## Overview #60834 brought the paged MXFP4 sparse indexer (dense path) to DeepSeek-V4 on ROCm gfx950. It was opt-in: ```bash --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype": "mxfp4"}' ``` Its measurements show the MXFP4 indexer is better than the FP8 one on almost every axis: - lower TTFT (up to -30.7%) and TPOT; - +9.2% KV cache capacity (68 B vs 132 B per compressed token); - near-lossless accuracy: GSM8K -0.16pt, and GPQA Diamond is unchanged at 0.7121. The results are copied below. This PR therefore makes MXFP4 the **default** indexer K cache dtype for DeepSeek-V4 (`model_type == "deepseek_v4"`, i.e. V4-Pro / V4-Flash) on ROCm CDNA4, and logs that it is enabled. ## Claims Nothing else changes: - CUDA, XPU and CPU behave as before; - DeepSeek-V4.1 keeps its current opt-in; - every other model is untouched. ## Validation ### Benchmark (from #60834, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) Fixed sequence length (`8k1k`, TP8, MTP=2): | Conc | Indexer | Output token throughput (tok/s) | Change | Mean TTFT (ms) | Change | Mean TPOT (ms) | Change | | ---: | :------ | ------------------------------: | ------: | -------------: | -------: | -------------: | ------: | | 1 | FP8 (old default) | 145.99 | — | 597.24 | — | 6.24 | — | | 1 | MXFP4 (new default) | 156.34 | 7.09% ↑ | 413.91 | 30.70% ↓ | 5.96 | 4.49% ↓ | | 4 | FP8 (old default) | 454.91 | — | 504.07 | — | 8.02 | — | | 4 | MXFP4 (new default) | 466.92 | 2.64% ↑ | 437.29 | 13.25% ↓ | 7.95 | 0.87% ↓ | | 16 | FP8 (old default) | 1020.90 | — | 744.88 | — | 14.51 | — | | 16 | MXFP4 (new default) | 1030.30 | 0.92% ↑ | 681.89 | 8.46% ↓ | 14.46 | 0.34% ↓ | | 64 | FP8 (old default) | 1629.53 | — | 1637.36 | — | 36.85 | — | | 64 | MXFP4 (new default) | 1656.28 | 1.64% ↑ | 1622.58 | 0.90% ↓ | 36.29 | 1.52% ↓ | Agentic replay (DP8, MTP=3, prefix caching): | Indexer | Output Token Throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | KV Cache Capacity (tokens) | |---|---|---|---|---| | FP8 (old default) | 697.25 | 2,442.24 | 46.01 | 4,589,684 | | MXFP4 (new default) | 675.83 (3.07% ↓) | 2,321.05 (4.96% ↓) | 43.42 (5.62% ↓) | 5,010,749 (9.17% ↑) | - **Latency improves:** mean TPOT -5.62% and mean TTFT -4.96%. - TPOT is the most consistent signal: both MXFP4 runs (44.60 / 42.24 ms) had lower TPOT than both FP8 runs (46.98 / 45.03 ms). - TTFT varied by up to 13% between runs of the same configuration, so treat its gain as indicative. - **Output throughput is within noise (-3.07%).** On this workload it is driven mainly by the trace replay and by output lengths. - **KV cache capacity: +9.17%.** Peak KV usage stayed below 40% here, so this workload does not yet turn the extra capacity into throughput. Higher-concurrency or longer-context workloads should benefit more. ### Accuracy (from #60834, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) GSM8K: | Task | Filter | n-shot | Metric | FP8 (old default) | MXFP4 (new default) | Change | | ----- | ---------------- | -----: | ------------- | ----------------: | ------------------: | -------: | | gsm8k | flexible-extract | 5 | exact_match ↑ | 0.9492 | 0.9477 | -0.16% ↓ | | gsm8k | strict-match | 5 | exact_match ↑ | 0.9500 | 0.9484 | -0.17% ↓ | GPQA Diamond: | Indexer | GPQA Diamond | Empty Responses (reasoning over budget) | |---|---|---| | FP8 (old default) | 0.7121 ± 0.0323 | 13 / 198 | | MXFP4 (new default) | 0.7121 ± 0.0323 | 11 / 198 | - **Accuracy is unchanged on GPQA:** both indexers score 0.7121. Per question, 124 are correct in both runs, and the disagreements are symmetric (17 vs 17, McNemar p = 1.0). - **This exercises the indexer's long-context path:** reasoning traces run to tens of thousands of tokens, far past the 4096 tokens where sparse top-k selection starts. - **The GSM8K change is negligible** (< 0.2% relative). ## Details ---

(Mandatory for agents, optional for humans). - [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR. - [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity. - [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI. - [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples. - [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.

title: [Perf][Mamba] Use the shared checkpoint exporter for Mamba2 and drop ssd_checkpoint
author: roikoren755
body:
## Overview Mamba2 prefill checkpoints now use the shared `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter` (introduced for GDN/KDA in #60050) instead of their own `ssd_checkpoint.py` kernel, which is deleted. Part of the internal prefill checkpoint work tracked in #52959. ## Claims - One checkpoint-store kernel for GDN, KDA and Mamba2 instead of two. Diff: +53 / -157 in `vllm/` (including the deleted 118-line file) and +35 / -17 in tests (the Mamba2 test retarget, plus new Mamba2 and wide-state cases in the exporter test). - Mamba2 checkpoint store time is faster than the removed kernel in 39 of 48 cases, and no TP1/2/4 case is slower. The 3 slower cases are all TP8 (Nano 30B at 1-2 rows, Super at 2 rows), by at most +2.9 µs per step. GDN/KDA are 13-37% faster at 4+ rows on TP1/2. Across 96 cases, 25 are slower than main by at most +15 µs per step, mostly at TP4/8 with 1-2 rows (details and numbers below). - Stops Mamba2 from writing skipped prefill checkpoints into the null block. Under the default sparse retention a non-final prefill chunk that spans two or more Mamba blocks gets a checkpoint offset but a null destination (by design since #59175, so that the export is masked); the removed kernel had no null check and wrote it into block 0, while the shared kernel skips it (reproduced with `check_mamba2_null_block_write.py`, which runs both kernels on a Super TP1 row whose column is null). Latent: no reader of block 0 was found (details under "Behavior of the swap"). ## Validation Hardware: one B200, torch 2.14.0+cu130. All outputs are bitwise equal to the baseline kernel before timing. Tests (all pass): ``` pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba2_checkpoint_state.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_checkpoint_exporter.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_prefill_flashinfer.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_mixer2.py tests/v1/attention/test_mamba2_prefill_checkpoints.py tests/v1/attention/test_gdn_metadata_builder.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_prefix_cache.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda_metadata.py tests/models/glm5next/test_kda_recurrent.py -v pytest tests/v1/e2e/general/test_mamba_prefix_cache.py -k mrv2_async_flashinfer -v ``` `tests/kernels/mamba` runs in CI (`.buildkite/test_areas/kernels.yaml`). No CI test exercises the Mamba2 mixer's internal checkpoints end to end (the kernel is covered by the unit test above), so that path was checked only by the Nemotron serving run below. The test changes are pointing `test_store_selects_the_checkpoint_from_all_chunk_states` at the shared exporter, and adding a `mamba2` caller and a wide recurrent state shape to `test_checkpoint_exporter.py`. The wide shape launches programs past the conv window, so the guard is covered for correctness (not speed). With `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, serving Nemotron 3.5 Super at TP1 (4224-token Mamba block) under the traffic below triggered no host-device sync from the exporter; afterwards the server was healthy and prefix-cache hits were recorded: ``` VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 --trust-remote-code 2>&1 | tee serve.log & M=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4; PORT=8000 B="vllm bench serve --model $M --port $PORT --seed 0 --num-warmups 4" # 1) one long prompt at a time (1 checkpoint row per step) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 32 \ --num-prompts 16 --max-concurrency 1 # 2) bursts of 2.7k-token prompts (below the Mamba block, so no checkpoints) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2700 --random-output-len 32 \ --num-prompts 120 --request-rate inf --max-concurrency 6 # 3) repeated long prefixes (checkpoint exports, then prefix-cache hits) $B --dataset-name prefix_repetition --prefix-repetition-prefix-len 6144 \ --prefix-repetition-suffix-len 1024 --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes 4 \ --prefix-repetition-output-len 32 --num-prompts 64 --request-rate inf # 4) mixed lengths, 600-11400 tokens (up to 3 checkpoint rows per step) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 6000 --random-range-ratio 0.9 \ --random-output-len 32 --num-prompts 64 --request-rate inf curl -s localhost:$PORT/health -o /dev/null -w "health: %{http_code}\n" grep -i -E "traceback|synchron|error" serve.log | head curl -s localhost:$PORT/metrics | grep -E "^vllm:prefix_cache_(queries|hits)" ``` GSM8K (`python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --num-shots 50`, 1319 questions, greedy) on the same server without `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK`. Every prompt starts with the same 50-shot prefix, longer than the 4224-token Mamba block, so the first prompts export checkpoints inside it and the rest resume from them (prefix-cache hit rate about 86% on both servers). Two runs per server: | | run 1 | run 2 | |---|---|---| | main (`24324ef0f6`) | 0.928 | 0.926 | | this PR | 0.926 | 0.926 | The two servers differ by at most 3 questions, within run-to-run variation. The two assertions added to `export()` (see "Behavior of the swap") were profiled in a real Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B step that exports a checkpoint in all 23 Mamba layers: one 4177-token prompt, one more than the 4176-token Mamba block, with fresh tokens every step (`profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.py`, attached, 30 profiled steps per run). They add about 1.4 µs of host time per `export()` call (75.1 vs 73.7 µs median, inflated by the profiler). The GPU idle time right before each store kernel is unchanged: 34.8 vs 36.0 µs median, within the 33-55 µs spread between steps. Benchmarks (microbenchmark scripts that are not part of this PR, attached). Shapes are per-rank states derived from the models' Hugging Face configs. Each arm is timed over 3 rounds in rotating order with fresh buffers; a second copy of the baseline is the noise control, and the `noise` column (mostly ≤0.03) is the floor a ratio has to clear. `step` = per-layer delta × layer count. Each attached output comes from one command, run from the repo root with the attached scripts saved under `benchmarks/kernels/`: ``` python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py # out_benchmark.log python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py --block-sweep # out_sweep_benchmark.log python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_checkpoint_exporter_callers.py --block-sweep # out_sweep_callers.log python benchmarks/kernels/scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py # out_ablation_sass.log python benchmarks/kernels/check_mamba2_null_block_write.py # check_mamba2_null_block_write.log ``` **What "rows" means.** A row is a request in the step that exports a checkpoint: its final prefill chunk spans more than one Mamba block, so the checkpoint falls inside this chunk (`is_mamba_prefill_checkpoint_valid`). Decodes and other prefills add no rows. 1 row is one long prompt finishing in the step; several rows are a burst of mid-length prompts finishing together. A step holds at most about `max_num_batched_tokens / mamba_block_size` rows. Super at TP1 has a 4224-token block, so at most 3 rows at the default 16k budget. The block size is set so an attention page is at least as large as a Mamba page, so it shrinks with TP once the attention KV heads are replicated and the per-rank Mamba state keeps shrinking; higher TP therefore allows more rows per step (not measured here). The kernel only reads 3 conv tokens and one state row per request, so lengths do not affect its time, only the row count does. Mamba2, new exporter vs the removed SSD store (`out_benchmark.log`): | shape | rows | SSD µs | new µs | ratio | step µs | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Super (128 heads) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 4.70 / 6.43 / 9.22 / 12.26 | 4.13 / 5.60 / 8.26 / 11.04 | 0.88 / 0.87 / 0.90 / 0.90 | -23 / -33 / -38 / -49 | | Super TP4 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.49 / 4.00 / 4.83 / 5.73 | 3.14 / 3.49 / 4.19 / 4.77 | 0.90 / 0.87 / 0.87 / 0.83 | -14 / -20 / -26 / -38 | | Super TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.17 / 3.36 / 3.94 / 4.22 | 3.17 / 3.39 / 3.74 / 4.26 | 1.00 / 1.01 / 0.95 / 1.01 | 0 / +1 / -8 / +1 | | Nano 30B TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.97 / 4.77 / 6.30 / 7.74 | 3.52 / 4.26 / 5.44 / 6.91 | 0.89 / 0.89 / 0.86 / 0.89 | -10 / -12 / -20 / -19 | | Nano 30B TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.10 / 3.36 / 3.46 / 3.68 | 3.23 / 3.46 / 3.42 / 3.58 | 1.04 / 1.03 / 0.99 / 0.97 | +3 / +2 / -1 / -2 | Across all 48 Mamba2 cases 39 are faster, 6 are within noise and 3 are slower: Nano 30B TP8 at 1 and 2 rows (+3 and +2 µs per step) and Super TP8 at 2 rows (+1). GDN/KDA, the exporter at 512 vs main's kernel (`out_sweep_callers.log`): | shape | rows | main µs | new µs | ratio | step µs | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Kimi K3 (KDA) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 6.18 / 9.92 / 17.41 / 24.86 | 4.83 / 6.91 / 11.30 / 15.81 | 0.78 / 0.70 / 0.65 / 0.64 | -93 / -208 / -422 / -625 | | Kimi K3 TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.04 / 3.36 / 4.35 / 5.28 | 3.14 / 3.42 / 4.10 / 4.51 | 1.03 / 1.02 / 0.94 / 0.85 | +7 / +4 / -18 / -53 | | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (GDN) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.71 / 5.09 / 7.65 / 10.24 | 3.62 / 4.16 / 5.47 / 6.98 | 0.97 / 0.82 / 0.71 / 0.68 | -3 / -28 / -65 / -98 | | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 2.91 / 3.04 / 3.17 / 3.42 | 3.26 / 3.13 / 3.30 / 3.39 | 1.12 / 1.03 / 1.04 / 0.99 | +11 / +3 / +4 / -1 | Across the 96 GDN/KDA cases (all six models, TP1/2/4/8, 1/2/4/6 rows) 63 are faster, 8 are within noise and 25 are slower: ratio up to 1.144 and up to +15.0 µs per step (both Qwen3-Next-80B TP8, 1 row), per-layer cost +0.06 to +0.42 µs. 21 of the 25 are TP4/8 and 21 are at 1-2 rows; the four at 4+ rows are all TP8 (ratio at most 1.05). At 4+ rows on TP1/2 all 24 cases are 13-37% faster. The slower cases are ~3 µs launches, where the same case moved by up to 0.4 µs between two runs of this benchmark (more than the in-run noise floor), so individual verdicts there are not stable; the counts and the TP1/2 results are. Not validated: end-to-end serving throughput (microbenchmarks only), how often real traffic reaches 4+ checkpoint rows in a step (3 at most for Super at TP1; higher TP allows more, but was not measured), and any hardware other than B200. ## Details **Why this swap makes sense now.** Before #60050 the two checkpoint-store kernels were not interchangeable: the shared one read each checkpoint's recurrent state from row `i` of the prefill output, while Mamba2's SSD store picked it out of all chunk states through `checkpoint_chunk_idx`. #60050 added `HAS_RECURRENT_ROWS` (`recurrent_rows`) to the shared kernel, which is exactly that selection. Since then the two kernels are basically identical: they differ in launch configuration (block size 1024 vs 256 on main), in the null-block and short-offset masks described under "Behavior of the swap" (the shared kernel already has them), and in how the conv window is addressed (the removed kernel took `x` as `(dim, tokens)`; the shared one takes `raw_qkv` as `(tokens, width)`, and the mixer now passes `x.transpose(0, 1)`). This PR sets the shared kernel's block size to 512 and makes its strides runtime arguments, so Mamba2 can use it without losing time and the duplicate can go. **Why the kernel changed.** Three changes to `store_cache_checkpoints_kernel`, each measured separately (the callers benchmark's `cx`, `guard` and `wide` arms each take one change out of the shipped kernel; `scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py` is a replica kernel that toggles one change at a time, with SASS diffs in `out_ablation_sass.log`): - **Block size 256 -> 512 (one value for all callers).** The removed Mamba2 kernel used 1024-wide blocks, and at 256 the shared kernel was 1.19-1.27x slower than it at 4-6 rows on large states (Super and Nano 4B at TP1), so Mamba2 would have regressed. 512 has a better worst case than 1024: 1024 is slower than the old kernel in 11 of the 24 TP4/TP8 cases, by up to about +12 µs per step, and it is ahead of 512 in only 7 of 48 cases (by 1-6%, mostly TP1/2 at 4+ rows). GDN/KDA share the kernel and get 512 as well. Keeping them at 256 was measured and is worse: with the conv guard below, 44 of 96 GDN/KDA cases were slower than main (up to ratio 1.19, +20 µs per step, both at Qwen3-Next-80B TP8 1 row), against 25 at 512 (up to ratio 1.14). A larger block means fewer programs, so the guard's fixed cost matters less. (The 256 and 1024 figures come from the block-size sweeps `out_sweep_benchmark.log` and `out_sweep_callers.log`, which time 256, 512 and 1024 side by side. `out_sweep_callers.log` is also the source of the GDN/KDA table; `out_sweep_benchmark.log` is a separate run from the Mamba2 table, so its 512 counts differ by a case or two.) - **Strides as runtime arguments, not `tl.constexpr`.** Specializing the 8 strides costs about 6% on average (`cx/cur` column of the callers benchmark: 0.97-1.20, mean 1.06 over the 144 Mamba2/GDN/KDA shapes), most at 1-2 rows (mean 1.08 and 1.07) and least on large states (TP1 at 4-6 rows: mean 1.015). The SASS has 192 vs 184 static instructions (216 vs 192 at TP8 shapes), with more IADD3/IMAD where runtime strides use LEA, and an identical sequence of global memory ops. On the conv-only Qwen4Exp PLE shape the two are within 2% (`cx/cur` 0.98-1.01). - **Skip the conv window in programs that don't cover it.** The conv section used to run, fully masked off, in every program. Guarding it on `program_id(1) * BLOCK_SIZE < WIDTH * STATE_LEN` cuts the time by 15-22% on large states in the ablation (for example 14.2 -> 11.1 µs at Super TP1, 6 rows) and is about neutral on small ones (-5% to +3% at Super TP4/TP8 and Nano 30B TP8). In the callers benchmark, removing it (`wide` arm) makes TP1 shapes at 4-6 rows 13-29% slower (mean 22%). **Tradeoff of the conv guard.** The guard is what makes the Mamba2 swap faster than the removed kernel. Removing it (`wide` arm: the shipped kernel without the guard) measured, by rows (mean over the 12 shapes per model kind; positive means removing it is slower): | rows | GDN | KDA | Mamba2 | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0% | +1% | -1% | | 2 | +6% | +2% | +4% | | 4 | +10% | +8% | +10% | | 6 | +14% | +12% | +15% | So the guard is about neutral on average at 1 row and wins from 2 rows up, by up to about 255 µs per step on TP1/2 (Kimi K3 TP1, 6 rows; Super TP1 at 6 rows about 125 µs). It loses on a few launch-bound shapes: 15 of the 72 1-2 row cases are 3% or more faster without it (13 of them TP4/8), by at most +0.5 µs per layer (+19 µs per step, Super TP8 2 rows). Without it Mamba2 would be slower than the removed kernel at TP1 with 2+ rows (Super TP1 about 1.03x at 2 rows and 1.15x at 6, from the ablation). On GDN/KDA's 1-2 row TP4/8 cases (2.6% slower than main on average) the guard accounts for about 1 point: removing it makes them 1.2% faster, while going back to 256 or to constexpr strides alone makes them 6% and 9% slower. The benchmarks' main kernel predates #63761's int64 cast; the `guard` arm (the shipped kernel with an int32 index) shows the cast is free (-2.4% to +2.0% per case), so the comparisons with main still hold. **Behavior of the swap.** The shared kernel also skips null destination blocks, which the removed kernel did not check, and for an offset shorter than the conv window it skips the conv window but still stores the recurrent state. The manager would cache such a block as a valid checkpoint, so `export()` now asserts that every nonzero offset covers the conv window, and that `recurrent_rows` has one entry per checkpoint row. Both are host-side checks with no device sync. Neither can fire today: a valid checkpoint's offset is at least `hash_block_size` (`query_start + hash_block_size <= checkpoint_position`), above the 3-token Mamba2 conv window, and every caller sizes recurrent_rows per checkpoint row. The null-block skip is reachable. Under the default sparse retention (`prefix_cache_retention_interval=0`) the manager reserves a checkpoint block only for the chunk that ends the prefill, and leaves the column null for earlier chunks so that the export is masked (#59175, `test_checkpoint_reservation_matches_worker`). An earlier chunk that spans two or more Mamba blocks still gets an offset, and the removed kernel wrote that checkpoint into the null block (block 0); the shared kernel skips it. `check_mamba2_null_block_write.py` reproduces this with Super TP1's geometry (a 12672-token first chunk, checkpoint offset 8448 in column 1): the removed store writes the row's checkpoint into block 0 and the shared exporter leaves it untouched, while a row with a real block is written identically by both. No reader of that write was found: Mamba's decode conv and SSU kernels skip `NULL_BLOCK_ID` rows, and cache groups overlay the same memory, so it also lands in attention's block 0, which only the FA4 restricted-sliding-window gap path assumes is zero (not used by full-attention hybrids such as Nemotron). That needs a prompt longer than the token budget and a budget of at least two Mamba blocks (Super TP1: prompts over 16k tokens at the default budget). The `mamba2` case in `test_checkpoint_exporter.py` covers the skip. Mamba2 passes the pre-conv activations through `x.transpose(0, 1)`, the same view the removed kernel read. **Considered: keeping main's launch shape for GDN/KDA.** A per-caller option that keeps GDN/KDA on 256-wide blocks without the guard, with only the runtime strides, is the callers benchmark's `wide256` arm. It is slower than main in 69 of 96 GDN/KDA cases (up to 1.04x, +58 µs per step at Kimi K3 TP1 with 6 rows) and gives up the 13-37% gains at 4+ rows on TP1/2. On the 1-2 row TP4/8 cases it would be 0.9% slower than main on average instead of 2.6%. So all callers share 512 and the guard. **Limitations.** Measured on B200 only; microbenchmarks, not serving. The shared kernel is also used by the ROCm Kimi-K3 KDA exporter (conv half only, `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_checkpoint.py`), so the 512 block size and conv guard apply there too; `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_checkpoint.py` covers it but needs gfx950 and was not run. The Qwen4Exp PLE short conv (#61601: conv-only with a token map, one layer) shares the kernel too. It is 2-6% slower than main at 1, 2 and 6 rows and within noise at 4, at most +0.19 µs per step, which comes from the 512 block size (at 256 the shipped kernel is up to 6% faster on that shape); its conv window spans every program, so the guard skips nothing there. **Related PRs.** No open PR does this swap (searched 2026-10-26: issue #52959 and open PRs that cite it, `ssd_checkpoint`, `store_cache_checkpoints_kernel`, `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter`, "Mamba2 prefill checkpoint"). #61601 (Qwen4Exp PLE checkpoints) and #61497 (Mamba2 SSD host overhead) are merged, and this PR is rebased on them. #59175 is where the manager leaves a non-final chunk's checkpoint column null for the exporter to skip (see "Behavior of the swap"). Open PRs near this code: #60659 (GDN Triton/FLA and AITER checkpoints) and #61951 (ROCm GLM-5.3-Flash KDA on Triton) add new `export()` callers without changing the exporter, so they pick up these kernel changes; #61501 (opt-in FlashInfer SSD prefill scan, draft) edits `conv_ssm_forward` next to the Mamba2 export but keeps checkpointed prefills on the Triton scan; #61466 (per-layer checkpoint alignment) edits `mamba_mixer2.py`'s imports and spec override; #60888 (checkpoints at or before the initial-state column, draft) changes the scheduler and manager rules, not the exporter, and like #59175 expects checkpoints into null columns to be skipped; #62232 (Mamba2 prefill checkpoints on CPU) adds a CPU path to `store_prefill_checkpoint`, which this PR deletes, and a test to `test_mamba2_checkpoint_state.py`; whichever lands second moves that path into `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter.export()`, which, like the removed kernel, always launches Triton (Mamba2 checkpoints on CPU are broken on main too, #62153).
Scripts and outputs
